headings: Frost, and the mistake that costs a crop
What this calendar deliberately leaves out
What can actually hurt you here
Shallow crustal earthquake on the Seattle Fault zone (M6.5-7.5)

docs.text: # Where You Are: Silverdale, Washington This is the real place the simulation is built on. Every number below comes from the same data the world itself is built from, so what you read here and what you walk around in cannot drift apart. **The setting.** Head of Dyes Inlet, an arm of Puget Sound, on the Kitsap Peninsula. **The shape of it.** Sea level to about 178 metres, averaging 64. Sea level in Dyes Inlet to about 178 m on the upland plateau. The town itself is low: the GNIS Silverdale point is 4.8 m (16 ft) and the Clear Creek mouth 2.8 m (9 ft), while the CDP centroid uphill is 15.7 m (51 ft) and Bucklin Hill is 69 m (227 ft). ## The year here Climate zone Csb, USDA hardiness zone 8b. About 1446 mm of rain a year and roughly 227 frost-free days. | Month | Average high | Average low | Rain | Daylight | |---|---|---|---|---| | January | 8.1 C | 2 C | 236 mm | 8.9 h | | February | 9.7 C | 1.7 C | 148 mm | 10.3 h | | March | 12.1 C | 3.2 C | 162 mm | 11.9 h | | April | 15 C | 5 C | 98 mm | 13.7 h | | May | 18.8 C | 8.1 C | 60 mm | 15.2 h | | June | 21.2 C | 10.6 C | 41 mm | 16 h | | July | 24.7 C | 12.6 C | 21 mm | 15.6 h | | August | 25.2 C | 12.8 C | 28 mm | 14.3 h | | September | 22.2 C | 10.6 C | 46 mm | 12.6 h | | October | 15.9 C | 7.1 C | 131 mm | 10.9 h | | November | 10.7 C | 3.7 C | 225 mm | 9.3 h | | December | 7.6 C | 1.7 C | 252 mm | 8.4 h | ### Frost, and the mistake that costs a crop Last spring frost: March 29 on average, as early as March 5 and as late as April 24. First autumn frost: November 14 on average, as early as October 26 and as late as December 1. The average is the 50th percentile: in half of all years the last spring frost falls AFTER it. Planting tender crops to the average kills them in half of all years. Plant to late_90pct (April 24), the date past which only one year in ten still delivers a frost, and have row cover ready by early_10pct in autumn (October 26), not by the average. All thresholds are 32 F. At the 36 F threshold, which is the honest one for seedlings on a clear calm night, the 10-percent-risk spring date is May 13. **Extremes on record.** 38.9 C at the highest, -13.9 C at the lowest. A building here should be designed for about -6 C in winter. ## What happens when The climate table above is the weather. This is the year as events: what comes into leaf, what fruits, what runs up the creek, what arrives and what leaves. Each entry says how confident it is, because a date from a published record and a regional generalisation are not the same claim. measured = computed here from raw observations or predictions, or taken from a NOAA normal computed from observations. published_range = a named source states this range, though usually for a region larger than Silverdale. local_consensus = the existing species record and regional sources agree, but no single publication gives the date. estimated = a regional generalisation applied here with no local source, and the event says so. Nothing in this file dresses an estimate as a measurement. Where the honest answer is that the timing varies too much to pin down, the event says that instead of giving a date. ### January The coldest and one of the wettest months: 236 mm of rain, a mean high of 8.1 C and only 8.9 hours of daylight. Nothing grows. The deep minus tides of the month all fall near midnight. This is maple sap season on a hard clear snap, and hazel catkins are already out on bare branches while eagles are settling onto nests. - **The wet half of the year**. October through March. These six months deliver 1,154 mm of the annual 1,446 mm, which is 79.8 percent of the year's water. December alone brings 252 mm, nearly as much as April through September put together (294 mm across six months). This is the half of the year to design drainage for, to expect saturated ground and landslide risk in, and to fill every cistern in. It is also the half in which soil work compacts rather than tills. - **Winter minus tides run at night**. November through February, the deep lows falling between roughly 22:00 and 02:00. The tide table will show you tides as low as any in June, and they are real, but they are in the dark and in the cold. Digging them means a headlamp, a falling tide you cannot see the edge of, and a long walk back over ground that is filling behind you. Treat a winter minus tide as an expert trip, not a family one, and note that the biotoxin question is unchanged by the season. - **King tides and the winter flood risk**. Late December and January, when the highest astronomical tides coincide with the storm season. The highest water ever observed at Bremerton, 4.74 m above MLLW on 27 December 2022, exceeded the highest astronomical tide by 0.45 m. That extra half metre was storm surge stacked on an already extreme tide. A shoreline structure has to survive the tide plus the surge plus the wind waves, not the tide alone, and the season for all three arriving together is the turn of the year. - **Marine biotoxin closures, which have no season**. Any month. There is no safe season and no pattern you can plan around. This is the one thing on this calendar that a calendar cannot answer. Paralytic, diarrhetic and amnesic shellfish poisoning come from algal blooms that the Washington Department of Health tests for continuously, and a closure can appear in any month. The water looks clear during a toxic bloom. Cooking and freezing do not destroy the toxin, because it is in the meat. Check the Department of Health Shellfish Safety Map or the hotline on 1-800-562-5632 on the day you harvest, every time, and never infer safety from a good tide or from last week's status. A separate authority answers a separate question. - **Shellfish beach seasons**. Beach by beach, set annually by WDFW. There is no statewide month you can rely on. Two independent gates must both be open before you may legally and safely harvest: the WDFW season for that specific beach, and the Department of Health biotoxin status for that specific beach. Neither implies the other, and a good tide implies neither. WDFW also publishes an annual best clam and oyster harvest tides chart, which is the tide half of the same planning problem. - **The winter steelhead run**. Late autumn into spring. The local fish are winter run. Unlike the salmon, steelhead do not all die after spawning, and they run through the months when nothing else does. Summer run fish are mostly east of the Cascades, so a steelhead in a Kitsap creek is a winter fish. Seasons here are tightly restricted and frequently closed outright; read the current rules rather than assuming an open season exists. - **Pacific herring spawn**. WDFW gives herring spawning in Puget Sound from January and into June. Herring spawn on nearshore vegetation and the event is visible from the beach: the water turns milky white or teal where a large spawn has happened. It is the hinge of the local food web in late winter. Wintering sea ducks switch from mussels and clams onto herring eggs during spring migration, which is what puts them in condition to fly north and lay, and the spawn draws gulls, eagles and predatory fish at the same time. If you want to know why the inlet suddenly gets busy in February, this is why. - **Surf smelt spawn, which has no single season**. Year round. Different beaches and stocks spawn at different times, and WDFW surveys for spawn year round. Surf smelt lay eggs about a millimetre across in the upper intertidal on mixed sand and gravel beaches, and a given beach may be a spawning beach in a season you would not expect. The practical consequence is not a harvest date but a construction constraint: WDFW protects documented forage fish spawning beaches from shoreline development, so upper intertidal work on a mixed sand and gravel beach is a permitting question in any month. - **Hazel catkins shed pollen**. January to March in the west coast states, with early March given for Oregon. Catkins expand 5 to 15 days before the leaves. Long yellow catkins on bare branches in the middle of winter, which is startling the first time you notice it and is the earliest flowering of any local shrub. It marks the shrub for you months before the leaves make it findable, so this is when to note where the hazels are if you want the nuts in September. - **Poison hemlock rosette, the dangerous anonymous stage**. The first year rosette stands through autumn, winter and early spring. It bolts and flowers in late spring and early summer, then sets seed and dies. The rosette is when poison hemlock looks most like parsley, and it is green at the exact time of year when a garden or field edge has little else green in it. This overlaps precisely with the wild carrot rosette, which is the root digging stage of an edible plant, and with the cow parsnip rosette. The dead standing stems remain poisonous. Never dig a white taprooted umbellifer in the rosette stage on the strength of leaf shape. - **Water hemlock root, dangerous in every month**. Shoots in spring, white umbels in summer, top dies back in autumn. The tuberous root is in the ground all twelve months. The most poisonous plant in North America grows in the same wet ground as water parsley, hemlock waterparsnip and cattail, all of which are gathered. In winter nothing above ground shows where it is, and the root is the most poisonous part. This is why the calendar cannot make wet ground digging safe at any time of year, and why the honest advice for winter root digging in a wet meadow is not to. - **Poison oak drops its leaves and keeps its oil**. Rain falls away to 98 mm. Ospreys return. Past 24 April only one year in ten still delivers a frost, so this is when tender crops can go out. All at the 32 F threshold. The average is the 50th percentile, which means that in half of all years the last frost falls AFTER March 29. In 2026 every daylight low tide at or below -2.0 ft MLLW fell between April 18 and August 12; across 2026 to 2029 the earliest is April 11 and the latest August 12. Dyes Inlet gets roughly the same number of deep minus tides every month of the year, but in the winter half they all happen in the middle of the night and in the summer half they all happen around midday. Approach slowly and stay out of the water: quick movement reads as a predator. - **Surf smelt spawn, which has no single season**. Year round. Different beaches and stocks spawn at different times, and WDFW surveys for spawn year round. Surf smelt lay eggs about a millimetre across in the upper intertidal on mixed sand and gravel beaches, and a given beach may be a spawning beach in a season you would not expect. The practical consequence is not a harvest date but a construction constraint: WDFW protects documented forage fish spawning beaches from shoreline development, so upper intertidal work on a mixed sand and gravel beach is a permitting question in any month. - **Poison hemlock rosette, the dangerous anonymous stage**. The first year rosette stands through autumn, winter and early spring. It bolts and flowers in late spring and early summer, then sets seed and dies. The rosette is when poison hemlock looks most like parsley, and it is green at the exact time of year when a garden or field edge has little else green in it. This overlaps precisely with the wild carrot rosette, which is the root digging stage of an edible plant, and with the cow parsnip rosette. The dead standing stems remain poisonous. Never dig a white taprooted umbellifer in the rosette stage on the strength of leaf shape. - **Water hemlock root, dangerous in every month**. Shoots in spring, white umbels in summer, top dies back in autumn. The tuberous root is in the ground all twelve months. The most poisonous plant in North America grows in the same wet ground as water parsley, hemlock waterparsnip and cattail, all of which are gathered. In winter nothing above ground shows where it is, and the root is the most poisonous part. This is why the calendar cannot make wet ground digging safe at any time of year, and why the honest advice for winter root digging in a wet meadow is not to. - **Poison oak drops its leaves and keeps its oil**. Leafless from late autumn through early spring. The Forest Service gives flowering March to June and fruit dispersal in summer and autumn. Losing the leaves removes the only identification character most people know, while the urushiol stays on the bare stems. A leafless, thornless vine in winter is not identified, and firewood gathering season is exactly when people handle unidentified bare stems. New spring leaves are often glossy and reddish. - **Deadly mushrooms fruit with the same rain as the good ones** (estimated). With the autumn flush. The exact season for Kitsap County is not established from any public source. Funeral bell fruits alongside honey mushroom and on the same wood, and it contains the same toxin as the death cap. The death cap season for western Washington is not established from any public source either, so this calendar cannot tell you a month to be careful in. Be careful in all of them. No seasonal rule substitutes for identification, and the autumn flush that brings chanterelles brings these at the same time and in the same woods. - **Madrone berries ripen**. Berries ripen from early autumn until December or January; seed collectors gather fruit from October to December. One of very few fruits still ripening as the year closes, which makes it disproportionately important to birds in early winter. Range wide dates rather than a Silverdale record, so treat the months as indicative. - **Bigleaf maple seed disperses**. Seeds ripe August to October, dispersing October to January, with some remaining on the tree until March. The paired winged samaras spin down through the whole wet season rather than dropping at once. Practically this is a gutter and drain problem as much as a botanical event, and it is the reason the tree seeds itself into every disturbed corner. - **The autumn mushroom flush, which rain triggers rather than the calendar**. There is no date. The National Park Service records for Olympic National Park, directly across Hood Canal, that while mushrooms can be found nearly year round, the peak season occurs after the start of fall rains up until the first major frosts. In practice that is the stretch between the September rains returning and the first hard freeze, which the frost normals put around the end of October at the earliest. This is the clearest case on the calendar of an event that a date would misrepresent. Fruiting here is triggered by the first sustained autumn rain after the summer drought, so in a year when the rain arrives in early September the season starts a month earlier than in a year when it holds off until October. Watch the forecast and the calendar together: count roughly from the first real soaking rain, not from a fixed day. The season ends at the first hard frost, which the climate normals put anywhere from 26 October to 1 December. - **Winter waterfowl arrive on the inlet**. WDFW records birds departing coastal moulting areas from late August through November and moving to wintering areas, primarily in Puget Sound. Most numerous here roughly October through April. The inlet changes character completely for half the year. Surf scoters are the most abundant of the diving ducks and feed on the mussels and clams of the same beaches people dig. They switch onto herring eggs during spring migration, so the waterfowl season and the herring spawn are the same story told twice. An empty looking Dyes Inlet in July is normal; an empty one in January means something is wrong. - **Varied thrush comes down into town** (local consensus). In the Silverdale lowlands mainly October through April. It breeds upslope in denser wetter forest and moves down into town for the winter, so its arrival is an altitude signal rather than a latitude one. It becomes most obvious feeding on the ground under shrubs during cold snaps, which makes it a good indicator that the weather has turned hard enough to push birds off the hills. - **Black-tailed deer rut**. November and December locally. The Forest Service gives the rut for the species as beginning as early as September and ending as late as March depending on location, with one studied population conceiving 75 percent of fawns between 21 November and 1 December. Bucks move far more than usual and lose their caution, and vehicle collisions peak with it. Drive the wooded roads at dawn and dusk in November expecting a deer in the road. Fawns follow from late May to mid July in the northern part of the range, which is when a doe will be aggressive near cover and when a fawn lying alone is not abandoned. - **Black bears feed hard before denning** (local consensus). Active roughly March through November in western Washington, with the heaviest feeding in late summer and autumn. Most bear conflict happens in the weeks before denning, when a bear needs enormous daily calories and stops being fussy about where they come from. That is exactly the season of ripe fruit, full compost heaps, and rubbish waiting for collection. They den through the coldest months rather than truly hibernating, so a mild winter can keep them up. ### December The wettest and darkest month: 252 mm and 8.4 hours of daylight. December alone brings nearly as much rain as April through September combined. King tides plus storm surge produce the highest water of the year, while the lowest tides fall near midnight. Maple sap can run on a cold snap, and madrone berries are among the only fruit left. - **First autumn frost**. October 26 at the 10th percentile, November 14 on average, December 1 at the 90th percentile. Have row cover ready by October 26, not by the average. One year in ten has already frozen by that date. This is also the end of the outdoor tomato and basil season and the point at which bracken and other soft growth dies back brown. - **The wet half of the year**. October through March. These six months deliver 1,154 mm of the annual 1,446 mm, which is 79.8 percent of the year's water. December alone brings 252 mm, nearly as much as April through September put together (294 mm across six months). It is also the half in which soil work compacts rather than tills. - **Winter minus tides run at night**. November through February, the deep lows falling between roughly 22:00 and 02:00. The tide table will show you tides as low as any in June, and they are real, but they are in the dark and in the cold. Digging them means a headlamp, a falling tide you cannot see the edge of, and a long walk back over ground that is filling behind you. Treat a winter minus tide as an expert trip, not a family one, and note that the biotoxin question is unchanged by the season. - **King tides and the winter flood risk**. Late December and January, when the highest astronomical tides coincide with the storm season. The highest water ever observed at Bremerton, 4.74 m above MLLW on 27 December 2022, exceeded the highest astronomical tide by 0.45 m. That extra half metre was storm surge stacked on an already extreme tide. A shoreline structure has to survive the tide plus the surge plus the wind waves, not the tide alone, and the season for all three arriving together is the turn of the year. - **Marine biotoxin closures, which have no season**. Any month. There is no safe season and no pattern you can plan around. This is the one thing on this calendar that a calendar cannot answer. Paralytic, diarrhetic and amnesic shellfish poisoning come from algal blooms that the Washington Department of Health tests for continuously, and a closure can appear in any month. The water looks clear during a toxic bloom. Cooking and freezing do not destroy the toxin, because it is in the meat. Check the Department of Health Shellfish Safety Map or the hotline on 1-800-562-5632 on the day you harvest, every time, and never infer safety from a good tide or from last week's status. A separate authority answers a separate question. - **Shellfish beach seasons**. Beach by beach, set annually by WDFW. There is no statewide month you can rely on. Two independent gates must both be open before you may legally and safely harvest: the WDFW season for that specific beach, and the Department of Health biotoxin status for that specific beach. Neither implies the other, and a good tide implies neither. WDFW also publishes an annual best clam and oyster harvest tides chart, which is the tide half of the same planning problem. - **The chum run** (local consensus). Late October into December in the local creeks. This is the biggest wildlife event of the year in central Kitsap and the easiest to see. Chum spawn in the lowest, most accessible reaches of the creeks, within a short walk of salt water, so Chico Creek and the other Dyes Inlet streams put spawning salmon within a few metres of a trail. NOAA records chum spawning from late summer to March with the peak in early winter when flows are high, and the local peak is November. The carcasses afterward are the year's biggest nutrient pulse into the creeks and draw eagles, gulls and bears. - **The coho run** (local consensus). September into December, later than the chum and pushing further upstream. Coho hold at the creek mouths and wait for the first heavy autumn rain to raise the water before running. That makes them the one salmon event you should watch the forecast for rather than the calendar: a dry October delays them, and a big early storm brings them in days. They spawn further up than chum, so they are the fish that reaches the smaller tributaries. Because juveniles then spend about a year and a half in fresh water, a creek only holds coho if it holds water all summer, which makes them the honest indicator of whether a stream is actually healthy. - **The winter steelhead run**. First, no month-by-month biotoxin season: closures have no season and the calendar must not imply the tide answers that question. Second, no mushroom dates: fruiting here is triggered by rain, not by the calendar, so a date would be a fabrication. Third, no fixed shellfish beach seasons: those are set beach by beach and annually, and reprinting last year's would be worse than silence. ## The ground The soil survey maps this area into named series. Winter-wet and summer-droughty on the same ground is the default condition, not an anomaly. ## Water **The watershed.** Kitsap (WRIA 15). WRIA 15 is named in RCW 90.94.030(2)(a) as one of eight watersheds with a Streamflow Restoration committee. Ecology adopted the WRIA 15 watershed plan in December 2024. **Where it goes.** Runoff at Silverdale reaches the open ocean through a chain of tidal basins, not a river. Each step below is the USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset 'tohuc' pointer, followed from the Silverdale HUC12 outward. **Surface water nearby.** Dyes Inlet, Clear Creek, West Fork Clear Creek, Strawberry Creek, Barker Creek, Koch Creek, Chico Creek, Dickerson Creek, Wildcat Creek, Mosher Creek. **Groundwater.** Yes. Groundwater is the normal domestic water source on the Kitsap Peninsula, and it is the only one: the peninsula is surrounded by saltwater and, as USGS puts it, 'the hydrologic setting is similar to that of an island'. There is no upstream river to divert from. ## The tide **Pattern.** Two highs and two lows per day, but the pair are markedly unequal. The mean diurnal high water inequality at Bremerton is 0.273 m and the mean diurnal LOW water inequality is 0.870 m, so it is the two lows that differ most. One of the two daily low tides is much lower than the other, which is why local low-tide beach access is so uneven day to day. **A caution about the numbers.** NOT a NOAA published datum. Derived here by applying NOAA's own subordinate-station ratio method to the Seattle datums. Use it for planning only; for anything you would wade or anchor by, use the live predictions for station 9445901 or the published Bremerton datums. **Currents.** Peak currents through the Narrows reach about 4.5 knots on the flood and 4 knots on the ebb, and the typical daily maximum is over 2 knots. That is faster than a person can swim. Slack water windows exist between each reversal and are the only safe crossing times. ## What can actually hurt you here Not a generic list. Somewhere on a subduction zone has a different honest preparedness answer from somewhere on a floodplain, and preparing for the wrong one is worse than not preparing at all. The column that matters most is warning time, because it decides whether preparation or reaction is the useful skill. ### Cascadia Subduction Zone megathrust earthquake (M~9) The defining regional event. Cascadia's fault is more than 800 km (500 miles) long and shaking from these earthquakes 'can last for a few minutes' (WA DNR). Silverdale sits well inland of the offshore rupture, so it is a long-duration, moderate-to-strong shaking problem rather than near-fault violent shaking: the hazards here are duration-driven - liquefaction of the Clear Creek delta fill at the head of Dyes Inlet and the waterfront, landslides on the Dyes Inlet bluffs, and multi-week loss of lifelines across a peninsula reached by two bridges and ferrie. Long-duration shaking; liquefaction risk concentrated on artificial fill, tidal flats and stream sediments (the Silverdale waterfront and Clear Creek mouth sit on exactly that); bluff landsliding around Dyes Inlet; prolonged isolation of the Kitsap Peninsula. **Likelihood:** 10-15 percent chance of an approximately magnitude 9 earthquake on the Cascadia Subduction Zone in the next 50 years (USGS, 2025). **Return period:** Full-margin ruptures approximately every 500 years; partial-margin ruptures approximately every 1,000 years (USGS Fact Sheet 2025-3050, fig. 4). The last event was the winter of 1699-1700, about 325 years ago. NOTE: the '330-year' figure in that fact sheet is for SOUTHERN Cascadia only and does not apply here. **Warning time:** No warning of the earthquake itself beyond ShakeAlert: in the Pacific Northwest warning times for people experiencing strong shaking are typically less than 10 seconds, and 50-80 seconds only for users far from the epicentre of an offshore megathrust. For the tsunami, see the Cascadia tsunami entry - hours, not minutes, inside Puget Sound. ### Deep intraslab (Benioff zone) earthquake, M6.5+ Moderate but widespread. Because the source is deep (tens of km), peak shaking intensity is lower than for an equivalent-magnitude shallow crustal earthquake, and these events rarely generate tsunamis. The three modern examples all damaged this region: 1949 M6.8 Olympia, 1965 M6.5 Seattle, 2001 M6.8 Nisqually. WA DNR notes the deep April 1949 Tacoma earthquake caused damage from southern Oregon to British Columbia. Shaking damage to unreinforced masonry and chimneys, liquefaction on waterfront fill, and landslides on saturated bluffs. The 1949 event triggered the Tacoma Narrows landslide, which generated a local wave. **Likelihood:** 85 percent chance of a magnitude 6.5 or greater deep (intraslab) earthquake in the Puget Sound region in the next 50 years (USGS, 2025). This is by far the most likely damaging earthquake to occur in a given lifetime here. **Return period:** Observed intervals in the instrumental record: 1949 to 1965 is 16 years, 1965 to 2001 is 36 years (USGS Fact Sheet 2025-3050, fig. 3). 24 years have now elapsed since 2001. **Warning time:** Seconds at most, via ShakeAlert (typically under 10 seconds where shaking is strong). No other warning. ### Shallow crustal earthquake on the Seattle Fault zone (M6.5-7.5) The worst-case shaking for this location, because it is shallow and close. The state/FEMA scenario models a M7.2 rupture on the northernmost strand from the Kitsap Peninsula to just east of Lake Sammamish (63 km / 40 miles). The 923-924 CE event lifted parts of Restoration Point on Bainbridge Island 23 feet straight up, generated a tsunami in Puget Sound, and triggered a large landslide into Lake Washington. Severe shaking, possible surface rupture, liquefaction, coseismic landsliding on the Dyes Inlet bluffs, and a locally generated tsunami arriving within minutes (see tsunami entry). **Likelihood:** 17 percent chance of a magnitude 6.5 or greater crustal fault earthquake in the Puget Sound region in the next 50 years (USGS, 2025). The Seattle fault zone passes immediately east and south of Silverdale; recent geologic mapping suggests it extends from the Olympic Mountains on the west to the Cascades on the east, and trenching at Waterman Point and Point Glover in Kitsap County found evidence of surface-rupturing earthquakes about 1,100 years ago. **Return period:** Uncertain and long. An 8,000-year investigation found evidence for possibly one additional earthquake about 6,900 years ago, 'suggesting a recurrence interval of thousands of years for large earthquakes'. Trenching on the Bainbridge Island scarp revealed evidence for up to three surface-rupturing earthquakes in the past 2,500 years. Last known event: winter 923-924 CE. **Warning time:** Effectively none. Silverdale is within the fault zone's near field, so ShakeAlert may deliver little or no useful lead time; strong shaking can arrive with the alert. ### Tsunami from a large Seattle Fault earthquake (the near-field, minutes-not-hours case) Modelled at the Silverdale point (47.64518, -122.68845): maximum amplitude 5 ft. Nearby modelled points: Bremerton/Sinclair Inlet 9 ft, Point White 16 ft, Liberty Bay 7 ft, Agate Passage 11 ft, Bangor 3 ft. The scenario is described by WGS as 'modeled after a simulated large magnitude Seattle fault earthquake, similar to that of the 923 CE event'. A roughly 5 ft wave at the head of Dyes Inlet about 5 minutes after shaking stops, on top of whatever the tide is doing (the GREAT DIURNAL range here, highest high to lowest low, is about 11.7 ft, so tide stage dominates the outcome). Low ground at the Silverdale waterfront, Old Town, and the Clear Creek mouth is the exposed area. **Likelihood:** Tied to a large Seattle Fault rupture (see above). The Washington Geological Survey's modelled inundation extent for this scenario does reach the head of Dyes Inlet at Silverdale. **Return period:** Governed by Seattle Fault recurrence: thousands of years between large earthquakes; last event 923-924 CE. **Warning time:** 5 minutes to the inundating wave at Silverdale (WGS modelled arrival time). Elsewhere on this shoreline it is worse: 'less than 3 min' at Bremerton/Sinclair Inlet, Point White and the Bainbridge ferry terminal. There is no time for an official warning. The earthquake itself is the warning - WA DNR states that for people in Washington, the single biggest warning of a potential tsunami is a large earthquake. This is a self-evacuation-on-shaking hazard, so preparation beats reaction. ### Tsunami from a Cascadia M9.0 megathrust earthquake (the far-field, hours case) Much smaller inside Puget Sound than the local Seattle Fault case, because the wave must refract through the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Admiralty Inlet. The WGS L1 M9.0 model has no separate Silverdale point; the nearest modelled point, Bremerton, gives a maximum amplitude of 2.5 ft. Bangor 9 ft, Lynch Cove 12 ft. Modest water-level surge and strong currents in Dyes Inlet hours after the shaking; the dominant local problem from Cascadia is the shaking and the multi-week infrastructure outage, not the wave. **Likelihood:** Accompanies the Cascadia megathrust event (10-15 percent in 50 years). **Return period:** Approximately 500 years for full-margin Cascadia ruptures. **Warning time:** About 2 hours 40 minutes to Bremerton (WGS modelled inundating-wave arrival). Hours of warning inside Puget Sound, unlike the outer coast. This is the one tsunami case here where official warning and organised evacuation are realistic. ### Seiche and landslide-generated waves in Puget Sound The concrete local precedent is the April 1949 deep M~7 earthquake, which triggered a large landslide on 90 m (300 ft) high bluffs at the Tacoma Narrows three days later; that slide caused a local tsunami. Dyes Inlet is a small, enclosed, steep-sided basin with bluffs around it, which is the geometry in which both effects occur. Sloshing and abrupt local waves in Dyes Inlet independent of any open-ocean tsunami; bluff collapse into the inlet displacing water. **Likelihood:** Not quantified in any source located. WA DNR defines a seiche as 'the sloshing of a closed body of water from earthquake shaking' and lists seiches among the secondary effects of both megathrust and shallow crustal earthquakes. Landslide-generated waves are separately documented: WA DNR states numerous deposits from landslide-generated tsunamis triggered by local earthquakes are found throughout Puget Sound, and that delta failures and landslides caused by shaking may create or amplify tsunamis. **Return period:** Not published for Dyes Inlet specifically. **Warning time:** None. Both are triggered by shaking and arrive within seconds to minutes; the delayed 1949 Narrows slide shows failures can also occur days after the earthquake, so the bluffs stay dangerous after the shaking ends. ### Landslides on coastal bluffs (the everyday geologic hazard here) Lethal and expensive. In the winter of 1996-1997 coastal landslides in Kitsap County destroyed millions of dollars of public and private property and killed a family of four on Bainbridge Island. NOAA's storm record for the Kitsap Peninsula zones logs 10 debris-flow events since 1996, including a 2007 fatality (a Mason County man killed in bed by a landslide) and a December 2010 episode causing about 1 million dollars of damage. Bluff failure around the Dyes Inlet shoreline, taking out shoreline houses, roads and the ground beneath them; road offsets at headscarps. Triggers are precipitation, coastal erosion at the bluff toe, and seismic shaking. **Likelihood:** High and recurring. USGS mapped 231 landslides in Kitsap County from lidar, covering 0.8 percent of the county's land area, and found that 67 percent of the mapped landslide area lies within 500 metres of the present coastline. About 77 percent of mapped landslides involve Vashon advance outwash deposits. Two mapped landslides sit directly on the Dyes Inlet shoreline near Silverdale: landslides 104a/104b (27,200 m2 and 5,030 m2, high confidence, on the coastal bluffs of the east shore and northern end of Dyes Inlet, with 'possible evidence of recent activity'), and landslide 139 (8,990 m2, west of Dyes Inlet, north of Chico). **Return period:** Not expressed as a return period. Empirically: landslide-producing winters recur on a scale of years, and Kitsap has about 338 km of saltwater coastline that is 'especially susceptible'. **Warning time:** Hours to days for the rainfall that drives them (NWS forecasts the atmospheric-river storms), but the failure itself is sudden and gives no useful warning. Above-normal precipitation was the principal triggering mechanism in 1996-1997. The mechanism is a perched water table: permeable Esperance-type advance outwash sand over the low-permeability Lawton Clay, so pore pressure builds during sustained wet weather and the bluff face fails. ### Winter windstorms Peak values in that record reach 77 mph (14 Dec 2000) and 71 mph (30 Mar 1997); the 14 Dec 2006 storm produced a measured 64 mph gust. Kitsap-specific documented effects: on 15 Nov 2006 about 8,000 people lost power in Kitsap County, three roads were closed or partly blocked by downed trees and power lines, and the Hood Canal Bridge was closed for several hours. The largest killer is indirect: the 14 Dec 2006 storm caused eight indirect fatalities from carbon monoxide poisoning from improper indoor use of barbecues and generators during the outage. Trees down across a heavily forested peninsula, multi-day power outages, closure of the Hood Canal Bridge, and carbon-monoxide deaths from generators and barbecues used indoors. In a peninsula community the outage, not the wind, is the hazard. **Likelihood:** Near-annual, and the most frequent damaging hazard here. In NOAA's storm record for the NWS zones covering the Kitsap Peninsula, 1996-2025, 24 of 30 years had at least one High Wind or Strong Wind event; 80 wind events total (45 High Wind, 35 Strong Wind). **Return period:** Empirically about 0.8 High/Strong Wind events per year in these zones over 1996-2025; a damaging regional windstorm roughly every 1-2 years, with the severe ones (65 mph+) clustering in 1997-2000 and 2006. **Warning time:** Hours to a few days. These are synoptic-scale Pacific storms that are forecast well in advance, and NWS Seattle issues High Wind Watches and Warnings for zone WAZ323. NWS does not publish a fixed numerical lead time - each office sets local criteria - but this is the one hazard on this list where preparation time is genuinely available. ### Flooding (coastal/tidal and small-stream) Localised rather than catastrophic - there is no large river here. NOAA logs 18 Flood and 3 Coastal Flood events for these zones since 1996. The coastal cases are tide-driven: on 17 Dec 2012 record high tides flooded roads and properties around Puget Sound (the Seattle gauge recorded 14.48 ft) with flooding of a street and apartment parking lots in Port Orchard; on 27 Dec 2022 flooding damaged business space in Port Orchard and Hood Canal water rose above Seabeck Highway. Saltwater flooding of the low Silverdale waterfront and Old Town at extreme high tides, and floodway flooding along Clear, Barker and Chico Creeks. The great diurnal range at the reference station, highest high to lowest low, is about 11.7 ft (the mean range of tide, high to low, is 8.0 ft), so tide stage governs. **Likelihood:** Mapped and regulated. FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer shows a 1-percent-annual-chance (100-year) special flood hazard area along the Dyes Inlet shoreline at Silverdale and up the creek corridors, with 0.2-percent-annual-chance (500-year) Zone X beyond it. Point checks: the Silverdale waterfront at the head of Dyes Inlet is Zone AE with a base flood elevation of 14 ft; the Chico Creek mouth is Zone AE with BFE 13 ft; the Barker Creek mouth is Zone AE FLOODWAY. The built-up upland of Silverdale (CDP centroid, Clear Creek at Silverdale Way, Bucklin Hill) is Zone X, area of minimal flood hazard. **Return period:** 1 percent annual chance (100-year) for the mapped AE zones; 0.2 percent annual chance (500-year) for the shaded X zone. Kitsap County FIRM panels covering Silverdale are effective 2010-11-04 and 2017-02-03, DFIRM 53035C, scale 1:6000. **Warning time:** Hours to days. Coastal flooding here is the predictable combination of a high astronomical tide, low barometric pressure and onshore wind, so NWS coastal flood advisories are issued in advance; small-stream flooding follows forecast heavy-rain events. ### Wildfire The westside Douglas-fir fire regime is infrequent but stand-replacing: the mapped historical events here are hundreds of thousands to over a million acres. The modern risk is a late-summer/early-autumn ignition in continuous second-growth timber during the annual summer drought, in a wildland-urban interface with limited road egress off the peninsula. Late-season timber fire in second-growth forest around Green and Gold Mountains and the peninsula interior; the constraint is evacuation off a peninsula, not fire behaviour alone. **Likelihood:** Low by Washington standards, but not zero, and it is the hazard most likely to be underestimated here. The interagency fire perimeter history contains no modern (post-1900) mapped fire perimeter within about 15 km of Silverdale; the only perimeters intersecting that area are three very large pre-settlement fire events dated 1308, 1508 and 1701 CE. NOAA's storm record logs a single Wildfire event for these zones in 30 years: 4-13 Oct 2012, 230 acres of timber north of Shelton, after 'little or no precipitation had fallen since mid July'. **Return period:** The mapped large-fire intervals near Silverdale are 1308, 1508, 1701 - roughly 200 and 193 years apart - with nothing mapped since. Treat as a centuries-scale, high-severity regime rather than an annual one. No published modern return period for this location was found. **Warning time:** Days for the fire-weather setup (NWS issues Red Flag Warnings for fire weather zone WAZ654), but minutes to hours for an actual fire run. ### Heavy snow and ice (included because the record says it outranks wind by count) Wet, heavy lowland snow near freezing, which loads trees and brings down limbs and power lines; combined with the terrain it isolates hillside neighbourhood. Power loss and road closures on the steep Bucklin Hill / bluff-top roads; same generator carbon-monoxide risk as windstorms. **Likelihood:** 48 Heavy Snow events, 19 Winter Weather, 4 Winter Storm and 3 Ice Storm events in NOAA's record for these zones since 1996 - more logged events than High Wind. Heavy-snow years occurred in 18 of the 30 years. **Return period:** Roughly 3 of every 5 winters produce at least one heavy-snow, winter-storm or ice-storm event in these zones. **Warning time:** Days. Forecast well in advance by NWS Seattle. ## Finding your way ## Who to ask Some questions have no general answer, only a local one: what may be taken, what may be planted, whether the shellfish are safe today, what water you may legally draw. These are the bodies that answer them here. - **WSU Extension, Kitsap County** (https://extension.wsu.edu/kitsap/) - **Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife** (https://wdfw.wa.gov/) - **Washington State Department of Health, Marine Biotoxins** (https://doh.wa.gov/community-and-environment/shellfish/recreational-shellfish/illnesses/biotoxins). Check before every shellfish harvest, not once. Cooking and freezing do not destroy paralytic shellfish poison. Hotline 1-800-562-5632. - **Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board** (https://www.nwcb.wa.gov/). Lists the county board contacts, including Kitsap. - **Washington State Department of Ecology, Water Rights** (https://ecology.wa.gov/water-shorelines/water-supply/water-rights). WRIA 15 overrides the statewide groundwater permit exemption, so what you may legally draw here is not the statewide answer. - **WSU Puyallup, Soils** (https://puyallup.wsu.edu/soils/) - **Puget Sound Clean Air Agency** (https://pscleanair.gov/). Declares burn bans for King, Kitsap, Pierce and Snohomish counties. Check on the day you intend to burn, not once a season. ## Sources Every figure above comes from a public-domain source, almost all of them US federal: NOAA for the climate normals and the tides, USDA NRCS for the soil survey, USGS for elevation and hydrography, FEMA and USGS for the hazards. The licence line inside each data file records which, so the claim can be checked rather than believed. The data itself lives in `data/locales/silverdale_wa/`. This document is GENERATED from it by `scripts/build-locale-doc.js`. Editing this page does nothing: edit the data and run the script.
