docs.text: # The Hazards Your Place Actually Has Most preparedness advice is written for nobody in particular, which means it is written for nowhere in particular. It tells you to buy a kit. It does not tell you that the kit a person needs on a floodplain and the kit a person needs on a subduction zone are different kits, and that the difference is not a detail. That matters more than it sounds, because attention and money are finite. Every hour and every dollar spent on the wrong hazard is an hour and a dollar not spent on the one that will actually come. Generic advice is not neutral. It has a cost, and the cost is paid on the day something happens. So this guide is not a list of things to buy. It is a method for answering one question about your own address: what does this place actually do, and how much notice does it give? Everything else follows from that answer. The worked example at the end is Silverdale, Washington, because that is the place this simulation is built on, and because a real answer is more instructive than a general one. If you live somewhere else, the method is the part that transfers. One honest boundary before anything else. This guide cannot tell you whether your house will stand up, whether your ground will liquefy, or whether the slope behind you is stable. Those are site-specific engineering questions, and the honest answer to all three is that somebody has to look at your particular ground. Ready.gov says the same thing about slopes: seek advice from a geotechnical expert for evaluating landslide hazards. What this guide can do is tell you which questions are worth paying someone to answer. ## Warning time is the organising idea Hazards are usually sorted by how frightening they are. That is the wrong axis. Sort them by how much notice they give, because notice decides which skill is useful. A hazard that gives you days of notice is a **plan**. You can watch a forecast, fill containers, charge things, move the car, call the person who lives alone up the road. Planning works because there is time to plan in. A hazard that gives you seconds is a **reflex**. There is no time to decide anything, so whatever you do in those seconds is whatever you already knew how to do without thinking. You cannot improve a reflex during the event. You can only have built it beforehand. A hazard that gives you minutes is the hardest case, because it looks like there is time to think and there is not. Minutes are enough to walk to high ground and not enough to gather your things first. The decision has to be pre-made, and the pre-made decision is the whole preparation. | Notice | What that makes it | What the preparation actually is | |---|---|---| | Seconds | A reflex | One trained response, practised until it needs no thought | | Minutes | A pre-made decision | Knowing your route and your high ground before the day | | Hours | A short plan | A checklist you can run without shopping | | Days | A full plan | Supplies, fuel, medication, and other people | | No notice, but slow onset | A siting decision | Answered before you buy, rent, or build | Notice this cuts across the usual categories. Two earthquakes in the same region can sit in different rows if one is offshore and one is under your feet. A tsunami can be a five-minute hazard or a three-hour hazard depending on which fault made it. The warning time, not the name, is what tells you what to do. ## How to find your own hazards This is the transferable part. Six questions, and a specific public body that answers each one. Every one of these is free and most are federal, which means you can check the answer rather than believe it. **Will the ground here shake, how hard, and how often?** The USGS National Seismic Hazard Model. It integrates what is known about "earthquake sources, crustal deformation, active faulting, and ground shaking" into maps of expected shaking, and it is the basis for the seismic provisions in building codes. It is expressed as probability: the 2023 maps show peak ground accelerations "having a 2 percent probability of being exceeded in 50 years, for a firm rock site." You can query it for your own coordinates through the USGS Earthquake Hazard Toolbox and the Unified Hazard Tool. What it does not answer: whether *your* soil amplifies that shaking. The model assumes firm rock. Soft fill, tidal flats and stream sediment behave differently, and that is a state or county question. **Is my address in a mapped flood hazard area?** The FEMA Flood Map Service Center, which describes itself as "the official public source for flood hazard information produced in support of the National Flood Insurance Program." Search by address. It returns your flood zone and, in the detailed zones, a base flood elevation. The vocabulary is worth learning because it is precise. A Special Flood Hazard Area is "the area that will be inundated by the flood event having a 1-percent chance of being equaled or exceeded in any given year." Shaded Zone X is the band out to the 0.2-percent-annual-chance flood. Unshaded Zone X is beyond that. "100-year flood" is the same thing as the 1-percent zone and is a much worse name for it, because it sounds like a schedule and it is a yearly probability. Ready.gov adds the caveat that matters: flooding does not follow lines on a map. Being outside the zone is not the same as being safe, it is the same as being unmapped. **What is the county-level picture across all hazards at once?** The FEMA National Risk Index, which "provides information for communities most at risk to 18 different natural hazards" and "offers a baseline risk measurement for expected annual loss, social vulnerability and community resilience at the Census tract or county level." Useful as a first sweep, because it will name hazards you had not thought of. Coarse by design: a county is a large thing and your street is not the county. **What is the ground itself going to do?** Two layers. Nationally, the USGS Landslide Hazards Program publishes a high-resolution map of landslide susceptibility for the entire United States and Puerto Rico, alongside the US Landslide Inventory. Locally, the deeper answer is usually your **state geological survey**, because the fine-grained mapping of landslides, liquefaction and tsunami inundation is state work. In Washington that is the Washington Geologic Information Portal, which carries landslide hazards, tsunami hazards and evacuation routes, earthquake ground response including "liquefaction, seismic site class, seismic design categories," and mapped faults. Every state has an equivalent body; what it has mapped varies a lot. **What has actually happened here, as opposed to what could?** Two NOAA sources. The National Centers for Environmental Information Storm Events Database is the logged record of severe weather events by state and county zone, with the damage, injuries and fatalities attached. The National Weather Service publishes local climate records for individual stations: average high, average temperature, average low, precipitation and snowfall, alongside record events. This is the step people skip, and it is the one that most often overturns an assumption. A thirty-year event log will tell you plainly that the thing your town actually deals with is not the thing your town talks about. **Who will tell me on the day, and where am I supposed to go?** Your local emergency management office, which holds the evacuation routes, the shelter locations, and the plan the county is actually operating. Ready.gov's framing of the household plan starts here: "Know what disasters and hazards could affect your area, how to get emergency alerts, and where you would go if you and your family need to evacuate." And make sure an alert can physically reach you. Wireless Emergency Alerts are short messages sent to any WEA-enabled mobile phone in a targeted area, with a distinctive sound and vibration repeated twice; there is no subscription and no charge. NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards is "a nationwide network of radio stations broadcasting continuous weather information directly from the nearest National Weather Service office," carrying non-weather emergencies too, from more than 1,000 transmitters. A battery radio keeps working when the tower, the mains and the internet do not. One thing none of these can do: predict. USGS is blunt about it. "Neither the USGS nor any other scientists have ever predicted a major earthquake," and what they can produce instead is "the probability that a significant earthquake will occur in a specific area within a certain number of years." Everything above tells you what is likely over years. Nothing tells you what is happening on Thursday. ## The worked example: Silverdale, Washington Here is what those six questions return for one real address at the head of Dyes Inlet on the Kitsap Peninsula. The full data, with the sourcing for every figure, is in [Where You Are: Silverdale, Washington](/library#silverdale-wa). What follows is that list resorted by warning time, because that is the sort that changes behaviour. ### Seconds, or none at all **A shallow crustal earthquake on the Seattle Fault zone, M6.5 to 7.5.** The worst shaking case for this location, because the fault is shallow and passes immediately east and south. USGS puts the chance of a magnitude 6.5 or greater crustal fault earthquake in the Puget Sound region at 17 percent in the next 50 years. The recurrence interval for large events is thousands of years and the last one was the winter of 923 to 924 CE, which lifted parts of Restoration Point on Bainbridge Island 23 feet. Warning time is effectively zero: Silverdale is in the near field, so an early-warning alert may arrive with the shaking rather than before it. **A deep intraslab earthquake, M6.5 or greater.** 85 percent in 50 years. This is the one most likely to happen in an ordinary lifetime here. Three have already: 1949 Olympia, 1965 Seattle, 2001 Nisqually, 16 years apart and then 36, with 24 years elapsed since. Because the source is tens of kilometres down, shaking is less intense than an equivalent shallow event and these rarely make tsunamis. Warning: seconds at most. **Cascadia megathrust shaking, M9.** 10 to 15 percent in 50 years, full margin ruptures approximately every 500 years, the last in the winter of 1699 to 1700. Silverdale sits well inland of the offshore rupture, so the local problem is not violent shaking but shaking that lasts for minutes: liquefaction of the fill and delta sediment at the waterfront and the Clear Creek mouth, landslides on the bluffs, and weeks without lifelines on a peninsula reached by two bridges and ferries. **Seiche and landslide-generated waves.** Sloshing in an enclosed basin, or a bluff collapsing into the water and displacing it. Dyes Inlet is small, enclosed and steep-sided, which is exactly the geometry for both. No warning at all, and a nasty detail: the 1949 earthquake triggered a large bluff landslide at the Tacoma Narrows three days later, which generated its own local wave. The bluffs stay dangerous after the shaking ends. ### Minutes **A tsunami from a large Seattle Fault earthquake.** The Washington Geological Survey models the inundation reaching the head of Dyes Inlet, with a maximum amplitude of 5 feet at the Silverdale point and an arrival time of 5 minutes. Along the same shoreline it is worse: less than 3 minutes at Bremerton, Point White and the Bainbridge ferry terminal. Nearby modelled amplitudes run higher than Silverdale's: Bremerton 9 feet, Agate Passage 11, Point White 16. And the tide is doing whatever it is doing on top of that, across a mean range of about 11.7 feet. Five minutes is not enough time for anyone to warn you. The earthquake is the warning. Washington DNR states plainly that for people in this state, the single biggest warning of a potential tsunami is a large earthquake, and Ready.gov's instruction is to evacuate on the natural sign without waiting: "DO NOT wait! Leave as soon as you see any natural signs of a tsunami or receive an official tsunami warning." ### Hours **A tsunami from the Cascadia megathrust.** Much smaller inside Puget Sound than the local case, because the wave has to refract through the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Admiralty Inlet: the nearest modelled point, Bremerton, gives 2.5 feet, and the modelled arrival is about 2 hours 40 minutes. This is the one tsunami case here where an official warning and an organised evacuation are realistic. The dominant Cascadia problem locally is the shaking and the multi-week outage, not the wave. **Coastal and small-stream flooding.** Mapped and regulated. The Silverdale waterfront is Zone AE with a base flood elevation of 14 feet, the Chico Creek mouth AE at 13 feet, the Barker Creek mouth AE floodway, while the built-up upland is Zone X, minimal hazard. There is no large river here, so this is localised rather than catastrophic: 18 flood and 3 coastal flood events logged since 1996, the coastal ones driven by high astronomical tide plus low pressure plus onshore wind, which is a combination the Weather Service can see coming. ### Days **Winter windstorms.** The most frequent damaging hazard here, and the one with real preparation time. In the NOAA record for the Kitsap Peninsula zones from 1996 to 2025, 24 of 30 years had at least one high or strong wind event, 80 in total, peaking at 77 mph in December 2000. On 15 November 2006 about 8,000 people in Kitsap County lost power, roads were blocked by downed trees and lines, and the Hood Canal Bridge closed for hours. Read the next sentence twice, because it is the single most useful fact in this document. The December 2006 storm caused eight indirect deaths from carbon monoxide poisoning, from barbecues and generators used indoors during the outage. The wind did not kill those people. The response to the outage did. **Heavy snow and ice.** 48 heavy snow events, 19 winter weather, 4 winter storm and 3 ice storm events logged since 1996, with heavy snow in 18 of the 30 years. Wet lowland snow near freezing loads trees, brings down limbs and lines, and isolates the steep bluff-top roads. Same generator and carbon monoxide risk as the windstorms. Worth being exact about the ranking, because it is a good lesson in reading a record honestly: heavy snow events alone (48) outnumber high wind events alone (45), but wind events of all kinds (80) outnumber winter events of all kinds (74). Which hazard "wins" depends on how you group the categories. The useful conclusion is not that one beats the other, it is that both are near-annual and both produce the same problem, which is a cold dark house. **Wildfire.** Low by Washington standards and not zero, and the hazard most likely to be underestimated here. No modern mapped fire perimeter within about 15 km; the only perimeters intersecting that area are three very large pre-settlement events in 1308, 1508 and 1701, roughly 200 and 193 years apart, with nothing mapped since. The westside Douglas-fir regime is infrequent and stand-replacing. Fire weather gives days of notice through Red Flag Warnings, but an actual fire run gives minutes to hours, and the binding constraint here is not fire behaviour, it is getting off a peninsula. ### The one with two different warning times at once **Landslides on coastal bluffs.** This is the everyday geologic hazard, and the one people forget while thinking about the megathrust. USGS mapped 231 landslides in Kitsap County from lidar, and 67 percent of the mapped landslide area lies within 500 metres of the coastline. Two sit directly on the Dyes Inlet shoreline near Silverdale with possible evidence of recent activity. The mechanism is a perched water table: permeable sand over low-permeability clay, so pore pressure builds through a sustained wet spell and the bluff face lets go. In the winter of 1996 to 1997 coastal landslides in Kitsap County destroyed millions of dollars of property and killed a family of four on Bainbridge Island. The NOAA storm record for these zones holds 10 debris-flow events since 1996, including a 2007 fatality. The two warning times are the point. The **rain** that drives it is forecast days ahead. The **failure** gives nothing. Ready.gov is direct about the fast kind: "the most dangerous, life-threatening and deadliest landslides are the ones that occur quickly, often with little notice," and "by the time you are sure a debris flow is coming, it will be too late to get away safely." So the preparation is not a reaction at all. It is knowing, before the winter, whether you live on or under a bluff. ## Why the everyday hazard usually matters more than the famous one Put the numbers side by side and the ranking inverts. A magnitude 9 on Cascadia is 10 to 15 percent in 50 years. A damaging deep earthquake is 85 percent in the same 50 years, which makes it between five and nine times as likely, depending on which end of the Cascadia range you take. A damaging windstorm has shown up in 24 of the last 30 years. Heavy snow in 18 of 30. A landslide-producing winter recurs on a scale of years. So in an ordinary lifetime at this address, the overwhelmingly probable emergency is not the one with a documentary about it. It is a week in February with no power, a road closed by a fallen tree, and a fridge full of food going over. Here is the part that makes this good news rather than a scolding, and it is reasoning from the figures above rather than a claim anyone has published. The preparation for the common case is most of the preparation for the rare one. Stored water, a way to stay warm without the mains, light, a battery radio, a month of medication and food that does not need a freezer, these are the same items whether the cause is a windstorm on Tuesday or the megathrust in fifty years. The megathrust adds duration and it adds the shaking reflex. It does not replace the list. Which means the honest advice is to prepare for the boring thing, and accept that you have substantially prepared for the frightening one as a side effect. ## What preparation looks like when the list drives it In this order. The ordering is a rule of thumb, not a published standard: it puts first the things that kill fastest and are hardest to improvise. **Water first.** The CDC says to store at least 1 gallon of water per person per day for 3 days, covering "drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, and other uses," and to try for a 2-week supply if possible. Ready.gov gives the same gallon "for several days," and notes that in very hot temperatures water needs can double, and that children, nursing mothers and sick people may need more. Washington's own emergency management division campaigns on "Be 2 Weeks Ready," two weeks rather than the federal three days, which is a reasonable thing for a state that expects lifelines to stay down. Everything about containers, sanitising, labelling, rotation and what to do about water you are unsure of is covered properly in two companion guides, and there is no point repeating it here: [Storing Water Safely](/library#storing-water-safely) and [Making Water Safe to Drink](/library#making-water-safe-to-drink). **Then warmth, and this is where people die.** Not from cold. From what they burn to fix the cold. CDC reports that more than 400 Americans die each year from unintentional carbon monoxide poisoning not linked to fires, and the symptoms read like ordinary winter illness: "headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, and confusion." The rules are absolute. Generators and fuel are used outdoors only, at least 20 feet from windows, doors, vents and attached garages. Never a generator inside a home or garage, even with the doors and windows open. Never charcoal indoors, never a portable gas camp stove indoors, never a gas oven as a heater. Install working carbon monoxide alarms on every level of the home. Eight people died that way in this region after one windstorm. That is the highest-value paragraph in this document and it costs about thirty dollars to act on. The rest of warmth is unglamorous: layers, blankets, sleeping bags, closing off one room. Know the signs of hypothermia (shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech, drowsiness) and warm the core first, which means chest, neck, head and groin. **Then light.** A flashlight for every household member, and spare batteries. Not candles, in a house that may have just been shaken. **Then information.** A battery or hand-crank radio, ideally a NOAA Weather Radio with tone alert, because it works when the network does not. A charged phone and a backup battery, because Wireless Emergency Alerts need no subscription and reach the phone directly. Local paper maps, for when the mapping app has nothing to talk to. **Then medicine.** Prescriptions, a first aid kit, and a real plan for anything that needs mains power or refrigeration; Ready.gov's advice is to talk to your medical provider about that plan before you need it, not during. On food in an outage, the numbers are specific: a refrigerator holds temperature about four hours, a full freezer about 48, and food held at 40 degrees Fahrenheit or above for two hours or more gets thrown out. **And the two-minute items that are not about disasters at all.** In any given year you are far more likely to have a house fire than an earthquake. The US Fire Administration's numbers: smoke alarms in every bedroom, outside each separate sleeping area, and on every level including the basement, interconnected so that when one sounds they all sound; test monthly; batteries at least once a year; replace the whole alarm 10 years from its manufacture date. Two ways out of every room, an outside meeting place in front of the house, and a drill that everyone in the household has actually walked. The reason is the number: you could have less than two minutes to get out once the alarm sounds. ## Drop, cover and hold on, done correctly For a seconds-of-warning hazard there is only the reflex. Here is the whole of it, from Ready.gov. **Drop** where you are, onto hands and knees. **Cover** your head and neck with one arm and hand. **Hold** until the shaking stops. For the cover step: "If a sturdy table or desk is nearby, crawl underneath it for shelter. If no shelter is nearby, crawl next to an interior wall (away from windows)." Stay on your knees and bend over to protect your vital organs. In bed: turn face down and cover your head and neck with a pillow. Do not get up and cross a dark room full of broken glass. In a vehicle: pull over and stop, and set the parking brake. Outdoors: move to an open area away from buildings, trees, streetlights and power lines. Using a cane: drop, cover and hold on, or sit on a chair or bed and cover your head and neck with both hands. Using a walker or wheelchair: lock your wheels, then get as low as possible, bend over, cover your head and neck, and hold on. **The error that injures people is running outside.** Ready.gov states it flatly: "If you are inside, stay and do not run outside; avoid doorways." Two reasons. Getting out means crossing a floor that is moving, on feet, past things that are falling, and then standing next to the outside of a building, which is where the glass, the cladding and the parapet land. And the doorway advice is a leftover from a different kind of building; in an ordinary modern house a doorway is not stronger than the rest of the structure and it will not protect your head. If you get a ShakeAlert, it is a trigger for that same reflex, nothing more. It gives "seconds before strong shaking arrives," and close to the epicentre it gives little or none. It is not a prediction; the earthquake has already started. USGS separates these carefully: early warning is seconds to tens of seconds after an earthquake begins, probabilities describe long-term chances over years, and prediction (a date, a place and a magnitude) is not yet possible. Then, and this is the part that belongs to shorelines: **when the shaking stops and you are near the water, go up and inland immediately, on foot, without waiting for anyone to tell you to.** Ready.gov's generic instruction is to shelter at least 100 feet above sea level or one mile inland, but the honest local instruction is simpler, because at Silverdale the modelled wave is 5 feet and arrives in about 5 minutes. Get off the low ground at the waterfront, Old Town and the Clear Creek mouth, get uphill, and stay there until somebody with authority says the sequence is over. You will feel foolish most times you do this. Do it anyway. ## The honest limits There are things a household cannot prepare for, and pretending otherwise is its own kind of failure. **You cannot store a bridge.** The Kitsap Peninsula is reached by two bridges and ferries. A Cascadia event means multi-week loss of lifelines across that whole peninsula. No quantity of tinned food fixes a road network. That problem is solved, to the extent it is solved at all, at the county and state level, and your part in it is to be one of the households that does not need rescuing in the first week. **You cannot prepare your way off bad ground.** If your house sits on liquefiable fill, or on top of an actively creeping bluff, or below one, no kit changes that. That is a siting question and it is answered before you sign anything: look up the address on the state hazard portal and FEMA's flood map, and pay a geotechnical engineer if the answer is ambiguous. Many people do not get this choice at all. Renters, people housed where housing exists, people who inherited the house. If that is you, then the thing you can control is knowing exactly what your ground does and exactly where you are going, which costs nothing. **You cannot stockpile your way out of dependence on other people.** Anyone on dialysis, oxygen, insulin or powered mobility equipment has a hard limit measured in days, and that limit is a medical plan, not a shopping list. Which brings the answer round to where it actually lives. After the frequent, boring, week-long version of every hazard on this list, what determines how a street comes through it is not equipment. It is whether anyone knows who lives alone, who has a generator and who knows how to use it safely outdoors, who has the chainsaw, who cannot get down their own steps, and which neighbour has the medical training. Washington's emergency management division organises its preparedness guidance around neighbourhoods for that reason, alongside families and pets. Ready.gov's household plan asks who you will contact and where you will meet before it asks what you will carry. That knowledge is local, it is unwritten, and it cannot be bought in a hurry. It is also, by a wide margin, the cheapest preparation on this page. ## How you know it worked - You can name the three hazards most likely to actually happen where you live, with a number attached to each, and say where the number came from. - You have looked up your own address on a flood map and on your state's geologic hazard portal, and you know what they said. - You can sort your hazards by warning time, and you know which of them give you seconds. - Drop, cover and hold on is something your household has practised, not something you have read. - If you are near a shoreline, every person in the house knows which way is uphill and goes there on the shaking, without discussion. - There is stored water, a way to stay warm, light, a battery radio and a month of medication, and a carbon monoxide alarm on every level. - You know the name of at least one neighbour who would notice if you did not come out for two days. None of that makes you safe, and nothing on this page should be read as a promise. What it does is move you from preparing for a hazard in general to preparing for the ones your ground actually has, which is the only kind of preparation that pays for itself. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. Government publications are listed first because they are public domain and can be redistributed with this guide; the rest cannot. ### United States government (public domain) - Federal Emergency Management Agency, Ready.gov. Build A Kit (one gallon of water per person per day, several-day food supply, the basic disaster supplies list). https://www.ready.gov/kit - Ready.gov. Water (the gallon, hot weather doubling needs, who needs more). https://www.ready.gov/water - Ready.gov. Food (several-day supply of non-perishable food, what kinds). https://www.ready.gov/food - Ready.gov. Earthquakes (Drop Cover Hold On in full, the bed, vehicle, outdoor and mobility-device variants, "stay and do not run outside; avoid doorways", going inland after shaking). https://www.ready.gov/earthquakes - Ready.gov. Tsunamis (natural warning signs, do not wait for an official warning, 100 feet above sea level or one mile inland). https://www.ready.gov/tsunamis - Ready.gov. Power Outages (generators 20 feet from windows, doors and attached garages; CO alarms on every level; fridge four hours, full freezer 48 hours; the 40 degree two-hour food rule; medical device plans). https://www.ready.gov/power-outages - Ready.gov. Winter Weather and Extreme Cold (heating safely, hypothermia signs, warming the core first). https://www.ready.gov/winter-weather - Ready.gov. Floods (Turn Around Don't Drown, six inches of moving water, the 30-day insurance waiting period, flooding does not follow lines on a map). https://www.ready.gov/floods - Ready.gov. Wildfires (evacuation alerts, go bag, 30 feet of defensible space). https://www.ready.gov/wildfires - Ready.gov. Landslides and Debris Flow (fast versus slow warning signs, "too late to get away safely", consult a geotechnical expert). https://www.ready.gov/landslides-debris-flow - Ready.gov. Make A Plan (knowing which hazards affect your area, contacts, meeting place, alerts). https://www.ready.gov/plan - Ready.gov. Be Informed (know what disasters and hazards could affect your area). https://www.ready.gov/be-informed - Ready.gov. Alerts and Warnings (Wireless Emergency Alerts need no subscription; the Emergency Alert System; NOAA Weather Radio; IPAWS). https://www.ready.gov/alerts - Federal Emergency Management Agency. Flood Map Service Center (the official public source for flood hazard information). https://msc.fema.gov/portal/home - Federal Emergency Management Agency. Flood Zones (Special Flood Hazard Area, the 1-percent-annual-chance definition, shaded and unshaded Zone X, the 0.2-percent zone). https://www.fema.gov/glossary/flood-zones - Federal Emergency Management Agency. National Risk Index for Natural Hazards (18 natural hazards; expected annual loss, social vulnerability and community resilience at Census tract or county level). https://www.fema.gov/flood-maps/products-tools/national-risk-index - United States Fire Administration. Smoke Alarms (every bedroom, outside each sleeping area, every level including basement; interconnected; test monthly; batteries yearly; replace the unit at 10 years). https://www.usfa.fema.gov/prevention/home-fires/prepare-for-fire/smoke-alarms/ - United States Fire Administration. Home Fire Escape Plans (two ways out of every room, outside meeting place, less than two minutes to escape). https://www.usfa.fema.gov/prevention/home-fires/prepare-for-fire/home-fire-escape-plans/ - United States Geological Survey. National Seismic Hazard Model (what it integrates, the 2 percent in 50 years framing, its role in building codes). https://www.usgs.gov/programs/earthquake-hazards/science/national-seismic-hazard-model - United States Geological Survey. Seismic Hazard Maps and Site-Specific Data (the Earthquake Hazard Toolbox and Unified Hazard Tool). https://www.usgs.gov/programs/earthquake-hazards/seismic-hazard-maps-and-site-specific-data - United States Geological Survey. Can you predict earthquakes? ("No. Neither the USGS nor any other scientists have ever predicted a major earthquake.") https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/can-you-predict-earthquakes - United States Geological Survey. What is the difference between earthquake early warning, forecasts, probabilities and prediction? (the timescales each one covers). https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/what-difference-between-earthquake-early-warning-earthquake-forecasts-earthquake-probabilities - United States Geological Survey. Earthquake Early Warning (the definition, seconds to minutes of advance warning). https://www.usgs.gov/programs/earthquake-hazards/science/earthquake-early-warning - ShakeAlert, operated by the United States Geological Survey (seconds before strong shaking, little or no warning near the epicentre, not prediction, Drop Cover and Hold On on alert). https://www.shakealert.org/ - United States Geological Survey. Landslide Hazards Program (the national landslide susceptibility map and the US Landslide Inventory). https://www.usgs.gov/programs/landslide-hazards - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. How to Create and Store an Emergency Water Supply (1 gallon per person per day for 3 days, the 2-week goal, what it covers, who needs more). https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/how-to-create-and-store-an-emergency-water-supply.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About Carbon Monoxide Poisoning (more than 400 unintentional non-fire deaths a year, symptoms, generators more than 20 feet from windows doors and vents, never charcoal or a camp stove indoors, never a gas oven as a heater). https://www.cdc.gov/carbon-monoxide/about/index.html - National Weather Service. NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards (a nationwide network broadcasting directly from the nearest NWS office; more than 1,000 transmitters; non-weather emergencies). https://www.weather.gov/nwr/ - National Weather Service, Western Region. Climate (NOWData and the local climate products: normals, records, snowfall, extremes). https://www.weather.gov/wrh/Climate - National Weather Service. Wind Safety (isolated wind damage at sustained 40 to 50 mph). https://www.weather.gov/safety/wind - NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. Storm Events Database (the logged severe weather record by state and county zone; the source of the event counts, damages and fatalities quoted for the Kitsap Peninsula zones). https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/stormevents/ ### State agencies (cited as the authority; text written here) State agencies are not covered by the federal public-domain rule, so these are cited for the fact and the sentences are ours. - Washington Emergency Management Division. Preparedness ("Be 2 Weeks Ready", and neighbourhoods as a preparedness category alongside families and pets). https://mil.wa.gov/preparedness - Washington State Department of Natural Resources, Washington Geological Survey. Washington Geologic Information Portal (landslide, tsunami, liquefaction and seismic site class, faults and historical earthquake damage). https://www.dnr.wa.gov/geologyportal ### The locale data this guide's worked example rests on Every Silverdale figure (probabilities, return periods, modelled tsunami amplitudes and arrival times, storm event counts, mapped landslides, flood zones and base flood elevations) comes from `data/locales/silverdale_wa/hazards.json`, which records its own source URL per hazard. Its provenance is USGS, FEMA, NOAA and the Washington Geological Survey. The generated reading copy is [Where You Are: Silverdale, Washington](/library#silverdale-wa). Two source notes for honesty. The Cascadia and Puget Sound probability and recurrence figures trace to USGS Fact Sheet 2025-3050, whose PDF at https://pubs.usgs.gov/fs/2025/3050/fs20253050.pdf returned HTTP 403 when this guide was written, so those numbers are quoted through the locale data file rather than from the fact sheet directly. The Seattle Fault scenario and the tsunami model outputs are Washington Geological Survey products, a state agency, restated here rather than copied. ### Companion guides in this collection - [Storing Water Safely](/library#storing-water-safely) - [Making Water Safe to Drink](/library#making-water-safe-to-drink) - [Where You Are: Silverdale, Washington](/library#silverdale-wa)
