Their seed comes out like the parent even when another variety is growing a few feet away. Others are pollinated by insects or by wind, which means a bee or a gust chose the other parent, and you find out next August. **Start here (self-pollinating, easy):** beans, peas, tomatoes, lettuce. Those four are on the University of Maine's self-pollinated list, and Minnesota names tomatoes, beans and peas as good choices, with "seeds that require little or no special treatment before storage." **Peppers: the sources disagree, so treat them as insect-pollinated.** Minnesota lists peppers among its beginner crops, but Maine's table puts pepper and eggplant in the insect-pollinated column, not the self-pollinated one. Follow Maine here, because the failure mode is specific and unpleasant: bees cross a sweet pepper with a hot one, and you discover the capsaicin next August in what you believed was a bell pepper. Grow only one pepper variety in any season you intend to save seed from. **Insect-pollinated (harder):** peppers, eggplant, squash, pumpkins, melons, cucumbers, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, carrots, radish. **Wind-pollinated (hardest):** corn, beets, Swiss chard. Four crops is not a limitation, it is a curriculum. Beans, peas, lettuce and tomatoes give you a protein crop, a cool-season crop, a salad crop, and the fruit almost everybody starts with. Learn on those. ## The traps, named **Hybrids.** Covered above. The most common disappointment there is. **Biennials.** Some crops we eat in their first year do not flower and make seed until their second. Carrots, beets, onions, parsnips, cabbage and their relatives are biennial, so saving their seed takes two growing seasons. In a cold climate it also means digging the roots in autumn and, as Maine Extension describes, storing them at or near freezing until spring so you can replant them. Minnesota simply notes that these "are harder to save since the plants need two growing seasons to set seed." None of this is impossible. It is a different and longer project, and it does not belong in your first year. **Squash and its relatives.** This is the trap that produces the famous inedible mystery squash. South Dakota State University Extension groups them by which will cross with which: - Group one, all of which cross with each other: zucchini, yellow crookneck, acorn, spaghetti, patty pan, delicata, pumpkins and gourds. - Group two, which cross with each other: butternut, buttercup, banana, Hubbard and turban squashes. - Group three, which cross with each other but not with squashes, pumpkins or cucumbers: muskmelon, cantaloupe, Charentais, honeydew, casaba, Armenian cucumber, snake melon. - Cucumbers, watermelon and loofah gourds cross only within their own kind, so they matter only if you grow two varieties of the same one. To keep a variety pure, SDSU says these need to be separated by "one-half to one mile," which no home garden has. Buildings, a thick stand of trees or a hill in between will shorten that, but the reliable home answers are simpler: grow only one variety from each group in a season, or hand-pollinate. To hand-pollinate, in early morning move pollen from a male flower to a female flower with a small paintbrush, do it within four hours of the female flower opening, and bag or tape the flower closed again afterward. **Corn.** Wind carries corn pollen a long way. Minnesota's example is the one to remember: "popcorn can pollinate a stand of sweet corn from a nearby garden on a windy day," which ruins both. Corn is not a beginner's seed-saving crop in a neighborhood. ## Choosing which plants to save from You are not only collecting seed, you are choosing the parents of next year's garden. So choose on purpose: - Save from plants that stayed healthy all season. Never save from a diseased plant; some diseases travel on the seed. - Save from plants that looked and tasted the way the variety is supposed to. If one bean plant matured three weeks before all the others, that is either a plant worth keeping or a stray from a different variety, and you have to decide which. - Save from several plants, not one. For the easy self-pollinating four, a handful is plenty. For anything cross-pollinated, SDSU suggests saving from 5 to 10 plants to keep a variety healthy, and 25 plants for a rare variety you are trying to preserve. - Let the seed crop stay on the plant far longer than the eating crop. Those plants are finished as food. They are seed factories now. ## Dry seeds: beans, peas, lettuce These are the simplest. The seed dries on the plant and you collect it. 1. Stop harvesting from a few chosen plants and let their pods stay on. Minnesota's finish line for beans and peas: leave the pods until "they are dry and start to turn brown, with the seeds rattling inside," which "may take as long as a month after you would normally harvest." 2. If a frost or a week of rain is coming, pull the whole plant and hang it somewhere dry and airy to finish. 3. Bring the pods indoors and dry them further before you open them. Minnesota says at least two weeks before shelling. 4. Shell the seed out. Maine describes the traditional way to do a large batch: put the dry pods in a sack and thresh them by crushing or treading, then winnow, which means pouring the mix from one bowl to another in front of a fan so the light chaff blows sideways and the heavy seed falls straight down. Lettuce works the same way but looks different. Let the plant bolt, which means send up a flower stalk, let the flowers turn into small dandelion-style puffs, and collect the puffs as they dry. Lettuce ripens over weeks rather than all at once, so plan on several passes. ## Wet seeds: tomatoes Tomato seeds arrive wrapped in a jelly that stops them sprouting inside the fruit, so they get a short deliberate ferment that removes it. It smells bad for a few days. That is normal. 1. Pick fully ripe, healthy fruit from a plant that stayed healthy. 2. Scoop the seeds and jelly into a jar and add water. 3. Leave it at room temperature and, in Minnesota's instruction, "stir or swirl the mixture twice a day. The mixture will ferment and the seeds should sink to the bottom within five days." 4. Pour off the floating pulp and the floating seeds. Maine's rule is that the "strong, viable seeds will sink to the bottom," so the floaters are the ones to discard. Rinse with clean water repeatedly until only clean seed is left. 5. Spread the seed in a single layer to dry. Maine notes that tomato seeds stick badly to paper towels and that coffee filters work better, and that you should shake them loose several times a day. Peppers need none of this. Minnesota: leave some fruit on the plant "until they become fully ripe and start to wrinkle," then remove the seeds and spread them out to dry. Wear gloves for hot peppers and keep your hands away from your eyes. ## Drying: the step people rush Wet seed rots or molds in the jar. This is the most common way a carefully saved harvest is lost after all the real work is finished. Colorado State University Extension is clearest on the target: "the drier the seeds, the longer they will store," and seed should be dried "to less than 8 percent moisture." Their method for finishing a batch is to dry seed at 100 degrees F for six hours. Do not use a microwave, and if you use an oven, keep it at its lowest setting with the door propped open so it never exceeds 100 F. Maine adds the ceiling that matters if you are drying in a warm room or a sunny window: the temperature must not exceed 96 F, and keep seed out of direct sun. For most home savers, a week or two spread on a plate or a screen in a dry, airy, shaded indoor spot does the job. A bean seed is dry enough when it shatters rather than dents under a hammer tap, and when you cannot mark it with a fingernail. ## Storing: cool, dry, dark, labeled Two things decide how long seed lives: how dry it is, and how cold it is. - **Container.** Colorado State says use "sealed cans or jars, rather than plastic bags," because those are genuinely moisture-proof. Minnesota says tightly sealed glass containers. A canning jar with a fresh lid is ideal and is probably already in the house. - **Temperature.** Minnesota says store between 32 and 41 F, which in practice means a refrigerator. Colorado says keep the temperature below 40 F, and a freezer also works for thoroughly dried seed. - **Humidity.** Colorado gives the numbers. At 15 percent relative humidity, seed settles at about 6 percent moisture and "will store safely in this condition for several years." At 90 percent humidity it reaches 19 percent moisture and "germination will be poor after one year." A rule of thumb used widely in the seed trade: the storage temperature in degrees Fahrenheit plus the relative humidity in percent should add up to less than 100. - **A drying agent, if your air is damp.** Minnesota suggests one to two tablespoons of silica gel, or powdered milk from a freshly opened package, wrapped in paper at the bottom of the jar. Powdered milk keeps absorbing moisture for about six months, then needs replacing. - **Label everything** with the crop, the variety, and the date you collected it. You will not remember. Nobody remembers. ## How long saved seed lasts Two extension services publish longevity tables, and they do not fully agree. That disagreement is itself worth knowing about. University of Maine, expected storage life in years: - **1 to 2 years:** onion, parsnip, sweet corn - **3 years:** bean, carrot, leek, pea - **4 years:** beet, pepper, pumpkin, tomato - **5 years:** Brussels sprouts, cabbage, cauliflower, cucumber, lettuce, melon, radish, squash, watermelon Colorado State's table gives lettuce 1 year and onion 1 year, with beans 3, peas 3, carrot 3, tomato 4, squash 4, and sweet corn 2. So Maine says lettuce keeps five years and Colorado says one. Both are real extension guidance. The gap is mostly about how well the seed was dried and how cold it was kept, which is exactly what you control. The honest way to use these tables: plan on the shorter number, and settle the question with a germination test rather than an argument. Minnesota takes the most conservative line of all and simply advises using saved seed within one year, because "the older the seed the lower the germination and vigor." ## The germination test: ten minutes, all doubt removed Do this in late winter, before you commit a season to seed that may be dead. Maine's method: 1. Count out 25 seeds of a large-seeded crop, or up to 100 of a small-seeded one. 2. Space them on a dampened paper towel, roll it up, and seal the roll in a plastic bag. 3. Leave it somewhere warm for 7 days. 4. Unroll it and count how many sprouted. Twenty out of 25 is 80 percent, which is fine; sow normally. Ten out of 25 is 40 percent, which is still usable if you sow twice as thickly. Two out of 25 means buy fresh seed, and be glad you found out in February instead of June. ## A note on seed-borne disease Some plant diseases ride on the outside of a seed into next year's garden. If you have had disease problems, Minnesota publishes two treatments: - A bleach soak: one part household bleach at 5.25 percent sodium hypochlorite to four parts water, with a drop of soap. Soak the seed for one minute, then rinse for 5 minutes. - A hot water treatment, for tomato seed only: warm at 100 F for 10 minutes, then hold at 122 F for 25 minutes, then rinse for 5 minutes. Both are precise for a reason. The hot water treatment needs a real thermometer, because a few degrees hotter kills the seed and a few degrees cooler accomplishes nothing. The bleach solution is for seed, never for skin and never for drinking. Mix it with ventilation, keep it away from children and pets, and never combine bleach with other cleaners. ## What can go wrong - **Everything came out wrong the following year.** Almost always the hybrid rule. Check the packet you saved from. If it says F1, that is the answer, and nothing you did in the harvesting or drying was at fault. - **The squash is a stranger.** Two varieties from the same crossing group flowered near each other. The fruit is usually still safe to eat and is occasionally good, but the variety is gone. Next year grow one variety per group, or hand-pollinate. - **Mold in the jar.** The seed was not dry enough, or the jar went into a warm humid cupboard. Discard moldy seed. Next time dry it longer, add a drying agent, and store it cold. - **Nothing germinated in the test.** Either the seed was harvested before it was mature, since green, soft, pale seed is not finished seed, or it was dried too hot. Both are common first-attempt mistakes. - **The lettuce fluff blew away.** It does. Cut the whole seed stalk into a paper bag and let it finish drying in there. - **You saved from the first plant to bolt.** For lettuce and the cabbage family, early bolting is the single trait you least want to breed for. Save from the last plants to bolt, not the first. ## How you know it worked - Your jar holds clean, hard, fully dry seed, labeled with crop, variety and date, sitting somewhere cold and dark. - A germination test in late winter comes back above roughly 70 percent. - Next season, the plants that come up look like the plants you saved them from. At that point something quiet and permanent has happened. You no longer depend on anyone's catalog to grow that crop again. The garden that fed you also reproduced itself, and it will keep doing that for as long as you keep choosing good parents. ## Sources University extension services (Minnesota, Maine, Colorado State, South Dakota State): - https://extension.umn.edu/planting-and-growing-guides/saving-vegetable-seeds - https://extension.umaine.edu/publications/2750e/ - https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/storing-vegetable-and-flower-seeds/ - https://extension.sdstate.edu/saving-seed-pumpkins-squash-cucumbers-melons-and-gourds

docs.title: Growing Food You Can Live On
headings: Growing Food You Can Live On
docs.text: # Growing Food You Can Live On A tomato is a wonderful first success and a nutritionally minor one. Here is the number that makes the point. Using USDA food composition data, a pound of raw tomatoes holds about 82 calories. A pound of potatoes holds about 350. A pound of dry beans holds about 1,550. You cannot live on tomatoes. That is not a criticism of the tomato, and Your First Tomato is still the right place to begin, because a first success teaches watering, light and patience faster than any reading does. But if the ambition is to feed yourself rather than to garnish a meal, the crops change, the arithmetic changes, and the honest numbers are worth seeing before you plan a garden around them. This guide covers the three crops that carry a beginner furthest: **potatoes** for calories, **dry beans** for protein and long storage, and **winter squash** for calories that keep for months without electricity. They are chosen because each one is forgiving, each one stores without a freezer, and together they are the classic backbone of a subsistence garden in most of the temperate world. One honest thing first, and it is a bigger one than usual: this guide tells you what a plot can produce, not what a person should eat. No three crops make a complete diet. Feeding yourself entirely from a garden is a serious nutritional project involving fats, vitamin B12, and much else, and it is a question for a dietitian, not for a garden guide. What follows is the scale, so you can see what a given piece of ground actually does. ## What the numbers actually say Every figure below comes from a university extension service or from USDA food composition data. The multiplication is ours and we show it, so you can check it or redo it with your own local figures. **Calorie density**, from USDA FoodData Central, per 100 grams raw. The conversion to pounds is ours, at 453.6 grams to the pound. - **Tomato**, red ripe, raw: 18 calories per 100 g, protein 0.9 g. Per pound, **about 82 calories**. - **Potato**, flesh and skin, raw: 77 calories per 100 g, protein 2.1 g. Per pound, **about 350 calories**. - **Winter squash**, butternut, raw: 45 calories per 100 g, protein 1.0 g. Per pound, **about 205 calories**. - **Dry beans**, black, mature seeds, raw: 341 calories per 100 g, protein 21.6 g. Per pound, **about 1,550 calories**. **Yield per 100 feet of row (extension figures):** - **Potatoes: 200 to 300 lb**, per Iowa State, whose figure is 20 to 30 lb per 10-foot row. - **Potatoes: 75 to 100 lb**, per Utah State. - **Dry beans: 20 to 25 lb**, per Utah State. - **Winter squash: 75 to 100 lb**, per Utah State. Look at the two potato figures. Two real extension services, both giving home-garden guidance, differ by a factor of three. That is not an error in either one. Iowa is deep prairie soil with a long humid summer; Utah is arid, high, and short-seasoned. Everything about garden yield depends on soil, water, season length, variety and how well the season goes, and a first-year garden on unimproved ground will land at the bottom of any published range or below it. So treat every yield figure you ever read, including these, as a planning estimate rather than a promise, and plan on the low number. **Putting them together (our arithmetic):** Calories from one 100-foot row, and how many days of one adult's food energy that is: - **Potatoes, Utah figure:** 26,000 to 35,000 calories, **13 to 18 days**. - **Potatoes, Iowa figure:** 70,000 to 105,000 calories, **35 to 53 days**. - **Dry beans:** 31,000 to 39,000 calories, **15 to 19 days**. - **Winter squash:** 15,000 to 20,000 calories, **8 to 10 days**. The days figures use 2,000 calories a day, which the FDA states is "used as a general guide for nutrition advice," while noting that your own needs "may be higher or lower and vary depending on your age, sex, height, weight, and physical activity level." A working adult doing physical labor needs more. Two cautions on those figures. The winter squash line is generous, because the yield figure is whole fruit and you do not eat the skin or the seed cavity, so the real number is lower. And the dry bean line understates what beans are for: their value is the 21.6 grams of protein in every 100 grams, which works out to roughly 4.3 to 5.4 pounds of protein from a 100-foot row, alongside a food that keeps for years in a jar. **How much ground is that?** Utah State spaces potato rows 30 to 36 inches apart and Iowa State says 2 to 3 feet, so a 100-foot potato row plus the walking space beside it occupies roughly 300 square feet. Bean rows at 18 to 24 inches occupy roughly 200 square feet per 100 feet of row. Winter squash is planted in mounds 4 feet apart, but the vines sprawl well past the row, so its real footprint is considerably larger than the row length suggests. Do not scale these figures up across a whole plot as though the whole plot were productive row; a real garden loses ground to paths, edges, shade and the corner where nothing grows. ## Potatoes: the calorie crop Potatoes produce more food energy per square foot than almost anything else a beginner can grow, they store for months without a freezer, and they are grown from pieces of potato rather than from seed. **Planting.** Utah State: plant 2 to 3 weeks before your last frost date, once soils are at least 50 F. Buy certified seed potatoes rather than using supermarket potatoes, which are often treated to suppress sprouting. Cut them so each piece weighs at least 2 ounces and has one or more eyes, the small dimples that sprout. You need 8 to 10 pounds of seed potatoes for every 100 feet of row. Seed potatoes are frequently treated with fungicide before sale, so plant them, do not eat them, and keep them away from the kitchen and out of reach of children. **Spacing.** Utah State: 4 to 6 inches deep, 10 to 12 inches apart in the row, rows 30 to 36 inches apart. Iowa State's version is a furrow 4 inches deep with pieces about 1 foot apart and rows 2 to 3 feet apart. Either works. **Growing.** Iowa State: at least six hours of direct sun each day, 1 inch of water per week through the season, and 1 to 2 pounds of all-purpose garden fertilizer such as 10-10-10 per 100 square feet. Keep cultivation shallow, 2 inches or less, because the tubers form near the surface and a deep hoe cuts them. Pull soil up around the stems as they grow, which is called hilling, so developing potatoes stay covered. **Harvest.** Iowa State: 90 to 120 days after planting for a full crop. You can steal a few new potatoes earlier once they are more than an inch and a half across, but use those within ten days; they have no skin to speak of and will not store. **Curing and storage.** Utah State: cure the tubers at 55 to 60 F with high humidity for 2 to 3 weeks after harvest, then store in the dark at 40 to 45 F through the winter. Iowa State's long-term figure is 40 F at 90 percent relative humidity, with a two-week cure at 50 to 60 F and 85 to 90 percent humidity first. Do not store potatoes with apples or other fruit, which give off a ripening gas that shortens their storage life. **The one real safety rule.** Potatoes exposed to light turn green and produce solanine, a natural toxin. Utah State: the chemical "tastes bitter after being cooked," and you should "discard very green tubers." Cut away small green patches generously; throw out badly greened potatoes. Store them in the dark, always. This is also why potato leaves and fruits are not food; the plant is in the nightshade family and only the tuber is edible. ## Dry beans: the protein crop A dry bean is the same plant as a green bean, left on the vine until the seed inside the pod is fully mature and hard. That one change turns a perishable vegetable into a food that stores for years at room temperature in a jar, and it is the single easiest protein a beginner can produce. **Planting.** Utah State: about 3 to 4 ounces of seed plants 100 feet of row. Sow 1 inch deep, 2 to 3 inches apart, in rows 18 to 24 inches apart. Beans need soil and air temperatures above 60 F; they rot in cold wet ground and they will not take a frost at either end of the season. **Timing matters more than for most crops.** Dry beans must stay on the plant to the very end of the season, so they need the whole season. Utah State's warning is worth taking seriously: dry beans planted after July 1 "generally will not mature in cooler areas of Utah but will produce mature seeds in the warmer regions of Southern Utah." Translate that to where you live by counting the frost-free days you get and comparing them to the days-to-maturity on the packet, with a few weeks of margin. If the margin is thin, choose the earliest variety you can find. Unlike snap beans, there is no picking through the summer. The whole crop comes in at once. **Harvest and drying.** Utah State: "Pull up the plants and lay in a row in the garden for 5 to 7 days. Once plants are dry, remove the pods, shell out the seeds and allow some additional time for the seeds to dry further." If rain is forecast during those days, move the plants under cover; a soaked, half-dried bean crop molds. **Storage.** Sealed containers in a cool dry place. Beans that are properly dry rattle hard and cannot be dented with a fingernail. **Dry beans must be fully cooked.** This is a real safety rule, not a matter of taste. Raw and undercooked dry beans contain a natural toxin called phytohaemagglutinin. The FDA's Bad Bug Book records that red kidney beans carry the most of it, and that as few as four or five improperly cooked red kidney beans can cause severe vomiting within a few hours, followed by diarrhea. Kansas State University Extension gives the procedure: soak the beans for at least five hours, drain and discard the soaking water, then boil in fresh water for at least 30 minutes. The toxin breaks down at boiling temperature in about 10 minutes, and the longer 30 minutes is the margin researchers advise. And the counterintuitive part: **do not cook dry beans in a slow cooker.** K-State's wording is blunt: "Don't use a slow cooker: it likely won't get hot enough." A slow cooker held below boiling can leave the toxin intact while making the beans soft enough to eat, which is how most poisonings happen. Boil first on the stove, then move them to the slow cooker if you want to. Canned beans from a store are already cooked and are not affected by any of this. **A bonus.** Dry beans are self-pollinating, which makes them one of the best crops to save your own seed from. See Saving Your Own Seeds. Once you grow an open-pollinated dry bean, you never need to buy that seed again. ## Winter squash: the storage crop Winter squash is not a variety of squash so much as a moment of harvest. It is left on the vine until the rind hardens into armor, and that armor is why it keeps for months in an unheated room with no processing at all. It costs you space, not effort. **Planting.** Utah State: plant 4 to 6 seeds in mounds 4 feet apart, 1 to 2 inches deep, once soils reach 65 F. After the seedlings have two leaves, thin to two plants per mound. **Harvest.** Utah State: squash are mature "when fruits are fully colored, when vines begin to die back, and when the rind is hard and impervious to scratching from a fingernail." Iowa State adds that mature squash have dull rather than glossy surfaces. Cut, do not pull, and leave about a 1-inch stem on each fruit; a squash that loses its stem rots at the scar. Bring them all in before a hard frost. **Curing.** Iowa State: cure winter squash, except acorn types, at 80 to 85 F and 80 to 85 percent relative humidity. Do not cure acorn squash. Curing hardens the skin and heals small scratches, and it is the difference between a squash that keeps and one that goes soft in November. **Storage.** Iowa State: a cool, dry, well-ventilated place at 50 to 55 F. Not the fridge, and not near apples or pears, which give off ripening gas that shortens storage. How long they keep depends entirely on type: Iowa State gives acorn about 5 to 8 weeks, butternut 2 to 3 months, and Hubbard 5 to 6 months. Utah State agrees on the pattern, noting that buttercup and banana squash store longer than butternut and acorn. If you want food in February, those storage numbers are the whole decision. Grow the long-keeping types. ## The honest counterweight Set the guides side by side. Your First Tomato is a container, six hours of sun, one plant, and a season that ends with something delicious that holds roughly 82 calories a pound. This guide is rows, a real plot, months of storage, and food that holds four to nineteen times as much energy per pound. Both are real gardening. The difference is that the first one teaches you to garden and the second one starts to feed you, and it would be dishonest to let the first stand in for the second. A garden that produces salad is a hobby with benefits. A garden that produces a winter's worth of potatoes, beans and squash is the beginning of not needing permission to eat. It is also, plainly, more work and more ground. A 100-foot row is not a balcony. If you have only a balcony, grow the tomato and the herbs, and use this guide as the map for the day you have soil, or as the reason to go looking for a community garden plot. ## What can go wrong - **The yield came in far under the published figures.** Expected, especially in year one. The published figures assume decent soil, adequate water and a full season. Improve the soil (see Your First Compost), water more consistently, and compare next year, which is the only comparison that means anything. - **Potatoes came out small and few.** Usually not enough water during the weeks when tubers are forming, or not enough sun, or the plants were crowded. Potatoes are thirsty; the 1 inch a week is not optional. - **Potatoes green in storage.** Light got in. Store them in the dark, in a box or a paper sack, and discard badly greened tubers. - **The dry beans never dried.** The season ended first. Either the variety needed more days than you have, or planting was too late. Next year plant at the earliest safe date with the earliest variety you can find. Beans caught by frost while still green are not wasted; shell and eat them fresh as shell beans. - **Beans molded on the drying plants.** Rain during the field-drying days. Move plants under cover next time. - **Winter squash went soft by November.** Either it was picked immature, or it lost its stem, or it was not cured, or it was stored too warm or next to fruit. Check those four in that order. - **Vines took over the garden.** They do. Winter squash is a land animal. Plant it at the edge where it can sprawl outward, or grow a bush variety, or plan for it next year. ## How you know it worked - You harvested a crop you had to find somewhere to store, rather than eat that week. - Potatoes are in the dark at around 40 F, dry beans are in sealed jars, and cured squash is on a shelf at around 50 F. - In February you cook a meal whose main ingredient you grew in July. That last one is the real threshold. Growing food in season is pleasant. Eating in winter from ground you tended in summer is a different capability, and it is the one that makes a household harder to squeeze. Next: Keeping What You Grew covers drying, freezing, root cellaring and canning, which is how the rest of the harvest joins these three in lasting. And Saving Your Own Seeds closes the loop, so next year's crop does not begin with a purchase. ## Sources University extension services (Iowa State, Utah State, Kansas State), USDA FoodData Central, and the US Food and Drug Administration: - https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/how-to/growing-potatoes-home-garden - https://extension.usu.edu/yardandgarden/research/potatoes-in-the-garden - https://extension.usu.edu/yardandgarden/research/beans-in-the-garden - https://extension.usu.edu/yardandgarden/research/summer-and-winter-squash-in-the-garden - https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/faq/what-proper-way-harvest-and-store-winter-squash - https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/how-to/storing-winter-storage-vegetables - https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/ (FoodData Central; entries used: potatoes flesh and skin raw 170026, beans black mature seeds raw 173734, squash winter butternut raw 169295, tomatoes red ripe raw year round average 170457) - https://www.fda.gov/food/nutrition-facts-label/how-understand-and-use-nutrition-facts-label - https://www.fda.gov/files/food/published/Bad-Bug-Book-2nd-Edition-(PDF).pdf (FDA Bad Bug Book, phytohaemagglutinin) - https://enewsletters.k-state.edu/youaskedit/2017/10/13/cooking-dry-beans-safely/

docs.title: Keeping What You Grew
headings: The one rule that everything else hangs on
Method 3: Root cellaring (the one that costs nothing)
Method 4: Water-bath canning, acid foods only
A complete tested procedure: crushed tomatoes
docs.text: # Keeping What You Grew A garden does not hand you food evenly. It hands you nothing for months and then, over about three weeks, more than you can eat. Preserving is what turns that spike into a supply, and it is the difference between a garden that decorates your summer and a garden that feeds your winter. There are four methods worth a beginner's time, and they are not interchangeable. Drying and freezing are easy and forgiving. Root cellaring is nearly free and requires only the right corner of a building. Canning is the one with real stakes. **Read this before anything else.** Home canning done wrong can kill people. The organism is *Clostridium botulinum*, and the poison it makes cannot be seen, smelled or tasted. The National Center for Home Food Preservation, which publishes the USDA's tested procedures, states it without cushioning: "Even a taste of food containing this toxin can be fatal." That risk is entirely manageable, because it is entirely understood. It is managed by following tested procedures exactly and by never improvising one. This guide gives you the safety architecture, one complete tested canning procedure, and clear boundaries around everything it does not teach. Where a method is outside its scope, it says so and points you to where the real instructions live, rather than teaching you half of it. ## The one rule that everything else hangs on Some foods are acidic enough that *C. botulinum* cannot grow in them. Everything else is not, and requires far more heat to make safe. NCHFP draws the line at **pH 4.6**. Acid foods have a pH of 4.6 or lower; low-acid foods are above it. - **Acid foods**, in NCHFP's list: "Fruits, pickles, sauerkraut, jams, jellies, marmalades, and fruit butters." - **Low-acid foods**, in NCHFP's list: "Red meats, seafood, poultry, milk, and all fresh vegetables except for most tomatoes." Read that second list again. **All fresh vegetables.** Green beans, corn, carrots, potatoes, peas, squash, beets, greens. Every one of them is low-acid. Now the heat. A boiling water canner reaches the temperature of boiling water, 212 F at sea level, and no higher; that is a physical ceiling, not a matter of boiling longer. A pressure canner reaches 240 to 250 F, operating at 10 to 15 pounds of pressure. NCHFP: "Botulinum spores are very hard to destroy at boiling-water temperatures; the higher the canner temperature, the more easily they are destroyed." Which produces the rule: > **Low-acid foods CANNOT be safely canned in a boiling water bath.** > **They require a pressure canner.** NCHFP: "Pressure canning is the only > recommended method for canning meat, poultry, seafood, and vegetables," > and "using boiling water canners for these foods poses a real risk of > botulism poisoning." Green beans, corn, carrots and meat in a water-bath canner are not a shortcut and not an old family tradition worth continuing. They are the classic route to botulism. A sealed jar is exactly the low-oxygen environment the organism wants: NCHFP lists its growth conditions as a moist low-acid food, a temperature between 40 and 120 F, and less than 2 percent oxygen. A sealed jar of green beans on a shelf is all three. **This guide does not teach pressure canning.** Pressure canning is safe, well documented, and genuinely worth learning, but it needs specific equipment, gauge testing, and a tested time and pressure for every single food, and it is not something to learn from a general article. Learn it from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning or from NCHFP directly, both linked in Sources, or from a class at your local extension office. Note also that NCHFP does not support using USDA canning processes in electric multicookers, even models with a "canning" button, because the processes were developed and tested for stovetop pressure canners. ## Method 1: Freezing (easiest, start here) Freezing keeps quality better than any other home method, and unlike canning it introduces no hazard of its own. What it does not do is kill anything. Freezing pauses spoilage; it does not sterilize. Food that was questionable going in is questionable coming out, and it starts spoiling again the moment it thaws, which is why frozen food is thawed in the refrigerator or under cold running water and not left out on the counter. **Temperature.** Colorado State University Extension: 0 degrees F or lower. A freezer compartment inside a refrigerator often runs warmer than that, which is why food stored there declines faster. **Blanching, and why it is not optional.** Vegetables carry enzymes that kept them growing, and those enzymes keep working in the freezer. CSU: after maturity, they "cause loss of quality, flavor, color, texture, and nutrients." Blanching, a brief scald, "slows or stops the enzyme action." Skip it and your green beans turn khaki and tasteless by January. CSU's method: 1. **Boiling water blanch:** at least 1 gallon of rapidly boiling water in a covered kettle. "Start counting time as soon as the vegetables are in the boiling water." 2. **Or steam blanch:** 1 to 2 inches of boiling water, vegetables held at least 3 inches above the bottom of the kettle. "Start counting steaming time as soon as the lid is on." 3. **Cool immediately.** Plunge the basket straight into a large quantity of cold water at 60 F or below, using about 1 pound of ice for each pound of vegetables. Cooling matters as much as the scald; vegetables left to cool slowly keep cooking. 4. **Drain, pack, freeze.** Times are per vegetable and per method, and they are short. CSU's examples: green beans 4 minutes in water; broccoli 4 minutes in water or 6 in steam; diced carrots 3 minutes in water. **Read that table's own footnote before you use those numbers.** It is a good lesson in where a published figure comes from. Colorado State notes that its "blanching times given are for 5,000 feet or higher. At altitudes below 5000 feet, subtract one minute from times given." Colorado is a high-altitude state and wrote its table for its own readers. Most of the world is below 5,000 feet, so for most readers those three examples are 3 minutes, 3 minutes (5 steaming), and 2 minutes. Get the full list from the CSU page in Sources, or from your own extension service, and check whose altitude a table was written for. Guessing a blanching time costs you quality rather than safety, but there is no reason to guess. **Packing.** CSU: leave 1/2 inch headspace at the top of rigid containers so the food can expand, and fill freezer bags to within 3 inches of the top. Press the air out of bags; air is what causes freezer burn. **How long.** CSU: "Most vegetables maintain high quality for 12 to 18 months at 0 degrees F or lower." That is a quality window, not a safety deadline. Food held continuously at 0 F stays safe indefinitely; it just stops being nice to eat. **The honest limitation.** Freezing depends on the power staying on. A freezer full of the year's harvest is a single point of failure, which is exactly why the other three methods in this guide exist. ## Method 2: Drying Drying removes the water that spoilage organisms need. It stores at room temperature, takes almost no space, and needs no power once the food is dry. **Temperature.** Penn State Extension: start at 145 F "when there is surface moisture on the fruit or vegetable," then "reduce the temperature to 135 to 140 F to finish drying." Starting hot while the surface is wet is safe because evaporation keeps the food itself cool; keeping it hot after that cooks the outside shut and traps moisture inside, a failure called case hardening, and food that is still damp in the middle will mold in the jar. **Equipment.** A food dehydrator is the straightforward answer. An oven works only if yours will genuinely hold a low temperature: Penn State says you need to set it to 140 to 150 F and prop the door open 2 to 3 inches. Many ovens will not go that low. **Sun drying is region-dependent.** It is a good example of why you should look up local guidance rather than trust any single article. Penn State says outright that "the high humidity in Pennsylvania makes this method impractical here." In a hot dry climate it is a traditional and effective method. The variable is your humidity, not your intent. **Knowing when it is done.** Penn State: fruit is done when it is "pliable and no beads of moisture form when pressed between your fingers." Vegetables are done when "tough, brittle, or crunchy." Test a piece after it has cooled, because warm food always feels softer. **Conditioning.** Pieces never dry evenly. Penn State: pack the cooled dried fruit loosely into an airtight glass or plastic container for several days so the remaining moisture spreads out evenly. Check daily. If you see condensation inside the jar, it is not dry enough; put it back in the dehydrator. **Insects.** Dried food from a home dryer can carry insect eggs. Penn State's treatment: heat in the oven at 160 F for 30 minutes, or freeze at 0 F or below for 48 hours, then store. **Storage.** Airtight, cool, dark. Cooler storage extends life substantially. ## Method 3: Root cellaring (the one that costs nothing) Some crops need no processing at all. They need the right corner. The insight worth carrying away is that there is no single set of "storage conditions"; there are three distinct climates, and putting a crop in the wrong one is why home storage usually fails. Iowa State University Extension's figures: - **Potatoes:** 40 F, 90 to 95 percent relative humidity, 5 to 8 months. - **Carrots:** 32 to 35 F, 98 to 100 percent humidity, 4 to 6 months. - **Beets:** 32 to 35 F, 95 percent humidity, 1 to 3 months. - **Onions:** 32 to 40 F, 65 to 70 percent humidity, 5 to 8 months. - **Winter squash:** 50 to 55 F, dry and well ventilated. Storage life by type: acorn 5 to 8 weeks, butternut 2 to 3 months, Hubbard 5 to 6 months. The three climates: - **Cold and very damp** for root crops. Carrots want humidity so high it is nearly condensing. Packed in damp sand or sawdust in a box is the traditional way to get there. - **Cold and dry** for onions and garlic. Same temperature as the roots, opposite humidity. They must not share a container with carrots. - **Cool and dry** for winter squash and pumpkins, notably warmer than the others. A refrigerator ruins winter squash. Two rules that apply throughout. Keep potatoes in the dark; light turns them green and bitter. And keep everything away from apples and pears, which give off a ripening gas that shortens storage life for potatoes and squash alike. Most homes have at least one of these climates somewhere: an unheated attached garage, a basement corner away from the furnace, an insulated crawl space, a spare room kept closed. Buy a cheap thermometer, put it where you are considering, and watch it for a week before you commit a harvest to it. ## Method 4: Water-bath canning, acid foods only Now the one with rules. Everything below applies **only** to acid foods: fruits, jams, jellies, pickles, sauerkraut, and tomatoes with acid added. Nothing else. Do not adapt it. ### Tomatoes and the acid problem Tomatoes sit right on the line, and they used to sit on the safe side of it. They no longer reliably do. As extension services now explain, newer varieties, over-mature fruit and tomatoes from frost-killed or dead vines can have a pH above 4.6, so tomatoes are no longer treated as acid foods, and the USDA requires acid to be added before processing. NCHFP's amounts, added directly to the jars before filling: - **Per pint jar:** 1 tablespoon bottled lemon juice, OR 1/4 teaspoon citric acid, OR 2 tablespoons of 5 percent vinegar. - **Per quart jar:** 2 tablespoons bottled lemon juice, OR 1/2 teaspoon citric acid, OR 4 tablespoons of 5 percent vinegar. NCHFP notes vinegar "may cause undesirable flavor changes." **It must be bottled lemon juice, not fresh.** This is not fussiness. Bottled lemon juice is standardized to a known acidity under FDA rules, while the acidity of a fresh lemon varies with variety, ripeness and growing conditions, and Iowa State Extension notes that fresh juice pH varies enough that you cannot rely on it for a safety margin. A lemon off your own tree is a lovely thing and it is not a measuring instrument. Never reduce the acid because the result tastes sharp. Add sugar if you must; the acid is not a seasoning. And note that acidification is required for tomatoes regardless of which canner you use. NCHFP is explicit that when a tomato procedure offers both a boiling water and a pressure option, every preparation step still applies, acidification included. Choosing the pressure canner does not excuse you from the lemon juice. **Use jars made for home canning.** NCHFP's procedures assume Mason-type canning jars with two-piece lids. Repurposed commercial food jars, mayonnaise jars and the like are not built for repeated heat cycling and break more often, sometimes during processing. ### A complete tested procedure: crushed tomatoes This is NCHFP's process, given in full so you can see what "tested procedure" means in practice. 1. Wash the tomatoes and dip them in boiling water for 30 to 60 seconds, or until the skins split. Dip in cold water, slip off the skins, and remove the cores. Trim any damaged areas and quarter them. 2. Heat about one-sixth of the pieces rapidly while crushing them to release juice. Add the rest, continuing to heat and stir until the whole pot is boiling, then keep it at a gentle boil for 5 minutes. 3. Add the bottled lemon juice or citric acid to each jar, in the amounts listed above. Optionally add 1 teaspoon of salt per quart. 4. Fill the jars immediately with the hot tomatoes, leaving 1/2 inch headspace. Wipe the rims, apply the lids. 5. Process in a boiling water canner for the time that matches your altitude: - 0 to 1,000 feet: pints 35 minutes, quarts 45 minutes. - 1,001 to 3,000 feet: pints 40 minutes, quarts 50 minutes. - 3,001 to 6,000 feet: pints 45 minutes, quarts 55 minutes. - Above 6,000 feet: pints 50 minutes, quarts 60 minutes. **Altitude is not optional.** Water boils cooler as you go up, so the same minutes deliver less heat. Look up your elevation once and write it inside your cupboard door. ### Running the canner NCHFP's boiling-water canner procedure: - Fill the canner about half full with clean warm water for a load of pints, and preheat the water to 140 F for raw-packed foods or 180 F for hot-packed foods. - Load the jars upright, using a jar lifter gripped below the neck. - Add boiling water until it stands at least 1 inch above the jar tops, or 2 inches above for any process longer than 30 minutes. Add more boiling water during processing if the level drops. - Start the timer only after the water is boiling, and time the full number of minutes. If the water stops boiling at any point, bring it back to a boil and start the timing over from the beginning. - When the time is up, turn off the heat and wait 5 minutes before removing jars, so the canner settles. - Set jars on a towel or a cooling rack with at least an inch between them, away from drafts and cold surfaces. - Leave them undisturbed for 12 to 24 hours. Do not tighten the ring bands and do not press the lid centers while they cool. - Remove the ring bands from sealed jars, label them, and store in a cool, dry, dark place. ### What not to do, ever - Do not water-bath any low-acid food. See the rule at the top. - Do not scale, halve, double or otherwise adjust a tested recipe. Processing times are tied to the exact contents and jar size tested. - Do not use a recipe without a tested source behind it. A recipe from social media, a blog, or a relative's notebook is not a tested process, however confident it sounds and however long it has been used without incident. Botulism is rare per jar, which is exactly why the anecdote "we always did it this way" is not evidence. - Do not can pureed or mashed vegetables. Pumpkin and winter squash are a standard example: NCHFP has a tested process for them cubed and pressure canned, and none for puree or butter, because in a dense puree there is no way to know the center of the jar reached temperature. No tested process means do not do it, not do it carefully. - Do not reuse the flat sealing lids. Rings are reusable; flats are not. ## When a jar goes wrong **Do not taste it.** NCHFP: "Do not taste food from a jar with an unsealed lid or food that shows signs of spoilage." Signs, in NCHFP's words: swelled lids and broken seals; "streaks of dried food originating at the top of the jar"; "rising air bubbles and unnatural color"; "cotton-like mold growth (white, blue, black, or green)"; unnatural odors; spurting liquid on opening. A jar can also be dangerous with no sign at all. That is the whole reason the procedures are strict. **Disposal, from NCHFP, and the first question is whether the jar is still sealed.** The two answers are different and it matters. *If the container is still sealed*, do not open it and do not heat it. Put it in a heavy garbage bag, close the bag, wrap it in duct tape and label it so nobody opens it, then put the bag in the regular trash or take it to a landfill. *If the container is unsealed, open or leaking*, it gets detoxified first. Wearing disposable rubber or heavy plastic gloves, place the containers and their lids on their sides in an 8-quart or larger stock pot or boiling-water canner. Add water carefully, avoiding splashing, until it is 1 inch above them. Put a lid on the pot, heat to boiling and boil 30 minutes. Then cool, and discard the containers, lids and food in the trash or at a landfill. Getting that branch the wrong way round is how somebody ends up boiling a sealed jar in an open pot, which is why it is the first question and not a footnote. **Cleanup.** NCHFP: use 1 part unscented liquid household chlorine bleach at 5 to 6 percent sodium hypochlorite to 5 parts clean water. Spray or wet the contaminated surfaces, let stand 30 minutes, repeat, then rinse thoroughly. Wash your hands afterward. Handle bleach in a ventilated space, keep it away from children and pets, and never mix it with other cleaners. **One more safety margin.** NCHFP: "Boiling food 10 minutes at elevations below 1,000 feet elevation should destroy this poison when it is present," and "for elevations at and above 1,000 feet, add 1 additional minute per 1,000 feet additional elevation." This is a sensible habit before serving home-canned low-acid food that was properly pressure canned. It is **not** a way to rescue food that was canned incorrectly, and it is not a reason to relax any rule above. Anything showing signs of spoilage gets the disposal procedure, not the stove. ## What can go wrong - **Jars did not seal.** Common causes: a chipped jar rim, food or acid left on the rim before the lid went on, a reused flat lid, headspace wrong, or the ring tightened too hard. An unsealed jar is not a disaster; refrigerate it and eat it within a few days, or freeze it. - **Liquid siphoned out during processing.** Usually the jars were cooled too fast or removed too soon. If the jar sealed, it is safe; it just looks poor. Wait the 5 minutes before removing jars next time. - **Frozen vegetables lost color and taste.** Blanching was skipped or cut short, or the freezer runs above 0 F. Check with a thermometer. - **Dried food molded in the jar.** It was not dry enough, or it was not conditioned. Redry the batch if you catch it early. Discard anything visibly moldy. - **Root-cellared carrots went limp.** Not humid enough. Pack in damp sand next time, or in perforated bags. - **Onions sprouted or rotted.** Too warm, or too humid because they were stored beside the roots. They need the cold dry corner. - **Potatoes turned green.** Light got in. Store them in the dark and discard badly greened tubers. ## How you know it worked - Every preserved item is labeled with what it is and the date. - Nothing you canned is a low-acid food in a water-bath jar. - Every canning recipe you used traces back to NCHFP, the USDA Complete Guide, or your extension service, without adjustments. - Your frozen food is at 0 F, your dried food shows no condensation inside the jar, and your stored roots, onions and squash are each in the climate the figures above say they want. - In February you open something you grew and it is good. ## The loop this closes Growing Food You Can Live On covers producing a real harvest. This guide is what stops that harvest turning into compost in September. Saving Your Own Seeds means next year's crop does not start with a purchase. Together they are a full year of food that runs on your labor and your ground rather than on anyone's permission, which is the entire point of the exercise. ## Sources The National Center for Home Food Preservation (which publishes the USDA's tested home canning procedures) and university extension services (Colorado State, Penn State, Iowa State): - https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/general-canning-information/ensuring-safe-canned-foods/ - https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/general-information/for-safetys-sake/ - https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/general-canning-information/using-boiling-water-canners/ - https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/how-do-i-can-tomatoes/tomato-acidification-directions/ - https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/how-do-i-can-tomatoes/crushed-tomatoes-with-no-added-liquid/ - https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/general-information/identifying-and-handling-spoiled-canned-food/ - https://nchfp.uga.edu/newsflash/canning-in-electric-multi-cookers - https://nchfp.uga.edu/resources/category/usda-guide (USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, 2015 revision, free to download) - https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/freezing-vegetables/ - https://extension.psu.edu/lets-preserve-drying-fruits-and-vegetables-dehydration - https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/how-to/storing-winter-storage-vegetables - https://blogs.extension.iastate.edu/answerline/2021/08/03/the-case-for-bottled-lemon-juice-in-canning/ - https://blogs.extension.iastate.edu/answerline/2021/10/05/preserve-pumpkin-and-squash-safely/

docs.text: # Why Canning Has Rules Take a jar of home-canned green beans off a shelf and look at it. The lid is domed down. The liquid is clear. It does not smell of anything, because it is sealed. Every single thing you can observe about that jar is consistent with it being perfectly good food. Every single thing you can observe about that jar is also consistent with it containing enough botulinum toxin to kill the person who eats it. That is the whole problem, and it is why canning is the one kitchen activity where a published procedure is not a suggestion. In most cooking, the feedback loop works: you taste, you adjust, you learn. Here the feedback loop is broken on purpose by the organism itself. You cannot taste your way to safety, and the one test everybody reaches for, opening the jar and having a careful sniff, is not a test at all. ## What this document does, and what it refuses to do This document explains **why** the rules exist and what each one is protecting against. It is the reasoning layer. Once you understand what the tested processes are actually doing, the parts that look excessive stop looking arbitrary, and, more usefully, you stop being able to guess which ones are safe to skip. The answer turns out to be none of them, but for a reason you can follow rather than on somebody's authority. **This document contains no canning process times, and you must not try to can anything from it.** It pairs no food with a time and a jar size anywhere, which is what a process actually is. It does contain some numbers with minutes and pressures in them, because you cannot explain why the rules exist without them: the range of temperatures a pressure canner reaches, the published boil that destroys the toxin at serving time, and USDA's own comparison of how long things take. Each of those is flagged where it appears. None of them tells you how to process a jar of anything. That distinction is deliberate. Process times are tied to one specific food, prepared one specific way, in one specific jar size, at one specific altitude, and a time lifted out of that context is worse than no time at all because it carries false confidence. The tested processes live in the **USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning**, which is a free public-domain download, and that is where you go when you want to actually do this. It is in the Sources section at the bottom. The practical companion inside this Library is [Keeping What You Grew](/library#keeping-what-you-grew), which walks through freezing, drying, root cellaring and water-bath canning, and which gives one complete tested procedure so you can see what "tested procedure" means in practice. This document is the theory behind the fence. Read both. Do neither instead of reading the USDA guide. One more honest boundary. Reading cannot make you a competent pressure canner. It can make you a person who understands why pressure canning exists, which is a genuinely different thing and is what this document is for. The mechanical skill, the gauge testing, the judgement about your own equipment, those come from the tested manual and ideally from somebody experienced standing next to you. ## The organism, and the four things it needs *Clostridium botulinum* is a bacterium that exists in two states. As a **spore** it is inert, tough, and effectively everywhere. FDA's Bad Bug Book describes the organism and its spores as "widely distributed in nature," found "in both cultivated and forest soils; bottom sediments of streams, lakes, and coastal waters; in the intestinal tracts of fish and mammals." The spores are on the carrot you just pulled up. They are on your hands, in your garden, in the dust. This is normal and it is not a hygiene failure. That last point deserves emphasis, because it is where people's intuition misfires hardest. Botulism is not a dirtiness problem. A spotless kitchen does not protect you, scrubbing the vegetables does not remove the spores, and no amount of care with [Handwashing and Personal Hygiene](/library#handwashing-and-hygiene) touches this hazard. Hygiene is genuinely important and it prevents a long list of other illnesses; it simply is not the control for this one. USDA's own passage here is worth reading in full rather than in the one line people usually pull from it, because the full version is more honest and still makes the point. Writing about "most bacteria, yeasts, and molds," USDA says they "are difficult to remove from food surfaces. Washing fresh food reduces their numbers only slightly. Peeling root crops, underground stem crops, and tomatoes reduces their numbers greatly. Blanching also helps, but the vital controls are the method of canning and making sure the recommended research-based process times, found in these guides, are used." So surface preparation is not useless, and peeling in particular does a lot. What USDA will not let you conclude is that any of it substitutes for the process. The phrase to hold onto is the last one: **the vital controls are the method of canning and the tested process times.** Cleanliness is worth doing and is not the control here. Spores are harmless to eat. You have eaten many. The danger begins only when a spore finds conditions that let it wake up into an actively growing cell, because the growing cell is what makes the toxin. USDA's Complete Guide states the conditions precisely. When conditions suit them, USDA says, the spores produce vegetative cells which multiply rapidly and "may produce a deadly toxin within 3 to 4 days of growth in an environment consisting of:" - "a moist, low-acid food" - "a temperature between 40 and 120 degrees F" - "less than 2 percent oxygen" Take those three lines seriously, because they are the master key to this entire subject. Everything else in this document is a consequence of them. Notice what USDA says next: "Botulinum spores are on most fresh food surfaces. Because they grow only in the absence of air, they are harmless on fresh foods." A fresh carrot on the counter has spores on it and is safe, because it is sitting in air. The spores are not the hazard. **The container is the hazard.** A sealed jar is an oxygen-free box, and if you put a moist low-acid food in it and store it at room temperature, you have deliberately built all three conditions at once and then put a lid on them. This is the thing that makes canning different from every other preservation method. Canning does not avoid the dangerous conditions. It creates them on purpose, because an airtight oxygen-free jar is exactly what keeps food edible for years. Then it relies entirely on having killed everything inside first. There is no second line of defence. That is why the process has to be right. ## The number that explains most of the rulebook: pH 4.6 Of the three conditions, acidity is the one you can control by choosing what to put in the jar, and it is the one the whole rulebook is organised around. USDA draws the line at **pH 4.6**, and draws it in both directions: - "Low-acid foods have pH values higher than 4.6. They include red meats, seafood, poultry, milk, and all fresh vegetables except for most tomatoes." - "Acid foods have a pH of 4.6 or lower. They include fruits, pickles, sauerkraut, jams, jellies, marmalades, and fruit butters." **What 4.6 means.** Below it, the food is acidic enough that *C. botulinum* cannot grow, so the jar cannot generate toxin no matter how long it sits. USDA: acid foods "contain enough acid to block their growth, or destroy them more rapidly when heated." Above it, the food will support growth, and the only thing standing between you and toxin is having killed every spore during processing. **What 4.6 does not mean.** It is not a flavour threshold and you cannot taste it. Plenty of things that taste sharp are above 4.6 and plenty of things that taste bland are below it. It is also not a property of a food category you can reason about from first principles; it is a measured number for a specific product, and mixtures behave in ways that surprise people. USDA is explicit that combining foods does not average out in your favour: "Most mixtures of low-acid and acid foods also have pH values above 4.6 unless their recipes include enough lemon juice, citric acid, or vinegar to make them acid foods." Adding a lot of tomatoes to a vegetable soup does not make the soup an acid food. A jar of mostly-fruit chutney with onion in it is not automatically safe. The tested recipe is what tells you where the mixture landed. Now read that low-acid list once more, slowly. **All fresh vegetables.** Green beans. Corn. Carrots. Potatoes. Peas. Beets. Asparagus. Greens. Squash. Every vegetable in your garden is a low-acid food, and so is every piece of meat, poultry and fish. The set of things that can go in a boiling-water canner is much smaller than most people assume, and it is almost entirely fruit, pickles and jam. **A note on measuring it yourself.** If you have a home water test kit from [Testing Water](/library#testing-water), you own pH strips, and it is natural to think you could just test the jar and settle the question. Do not do this. Household pH strips and inexpensive meters are made for a different job at a different precision, the reading you need is the *finished equilibrium* pH of the whole sealed product rather than the pH of the liquid you dipped into, and being slightly wrong here is not a slightly wrong answer, it is a lethal one. The reason the tested recipes specify measured amounts of a standardised acid is precisely so that nobody has to measure pH at home. Follow the recipe instead of testing. ## Tomatoes, the classic trap Tomatoes are where this goes wrong most often, because they sit almost exactly on the line and because everybody's grandmother canned them in a water bath without incident. USDA: "Although tomatoes usually are considered an acid food, some are now known to have pH values slightly above 4.6. Figs also have pH values slightly above 4.6. Therefore, if they are to be canned as acid foods, these products must be acidified to a pH of 4.6 or lower with lemon juice or citric acid. Properly acidified tomatoes and figs are acid foods and can be safely processed in a boiling-water canner." Read the structure of that carefully, because it is doing something specific. It does not say tomatoes are acid foods. It says tomatoes are acid foods **if you make them so**, and that the acidification is what moves them across the line into the category where a boiling-water bath is the correct tool. The acid is not an ingredient in the recipe sense. It is part of the safety process, in the same way the processing time is. A tomato recipe without added acid is not a variant, it is an incomplete process. **"Acidified" means the acid went in, in the measured amount, before processing.** Not stirred in afterwards, not approximated, not adjusted down because the result tasted too sharp. NCHFP's tomato acidification directions anticipate exactly that temptation and answer it: sugar may be added to balance the acidic taste if you want, but the acid is not to be left out. Sugar changes how it tastes without undoing the chemistry. Reducing the lemon juice undoes the chemistry. This is also the single most common place where a reader half-remembers a rule and applies it backwards, so here it is at the point of the mistake: **choosing a pressure canner does not excuse you from acidifying tomatoes.** The acidification and the heat process are two separate controls doing two separate jobs. NCHFP's acidification directions are explicit that the specified acid is added to ensure safe acidity for both pressure and boiling water bath processing, so the step belongs to the tomatoes, not to the choice of canner. The measured amounts per jar size are in those directions and in [Keeping What You Grew](/library#keeping-what-you-grew); they are deliberately not reproduced here. Why did this change? Because the reference point moved. The varieties in cultivation now are not the varieties the old family method was worked out on, and USDA's current position is the one quoted above: some are now known to sit above the line. Your grandmother was not being reckless with the tomatoes she had. She was working with a different input and, in all likelihood, getting lucky some of the time as well. There is more on picking tomatoes at a sensible stage in [Your First Tomato](/library#your-first-tomato), and on planning a harvest that does not force you into preserving a glut of over-ripe fruit in a panic in [The Growing Calendar Where You Live](/library#the-growing-calendar). There is a second, stranger number in this area, and it is worth knowing about specifically so that you do not get caught out by it. The federal regulation covering **commercially** canned foods, 21 CFR 113.3, defines low-acid foods as "any foods, other than alcoholic beverages, with a finished equilibrium pH greater than 4.6 and a water activity (aw) greater than 0.85," and then adds: "Tomatoes and tomato products having a finished equilibrium pH less than 4.7 are not classed as low-acid foods." So there is a real, published, federal **4.7** for tomatoes. If you meet it in isolation it looks like permission to relax. It is not. **That number is scoped to commercial processors** operating under a scheduled process, with laboratory pH measurement, process authority oversight and batch records, inside a regulation about hermetically sealed containers in a factory. It is a regulatory classification boundary that decides which rulebook a cannery falls under. It is not home-canning guidance, it does not appear in the home-canning guidance, and there is no version of your kitchen in which it applies to you. For home canning the number is 4.6 and the instruction is to acidify. If you ever see somebody online cite 4.7 to argue that tomatoes are fine unacidified, they have taken a factory regulation and pointed it at a kitchen. ## Why a boiling-water bath is not enough for low-acid food Here are two facts. They are about two different things at two different temperatures, and mixing them up is the mistake that puts people in intensive care. Read them as a pair and keep them apart. **Fact one: boiling water does not reliably destroy the spores.** USDA: "Botulinum spores are very hard to destroy at boiling-water temperatures; the higher the canner temperature, the more easily they are destroyed. Therefore, all low-acid foods should be sterilized at temperatures of 240 to 250 degrees F, attainable with pressure canners operated at 10 to 15 PSIG." A boiling-water canner cannot get there. Water boils at a fixed temperature for a given pressure, and open to the air that is a ceiling, not a target you can push past by boiling harder or longer. The jars sit at the temperature of boiling water and no higher, however vigorous the bubbling looks. **Fact two: boiling does destroy the toxin, once it has been made.** The toxin is a protein and it is far less heat-tolerant than the spore that produced it. CDC's instruction is to "Boil some foods for 10 minutes before eating them," and it carries the altitude correction in the same breath: "Add 1 minute for each additional 1,000 feet of elevation." NCHFP, which publishes USDA's tested procedures, gives the same figures and is explicit that the target is the toxin: 10 minutes of boiling below 1,000 feet should destroy it where it is present. Now the part that matters. These two facts are about **different targets**, and the gap between them is exactly where people hurt themselves. The spore is the seed and the toxin is the poison the sprouted seed makes. Boiling handles the poison. Boiling does not handle the seed. So a boiling-water bath applied to low-acid food leaves surviving spores in a sealed, oxygen-free, moist, low-acid jar held at room temperature, which is the complete list of conditions the organism needs, and then you put it on a shelf and wait months. USDA says toxin can appear within 3 to 4 days of growth. You have given it a year. If you want a sense of how far a water bath falls short, USDA quantifies it, and the numbers are startling: "At temperatures of 240 to 250 degrees F, the time needed to destroy bacteria in low-acid canned food ranges from 20 to 100 minutes... The time needed to safely process low-acid foods in a boiling-water canner ranges from 7 to 11 hours; the time needed to process acid foods in boiling water varies from 5 to 85 minutes." Sit with that. **Seven to eleven hours.** The gap between a water bath and a pressure canner for low-acid food is not a twenty percent safety margin that a careful person might shave. It is most of a working day of boiling, against a pressure process measured in tens of minutes. When somebody says they water-bathed their green beans and everyone was fine, they did not find a shortcut through that gap. They rolled dice that mostly come up blank, because most jars do not happen to contain a spore that germinates. Those ranges are given here to show the size of the gap, and for no other purpose. They are not process times. Do not use them as one. CDC compresses all of the above into one sentence, and it is the single line to remember out of this whole section: **"Pressure canning is the only recommended method for canning low-acid foods."** Not the preferred method, not the method for the cautious. The only one. This is also why the spores, not the bacteria, are what the process is aimed at. FDA's Bad Bug Book puts the durability plainly: "The spores are heat-resistant and can survive in foods that are incorrectly or minimally processed." A process that kills every living cell in the jar and leaves the spores has not made the food safe, it has only reset the clock. **And the 10-minute boil is not a rescue.** This is the second half of the trap, so here it is at the point of the mistake: the fact that boiling destroys the toxin does not mean you can water-bath low-acid food and then boil it before serving. The two bodies scope the pre-serving boil slightly differently, and you should follow the broader one. NCHFP aims it at low-acid and tomato foods that were not canned according to the tested recommendations, and is emphatic that it applies even when you can detect no signs of spoilage at all. CDC recommends it more generally, listing home-canned tomatoes, low-acid home-canned foods and fermented Alaska Native foods among the things to "Boil some foods for 10 minutes before eating them." Treating it as a standing habit for any home-canned low-acid food, however confident you are in the batch, is the safer reading and costs nothing. NCHFP also notes that CDC's own position since 2013 has been to discard any home-canned food that might contain the toxin, and is explicit that the boil is not a guarantee against every defect in a badly made jar. Both points cut the same way as the paragraph below. What it is not is permission. It is damage limitation for food that already exists and should not have been made, not a licence to make more of it. It depends on you boiling every portion thoroughly, every time, for the full time, with the altitude correction, and on nobody ever tasting the jar while cooking. A safety margin that a distracted person can skip in one second is not a process. Use it as the habit it is meant to be, and can the food correctly in the first place. ## Why you cannot judge a jar by looking This is the core of the guide, and it is the part people resist most, because refusing to trust your own senses feels like superstition. There are real published warning signs, and you should know them. USDA describes what to check: examine the lid for tightness and vacuum, because "lids with concave centers have good seals"; then, "while holding the jar upright at eye level, rotate the jar and examine its outside surface for streaks of dried food originating at the top of the jar. Look at the contents for rising air bubbles and unnatural color." Then, "while opening the jar, smell for unnatural odors and look for spurting liquid and cotton-like mold growth (white, blue, black, or green) on the top food surface and underside of lid." Learn those. A swollen lid, a broken seal, streaks down the outside, bubbles, odd colour, mould, a bad smell, liquid that spurts when the seal breaks. Any one of them means the jar is finished and you do not taste it to check. USDA: "Do not taste food from a jar with an unsealed lid or food that shows signs of spoilage." **And now the sentence this whole document is built around.** USDA, on low-acid foods: "Spoiled low-acid foods, including tomatoes, may exhibit different kinds of spoilage evidence or very little evidence. Therefore, all suspect containers of spoiled low-acid foods, including tomatoes, should be treated as having produced botulinum toxin and handled carefully." **Very little evidence.** The warning signs are useful in one direction only. Their presence tells you a jar is bad. **Their absence tells you nothing at all.** A jar can be sealed, clear, correctly coloured, pleasant-smelling and lethal, because botulinum toxin is not a spoilage product in the sense your nose understands. Your nose evolved to detect the bacteria that rot food and make it smell of rot. This organism is not one of those. It can grow in a jar and leave the contents looking like dinner. CDC puts the same fact in one line, and then closes the obvious loophole in the next: **"You cannot see, smell, or taste the toxin that causes botulism. But taking even a small taste of food containing the toxin can be deadly."** That second sentence is there because the natural response to "you cannot taste it" is to try a cautious little taste anyway. A cautious little taste is not a smaller version of the test. It is the exposure. This is why the inspection ritual, however carefully performed, is not a safety system. It is a filter that catches the obvious failures. The process is the safety system. The tested time and pressure are the only thing that ever protected you, and if the process was wrong, no amount of looking at the jar afterwards recovers the situation. That is the entire argument for following the published procedure exactly: it is the only control in the chain, and you get no feedback on whether it worked. It also explains the rule that frustrates people most, which is that "we have always done it this way and nobody ever got sick" carries no information. Botulism is rare per jar. A method with a small failure rate per jar produces a long run of uneventful years and then one event, and the uneventful years are not evidence the method works. They are what a small failure rate looks like from the inside. **If you do find a suspect jar, do not improvise the disposal either.** The toxin is dangerous by contact as well as by mouth, which most people do not expect. USDA: "Contact with botulinum toxin can be fatal whether it is ingested or enters through the skin. Take care to avoid contact with suspect foods or liquids. Wear rubber or heavy plastic gloves when handling suspect foods or cleaning up contaminated work surfaces and equipment." **The published procedure splits on whether the jar is still sealed, and the two branches are opposite. Do not mix them up.** USDA sends a suspect container that is "still sealed" into "a heavy garbage bag," closed and put in the trash or taken to a landfill. It is only a container that is "unsealed, open, or leaking" that gets the detoxification boil, laid on its side in a large pot and boiled for 30 minutes. Boiling a still-sealed jar is not the instruction, and treating it as one risks bursting a sealed jar of toxin-bearing food in an open pot, which is exactly the contact exposure the glove warning above exists to prevent. There is also a specified bleach solution for the surfaces afterwards. The whole procedure, both branches and the cleanup, is written out step by step in [Keeping What You Grew](/library#keeping-what-you-grew) and in the USDA guide; read it there rather than working from this summary. Do not pour a suspect jar down the sink and rinse it. ## Why altitude changes the numbers Water boils at a lower temperature as you go up, because there is less atmosphere pressing on it. The bubbles look identical. The thermometer does not agree. USDA: "Water boils at lower temperatures as altitude increases. Lower boiling temperatures are less effective for killing bacteria. Increasing the process time or canner pressure compensates for lower boiling temperatures. Therefore, when you use the guides, select the proper processing time or canner pressure for the altitude where you live." So the published times and pressures are not one number, they are a small table, and the row you need depends on where you are standing. Using the sea-level row in the mountains means your jars were held at a lower temperature than the process assumed, for the length of time the process assumed. You under-processed them, and, because of everything in the previous section, you have no way to tell from the outside. USDA names 1,000 feet as the point where this starts to matter: failing to adjust can "result in spoilage if you live at altitudes of 1,000 feet or more." Two practical consequences. First, the correction is not always a smooth dial. A dial-gauge canner can be set to an intermediate pressure, but a weighted-gauge canner only has fixed steps, so above 1,000 feet USDA has it jump to the next weight up rather than trim the pressure finely. The actual weights are in the process tables, paired with the food and jar size they belong to, and that pairing is the reason they are not reproduced here. Second, the altitude correction also applies to the pre-serving boil described earlier, at one extra minute per 1,000 feet. Look up your elevation once, from a mapping service or your local extension office, and write it somewhere permanent near where you can. It is a single number you will use every season, and it is the easiest of all these rules to get right. The same physics shows up elsewhere in this Library, which is a useful cross-check on whether you have understood it: [Making Water Safe to Drink](/library#making-water-safe-to-drink) carries CDC's instruction to boil water for 1 minute, and for 3 minutes above 6,500 feet, for exactly the same reason. If the altitude adjustment there makes sense to you, the one here is the same idea applied to a jar. **For Silverdale, Kitsap County, Washington**, the local case is comfortable: the town sits on Dyes Inlet at close to sea level, so the sea-level row is the right row for most of the settled area. That is a local fact and not a general one. It is also exactly the kind of fact that travels badly, because a person who learned to can at sea level and then moves inland and uphill carries a set of habits that are now quietly wrong.
