The habit to build is not "use the sea-level row," it is "look up the row for where I am." ## Which methods cannot produce this problem at all Canning is the risky one. It is worth being clear about why the others are not, because the reasoning is more useful than the list. Go back to USDA's three conditions: a moist low-acid food, a temperature between 40 and 120 degrees F, and less than 2 percent oxygen. All three must hold at once. **Remove any single one and the organism cannot grow, so no toxin can be produced, so the hazard does not exist.** Every safe preservation method below is a different way of removing one of them. **Freezing removes the temperature.** A freezer is far below the bottom of the growth range, so the spores simply sit there inert. Note what freezing does not do: it does not kill the spores, and USDA notes that accidental freezing of canned food "will not cause spoilage unless jars become unsealed and recontaminated." Freezing is a pause, not a sterilisation. When frozen food thaws it re-enters the growth range, which is why thawed food goes in the refrigerator and not back on the counter. Refrigeration works the same way with a much smaller margin. CDC's two everyday examples are worth knowing precisely, because both are the canning hazard rebuilt without a canner. For homemade flavoured oils: "Refrigerate homemade oils made with garlic or herbs. Throw the oils away after 4 days." Garlic is a low-acid food and a layer of oil is an air barrier, so a bottle of garlic in oil on a warm counter has assembled all three conditions on your kitchen shelf. The second is more specific than people remember, so note its exact scope. CDC's guidance here is about **potatoes that were baked in foil**, not about leftovers in general. Under the heading "For potatoes that were baked in foil," CDC says to either "Keep them at 140 degrees F or hotter until they're served" or "Refrigerate them at 40 degrees F or colder with the foil loosened so they get air." That last clause is not housekeeping advice, it is the whole mechanism: the foil is the anaerobic seal, and loosening it readmits the oxygen that keeps the organism dormant. A foil-wrapped baked potato left on a counter to cool is a moist, low-acid food wrapped away from air at room temperature, which is the same three conditions again in a form nobody thinks of as canning. **Drying removes the moisture.** The organism needs liquid water available to it, and the measure of that is water activity, written aw. The regulation defines it precisely; 21 CFR 113.3 calls it "a measure of the free moisture in a product and is the quotient of the water vapor pressure of the substance divided by the vapor pressure of pure water at the same temperature." FDA's technical guidance then gives the biological threshold: "The minimum aw level for the growth of *C. botulinum* is approximately 0.93. Depending on various product characteristics this minimum level can be as high as 0.96." Below that, it cannot grow whatever else you do to it. Two cautions on that number, because it is easy to misuse. **0.93 is a minimum for growth, not a home target**, and it is a laboratory measure of free water, not a percentage of moisture you can estimate by feel; there is no way to check it in a kitchen. There is a second published figure, 0.85, which comes from the commercial regulation quoted earlier and is the level at which a product falls outside the low-acid canned food rules entirely; that one is a regulatory boundary for factories, not a home drying instruction. What you should take from both is the mechanism, which is that properly dried food is safe from this particular organism because there is not enough available water in it, and that "properly dried" is defined by the tested drying guidance rather than by your judgement of when something feels crisp. Under-dried food that gets sealed in a container is the failure mode, and it usually announces itself as mould rather than as botulism. **Acid removes the low-acid condition**, which is the pH 4.6 line already covered. This is why jam, pickles and fruit are the easy cases. **Salt and sugar work mainly by taking the water away.** They dissolve into the water that is present and hold onto it, lowering water activity, which is why FDA notes that water activity "is usually controlled by the use of salt or sugar." That is the same mechanism as drying, reached by a different route. **Now a distinction that most writing on this gets wrong, including an earlier draft of this document: whether the salt is doing a safety job depends entirely on the method, and USDA splits it cleanly.** In ordinary canning, salt is seasoning and you may leave it out. USDA: "To can tomatoes, vegetables, meats, poultry, and seafood, use the procedures given in Guides 3 through 5, but omit the salt. In these products, salt seasons the food but is not necessary to ensure its safety." Fresh-pack pickles are the same: they "may be prepared safely with reduced or no salt," at some cost to quality, because there the vinegar is doing the safety work. In **fermented** products it is the opposite, and USDA says so in the very next breath: the salt in fermented sauerkraut and brined pickles "not only provides characteristic flavor but also is vital to safety and texture. In fermented foods, salt favors the growth of desirable bacteria while inhibiting the growth of others." Hence: "Caution: Do not attempt to make sauerkraut or fermented pickles by cutting back on the salt required." Note that this second case is not purely a water-activity effect. USDA describes it as selective inhibition, salt tilting the competition toward the organisms you want, which is a different mechanism from simply drying the food out. So the rule to carry is not "never reduce salt." It is: **reducing salt is a quality decision in canning and a safety decision in fermenting**, and you need to know which one you are doing. **Fermentation deserves its own paragraph, because it is safe for a reason that can fail.** A successful ferment is safe because the lactic acid bacteria you are cultivating drop the pH below the line. The acid is the safety, and the acid is a *product* of the process rather than an ingredient you added. That means the safety is contingent on the ferment actually working. A ferment that stalls, that was made with too little salt so the wrong organisms won, or that was diluted away from the tested proportions, is not a slightly worse ferment. It is a jar of low-acid vegetables in brine with no acid in it, which is a different and dangerous object wearing the same clothes. USDA states the requirement plainly: "There must be a minimum, uniform level of acid throughout the mixed product to prevent the growth of botulinum bacteria." USDA's matching caution is written for pickled products, where the acid arrives in a bottle: "Do not alter vinegar, food, or water proportions in a recipe or use a vinegar with unknown acidity. Use only recipes with tested proportions of ingredients." A sauerkraut ferment contains no vinegar, so read that as the general principle rather than the literal instruction: in a ferment the proportion you must not alter is the salt, which is what steers the acid-producing organisms, and the tested recipe is still the thing you follow rather than adjust. Note the phrase **minimum, uniform**. Uniform is doing work there. An average pH of 4.4 across a jar that has an un-acidified pocket in the middle is not a safe jar, which is also why tested procedures care so much about how food is packed, and why pureeing is restricted. Be precise about that restriction, because it is not a blanket ban. USDA permits pureed *fruit*, which is acid. What it forbids is the low-acid case: "Do not attempt to can pureed vegetables, red meats, or poultry meats, because proper processing times for pureed foods have not been determined for home use." Its alternative is to can those foods by the standard procedure and puree them at serving time instead. The reasoning is the same as everywhere else in this document: in a dense low-acid puree nobody can guarantee what happened in the centre of the jar, so no tested process exists, and no tested process means do not do it rather than do it carefully. **Now the general tool.** If you meet a preservation method this document did not list, you do not need somebody to rule on it. Ask which of the three conditions it removes, and ask whether it removes it reliably or only usually. - A method that keeps the food cold enough, dry enough, or acid enough, and does so dependably, is working on the mechanism. - A method that leaves a moist, low-acid food sealed away from air at room temperature is building the hazard, whatever it is called and however traditional it is. Oil is an air barrier. Wax is an air barrier. A tight lid is an air barrier. Vacuum sealing removes oxygen deliberately. - A method whose safety depends on something *happening* rather than something *being*, like fermentation, is only as safe as the thing that has to happen. That test will not give you a process time and it is not a substitute for a tested procedure. It will reliably tell you when something sounds wrong, which is most of the value. ## Honey and infants This is a separate mechanism from everything above and it needs its own section so that the two do not blur together. In ordinary foodborne botulism, which is what the rest of this document is about, the bacteria grow in the food and you swallow toxin that was already made. **Infant botulism is different: the infant swallows spores, and the spores grow inside the intestine and make the toxin there.** CDC describes it as infants getting "botulism when the spores get into their intestines, grow, and produce the toxin." The food does not have to be spoiled, contaminated in any visible way, or badly handled. It only has to contain spores, which honey sometimes does. The published threshold is an age, and it is 12 months. CDC: **"Do not feed honey to a child who is younger than 1 year old."** CDC's infant nutrition guidance states the reason and closes the obvious loopholes: "Honey given to children younger than 12 months may cause a severe food poisoning called botulism," and "Do not add honey to your baby's food, water, infant formula, or pacifier." NIH's MedlinePlus encyclopedia states the same rule with the same force and extends it in two ways worth carrying: it applies the under-one-year rule to corn syrup as well as honey, and it is explicit that even a small taste on a pacifier counts. (That page is licensed medical content rather than a federal work, so its facts are restated here rather than quoted. See Sources.) Three things that are commonly assumed and that I will not tell you, because the pages I opened do not support them. **Cooking or baking the honey is not addressed** on those pages as a way to make it safe, so do not treat heat as a solution. **Pasteurised honey is not distinguished from raw** on CDC's page; the guidance is written about honey, without that carve-out, so applying it to all honey is the reading the source supports. And while it is clear that this affects infants and not older children or adults, **the reason is not settled**, and CDC says so itself rather than leaving it to be inferred. Its sentence on infant botulism opens: "For reasons we do not understand, some infants get botulism when the spores get into their intestines, grow, and produce the toxin." That is a federal health agency stating plainly that the mechanism is not understood. Treat any confident explanation you meet elsewhere with that in mind, and take the rule regardless: the rule is well established even though the explanation behind it is not. Worth knowing: the age threshold is not the only route. CDC lists **adult intestinal toxemia**, which "can happen if the spores of the bacteria get into an adult's intestines, grow, and produce the toxin." It is rare. It is mentioned here only so that "infants get it from spores, adults cannot" is not filed away as a law of nature. ## What the outbreak record actually shows CDC publishes an annual National Botulism Surveillance Summary. Reading three consecutive years is more informative than any general claim about how dangerous canning is, and it corrects two opposite errors at once. Here is what CDC reported, quoted with its own framing: - **2021:** "health departments reported 273 cases of botulism to CDC. Of those, 243 cases were laboratory-confirmed and 30 were probable. The cases were of the following types: 181 (66%) infant, 66 (24%) wound, 22 (8%) foodborne, and 4 (1%) other." - **2020:** "health departments reported 226 cases of botulism to CDC. Of those, 202 cases were laboratory-confirmed and 24 were probable. The cases were of the following types: 159 (70%) infant, 55 (24%) wound, 9 (4%) foodborne, and 3 (1%) other." - **2019:** "health departments reported 215 cases of botulism to CDC. Among those cases, 201 were laboratory confirmed and 14 were probable." The types were "152 (71%) infant," "41 (19%) wound," "21 (10%) foodborne," and "1 (<1%) other." **The scope of those figures matters more than the figures.** These are cases reported to CDC by health departments in the United States, for one calendar year each, counting all routes of botulism and not only food. Each year's counts and percentages are given as shares of the **total reported** cases, confirmed and probable together, which is why the laboratory-confirmed subtotal is always smaller. If you see a foodborne figure quoted somewhere as 18 for 2021 rather than 22, or 19 for 2019 rather than 21, that is the laboratory-confirmed count rather than the reported count, and the two are easy to mix up because the same page carries both. Quote whichever you like, but say which one you are quoting. I checked the arithmetic in all three years and the counts reconcile: the four type counts sum to the reported total in each year (181 + 66 + 22 + 4 = 273; 159 + 55 + 9 + 3 = 226; 152 + 41 + 21 + 1 = 215), and the confirmed and probable counts sum to the same totals (243 + 30; 202 + 24; 201 + 14). The percentages behave differently between years, and it is worth saying so rather than waving at rounding. For 2021 and 2020 the four rounded percentages sum to 99 (66 + 24 + 8 + 1, and 70 + 24 + 4 + 1). For 2019 the three stated percentages already sum to 100 on their own (71 + 19 + 10), because the fourth category is given as "<1%" rather than as a rounded 1 percent. Both are ordinary rounding behaviour and neither is an error, but they are not the same pattern, and a single sentence claiming they always sum to 99 would have been wrong for one year in three. Across those three years, **52 foodborne cases were reported out of 714 botulism cases in total**, which is about 7 percent. Infant botulism is the large majority at 492 cases, about 69 percent. **Now the part that matters for this document: which foods.** Not speculation, the actual named items. In 2021, the foodborne outbreaks were traced to seal oil, fermented beluga whale, an unknown source, and **home-canned potatoes and sausages**. The single cases included **home-canned beans**, **home-canned meat**, **home-canned potatoes**, improperly stored clam chowder, and a commercially canned soup. In 2020, the named items were **home-canned asparagus**, **home-canned green chili peppers with onions**, **home-canned peaches**, an unspecified home-canned food, and an expired canned food. In 2019, they included **home-canned green beans**, **homemade pickled eggs**, **home-canned mushrooms and apples**, **home-canned salmon**, an unidentified home-canned food, an unidentified homemade food, and **fermented beluga flipper**. That year also had two commercial outbreaks, from commercially pre-packaged roasted potatoes and from commercially prepared preserved peppers. And it had one case that belongs to none of those categories: Maryland, June 2019, "Inadequately refrigerated macaroni & cheese and green beans from a fast-food restaurant." Look at that list against the pH rule. Potatoes, asparagus, green beans, mushrooms, peppers with onions, meat, sausages, salmon. **Low-acid foods, every one.** The outbreak record is not a random scatter across the whole of home preserving. It lands, year after year, mostly where the theory says it will: low-acid vegetables and meats in jars. Several items on those lists are not that, and they are worth keeping in view rather than trimming away, because each teaches something the tidy version would hide. **Peaches, pickled eggs, and mushrooms with apples** all sit at least partly on the acid side of the line, and all appear in the record anyway. Peaches are fruit; pickled eggs are pickled precisely to acidify them; the mushrooms were canned with apples. So being in the easy category, or intending to be, is not the same as being exempt. Acidity protects you only when the finished product really is below the line, uniformly, and the rest of the process was done properly. A jar whose acid was assumed rather than measured into it by a tested recipe is not an acid food just because its ingredients sound like one. **The 2019 macaroni and cheese, and the clam chowder in 2021**, were never canned at all. Both were low-acid foods held at the wrong temperature, one from a restaurant and one stored badly at home. They are a reminder that the three conditions do not care whether a jar was involved. Canning is the activity that most reliably assembles all three on purpose, which is why this document is about canning, but "I do not can" is not the same as "this cannot happen to my food." **Two conclusions, and they point in opposite directions. Hold both.** Botulism is genuinely rare. Foodborne cases reported nationally ran to 22, 9 and 21 in those three years, in a country of hundreds of millions and against a very large number of jars canned every autumn. That is a small number, and it is worth stating it as the actual figure rather than as a vague "dozens," because the vague version drifts upward every time it is repeated. You should not be frightened of a jar of jam, and you should not take from this document that home preserving is reckless. It is not. And the rarity is not reassurance about your method, because the cases that do occur are overwhelmingly home-preserved low-acid food. Rare events concentrated in one specific practice tell you that the practice is the risk factor. The correct reading is not "this almost never happens so I can relax," it is "this almost never happens, and when it does, it happens to people doing the exact thing the rules tell you not to do." ## Symptoms, and what to do If you ever need this section, you need it quickly, so it is short and specific. **When.** FDA's Bad Bug Book gives both a typical window and an outer range: "Onset: Adult: Usually 18 to 36 hours after ingesting food containing the toxin, although times have varied from 4 hours to 8 days." NIH's MedlinePlus encyclopedia gives a narrower typical window, of roughly 8 to 36 hours, which is consistent with the same picture; the numbers below follow FDA because it states the outer bound as well. Take the wider figure seriously, because it is the one that prevents a specific mistake. **Feeling fine the next morning is not the all-clear.** Onset has been recorded as late as 8 days, so a person who ate from a suspect jar three days ago and has no symptoms has not proved anything, and should still be told to watch for the pattern below. Equally, the typical window is long enough that the meal will not be an obvious suspect by the time symptoms start, and long enough that somebody may have eaten from the same jar more than once before the first one made them ill. If a jar is implicated, think about everyone who ate from it, not just the person who is currently unwell. **What.** CDC's list: "Difficulty swallowing, Muscle weakness, Double vision, Drooping eyelids, Blurry vision, Slurred speech, Difficulty breathing, Difficulty moving the eyes." With foodborne botulism CDC also lists "Vomiting, Nausea, Stomach pain, Diarrhea." **The pattern to recognise.** The distinctive thing is where it starts and how it spreads. It starts in the head, with the eyes, the eyelids, speech and swallowing, and moves downward into the body. FDA's Bad Bug Book describes the result as "flaccid paralysis of muscles, including those of the respiratory tract," and MedlinePlus describes the weakness as affecting both sides of the body equally. So: symmetrical, both sides together, starting with the face and eyes, descending. A person with double vision and drooping eyelids and slurred speech who is not drunk, not feverish and still mentally clear is the picture to hold in mind. That combination is unusual enough to be worth acting on. In an infant, the presentation is different and quieter, which is why it gets missed. CDC lists "Constipation, Poor feeding, Drooping eyelids, Pupils that are slow to react to light, Face showing less expression than usual, Weak cry that sounds different than usual." A floppy, poorly feeding baby with a weak cry is an emergency even though nothing about it looks dramatic. **What to do.** This is not a wait-and-see illness, and the reason is the treatment. The treatment is an antitoxin, and an antitoxin can only neutralise toxin that has not yet bound to the nerve endings. Every hour of delay is more toxin bound and more paralysis that the drug can no longer prevent. That is why the Bad Bug Book ties the outcome directly to the delay: "The mortality rate is high if treatment is not immediately administered. The disease is generally fatal in 5% to 10% of cases." MedlinePlus makes the same point in plainer terms, that prompt treatment greatly reduces the risk of death. Read those two sentences together rather than separately, and note what the source does not say. It gives one overall figure, 5 to 10 percent, without splitting it into treated and untreated cases, so do not read the 5 to 10 percent as "the odds if you get to hospital" or as "the odds if you stay home"; the page I took it from does not break it down that way. What it does say is that mortality is high specifically when treatment is not immediate, which is the half of the statement that should govern what you do in the next hour. And a non-fatal case is not a mild one: the Bad Bug Book notes that with antitoxin, other treatment "and the help of a breathing machine, the paralysis usually goes away within weeks or, in severe cases, months." So the instruction is the emergency one. MedlinePlus tells you to go to the emergency room or call 911, or your local emergency number, if you suspect botulism. CDC: "If you or your child has signs and symptoms of botulism, immediately see your doctor or go to the emergency room. Do not wait." Do not phone a friend who cans. Do not wait until morning to see whether it settles. Do not let the fact that the person can still walk about reassure you: descending paralysis means the limbs and the breathing muscles are what goes last, so someone still on their feet can already be well into it. Note that speech and swallowing are not a late sign but an early one, which is why slurring in a person who has not been drinking belongs on the list of things that get a phone call rather than a night's sleep. If you suspect it, call emergency services, say the word botulism, and say what was eaten and when. If the suspect jar still exists, keep it, sealed and out of reach of everyone including pets, since it may be needed to identify the toxin type. Do not clean it up and do not throw it away. ## The data layer behind this topic Inside the simulation, this hazard is backed by a record in `data/chemistry/toxins.csv` with the id **`botulinum_toxin`**. Reading it against the sources is a good illustration of what a data layer is and is not. The record classifies the toxin as biological, names its source as *Clostridium botulinum*, gives its antidote as heptavalent antitoxin serum, lists its effects as muscle paralysis, blurred vision, difficulty swallowing and respiratory failure, and describes it as the most toxic substance known, acting by blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. Two things to say plainly about that record, in the spirit of the rest of this document. The symptom list and the antitoxin match the federal sources well; CDC's symptom list and the heptavalent antitoxin are both real and consistent with what is written above. CDC describes botulinum toxin as "one of the most lethal toxins known," which is slightly more measured than the record's "most toxic substance known," and CDC's phrasing is the one to use in anything you write. The record's `onset_time_minutes` field holds 720, which is 12 hours. That is a single number where the published figure is a range, and it sits outside the part of the range that matters most. FDA gives the usual window as 18 to 36 hours, with recorded times from 4 hours to 8 days. Twelve hours is inside the outer range but below the usual one, so a simulation that fires symptoms at exactly 12 hours every time is modelling an early case as if it were the typical case, and it cannot represent the late-onset possibility at all. If you are reasoning about real food, use the published range and not the record's single value. The record's lethal-dose field holds 0.000001 mg per kg, which is 1 nanogram per kilogram of body weight. I could not find a federal page stating a dose in those units, so I cannot confirm the figure as written. What I can say is that the order of magnitude is not invented: the Bad Bug Book gives the infective dose as "An extremely small amount, a few nanograms, of the toxin can cause illness." Nanograms is the right scale. Whether the specific per-kilogram value is right, and what route of exposure it was derived for, I could not verify, so treat that field as a simulation parameter rather than as a sourced medical fact. ## Where the real instructions live Everything above is reasoning. None of it is a process. When you want to actually preserve food: **The USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning** is the authority for every tested process time, pressure, jar size and altitude adjustment. It is a US government work, it is free, and it is a download rather than a paywall. That single document is what all the trustworthy advice you will encounter is ultimately quoting. It is `usda-canning-guide` in this project's source registry, and the link is in Sources below. Alongside it, **the National Center for Home Food Preservation** hosts the guide and publishes current procedures and updates. Your **local extension office** is the other good route, and has the advantage of being able to test your pressure canner's dial gauge, which is a real annual maintenance task that nothing in a book can do for you. Inside this Library, [Keeping What You Grew](/library#keeping-what-you-grew) is the practical guide: four methods, their trade-offs, and one complete tested canning procedure written out so you can see the shape of one. Three rules to carry out of here, which between them prevent almost every way this goes wrong: 1. **Know whether the food is above or below pH 4.6**, and if it is above, it needs a pressure canner. All fresh vegetables and all meats are above. 2. **Use a tested process, unaltered**, including the altitude row, the jar size, the headspace, and the acid where acid is called for. Do not scale, halve, double or substitute. 3. **Never use your senses as the safety check.** They catch obvious failures and miss the one that matters. The rules are not there because somebody wanted the hobby to be bureaucratic. They are there because this organism produces no warning, the container you preserve in is the container it prefers, and the only moment you have any control over the outcome is the moment you are processing the jar. Get that moment right and home canning is a safe, ordinary, immensely useful skill that will feed you in February from a garden that stopped producing in September. ## Sources Every URL below was opened while writing this document. Federal works (USDA, FDA, CDC) are public domain under 17 USC 105 and their wording is quoted directly. Anything from a university or state body is restated rather than quoted, because those are not public domain. **Two sources need care and are flagged here rather than buried.** Facts are not copyrightable (Feist v. Rural Telephone, 1991); the expression is. So both of these are restated in our own words and neither is quoted anywhere in this document. The **MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia** article used below is hosted by the National Library of Medicine but is not a federal work: it carries the notice "(c) 1997- 2026 A.D.A.M., a business unit of Ebix, Inc. Any duplication or distribution of the information contained herein is strictly prohibited." MedlinePlus pages written by NLM itself are a different case from the A.D.A.M.-licensed encyclopedia articles under `/ency/article/`, and the distinction is easy to miss because both sit on the same domain. This project's source registry already records MedlinePlus as mixed licensing, restate-only, which is the correct handling. **NCHFP** is hosted by the University of Georgia and the registry records it as restate-only as well, so although it publishes USDA's tested procedures, its wording is paraphrased here rather than quoted. The underlying USDA guide is public domain and is quoted directly throughout. Where a federal page prints a degree symbol, it is rendered here as "degrees F" to keep the document plain ASCII. No other wording inside a quotation has been altered, except that hyphenation introduced by PDF line breaks has been closed up and extraction artefacts noted below. **USDA, Complete Guide to Home Canning, Guide 1: Principles of Home Canning (2015 revision)** https://nchfp.uga.edu/papers/guide/GUIDE01_HomeCan_rev0715.pdf The central source. Supplied: the pH 4.6 definitions and both food lists; the three growth conditions and the 3 to 4 day toxin timeline; the 240 to 250 degrees F sterilisation temperature at 10 to 15 PSIG; the 20 to 100 minute, 7 to 11 hour and 5 to 85 minute comparison; the tomato and fig acidification requirement; the altitude explanation and the 1,000 foot threshold; the weighted-gauge pressure step-up; the spoilage inspection sequence and the "very little evidence" warning; the contact-toxicity and glove warning; and the fermentation and pickling acidity and salt cautions. The PDF would not convert through the ordinary fetch path, so it was downloaded and its text extracted locally before reading. Note that the extraction drops "fi" and "fl" ligatures, so "acidified" appears as "acidied" in the raw text; quotations above restore them. **USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, landing page (registry id `usda-canning-guide`)** https://nchfp.uga.edu/resources/category/usda-guide The download point for the full guide, and the citation target readers should be sent to for process times. **NCHFP, For Safety's Sake** https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/general-information/for-safetys-sake/ Supplied, restated rather than quoted: the pre-serving boil of 10 minutes below 1,000 feet plus 1 minute per additional 1,000 feet; that it applies to low-acid and tomato foods not canned according to the USDA guide even where no sign of spoilage can be detected; that CDC's position since 2013 has been to discard any home-canned food that might contain the toxin; and that the boil is not offered as a guarantee against every defect in an underprocessed jar. **NCHFP, Tomato Acidification Directions** https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/how-do-i-can-tomatoes/tomato-acidification-directions/ Supplied, restated rather than quoted: that the specified acid is added to ensure safe acidity for both pressure and boiling water bath processing, so acidification is not waived by choosing a pressure canner; and that sugar may be added to balance the acidic taste but the acid must not be left out. The page also carries the per-jar amounts, which are deliberately not reproduced in this document. **NCHFP, Ensuring Safe Canned Foods** https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/general-canning-information/ensuring-safe-canned-foods/ Confirmed the three growth conditions and the 3 to 4 day figure independently of the PDF. **NCHFP, Identifying and Handling Spoiled Canned Food** https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/general-information/identifying-and-handling-spoiled-canned-food/ Opened and read. It carries the spoilage and disposal material but **not** the pre-serving 10-minute boil, which is why that claim is cited to For Safety's Sake above. **CDC, Botulism Prevention** https://www.cdc.gov/botulism/prevention/index.html Supplied "You cannot see, smell, or taste the toxin that causes botulism. But taking even a small taste of food containing the toxin can be deadly"; "Boil some foods for 10 minutes before eating them" with "Add 1 minute for each additional 1,000 feet of elevation"; the foil-baked potato guidance ("Keep them at 140 degrees F or hotter until they're served" or "Refrigerate them at 40 degrees F or colder with the foil loosened so they get air"); "Pressure canning is the only recommended method for canning low-acid foods"; the honey rule for children under 1 year; and the garlic and herb oil guidance including the 4-day limit. **CDC, Botulism Signs and Symptoms** https://www.cdc.gov/botulism/signs-symptoms/index.html The adult and infant symptom lists, and "immediately see your doctor or go to the emergency room. Do not wait." **CDC, About Botulism** https://www.cdc.gov/botulism/about/index.html The transmission categories including infant botulism and adult intestinal toxemia, "one of the most lethal toxins known," and CDC's own admission that "For reasons we do not understand, some infants get botulism when the spores get into their intestines, grow, and produce the toxin." This page carries no onset window at all, which is why the onset figures come from FDA's Bad Bug Book instead. **CDC, National Botulism Surveillance Summary, 2021** https://www.cdc.gov/botulism/php/national-botulism-surveillance/2021.html **2020:** https://www.cdc.gov/botulism/php/national-botulism-surveillance/2020.html **2019:** https://www.cdc.gov/botulism/php/national-botulism-surveillance/2019.html The three years of case counts, type breakdowns, and the named implicated foods. Arithmetic in all three was checked and reconciles. **CDC, Foods and Drinks to Avoid or Limit (Infant and Toddler Nutrition)** https://www.cdc.gov/infant-toddler-nutrition/foods-and-drinks/foods-and-drinks-to-avoid-or-limit.html "Honey given to children younger than 12 months may cause a severe food poisoning called botulism," and the instruction not to add honey to food, water, formula or a pacifier. **MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia, Botulism** (A.D.A.M. licensed content hosted by NIH/NLM, NOT public domain, restated not quoted) https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000598.htm Supplied, as restated facts: a typical onset window of roughly 8 to 36 hours; that the weakness affects both sides of the body equally; that the under-one-year rule covers corn syrup as well as honey and includes a taste on a pacifier; that you should go to the emergency room or call 911 or your local emergency number on suspicion; and that prompt treatment greatly reduces the risk of death. The onset figure quoted in the body of this document is FDA's rather than this page's, because FDA is a federal work and also states the outer range. **FDA, Water Activity (aw) in Foods, Inspection Technical Guide** https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/inspection-technical-guides/water-activity-aw-foods "The minimum aw level for the growth of C. botulinum is approximately 0.93. Depending on various product characteristics this minimum level can be as high as 0.96"; the 0.85 regulatory boundary; and that water activity is usually controlled with salt or sugar. **21 CFR 113.3, Definitions (GPO print edition)** https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2023-title21-vol2/pdf/CFR-2023-title21-vol2-sec113-3.pdf The verbatim definition of low-acid foods, including the pH 4.6 and aw 0.85 thresholds and the tomato exclusion at pH less than 4.7, and the definition of water activity. Downloaded and extracted locally. Read with its scope in mind: this regulation governs commercial thermal processing, not home canning. **FDA, Bad Bug Book, 2nd edition, Clostridium botulinum chapter** https://www.fda.gov/files/food/published/Bad-Bug-Book-2nd-Edition-(PDF).pdf The environmental distribution of the organism and its spores, the heat-resistance of spores in "incorrectly or minimally processed" foods, the toxin types that cause human illness, and "flaccid paralysis of muscles, including those of the respiratory tract." Also the onset figures ("Usually 18 to 36 hours after ingesting food containing the toxin, although times have varied from 4 hours to 8 days"), the mortality statement ("generally fatal in 5% to 10% of cases"), the recovery description involving a breathing machine and "weeks or, in severe cases, months," and the infective dose ("An extremely small amount, a few nanograms, of the toxin can cause illness"). Downloaded and extracted locally. **Simulation data:** `data/chemistry/toxins.csv`, record id `botulinum_toxin`, read from the repository. ### Sources I could not use - **USDA FSIS, Clostridium botulinum and Botulism** (https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/foodborne-illness-and-disease/illnesses-and-pathogens/botulism) returned HTTP 403 and would not load. It is not cited anywhere above and nothing has been paraphrased from it. - **eCFR** (ecfr.gov) redirected to an anti-automation gate on every attempt, so 21 CFR 113.3 is cited to the GPO print edition instead, which did load. - **USDA NIFA, Preventing Foodborne Illness: Clostridium botulinum** timed out twice and was never read. Not cited. - **A dedicated CDC infant botulism page** could not be located at a working URL; two candidates returned 404. The infant material above is therefore drawn only from CDC's About, Prevention and infant nutrition pages, and from MedlinePlus. ### What I could not source - **Why infants specifically are susceptible** to intestinal colonisation when older children and adults generally are not. This turned out not to be a gap in my reading: CDC states outright that the reason is not understood ("For reasons we do not understand"). The document now says that the cause is unsettled and attributes that to CDC, rather than hedging about what I personally could find. It is a genuinely open question, not a missing citation. - **Whether cooking or baking honey makes it safe for an infant**, and **whether pasteurised honey is treated differently from raw.** Neither distinction appears on the CDC pages I opened. The document declines to infer either way and applies the guidance as written. - **The lethal dose figure** in the `botulinum_toxin` record, as a per-kilogram value. FDA's Bad Bug Book confirms the scale ("a few nanograms") but states an infective dose in absolute terms, not per kilogram of body weight, and does not name a route of exposure for it. The document reports what is corroborated, says what is not, and flags the field as a simulation parameter. - **The exact boiling point of water at sea level (212 degrees F)** does not appear in the extracted text of USDA Guide 1. It is ordinary physics and is not controversial, but since it could not be quoted from a source opened this session, the document describes the ceiling qualitatively instead of asserting the number.

docs.title: Telling Spoiled From Safe
headings: The central idea: spoiled and dangerous are two different axes
What spoilage actually is: four processes, four signatures
What your senses genuinely tell you
Bacterial pathogens on food that looks fine
Scombroid, or why the fish that smells fine is the problem
What does and does not work as a rescue
How you know you have this
What in this document is a rule of thumb rather than a sourced fact
docs.text: # Telling Spoiled From Safe Take the container of Sunday's leftovers out of the refrigerator, lift the corner of the lid, and smell it. Everybody does this. It feels like a test. It feels like the moment where you find out. What you have actually done is measure one thing and then draw a conclusion about a different thing, and the gap between those two things is what this document is about. Your nose is a good instrument. It detects the waste products of organisms that are busy breaking your food down. It is nearly useless at detecting the organisms and poisons that will send you to a hospital, because those mostly do not produce a smell, and in several important cases the food they are in tastes perfectly normal right up until it hurts you. **This document will not give you a way to smell your way to safety, because there is not one.** What it will give you is the shape of the problem: what spoilage actually is, which of your senses are worth trusting and for exactly what, the specific hazards that give no sensory warning at all, what cooking can and cannot undo, and a decision procedure you can run in front of an open refrigerator in ten seconds. It will also be honest about the size of the other error. Throwing away good food is not free. FDA puts it at "Between 30 and 40 percent of food in the United States goes uneaten," which it describes as "as much as 20 pounds of food per person per month," adding up to "the equivalent of $165 billion in food each year." A guide that just says "when in doubt, throw it out" and stops has told you to solve one problem by making another one worse. The useful skill is knowing which doubts are the real ones. ## The central idea: spoiled and dangerous are two different axes Here is the sentence that reorganises everything else, and it comes straight from FDA: > "You may be surprised to learn that food can make you very sick even > when it doesn't look, smell, or taste spoiled. That's because foodborne > illnesses are caused by pathogenic bacteria, which are different from > the spoilage bacteria that make foods 'go bad.'" Read that twice. **They are different organisms.** The bacteria, yeasts and moulds that turn milk sour, make meat slimy and put fur on bread are in the business of eating your food. They are good at it, they produce smells and colours and textures while they work, and most of them have no particular interest in you. The organisms that cause foodborne illness are in a different line of work. They can multiply to an infectious dose while leaving the food looking, smelling and tasting exactly as it did when it was safe. Penn State Extension states the consumer half of this plainly in its material on spoilage signs: we cannot see, smell or taste pathogenic microorganisms, though we can see or smell some signs of spoilage. Those are two separate observations about two separate populations. So there are two independent questions about any piece of food: 1. **Is it spoiled?** Has it been chemically and microbially degraded to the point where it is unpleasant or inedible? Your senses are reasonably good at this. 2. **Is it dangerous?** Does it carry enough pathogenic organisms or preformed toxin to make you ill? Your senses are close to useless at this. The folk rule "trust your nose" quietly assumes these two questions are the same question. They are not, and the direction of the error matters: the rule fails safe in one direction and fails fatal in the other. If you throw out food because it smells bad, you have probably wasted something that would not have hurt you. If you eat food because it smells fine, you have learned nothing about whether it will. **Two things this argument does not say, and it is important not to hear them.** It does not say spoiled food is safe. Spoilage and contamination can and do occur in the same piece of food, and one is a hint about the conditions that produce the other. USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service makes this point directly about mould: "Foods that are moldy may also have invisible bacteria growing along with the mold." Visible spoilage is evidence that something has been growing in there under conditions favourable to growth, and that is not a reassuring thing to learn about something you were about to eat. It also does not say your senses are worthless. They are the cheapest instrument you own and they detect real conditions. It says they answer question one and not question two, and that you must stop using an answer to one as an answer to the other. ## What spoilage actually is: four processes, four signatures "Going off" is not one process. It is at least four, they have different causes, they produce different evidence, and they carry different amounts of risk. A reader who can tell them apart makes better decisions than one who lumps them together, because two of the four are almost purely quality problems and one of them is where the danger lives. ### 1. Microbial growth Bacteria, yeasts and moulds land on food and eat it. Breaking down its carbohydrates, proteins and fats releases the by-products you detect: sour, sulphurous, yeasty, ammoniac smells, gas, slime, visible colonies. **This is the process that overlaps with danger,** because pathogens are also microbes and grow under broadly similar conditions. It is also the process we have the most control over, because microbial growth has requirements, and if you remove one of them, growth stops or slows dramatically. Iowa State University Extension's summary of those requirements is the standard one: bacteria want warmth, moisture, a food source, near-neutral acidity, time, and (for most, though not all) the right oxygen conditions. Two of those thresholds are worth memorising because so many other rules hang off them: - **pH 4.6.** Above it, a food is "low-acid" and supports the growth of the organisms we worry about most. At or below, it is acid food. This is the line the whole discipline of home canning is built on, and it gets its own treatment in [Keeping What You Grew](/library#keeping-what-you-grew). - **Water activity about 0.85.** Iowa State cites FDA's use of water activity above 0.85 as the mark of a food able to support microbial growth. Water activity is not the same as wetness; it is how much of the water is chemically available. This is why honey, jam, dried beans and hard salami keep at room temperature: salt and sugar tie up the water. It is also why moulds beat bacteria in those foods, because moulds tolerate low water activity better. ### 2. Enzymatic change Food is made of tissue that was recently alive, and it is full of enzymes that were doing jobs. Those enzymes keep working after harvest or slaughter. Penn State Extension describes them as a natural component of food that, when active, change its colour, texture, flavour and nutritional content. This is the browning of a cut apple, the toughening of asparagus, the overripening of a pear on the counter. It is a chemical process running inside the food's own cells, not an infection, and it is why blanching exists: a brief scald denatures the enzymes before freezing so they are not still working slowly in the freezer for the next eight months. The blanching procedure itself belongs to [Keeping What You Grew](/library#keeping-what-you-grew). **Enzymatic change is a quality process.** Left long enough it produces conditions that invite microbes, but the browning itself is not the hazard. ### 3. Oxidation Fats react with oxygen and go rancid. The signature is unmistakable once you have learned it: the flat, stale, crayon-and-old-nuts smell of an opened bag of walnuts left in a warm cupboard, or cooking oil from the back of the shelf. Light, heat and air drive it, which is why oils belong in dark bottles in cool places and why nuts keep far longer in a freezer than a pantry. Rancidity is a real signal and worth acting on, but it is a signal about palatability and nutritional degradation rather than about infection. **I could not open an agency page stating whether eating rancid fat is harmful in the short term, so this guide does not make a claim either way.** Treat it as a strong reason not to eat something and not as evidence of a pathogen. ### 4. Physical change Freezer burn, bruising, wilting, crystallised honey, separated sauce. Nothing is growing and nothing is oxidising in the fat; the food has been physically damaged or dehydrated. FDA is unusually direct that this class is not a safety class: "Freezer burn does not mean food is unsafe. Freezer burn is a food-quality issue, not a food safety issue. It appears as grayish-brown leathery spots on frozen food." Penn State agrees, adding that you will not become ill from eating a food with freezer burn, though the product is less desirable. Physical damage does matter indirectly: a bruise is broken tissue with its juices exposed, which is an excellent place for microbes and moulds to start. That is precisely the mechanism behind patulin in apples, below. **The practical payoff of separating the four:** if you can name which process you are looking at, you can usually name whether you are making a quality decision or a safety decision. Grey leathery patches on frozen beef is a quality decision. Fuzz on the bread is a different decision. Sour cream that smells like acetone is a different decision again. ## What your senses genuinely tell you A guide that says your senses are useless deserves to be ignored, because they plainly are not. Be specific about where they work. **Your senses are reliable for these.** - **Visible mould is real information.** If you can see it, it is there, and there is more of it than you can see. FSIS: "you only see part of the mold on the surface of food," and "When a food shows heavy mold growth, 'root' threads have invaded it deeply." - **Slime on meat, fish or vegetables** is a bacterial film. It means a population has had time and conditions to build. - **Gas.** A bulging can, a jar with a domed lid, a vacuum pack that has inflated, a bottle of juice that fizzes when it should not. Something living has been producing gas inside a sealed container. Penn State's list of spoilage signs in preserved food is worth knowing by heart: unsealed, bulging or loose lids, rising air bubbles, leaking, foam, foul odour, unnatural colours, sliminess, dried food on the outside at the top of the jar, and cotton-like mould growth in white, blue, black or green. - **Rancidity.** Your nose is genuinely sensitive to oxidised fat. - **Obvious visual wrongness:** grey-green meat, pink or slimy patches on cooked chicken, a sauce that has separated and darkened. FDA's consumer guidance treats these as actionable: "Anything that looks or smells suspicious should be thrown out." **Your senses are unreliable, in a way you cannot train away, for these.** Each of the following can be present in food that looks, smells and tastes completely normal: - *Salmonella*, *Campylobacter*, *Listeria monocytogenes*, Shiga toxin-producing *E. coli* and the other bacterial pathogens. - Staphylococcal enterotoxin. - Botulinum toxin. CDC: "You cannot see, smell, or taste the toxin that causes botulism." - Aflatoxin and other mycotoxins, which are invisible at the concentrations that matter. - Histamine in fish. FDA's Bad Bug Book, on scombrotoxin: "The fish might not look or smell bad, but can cause illness," and, in the technical section, "Common sensory examination by the consumer cannot ensure the absence or presence of the toxin." - Shellfish biotoxins. In most cases the toxin has no effect on the shellfish itself, so the animal looks and behaves normally. **One more thing about the sniff test: it is not even free.** FSIS's instruction on mouldy food is "Don't sniff the moldy item. This can cause respiratory trouble." Deliberately inhaling from a colony of sporulating mould is a bad idea on its own terms, quite apart from what it fails to tell you about the food. ## The invisible things Five hazards, five different mechanisms. They are grouped here because they share the property that made this document necessary: **no sensory warning.** ### Bacterial pathogens on food that looks fine This is the ordinary case, the one behind most foodborne illness. The food was contaminated at some point, sat at a temperature where bacteria multiply, and reached a dose that makes you ill, all without changing appearance. **The Danger Zone.** CDC: "Bacteria can multiply rapidly if left at room temperature or in the 'Danger Zone' between 40 degrees F and 140 degrees F." FDA gives the rate: "at room temperature, the numbers of bacteria that cause foodborne sickness can double every 20 minutes." Sit with that doubling figure for a moment, because it explains why the time limits are so short. Doubling every 20 minutes is eight-fold per hour. It is exponential, so the last hour of a four-hour lapse does far more damage than the first. This is also why the number is a rate and not a promise: it is what fast-growing bacteria can do under favourable conditions, not a guarantee of what any particular organism in any particular food did. **The two-hour rule, with its scope.** FDA: "Never allow meat, poultry, seafood, eggs, or produce or other foods that require refrigeration to sit at room temperature for more than two hours, one hour if the air temperature is above 90 degrees F." CDC gives the same limits. Note what the rule is scoped to: **perishable foods that require refrigeration.** It is not a rule about bread, dry pasta, jam or an unopened tin. It also applies to leftovers, restaurant doggie bags and take-out, and FDA notes the same two hours applies to groceries in a car, which is usually hotter than a room. **Storage temperatures.** FDA: "Keep the refrigerator temperature at or below 40 degrees F (4 degrees C). The freezer temperature should be 0 degrees F (minus 18 degrees C)." Buy an appliance thermometer; they cost very little, and the dial on the door of a refrigerator is a setting, not a measurement. **Cold slows growth, it does not stop it, and one important pathogen ignores the rule.** FDA notes that *Listeria* can grow at refrigerated temperatures, which is why it singles out refrigerated ready-to-eat foods such as luncheon meats: the longer they sit, the more chance *Listeria* has to grow, "especially if the refrigerator temperature is above 40 degrees F." *Listeria* infection is rare, but CDC calls it "the fourth leading cause of death from foodborne illness in the United States," and it falls hardest on pregnant women, newborns, adults over 65 and people with weakened immune systems. If you are in one of those groups, the rules in this section are not conservative advice, they are the actual risk boundary. **How long leftovers keep.** The figure FSIS gives on its mould page is to use leftovers within 3 to 4 days, and it gives that number for a specific reason: "so mold doesn't have a chance to grow." That is the scope I can source, and it is a good working number. **The scale of the thing.** CDC: "CDC estimates that each year 48 million people get sick from a foodborne illness, 128,000 are hospitalized, and 3,000 die." Most of those illnesses are a bad day or two on food that looked fine. Some of them are not. ### Mycotoxins Now the part that people get wrong most often, because the folk rule here is not just unreliable, it is applied to exactly the foods where it is most dangerous. Moulds are fungi, and most of them are harmless nuisances. FSIS is careful about this: "some molds cause allergic reactions and respiratory problems. And a few molds, in the right conditions, produce 'mycotoxins,' poisonous substances that can make people sick." A few. In the right conditions. Mould on food is usually a quality problem, and FDA's consumer page says as much: "Mold is not a major health threat, but it can make food unappetizing." The trouble is that "usually" is doing real work in that sentence, you cannot tell which mould you have by looking, and the toxins are not confined to the fuzzy part you can see. **Why cutting the mould off is not a general rule.** A mould is not a stain on a surface. FSIS: "Molds have branches and roots that are like very thin threads. The roots may be difficult to see when the mold is growing on food and may be very deep in the food." And on where the poison sits: "In dangerous molds, poisonous substances are often contained in and around these threads. In some cases, toxins may have spread throughout the food." So whether you can cut it off depends entirely on whether the threads can get through the food, which depends on how dense and how wet it is. FSIS publishes this as a food-by-food table rather than a principle, and the table is the authority. **Here is the actual rule, with the actual depth.** **Cut it off, and here is how:** - **Hard cheese** (not cheese where mould is part of the process). FSIS: "Cut off at least 1 inch around and below the mold spot (keep the knife out of the mold itself so it will not cross-contaminate other parts of the cheese). After trimming off the mold, re-cover the cheese in fresh wrap." The reason given: "Mold generally cannot penetrate deep into the product." - **Firm fruits and vegetables**, and FSIS gives cabbage, bell peppers and carrots as its examples. Same instruction: cut off at least 1 inch around and below the spot, keeping the knife out of the mould. The reason: "It's difficult for mold to penetrate dense foods." - **Hard salami and dry-cured country hams**, where surface mould is normal for the product: scrub the mould off the surface. **Discard, no trimming:** - Luncheon meats, bacon, hot dogs. - Cooked leftover meat and poultry, cooked casseroles, cooked grain and pasta. - Soft cheeses such as cottage, cream cheese, Neufchatel and chevre, and **all** crumbled, shredded and sliced cheeses of any type, because the cutting instrument can have contaminated them. - Yogurt and sour cream. - Jams and jellies. FSIS's reason here is the sharpest sentence in the table: "The mold could be producing a mycotoxin. Microbiologists recommend against scooping out the mold and using the remaining condiment." - Soft fruits and vegetables, with cucumbers, peaches and tomatoes given as examples. - Bread and baked goods, because porous foods can be contaminated below the surface. - **Peanut butter, legumes and nuts.** The one-inch figure is a margin around a visible spot on a dense food, not a universal permission. Note also what FSIS says to do with the rest of the environment: clean the refrigerator or pantry where the food was stored, and check nearby items the mouldy food might have touched, because "Mold spreads quickly in fruits and vegetables." **A note on a second, stricter rule you will meet.** Penn State Extension's spoilage material says that because mould filaments grow down into food, scraping surface mould does not eliminate mould or the toxins it may have produced, and concludes: throw mouldy food away. That is written inside a section about canning and preserved food in jars, where discarding is unambiguously correct, and it is not in conflict with the FSIS table once you keep each one's scope attached to it. If you want a single rule to carry around, the FSIS table is the more specific instrument and it is the one this guide follows. If you are looking at a jar of anything home-preserved, both sources say the same thing: discard. **Aflatoxin.** This is the mycotoxin that earns its reputation. FSIS: "Aflatoxin is a cancer-causing poison produced by certain fungi in or on foods and feeds, especially in field corn and peanuts." FDA's Bad Bug Book is blunter: "AFB1 is the most potent known natural carcinogen and is the most abundant of the AFs," and the International Agency for Research on Cancer has classified AFB1 as a group 1 carcinogen. The US National Toxicology Program's Report on Carcinogens lists aflatoxins as "known to be human carcinogens based on sufficient evidence of carcinogenicity from studies in humans," a listing revised upward from "reasonably anticipated" in 1991. It is produced mainly by *Aspergillus flavus* and *A. parasiticus*, and the Bad Bug Book is specific about when: "In adverse weather or under poor storage conditions." **Storage is the half you control.** In the US the foods it is commonly found in are corn, sorghum, rice, cottonseed, peanuts, tree nuts, copra, cocoa beans, figs, ginger and nutmeg. Four properties make it different from a bacterial hazard. *It is chronic before it is acute.* At the doses a US consumer is realistically exposed to, aflatoxin is a cancer risk, not a poisoning. The Bad Bug Book records that no human aflatoxicosis outbreak has been reported in the United States, crediting strict regulation since 1971, FDA monitoring, and a diverse diet. Acute outbreaks are real but they happen where a single contaminated staple dominates the diet: 397 illnesses and 108 deaths in northwest India in 1974; and in rural Kenya in 2004 and 2005, 317 people ill and 125 dead, from home-grown maize averaging 354 ng/g, which is about eighteen times the US action level below. *It survives cooking.* WHO states that most mycotoxins are chemically stable and survive food processing. For aflatoxin specifically, the peer-reviewed review literature (Kutasi and colleagues, *International Journal of Molecular Sciences*, 2021) reports that aflatoxins remain stable above 100 degrees C and that significant decontamination was reported only at heating or roasting temperatures of 150 degrees C (302 degrees F) or higher. Boiling is 100 degrees C. **Cooking a mouldy peanut does not fix a mouldy peanut.** I did not find a federal page giving an aflatoxin-specific temperature threshold, so treat the 150 degrees C figure as the research literature's number and not as a US agency position. *It is wildly unevenly distributed, which is why sampling is hard and looking is useless.* The Bad Bug Book: "There have been reports of AF concentrations in excess of 1,000,000 ng/g for individual peanut kernels; 5,000,000 ng/g for cottonseed; and more than 4,000,000 ng/g in corn kernels," and sampling variability "is the largest in the total testing procedure." A single kernel can carry an enormous dose while the ones beside it carry none. There is no version of eyeballing a bag of nuts that samples it properly. *It is regulated, and the regulation is doing the work.* FDA's action levels are the limits "at or above which FDA will take legal action to remove products from the market." For aflatoxin they are **20 ppb for foods**, 20 ppb for peanuts and peanut products, and **0.5 ppb for aflatoxin M1 in milk**, the lower figure because, as the Bad Bug Book explains, milk makes up such a large part of the diet of infants and children. The published action level list states that it is current as of August 2000 and that it is the user's responsibility to keep up with changes, so check FDA's current guidance before quoting these as today's numbers. WHO's practical advice for consumers is the part you can act on: inspect whole grains and nuts for evidence of mould and discard any that look mouldy, discoloured or shrivelled, and avoid damaging grain before, during and after drying, since damaged grain is more prone to mould invasion. Note that this is advice about visible mould and damage, which is the only handle you have; it is not a claim that clean-looking nuts are guaranteed clean. *This guide's simulation data.* The toxin table carries a record `aflatoxin_b1` in `data/chemistry/toxins.csv`, describing aflatoxin B1 as the most potent natural carcinogen known, contaminating corn, peanuts and tree nuts in storage, with liver damage, jaundice and hepatocellular carcinoma as effects and no specific antidote. That matches the sources above. Its two numeric fields should not be read as human figures. The record carries a lethal dose of 0.5 mg per kg and an onset of 1,440 minutes, but FDA's Bad Bug Book says plainly that "The toxic level of AF in humans is largely unknown," gives its dose figures as animal LD50 values ranging from 0.3 mg/kg in rabbits to 18 mg/kg in rats, and lists onset for aflatoxin as "Not applicable," because the characteristic harm is a cancer risk accumulated over years rather than an event with a waiting time. **Patulin**, the other mycotoxin you are likely to meet, is the one that makes bruising matter. FDA's compliance programme for mycotoxins describes it as "a toxic substance produced by Penicillium, Aspergillus, and Byssochlamys molds that may grow on apples, and may be present if rotten, moldy or damaged apples are used to make apple juice," and states that "Patulin is not destroyed by heat processing, and can occur at high levels in apple juice, including pasteurized apple juice." FDA's action level is 50 micrograms per kilogram, that is 50 parts per billion, measured on single strength apple juice. WHO adds that patulin turns up in other mouldy fruits and grains as well, with apples and apple juice the major dietary source. The lesson for a home cider press or a bucket of windfalls is exact: **the rot goes into the juice and the pasteuriser does not take it out again.** Cut generously around damage on apples destined for juice, and do not press fruit that is actually rotting. ### Botulinum toxin, in one paragraph *Clostridium botulinum* grows without oxygen in low-acid food and produces a neurotoxin that causes flaccid paralysis, starting with the eyes and face and descending; when the diaphragm is involved, death is by asphyxia. The Bad Bug Book gives onset as 4 hours to 8 days, usually 18 to 36 hours, and notes that "Often, there's no visible sign that a food is contaminated, but sometimes a can is swollen." The spores are heat-resistant and survive incorrect processing; the toxin itself is not, and CDC's advice is to boil some foods for 10 minutes before eating them, adding 1 minute for each additional 1,000 feet of elevation. CDC also disposes of the idea that a cautious nibble is a test: "You cannot see, smell, or taste the toxin that causes botulism. But taking even a small taste of food containing the toxin can be deadly." Home-canned low-acid food is the classic source, and CDC also flags two everyday anaerobic traps: refrigerate homemade oils made with garlic or herbs and throw them out after 4 days, and keep foil-baked potatoes at 140 degrees F or hotter, or refrigerate them at 40 degrees F or colder with the foil loosened. **The full treatment, including the pH 4.6 rule, why low-acid food cannot be water-bath canned, and the disposal procedure for a suspect jar, is in [Keeping What You Grew](/library#keeping-what-you-grew), and that is where to read it before you can anything.** Do not use the ten-minute boil as a way to rescue food that was canned incorrectly. ### Scombroid, or why the fish that smells fine is the problem Scombroid poisoning is the clearest illustration in this whole document of the difference between an organism and the chemistry it leaves behind. Here is the mechanism, from FDA's Bad Bug Book. Certain fish carry a lot of the amino acid histidine in their flesh. Bacteria that normally inhabit the fish, and which the Bad Bug Book pointedly notes "do not sicken" it, make decarboxylase enzymes. If the fish is not chilled fast enough after it is caught, those enzymes convert histidine into histamine. Then you can cook the fish, can it, or freeze it. The bacteria die. **The histamine does not care.** FDA: "Cooking, canning, and freezing do not reduce the toxic effects." This is not spoilage bacteria making you ill. It is a stable small molecule sitting in the flesh, produced during an episode of poor refrigeration that may have happened on a boat weeks before you bought the fish. - **The fish involved:** tuna, mahi-mahi, bluefish, sardines, mackerel, amberjack, anchovies, and others. Histamine can also form in other foods, and FDA names cheese and sauerkraut. - **What it does:** tingling or burning in or around the mouth or throat, rash or hives, a drop in blood pressure, headache, dizziness, itching, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, asthma-like constriction of the airway, heart palpitations and respiratory distress. - **How fast:** onset is rapid, "ranging from minutes to a few hours after consumption." Symptoms commonly last several hours, occasionally several days. - **How serious:** the Bad Bug Book records that no deaths have been confirmed from scombrotoxin poisoning, but severe cardiac and respiratory reactions do occur rarely, and people taking certain medicines, the anti-tuberculosis drug isoniazid named specifically, are at increased risk. It is treated with antihistamines by a medical professional. **If you or somebody you are with reacts this way after eating fish, say what was eaten and when: it helps the diagnosis.** - **How common:** one of the most common forms of fish poisoning in the US, with 379 outbreaks involving 1,726 people reported to CDC between 1990 and 2007, and FDA believes the true number is far greater. - **The numbers FDA works to:** histamine at 50 ppm or greater indicates a fish in a state of decomposition; 500 ppm or greater is treated as a public health hazard. Those are regulatory guidelines for evaluating product, not something you can assess at home. Two consequences worth holding onto. First, **the toxin is unevenly distributed**, within a single fish and between cans in the same lot, so one person at the table can be ill and another fine from the same purchase. Second, since you cannot detect it and cooking will not remove it, the entire defence is upstream: buy fish from somewhere that keeps it properly cold, get it home cold, and keep it at 40 degrees F or lower until you cook it. Prevention is the whole of the treatment. ### Shellfish biotoxins, in one paragraph Filter-feeding shellfish concentrate toxins made by algae, and the important property is the same one that runs through this section: "In most cases, the toxin has no effect on the shellfish itself," so contaminated shellfish look and smell entirely normal, and FDA's consumer summary states that "These poisons aren't destroyed by cooking, freezing, or other food preparation." Paralytic shellfish poisoning is the lethal one, with onset generally within 30 minutes and death reported as soon as 3 to 4 hours after the meal. Because the hazard is in the water on a given day rather than in the animal's appearance, the control is a monitoring programme and a closure notice, not an inspection you perform yourself. **This is the local case here, and it is covered properly in [Reading the Tide](/library#reading-the-tide), which carries Washington's closure hotline and the rule that you check on the day you harvest, every time.** Read that before you take anything off a beach. [The Species Where You Live](/library#the-species-where-you-live) covers which authority answers which question. ## What does and does not work as a rescue The single most useful idea in food safety is this one: > **Killing an organism and destroying the toxin it already made are > different operations, and the second is much harder than the first.** Almost every "can I save this?" question resolves once you ask which of those two you need. Here is each common rescue, with what it does and what it does not touch. **Cooking.** Kills vegetative bacteria. CDC's safe internal temperatures are 145 degrees F for beef, veal, lamb, pork and fish, with a 3 minute rest for the meats, 160 degrees F for ground meats, and 165 degrees F for poultry; a thermometer is the only way to know you got there, since colour and texture do not tell you. What cooking does **not** do: - It does not destroy staphylococcal enterotoxin. FDA: "Destruction of viable cells by heat does not destroy the biological activity of preformed staphylococcal enterotoxins. These toxins are highly heat stable and can remain biologically active." The consumer summary is even plainer: *S. aureus* "can make toxins (enterotoxins) that might not be destroyed by cooking, although the bacterium itself can be destroyed by heat." Onset is 1 to 7 hours, and because *Staph* lives on the skin and in the nose and throat of half or more of healthy people, the classic vehicles are heavily handled foods left warm: egg, tuna, chicken, potato and macaroni salads, cream-filled pastries, sandwich fillings. - It does not destroy *Bacillus cereus* emetic toxin. That toxin, cereulide, is "pH-stable and heat- and protease-resistant" and remains stable "after heating at 121 degrees C for 30 minutes," which is about 250 degrees F, hotter and longer than any kitchen cooking. This is the reheated-rice case: emetic illness starts 0.5 to 6 hours after eating, and the vehicle is typically rice or another starchy food held warm. FDA's own summary of the lesson: "Cooking may kill the bacteria, but it might not disable the toxin that causes the vomiting type of illness." - It does not touch aflatoxin, patulin, histamine or shellfish biotoxin, for the reasons given above. - It does not make mushroom poisoning safe. FSIS, on the same page as the mould table: "Most mushrooms that cause human poisoning cannot be made safe by cooking, canning, freezing, or any other processing." See [Identifying Wild Plants](/library#identifying-wild-plants) for why the identification, not the preparation, is the entire safety step. **Reheating leftovers.** CDC gives 165 degrees F for leftovers. This kills organisms that grew during storage. It does not undo toxin produced while the food sat warm before it went into the refrigerator, which is exactly why the two-hour rule matters more than the reheating temperature. **A thorough reheat is not a reset button on a bad afternoon.** **Freezing.** FDA: "While freezing does not kill most bacteria, it does stop bacteria from growing," and "Though food will be safe indefinitely at 0 degrees F, quality will decrease the longer the food is in the freezer." Freezing is a pause, not a sterilisation. Whatever was in the food goes into the freezer with it and wakes up on thawing, which is why thawing happens in the refrigerator, in cold water or in the microwave rather than on the counter. For a thawed freezer after a power cut, FDA gives the one genuinely useful test, and prefaces it with the sentence this whole document has been arguing: "You can't rely on appearance or odor. If the food still contains ice crystals or is 40 degrees F or below, it is safe to refreeze or cook." For the refrigerator: food should be safe if the power was out no more than four hours with the door kept shut, and you discard perishables that have been above 40 degrees F for four hours or more. **Cutting away.** Works only for the specific foods in the FSIS table above, at 1 inch around and below, with the knife kept out of the mould. It does not work for soft, porous, high-moisture or pre-cut foods, because in those the threads and the toxins are already past the point you would be cutting to. **Skimming.** Taking the mould off the top of a jam, a sauce or a stock and using what is underneath is the single most common version of this mistake, and FSIS addresses jams and jellies by name: the mould could be producing a mycotoxin, and microbiologists recommend against scooping it out and using the rest. Skimming removes the evidence and leaves the question. **Re-canning or re-boiling a suspect jar.** No. A jar showing signs of spoilage gets the disposal procedure, not the stove, and that procedure is in [Keeping What You Grew](/library#keeping-what-you-grew). Reprocessing food that was canned by an untested method does not convert it into food that was canned by a tested one. **Washing.** Worth doing for produce, and it reduces surface contamination, but it does not sterilise and it will not reach anything that has got inside the tissue. Your hands are the more important surface, and that belongs to [Handwashing and Hygiene](/library#handwashing-and-hygiene). If the water itself is the uncertainty, see [Making Water Safe to Drink](/library#making-water-safe-to-drink) and [Testing Water](/library#testing-water). ## The decision procedure Run these in order. The order matters, because the first question is the one that actually carries the information and the one everybody asks last. **1. What is its history?** Where has this been, at what temperature, for how long? A container that went from the stove into a shallow dish into the refrigerator within two hours and has been at 40 degrees F or below for three days is in good standing regardless of what your nose reports. A dish that sat out overnight is not, no matter how good it smells. **If you cannot reconstruct the history, treat it as unknown, and unknown is not the same as fine.** **2. Is this a food class with a known invisible hazard?** Home-canned low-acid food. Fish in the scombroid group. Shellfish. Nuts, grain, peanut butter and dried figs. Rice or pasta held warm. Anything from a bulging or damaged can, a jar with a compromised seal, or an inflated vacuum pack. If yes, the class rule governs and your senses do not get a vote. **3. Now look and smell.** A positive result here is meaningful: mould, slime, gas, rancidity, wrong colour. A negative result here is not evidence of safety; it just means you have failed to detect the one category of problem your senses can detect. **4. If there is mould, which column is this food in?** Hard cheese and firm vegetables get 1 inch cut around and below. The discard list gets discarded. Then clean the spot where it was stored and check its neighbours. **5. Decide, and be honest about which decision you are making.** Is this a quality judgement (freezer burn, a limp carrot, a stale cracker) or a safety judgement? Quality judgements can be made with your own preferences. Safety judgements are made with the rules. **The standing rule: throw it out regardless of how it looks, if any of these is true.** - It is home-canned low-acid food that was not processed by a tested procedure, or the jar is bulging, leaking, spurting, mouldy or smells wrong. - It is a perishable food that has been above 40 degrees F for more than four hours, or out at room temperature for more than two hours, or more than one hour above 90 degrees F. - It is mouldy and on the discard list, particularly nuts, peanut butter, bread, soft cheese, jam, soft fruit or cooked leftovers. - It is fish you have reason to think was warm at any point in its history. - It is shellfish from an area you have not checked for closures on the day. - You cannot account for where it has been. **And one rule that changes the threshold rather than adding to the list.** When you are feeding somebody in a higher-risk group, that is a pregnant woman, a child under 5, an adult over 65, or anybody with a weakened immune system, every marginal call above resolves toward discarding. The same food is a different decision for a different eater, and this is the single most important adjustment in the whole document. CDC names those four groups as the ones more likely to get very sick from foodborne germs, and *Listeria*, which grows in your refrigerator, falls hardest on exactly them. **The cost calculus, plainly.** On one side: the food. A container of leftovers, a bag of nuts, a piece of fish. Call it a few dollars, and the waste is genuine, which is why the earlier steps exist at all. On the other side: an illness that at best costs you two days and at worst is one of the 128,000 hospitalisations or 3,000 deaths CDC counts each year, plus, for aflatoxin, a cancer risk that does not present a bill for decades. **The asymmetry is enormous and it is not close.** No plate of food is worth a hospital visit.
