The discipline is to make the earlier steps good enough that you rarely reach a genuine coin-flip, because then you are neither gambling nor throwing away food you did not need to. ## Dates and labels Most of what people believe about the dates printed on food is wrong, and in the United States the truth is startling once you see it stated. **Almost no date on a food package is a safety date, and almost none of them is required at all.** FDA: "Except for infant formula, manufacturers are not required by Federal law or regulation to place quality-based date labels on packaged food." It gets looser. FDA: "There are no uniform or universally accepted descriptions used on food labels for open dating (calendar dates) in the United States. As a result, there are a wide variety of phrases used for product dating." Sell By, Best By, Expires On and the rest are chosen by manufacturers at their own discretion, and FDA says the most common reason for applying one is to tell you and the retailer how long the food can be expected to keep its intended quality and flavour. FDA supports standardising on **"Best if Used By"** precisely because the phrase says what it means: "the date when a product will be at its best flavor and quality." It is not a safety date, and it is not a deadline. FDA's own instruction for food past it is to examine it: if the product has changed noticeably in colour, consistency or texture, you may want to avoid eating it. That is a quality inspection, and, as everything above this section has argued, a quality inspection is not a safety verification. The stakes of the confusion are real in the other direction too. FDA: "Confusion over date labeling accounts for an estimated 20 percent of consumer food waste." **The one exception, and it is the answer to "which label IS a safety date".** Infant formula. FDA: "The 'use by' date is required by FDA regulations on each container of infant formula." And what it means is specific: "The 'use by' date on infant formulas is a date, selected by the manufacturer based on tests and other information, to inform retailers and consumers about the quality of the infant formula. Until that declared date, the infant formula will contain no less than the amount of each nutrient declared on the product label and will otherwise be of acceptable quality." Be precise about what that does and does not say, because it is easy to over-read. It is the only federally required date on food. It is a guarantee that runs **until** the date: up to it, the formula holds the nutrient levels on the label. Past it, the guarantee is gone, and for an infant who is getting all of their nutrition from that tin, a shortfall in declared nutrients is itself the harm. So it functions as a date you obey, but its basis is nutrient content and quality rather than contamination. **Use infant formula by the date on the tin.** Two practical consequences for everything else. First, **a date is a manufacturer's estimate of quality under proper storage, and it knows nothing about your storage.** Milk that spent an afternoon in a warm car is not made safe by the date on the carton, and an unopened jar of something shelf-stable is not made dangerous by passing it. History beats the printed date in both directions. Second, if you want actual storage times, they exist and they are specific to the food. FDA points to the FoodKeeper, developed with USDA, Cornell University and the Food Marketing Institute, and to the Refrigerator and Freezer Storage Chart. Those are tables, not principles, and looking one up takes less time than arguing with yourself over a carton. ## Where this is local In Silverdale, on Dyes Inlet in Kitsap County, at about 47.65 degrees north, two parts of this document stop being general and become specific. **Shellfish.** You can gather them here, which means the biotoxin paragraph above is not an abstraction but a thing to check before you walk down to the water. Cooking and freezing do not touch paralytic shellfish poison, the animal gives you no sign, and the only control is the state health department's marine biotoxin programme and its closure information. [Reading the Tide](/library#reading-the-tide) carries the hotline number and the procedure, and the standing instruction there is the right one: check on the day you harvest, every time, not once a season. **Damp.** This is a cool marine climate with a long wet season, and mould grows on warmth and humidity. FSIS's advice to keep household humidity below 40 percent is written for the general case and is a demanding target in a Puget Sound winter, but the direction is right: storage areas that stay damp will grow mould on food faster than a dry pantry will, and the pantry, not the refrigerator, is where nuts, grain and flour sit. Keeping the house dry is its own subject, in [Ventilation, Damp and Mould](/library#ventilation-damp-and-mould). Note that the household mould problem and the food mould problem are related by mechanism but are not the same decision: a damp wall is a building problem, a furred loaf is a food one. For anything grown or preserved here, the storage conditions by crop, the four preservation methods and the canning rules are in [Keeping What You Grew](/library#keeping-what-you-grew). ## How you know you have this - You can say which of the four processes you are looking at when something has gone wrong, and therefore whether you are making a quality or a safety decision. - You reach for the history of a food before you reach for your nose. - You know the two-hour rule, the 40 and 140 degrees F boundaries, and what they are scoped to. - You know that cutting mould off is a rule for hard cheese and firm vegetables at 1 inch, and not a rule for bread, jam, nuts or soft fruit. - You no longer believe that cooking fixes things, and you can name three toxins it does not touch. - You have an appliance thermometer in the refrigerator and you have actually looked at it. - Nothing in your house is being evaluated primarily by the date printed on it. - You waste less food than you did, because you stopped throwing out perfectly good things on the strength of a date, and you stopped gambling on things whose history you could not account for. ## What in this document is a rule of thumb rather than a sourced fact Kept separate on purpose, so you can tell which is which. - **The four-process division** (microbial, enzymatic, oxidative, physical) is this guide's organising scheme. Each process is described by the sources cited, but the framing of them as four distinct signatures to be told apart is ours. - **The five-step decision procedure and its ordering** is ours. Every individual rule inside it is sourced; putting history first and the sniff test third is a judgement about what carries information. - **"Unknown history means treat as unsafe"** is a rule of thumb. No agency page opened for this guide states it in those words; it follows from the time-and-temperature rules, which do nothing for you if you cannot reconstruct the time or the temperature. - **The claim that most obviously spoiled food would not have badly hurt you** is the weakest claim in this document and it is stated carefully above. What is sourced is the mechanism: spoilage organisms and pathogens are different populations, and FDA says mould is not a major health threat but makes food unappetising. What I could not source is any quantitative statement about what fraction of visibly spoiled food is harmless, so this guide does not make one, and it does not tell you to eat anything on that basis. - **Whether rancid fat is harmful to eat** is not answered here, because I could not open a source that answers it. - **The 150 degrees C aflatoxin figure** is from the peer-reviewed review literature, not from a US agency, and is labelled as such where it appears. - **Household humidity in a marine climate.** FSIS's below-40-percent figure is sourced; the observation that this is hard to achieve in a Puget Sound winter is ours. ## Sources Every URL below was opened while writing this document. Patulin produced by *Penicillium*, *Aspergillus* and *Byssochlamys* on apples, present if rotten, mouldy or damaged apples are used, "not destroyed by heat processing", occurring at high levels even in pasteurised apple juice. **Centers for Disease Control and Prevention** - https://www.cdc.gov/food-safety/about/index.html The annual US estimates: 48 million illnesses, 128,000 hospitalisations, 3,000 deaths; the higher-risk groups. - https://www.cdc.gov/food-safety/prevention/index.html The Danger Zone defined as 40 to 140 degrees F; the two-hour and one-hour rules; safe internal cooking temperatures of 145, 160 and 165 degrees F and 165 degrees F for leftovers; safe thawing methods; that colour and texture do not tell you whether food is safely cooked. - https://www.cdc.gov/botulism/prevention/index.html "You cannot see, smell, or taste the toxin that causes botulism"; boil for 10 minutes plus 1 minute per additional 1,000 feet of elevation; garlic and herb oils refrigerated and discarded after 4 days; foil-baked potatoes held at 140 degrees F or refrigerated at 40 degrees F with the foil loosened. - https://www.cdc.gov/botulism/about/index.html Botulinum toxin attacks the nerves and causes paralysis and death; improperly canned, preserved or fermented home foods as the main vehicle. - https://www.cdc.gov/listeria/about/index.html *Listeria* infection is rare but serious, the fourth leading cause of death from foodborne illness in the US, and the higher-risk groups. **National Institutes of Health** - https://ntp.niehs.nih.gov/sites/default/files/ntp/roc/content/profiles/aflatoxins.pdf National Toxicology Program, Report on Carcinogens, fifteenth edition: aflatoxins listed as "known to be human carcinogens based on sufficient evidence of carcinogenicity from studies in humans", first listed in 1980 and revised to "known" in 1991. **USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service** - https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/molds-food-are-they-dangerous The whole mould section: root threads invading deeply, toxins in and around the threads and sometimes throughout the food, invisible bacteria alongside mould, what mycotoxins are, aflatoxin as a cancer-causing poison especially in field corn and peanuts, the complete discard and cut-off table with the 1 inch depth and the knife instruction, "Don't sniff the moldy item", leftovers within 3 to 4 days, perishables not out more than 2 hours, moulds growing at refrigerator temperatures and tolerating salt and sugar, household humidity below 40 percent, cleaning the storage spot and checking neighbours, and mushroom poisoning not being fixed by cooking. **Sources that would not load** - USDA FSIS "Food Product Dating", "Danger Zone 40 F - 140 F", "Refrigeration and Food Safety" and "Leftovers and Food Safety" all returned HTTP 403 to every route tried, including the Internet Archive. **This guide therefore does not quote FSIS's definitions of "Best if Used By", "Sell-By", "Use-By" and "Freeze-By", because I could not read them.** The date-label section is built entirely on the FDA pages above, which state the federal position directly. The one FSIS page that did load, on moulds, was read through an Internet Archive capture rather than from fsis.usda.gov. - https://www.foodsafety.gov/food-safety-charts/danger-zone-temperatures also returned 403 and is not cited. **State extension services, WHO and the research literature (restated, not quoted, because these are not public domain)** - https://extension.psu.edu/signs-of-food-spoilage Penn State Extension. Enzymes as a natural component of food that change colour, texture, flavour and nutritional content; that we cannot see, smell or taste pathogenic microorganisms though we can detect some spoilage; the list of spoilage signs in jars; freezer burn described and identified as not a cause of illness; and the instruction to discard mouldy food, which appears in its canning section. - https://blogs.extension.iastate.edu/answerline/2024/09/26/foodborne-illness-environmental-factors-affecting-microbial-growth/ Iowa State University Extension. The conditions bacteria need; the pH 4.6 low-acid threshold; FDA's water activity figure above 0.85; the 40 to 140 degrees F range; aerobic, anaerobic and facultative organisms. - https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mycotoxins World Health Organization. That most mycotoxins are chemically stable and survive food processing; the crops affected by *Aspergillus*; patulin in rotting apples and apple products; aflatoxin causing acute aflatoxicosis at large doses and liver cancer; and the consumer advice to inspect grains and nuts and discard any that look mouldy, discoloured or shrivelled. - https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8704553/ Kutasi K and colleagues, "Approaches to Inactivating Aflatoxins, A Review and Challenges", *International Journal of Molecular Sciences* 22(24):13322, 2021. Aflatoxins remaining stable above 100 degrees C, with significant decontamination reported only at 150 degrees C or higher. Used only for the heat-stability figure, and labelled in the text as research literature rather than an agency position. **Simulation data referenced** - `data/chemistry/toxins.csv`, record `aflatoxin_b1`. ## Related reading in this Library - [Keeping What You Grew](/library#keeping-what-you-grew), for the four preservation methods, the pH 4.6 rule, why low-acid food needs a pressure canner, and what to do with a jar that has gone wrong. Read it before you preserve anything. - [Reading the Tide](/library#reading-the-tide), for shellfish, closures and the biotoxin hotline. - [The Species Where You Live](/library#the-species-where-you-live), for which authority answers which question about a living thing. - [Identifying Wild Plants](/library#identifying-wild-plants), for why preparation never rescues a misidentification. - [Handwashing and Hygiene](/library#handwashing-and-hygiene), for the contamination route that starts in your own kitchen. - [Making Water Safe to Drink](/library#making-water-safe-to-drink) and [Testing Water](/library#testing-water), for the other half of what goes into your food. - [Ventilation, Damp and Mould](/library#ventilation-damp-and-mould), for the building-side of the damp problem that feeds the food-side.

docs.title: Your First Compost
headings: How you know it is done
docs.text: # Your First Compost Composting is letting food scraps and yard waste rot on purpose, in a controlled spot, until they turn back into dark, crumbly soil. You are not really doing the work; billions of bacteria and fungi are. Your whole job is to keep them fed, damp, and supplied with air. Do that even roughly right and you get free fertilizer while keeping waste out of the trash. Your first pile may go wrong. It may smell one week, sit cold the next, or take twice as long as you hoped. That is normal and useful: every problem has a smell or a look that tells you exactly what to fix, and this guide covers them all. Nobody composts perfectly the first time. ## What you need Cheap or free options first: - A spot of bare ground about 3 feet by 3 feet (roughly one big stride each way), or a container. Options, simplest first: - An open pile. Free. Works fine. Looks messy, and animals can reach it. - A homemade bin: a circle of wire fencing, a ring of pallets, or a plastic storage bin with air holes drilled in the sides. Nearly free. - A bought compost bin or a tumbler (a barrel on a stand that you spin to mix the contents). Costs money, but keeps animals out and mixing easy. Good for small yards. - No yard at all? A worm bin works indoors: red wiggler worms in a plastic tub about 21 by 15 inches, kept at 55 to 75 degrees F, eat your scraps and leave behind rich compost. It deserves its own guide; search "vermicomposting" plus your state university extension. - A garden fork, shovel, or sturdy stick for mixing. - A steady supply of two kinds of material, described next. ## Greens and browns Everything you compost is one of two kinds: - Greens are fresh and moist, and rich in nitrogen (the nutrient that feeds fast bacteria). Everyday examples: fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, tea bags (paper ones), crushed eggshells, fresh grass clippings. - Browns are dry and dead, and rich in carbon (the energy source). Everyday examples: dry autumn leaves, straw, shredded cardboard, shredded newspaper, small twigs, untreated wood chips or sawdust. The practical ratio: about 2 to 3 parts browns for every 1 part greens, measured by volume, not weight. A bucket of scraps means two to three buckets of leaves. You do not need to be exact; when in doubt, add more browns. Almost every compost problem is too many greens, not too few. ## What never goes in - Meat, fish, and bones: they attract rats and raccoons, and a home pile rarely gets hot enough to break them down safely. - Cheese, dairy, fats, oils, and grease: same reasons. - Dog or cat waste, and cat litter: pets can carry disease organisms that home compost does not reliably kill. - Diseased plants and weeds that have gone to seed (flowered and formed seed heads): a cool pile will not kill the disease or the seeds, and you will spread them later. - Treated or painted wood, and coal or barbecue ash: chemicals you do not want in your soil. ## Building and running the pile 1. Pick a spot with decent drainage, ideally on bare soil, out of any spot that floods. Shade or sun both work. 2. Start with a layer of bulky browns about 4 to 6 inches deep. Twiggy stuff at the very bottom helps air get in. 3. Add your greens. Chopping scraps into 1 to 2 inch pieces speeds everything up, because the bacteria work on surfaces. 4. Cover every addition of food scraps with 4 to 8 inches of browns. Buried food does not smell and does not attract animals. This one habit prevents most beginner problems. 5. Check moisture. Squeeze a handful of the mixed material from inside the pile (not the dry cover layer): it should feel like a wrung-out sponge, clearly damp but yielding at most a drop or two of water. Too dry, sprinkle water as you mix. Too wet, mix in dry browns. Gloves are a good habit, and always wash your hands after working the pile. 6. Turn the pile (mix it with a fork, bottom to top) every week or two if you want speed, or once or twice a month if you are patient. Turning feeds air to the bacteria. Skipping it does not ruin anything; it just slows things down. 7. Keep adding as scraps appear. When the pile reaches about 3 by 3 by 3 feet, it can hold enough heat inside to really cook. Smaller piles still compost, just slowly and coolly. A well-fed pile of that size warms up inside within days. The middle of a working pile feels distinctly hot to a quick touch; a compost thermometer will read about 130 to 160 degrees F (do not hold a bare hand in material that hot). Heat is a bonus, not a requirement: it speeds things up and helps kill weed seeds, but a cool pile still turns into compost eventually. ## The honest timeline Months, not weeks. Anyone promising two-week compost is selling something. - A tended pile (good ratio, kept damp, turned regularly): roughly 2 to 5 months. University sources vary in this range because climate, materials, and effort vary; warm weather is faster. - A well-managed tumbler: as little as a couple of months. The sealed container holds heat despite its small size, and spinning it makes the frequent mixing easy, which is why it can beat an open pile. - An ignored pile you just keep adding to: about a year, sometimes two. This is a legitimate method. Lazy composting works; it is only slow. After the pile stops heating, let it sit and finish for at least 4 more weeks (called curing). Half-finished compost can rob nitrogen from your plants instead of feeding them. ## How you know it is done Finished compost is dark brown, loose, and crumbly, smells like fresh earth after rain, and no longer looks like what you put in. The pile will have shrunk to about half its original height. A few stubborn bits (eggshells, avocado pits, corncobs) may remain; sift them out and toss them back into the next batch. ## Using it Spread a layer about 1/2 to 1 inch deep over garden beds and work it gently into the top of the soil, or ring it around existing plants, keeping it a few inches away from stems. Mix some into the soil when planting. Compost is far more forgiving than fertilizer, but more is not better: stick to the 1/2 to 1 inch a year. Years of heavy applications can build up excess nutrients in the soil. ## Troubleshooting - Smells like rotten eggs, rancid butter, or vinegar: not enough air, usually because the pile is too wet or packed down. Fluff and turn the whole pile and mix in dry browns. - Smells like ammonia (sharp, like window cleaner): too many greens. Mix in more browns. - Rats, raccoons, or other animals: something meaty, oily, or dairy got in, or food is sitting exposed. Remove it, always bury new scraps under browns, and if it continues, switch to a closed bin; cover any vent holes with fine metal mesh (hardware cloth). - Clouds of fruit flies: annoying, harmless. Bury scraps deeper under browns. Freezing scraps before adding them kills fruit fly eggs that ride in on fruit skins. - Pile will not heat up: it is too small (under about 3 by 3 by 3 feet), too dry, or too brown-heavy. Grow it, water it while turning, or mix in fresh greens like grass clippings. Or it may simply be finished; done compost runs cool. - Soggy mess: too much rain or too many wet greens. Turn it, add plenty of dry browns, and cover the top during long wet spells. - Bone dry and nothing happening: sprinkle water as you turn until it passes the wrung-out-sponge test. - Bugs, worms, and slugs everywhere inside the pile: good news, not a problem. They are decomposers doing the work. ## The loop this closes The scraps from your kitchen become the dark, living soil that a tomato seedling wants to grow in. Compost feeds the garden, the garden feeds you, and the trimmings go back into the pile. Waste stops being waste. Start the pile now and it will be ready for planting season. ## Sources - https://www.epa.gov/recycle/composting-home - https://extension.umn.edu/managing-soil-and-nutrients/composting-home-gardens - https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/extension-gardener-handbook/2-composting - https://extension.unh.edu/resource/composting-home-gardener-fact-sheet - https://ccetompkins.org/resources/compost-troubleshooting-your-compost - https://extension.umd.edu/resource/indoor-worm-composting-or-vermicomposting

docs.text: # What Soil Is Put a spade into the ground and turn it over. What comes up tells you more about what will grow there than the seed packet does. Soil is not an inert material that holds plants upright while you add fertilizer. It is ground-up rock, dead things, water, air, and a very large amount of life, and the proportions of those five decide most of what you will experience as a gardener: how often you water, whether a bed drains after rain, how deep roots go, and whether the fertilizer you bought does anything at all. This guide is about reading what you already have. It is the thing to understand before you test your soil, before you plan a planting calendar, and before you spend money correcting a problem you have not identified. Nothing here is hazardous, and nothing here needs equipment. Most of it you can do this afternoon with your hands, a spade, and a jar. ## What soil is actually made of Take a spadeful of good topsoil and sort it by volume. USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service describes the surface layer as roughly half solids and half pore space. Of the whole volume, about 45 percent is mineral particles, meaning ground-up rock; about 5 percent or less is organic matter; and the remaining 50 percent is pore space, filled with water and air in a ratio that changes every time it rains. Four things follow from that, and they are worth sitting with. **Half of good soil is nothing.** The pore space is not wasted volume, it is the working part. Roots grow into it, water moves through it, and air reaches the roots and the microbes through it. When you compact soil, what you destroy is this half. **Water and air share one space.** They are in direct competition. A soil holding all the water it can hold is a soil with no air in it, which is why waterlogged ground kills plants that are not adapted to it. NRCS notes that once more than about 80 percent of the pore space is filled with water, soil respiration falls to a minimum and nitrogen starts being lost to the air as gas. **Organic matter is the smallest ingredient by a wide margin**, at 5 percent or less, and it matters far out of proportion to that. There is a section on it below. **It is alive, and that is not a metaphor.** NRCS defines soil health as "the continued capacity of soil to function as a vital living ecosystem that sustains plants, animals, and humans." The bacteria, fungi, worms and arthropods in the ground are not passengers. They are what turns dead material into plant food and glues loose particles into crumbs. ## Sand, silt and clay are sizes, not substances This is the single most useful thing in the guide, and almost everyone gets it slightly wrong at first. Sand, silt and clay are not three different materials. They are three size ranges of the same ground-up rock. USDA defines them by diameter: | Name | Diameter | How it behaves in your hand | |---|---|---| | Sand | 2.0 down to 0.05 mm | Gritty. You can see individual grains with the naked eye | | Silt | 0.05 down to 0.002 mm | Smooth, like flour. Invisible without magnification | | Clay | smaller than 0.002 mm | Sticky when wet, hard when dry | Anything 2 mm or larger is not counted in the texture at all. USDA calls the material below 2 mm the "fine earth" and treats everything above it separately as rock fragments, which are described by how much of the soil volume they occupy. Those three lines look like a small difference. They are not. Because the particles get smaller by roughly a thousandfold from sand to clay, the surface area goes up enormously. NC State Extension publishes a comparison that makes the point better than any argument: one gram of coarse sand offers a surface area of about 23 square centimeters, while one gram of clay offers about 8 million. Surface area is where everything happens in soil. Water clings to surfaces. Nutrients stick to surfaces as charged ions. Microbes live on surfaces. So a clay particle does thousands of times more chemistry than a sand grain of the same weight, and a soil's clay content largely decides how much water and how many nutrients it can hold. The flip side is drainage. Water moves fast through the large gaps between sand grains and slowly through the tiny gaps between clay plates. NRCS gives these average steady-state infiltration rates, the speed at which water soaks in once the soil is already wet: | Soil type | Water soaks in at | |---|---| | Sand | more than 0.8 inches per hour | | Sandy and silty soils | 0.4 to 0.8 inches per hour | | Loam | 0.2 to 0.4 inches per hour | | Clayey soils | 0.04 to 0.2 inches per hour | Those are averages and NRCS is explicit that they should not be generalized to all soils, but the spread is the point: water enters a sandy soil several times faster than a clayey one, and at the extremes of that table more than ten times faster. This is why the same watering habit produces a drought in one garden and root rot in another. Sandy ground drains fast, dries fast, warms early in spring, and loses nutrients downward with the water. Clay ground holds water and nutrients, stays cold and wet late into spring, and turns to a brick when it dries. Silt sits between the two: it holds more water than sand and lets it through faster than clay. One honest complication: clay holds a lot of water but does not give all of it back. NRCS points out that a great deal of the water held by clay is bound too tightly for plants to use, while organic matter can hold up to 90 percent of its own weight in water and releases nearly all of it. A clay soil can be wet and a plant in it can still be thirsty. ## Texture is the proportions, and you are not going to change it Soil texture is simply the percentage of sand, silt and clay, by weight, in the fine earth. USDA sorts every possible combination into twelve texture classes: sands, loamy sands, sandy loams, loam, silt loam, silt, sandy clay loam, clay loam, silty clay loam, sandy clay, silty clay, and clay. They are laid out on a triangular chart, the texture triangle, where each corner is 100 percent of one separate. Note where "loam" sits. A loam is not an equal mix and it is not a quality rating. USDA defines it as 7 to less than 27 percent clay, 28 to less than 50 percent silt, and 52 percent or less sand. It is a particular corner of the chart that happens to balance the useful behaviors of all three sizes. Texture is effectively permanent. NC State Extension makes the arithmetic vivid: a typical mineral soil 6 inches deep across one acre weighs about 2 million pounds, so shifting the sand content by one percentage point means adding 10 tons of sand, and a change you would actually notice means something closer to 100 tons. So stop trying to fix texture. You cannot afford it and it will not work. The sand you dig into a clay bed does not make it sandy, it fills the gaps and makes it denser. What you can change, and change a great deal, is structure. ## Structure is a different thing, and compaction is what quietly ruins ground Texture is what the particles *are*. Structure is how they are *arranged*. Soil particles stick together into units, and USDA calls a unit that formed through soil development a ped. The surfaces of peds survive repeated wetting and drying, which is what distinguishes them from a clod you made with a plow. Good topsoil typically has granular structure, roughly rounded crumbs. NC State Extension describes it as looking like chocolate cookie crumbs, which is exactly right and is the image to hold. Those crumbs leave large gaps between them for air and water, and small gaps inside them that hold water. Soil with no structure at all is either loose single grains, like beach sand, or massive, a single coherent block. Structure is what compaction destroys, and compaction is the failure that does the most damage while announcing itself the least. It has no symptom of its own. It shows up as poor drainage, stunted plants, puddles that sit for days, roots that turn sideways at a certain depth, and it gets blamed on all sorts of other things. The measurement behind it is bulk density, the oven-dry weight of soil per unit volume. NRCS publishes the values at which roots start to struggle, and they depend on texture: | Texture | Ideal for plant growth | Restricts root growth | |---|---|---| | Sand, loamy sand | under 1.60 g/cm3 | over 1.80 g/cm3 | | Sandy loam, loam | under 1.40 g/cm3 | over 1.80 g/cm3 | | Silt, silt loam | under 1.40 g/cm3 | over 1.75 g/cm3 | | Clay, more than 45 percent clay | under 1.10 g/cm3 | over 1.47 g/cm3 | NRCS notes the table does not apply to red clayey soils or to volcanic ash soils, which matters in parts of the western United States. You will not measure this at home, and you do not need to. The useful lesson is in the shape of the table: clay soils reach a root-restricting density at a far lower number than sandy soils do, which is the technical version of "clay compacts easily and sand does not." Clay particles are small and plate-shaped, so pressure slides them into alignment, especially when wet. Which gives you the two rules that actually protect soil, both of them free. Do not work soil when it is wet. Do not walk on your beds. NRCS also notes that bulk density normally rises with depth anyway, because deeper layers have less organic matter and less root activity, so the subsoil starts out denser before you add anything to it. ## Horizons, and what topsoil really means Dig a deep enough hole and you will see the soil change in bands as you go down. Those bands are horizons, and USDA gives them letters: - **O** is an organic layer, mostly leaves, needles, twigs and moss in various stages of decay, lying on top. - **A** is the mineral topsoil: rock particles thoroughly mixed with humified organic matter. It is usually the darkest layer and holds most of the roots. - **E** is a bleached, lighter layer, found in some soils, where clay, iron and aluminum have been washed downward, leaving sand and silt behind. - **B** is the subsoil, where the material washed out of the layers above accumulates. It is often more clayey, denser, and a different color. - **C** is little-altered parent material: the sediment, weathered rock or geologic deposit the soil formed in. - **R** is bedrock, coherent enough that hand-digging with a spade is impractical. Not every soil has all of them, and USDA sets the lower boundary of soil, for classification purposes, at an arbitrary 200 cm. "Topsoil" in the ground means the O and A horizons, and it is where the organic matter, the biology and the roots are. "Topsoil" in a bag or on a truck means whatever the seller decided to call topsoil. NC State Extension warns plainly that there are no standards for material sold under that name, that it can bring in weed seeds and disease, and that dumping a layer of it over compacted ground creates a new drainage problem where the two layers meet. Buying topsoil is not a shortcut past the work. ## pH, and why most crops want a narrow band pH measures how acid or alkaline the soil solution is. Seven is neutral, lower is acid, higher is alkaline. The scale is logarithmic, so each whole number is a tenfold change: pH 5 is a hundred times more acid than pH 7, not 40 percent more. USDA puts the full range of soils from slightly below 2.0 to slightly above 11.0, and names the bands like this: | Class | pH | |---|---| | Extremely acid | 3.5 to 4.4 | | Very strongly acid | 4.5 to 5.0 | | Strongly acid | 5.1 to 5.5 | | Moderately acid | 5.6 to 6.0 | | Slightly acid | 6.1 to 6.5 | | Neutral | 6.6 to 7.3 | | Slightly alkaline | 7.4 to 7.8 | | Moderately alkaline | 7.9 to 8.4 | The scale continues past both ends of that table. USDA calls anything below 3.5 ultra acid and anything above 9.0 very strongly alkaline. Soils that extreme do exist, but they are uncommon and they are not the sort of thing a bag of lime fixes. pH matters because it controls what is chemically available, not what is present. A soil can hold plenty of a nutrient that the plant cannot take up because the pH has locked it away. NC State Extension notes that lowering pH increases the solubility of manganese, zinc, copper and iron, and that below about 5.5 those, along with aluminum, can reach levels that damage plants. So a very acid soil can poison a crop as well as starve it. Most food crops want the slightly acid to neutral band. NC State Extension describes a pH of 6.5 to 7.0 as what is often considered ideal for most plants, while adding the caveat worth repeating: the optimum differs by species, and it is worth looking up the plants you actually intend to grow. Blueberries and azaleas are genuinely happy near 5.0. Asparagus tolerates up to about 8.0. What makes soil acid is mostly rain and time. NC State Extension describes soils across the southeastern United States being acidified over thousands of years by acids arriving in rainfall, by the decay of plant and animal residues, and by the steady washing of basic cations such as calcium and magnesium down out of the root zone. Where rainfall is low, those bases are not washed away, carbonates accumulate, and soils tend alkaline instead. The parent rock matters too: soil formed over limestone starts with a large reserve of calcium carbonate. Raising pH means adding lime, lowering it usually means adding elemental sulfur, and both are slow and easy to overdo. That belongs to Testing and Correcting Soil, not here. The point of this section is that you should know your number before you buy anything. ### A regional note: the Pacific Northwest leans acid The canonical world for this project sits in the Pacific Northwest, and forest soils there tend toward the acid end. You can check that against the actual survey rather than taking anyone's word for it. USDA's Official Series Descriptions give the reaction range for each mapped soil, and three of the common Puget lowland soils, all formed under Douglas fir, western hemlock, western redcedar and red alder, read as follows: Alderwood, pH 5.1 to 6.5; Everett, pH 4.5 to 6.0; Kitsap, pH 5.1 to 7.3. Alderwood receives about 1000 mm of rain a year, which is the mechanism in one number. That is a regional fact, not a universal one, and even within that region Kitsap runs up into the neutral range. If you garden elsewhere, look up your own ground in USDA's Web Soil Survey rather than assuming it behaves the same way. ## Organic matter, the 5 percent that does the heavy lifting Organic matter is the decomposing and decomposed remains of living things, plus the living organisms themselves. NRCS calls it the most important single indicator of soil health, and for a component that is 5 percent or less of the volume, the list of what it does is absurdly long: it holds water like a sponge and gives nearly all of it back, it feeds the microbes, it releases nutrients as it breaks down, it buffers acidity, it glues particles into the aggregates that give soil its structure, it reduces crusting and compaction, and it makes water soak in rather than run off. Some numbers to anchor it. NRCS reports that soils holding 2 to 5 percent organic matter can maintain that level under ordinary management, and that in temperate regions roughly 1.5 percent of the organic matter present mineralizes each year, which is to say it is continuously being consumed and must be continuously replaced. Each percentage point of organic matter in the top 6 inches of a medium-textured soil releases roughly 10 to 20 pounds of nitrogen, 1 to 2 pounds of phosphorus and 0.4 to 0.8 pounds of sulfur per acre per year. And the sobering one, which explains why building organic matter is a long game: an acre of soil 6 inches deep weighs about 2 million pounds, so one percent of organic matter is about 20,000 pounds of it. Since roughly 10 pounds of raw organic material decomposes down to 1 pound of stable organic matter, raising an acre by a single percentage point takes on the order of 100 tons of material. You do this over years, with compost and mulch and roots left in the ground, or you do not do it. There is a reason forest soil is often less rich than it looks. NRCS explains that soils under forest commonly carry relatively low organic matter, because trees put far less root mass into the ground than grasses do and do not die back and decompose every year. Most of the carbon in a forest is standing up in the trunks. Grass, by contrast, dies back top and root every season and puts that material straight into the upper soil, which is why grassland soils are the deep dark ones. ## How to tell what you have, today ### The ribbon test This is the method soil surveyors actually use in the field, and USDA publishes the flowchart for it. It takes practice, and it is worth the practice, because it needs nothing but your hands and a little water. 1. Take about 25 grams of soil into your palm, roughly a heaped tablespoon, and pick out any stones. 2. Add water a few drops at a time and knead it until every lump is broken down. It is ready when it feels like moist putty: plastic and moldable, not runny. 3. Squeeze it into a ball. If it will not hold a ball at all, and it is neither too wet nor too dry, it is **sand**. Stop. 4. Put the ball between your thumb and forefinger and push it upward with your thumb into a flat ribbon of even thickness, letting the ribbon hang out over your finger until it breaks under its own weight. If it will not form a ribbon at all, it is **loamy sand**. Stop. 5. Measure the ribbon you got before it broke. Under 2.5 cm is a weak ribbon, 2.5 to 5 cm is medium, over 5 cm is strong. More clay makes a longer ribbon. 6. Now wet a fresh pinch of the soil thoroughly in your palm and rub it with a finger. Judge whether it feels distinctly gritty, distinctly smooth, or neither. Put the two answers together. Weak ribbon plus gritty is a sandy loam; weak plus smooth is a silt loam; weak plus neither is a loam. Medium ribbon gives you the three clay loams in the same order: sandy clay loam, silty clay loam, clay loam. A strong ribbon gives you sandy clay, silty clay, or clay. USDA is candid that this is a skill rather than a measurement, and that certain soils will fool you. In humid climates clay can be cemented by iron oxide into aggregates that feel like fine sand until you rub them for a long time, and some granite-derived soils contain soft grains that only reveal themselves as clay under prolonged rubbing. If a result surprises you, rub harder and try again. ### The jar test The jar test is the other method people are taught, and it works on the same principle as the laboratory hydrometer method USDA uses: bigger particles settle out of water faster than small ones. Put two or three inches of soil in a straight-sided jar, pick out the stones and roots, fill the jar most of the way with water, add a small squirt of dishwashing liquid to stop the clay clumping, cap it, and shake it hard for several minutes. Then set it down and leave it alone. The sand drops out almost immediately, the silt settles over the next few hours, and the clay may take a day or more to clear. Measure the three bands and you have rough percentages to take to the texture triangle. Treat the timings as a rule of thumb rather than a measured standard. The published settling times vary from source to source, organic matter floats rather than settling and will sit on top, and the same cemented clay aggregates that fool the ribbon test will settle out early here and read as sand. The jar test is a good way to *see* your soil's three fractions separated out, which is genuinely worth doing once. The ribbon test is the one to learn for real use. ### Look at the structure while you are there Dig a spadeful from a spot you have not walked on and let it fall apart on its own. Does it break into rounded crumbs, or into hard angular blocks, or not at all? Crumbs are good structure. A solid mass that needs force to break, especially with a flat, smooth face where it gives way, suggests compaction. Look for where the roots stop, and for whether they turn sideways at a particular depth, which usually means they have hit something they cannot get through. ## One thing to check before you grow food in unfamiliar ground Soil texture and pH are gardening problems. Contamination is a health problem, and it is invisible. EPA notes that lead levels are typically higher in soil near roads, because of decades of leaded gasoline exhaust; along the dripline of buildings painted before 1978; and near industrial sites, smelters and hazardous waste sites. Their practical advice for growing food is worth following: test the soil you intend to use for food crops; keep food beds at least 10 feet away from buildings, roads and driveways; and use raised beds or containers of clean soil where levels are higher. EPA also notes that root vegetables such as carrots and leafy greens take up more lead than fruiting crops like tomatoes, peppers and cucumbers, and that produce should be washed thoroughly, root crops peeled, and the outer leaves of leafy vegetables discarded. Many state university extension offices will test soil for lead for a modest fee, and that is the right place to start if you have any doubt about the history of the ground. ## So what is "good soil"? The honest answer is that it depends what you are growing, and anyone who gives you a single answer is selling something. A blueberry wants soil at about pH 5.0, which NC State Extension gives as its preference and which would starve most vegetables. Asparagus, by the same source, tolerates up to about 8.0. Beyond those two, the familiar examples are ordinary gardeners' knowledge rather than measured values, and each is worth confirming for the variety you actually plan to grow: that carrots want loose, deep, stone-free ground because the root forks around any obstacle, that rice wants the standing water that would kill a tomato, and that lavender and most Mediterranean herbs want the fast-draining, lean ground a squash would sulk in. What is nearly always true is narrower and less exciting: a soil that lets water in, holds some of it without staying saturated, lets air reach the roots, has enough organic matter to feed its own biology and hold itself together in crumbs, and sits at a pH where the nutrients present are actually available. Get those and the texture you happen to have stops mattering very much. Which is the useful conclusion, because the texture is the one thing you were never going to change anyway. You now know what to call what you have, why it behaves as it does, and which of its properties you can move. The next step is to measure the things you cannot judge by hand, which is pH and nutrients, and that is Testing and Correcting Soil. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. United States government publications are listed first because they are public domain and can be redistributed with this guide; the rest cannot. ### United States government (public domain) - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. Soil Survey Manual, Agriculture Handbook 18, Chapter 3, Examination and Description of Soil Profiles (particle-size separates, soil texture and the twelve texture classes, soil structure and peds, master horizons O through R, soil reaction and the pH class terms). https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-09/SSM-ch3.pdf - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. Soil Survey Manual, complete volume. https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-09/The-Soil-Survey-Manual.pdf - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. Soil Health, Guides for Educators: Bulk Density, Moisture and Aeration (May 2019) (the 45 percent mineral, 5 percent organic matter, 50 percent pore space split; the bulk density and root growth table; water-filled pore space). https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-10/Soil%20Bulk%20Density%20Moisture%20Aeration.pdf - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. Soil Health, Guides for Educators: Organic Matter (May 2014) (what organic matter does, the 2 to 5 percent maintenance range, mineralization rate, nutrient release per percentage point, the 2 million pounds per acre-6 inches figure, forest versus grassland organic matter). https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-10/Soil%20Organic%20Matter.pdf - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. Soil Health, Guides for Educators: Infiltration (May 2014) (steady-state infiltration rates by texture class). https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-10/Soil%20Infiltration.pdf - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. Guide to Texture by Feel (the field flowchart, and the soils that fool it). https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-11/texture-by-feel.pdf - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. Soil Texture Calculator (the texture triangle and a calculator for percentages). https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/resources/education-and-teaching-materials/soil-texture-calculator - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. What is Soil? (the Soil Taxonomy definition of soil and its 200 cm lower boundary). https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/resources/education-and-teaching-materials/what-is-soil - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. Soil Health (the definition of soil health used above). https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/conservation-basics/soil/soil-health - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. Official Series Description, ALDERWOOD series (western Washington; reaction pH 5.1 to 6.5; mean annual precipitation about 1000 mm; Douglas fir, western hemlock, western redcedar and red alder vegetation). https://soilseries.sc.egov.usda.gov/OSD_Docs/A/ALDERWOOD.html - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. Official Series Description, EVERETT series (northwest Washington; reaction pH 4.5 to 6.0). https://soilseries.sc.egov.usda.gov/OSD_Docs/E/EVERETT.html - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. Official Series Description, KITSAP series (western Washington; reaction pH 5.1 to 7.3). https://soilseries.sc.egov.usda.gov/OSD_Docs/K/KITSAP.html - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. Web Soil Survey (look up the mapped soils on your own ground). https://websoilsurvey.nrcs.usda.gov/app/ - United States Environmental Protection Agency. Lead in Soil (where lead concentrates, testing, the 10 foot setback, raised beds, and which crops take up the most lead). https://www.epa.gov/lead/lead-soil ### University extension (copyrighted; cited as the authority, restated here in our own words) - NC State Extension. Extension Gardener Handbook, Chapter 1: Soils and Plant Nutrients (particle surface area per gram, the arithmetic of changing texture, granular structure, why clay compacts, purchased topsoil, the pH scale and the pH most plants prefer, nutrient solubility and aluminum toxicity below about 5.5, and how soils become acid over time). https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/extension-gardener-handbook/1-soils-and-plant-nutrients

docs.text: # How Plants Work Go outside on an overcast day and stand there a minute. Then come back in and stand in the middle of the room with the lights on. Both places look like daylight. Your eye adjusts so completely between them that you will not feel any difference worth mentioning. NC State Extension publishes what a light meter says about places like those. Outdoors in full sun is about 10,000 foot-candles. Outdoors under overcast is about 1,000. An office is about 50, and a library about 20. So the dull grey day you were just standing in is about a tenth of a bright one, and the lit interior of a building is about a twentieth of the grey day, which is about a two-hundredth of full sun. Your eye smoothed over a factor of two hundred and reported all three as "daylight". A plant cannot smooth over it, because a plant is not looking at the light, it is eating it. The window itself is the interesting case. NC State classes areas within 4 feet of large windows facing south, east or west as high light, 4 to 8 feet from south and west windows as medium, and more than 8 feet from a window as low. Which means that in the room you are standing in, the difference between a good place for a plant and a slow death for one is about six feet of floor and which wall the window is in, and you cannot see either. That is the whole shape of this guide. Almost every piece of growing advice you have ever been given is the visible end of a mechanism, and once you can see the mechanism the advice stops being a list of rules to memorise and starts being something you can work out for yourself. ## What this guide does and does not do It explains how a plant makes food, moves water, feeds, grows, changes shape, flowers, and starts from seed, and after each mechanism it says what that mechanism predicts. The prediction is the point. If you finish this and can answer "why would that be true?" about a growing instruction you meet somewhere else, it worked. It does not tell you when to plant. Your dates depend on where you live, and [The Growing Calendar Where You Live](/library#the-growing-calendar) does that properly with real frost data and soil temperatures. It does not tell you what your ground is made of. That is [What Soil Is](/library#what-soil-is), and for your specific address, [Your Soil, Specifically](/library#your-soil-specifically). This guide leans on both and deliberately does not repeat their numbers. It does not qualify you to eat anything. Knowing how a plant works tells you nothing about whether a particular plant will kill you. [Identifying Wild Plants](/library#identifying-wild-plants) opens by refusing to be a field guide, and it is right to. And the honest limit: understanding does not substitute for a season. You will still kill things. The difference is that you will know which of the four or five possible reasons you are looking at, which is worth a great deal when you only get one attempt a year. --- ## Part 1: The budget ### Light in, sugar out A plant is a chemical factory with one product and one power source. NC State Extension gives the reaction as carbon dioxide plus water plus light making sugar and oxygen and water, and summarises it as plants using "energy from sunlight, carbon dioxide from air, and water from the soil to produce simple carbohydrates." Notice what is not on that ingredient list. There is no fertiliser in it. The carbon, hydrogen and oxygen that the sugar is built from come out of the air and out of water. Everything you buy in a bag is for a different job entirely, and we will get to it. The sugar can be used at once, moved elsewhere in the plant, or stored as starch. Every potato, every carrot, every grain of wheat and every drop of maple sap is that sugar, parked. Leaves are where most of it happens. Any green tissue can photosynthesise, but NC State notes that "leaves are generally the site of most food production", because their internal tissue, the mesophyll, is packed with the chloroplasts that hold the green pigment, chlorophyll, that actually catches the light. ### The bill that never stops Here is the half that gets left out of school diagrams. The plant spends that sugar continuously, in a process called respiration, which NC State describes as converting the carbohydrates produced by photosynthesis back into usable energy. The equation runs the other way: sugar plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water plus energy. Two things about respiration matter more than anything else in this guide. **It happens in every cell, and it does not stop at night.** NC State: "Respiration occurs in all life forms and in all cells." Photosynthesis needs light. Respiration does not. A plant in the dark is still burning sugar, all night, every night, the way you burn calories while asleep. **It does not stop at harvest either.** NC State: "Respiration continues in flowers, fruits, and vegetables even after they are harvested", which is exactly why refrigeration extends the shelf life of produce. The lettuce in your fridge is still alive and still spending. You are not preserving it, you are slowing its metabolism down. That is the mechanism under everything in [Keeping What You Grew](/library#keeping-what-you-grew). So growth is not photosynthesis. Growth is photosynthesis minus respiration. A plant that makes exactly as much sugar as it burns is not growing slowly. It is not growing at all. ### The break-even point, named That break-even has a name and a definition, and the definition is worth having exactly. A US Forest Service synthesis of forest physiology defines the photosynthetic light compensation point as "the light level at which gross photosynthesis equals leaf respiration and net photosynthesis is zero." Below that light level the plant runs a deficit. It is not idling, it is drawing down reserves, and eventually it dies of a slow financial problem rather than any disease you can name. The same source shows what evolution does with this. Light under a closed northern hardwood canopy is "typically less than 1 or 2% of full sunlight". Shade-tolerant trees survive there by pushing their compensation point below 5 percent of full sunlight, achieved "by minimizing leaf respiration per unit of light-absorbing leaf area, which can be accomplished by having thin leaves with only a single layer of chlorophyll-containing mesophyll cells." And they pay for it. Those same thin leaves cannot use bright light when it arrives: they saturate early, at something like 15 percent of full sun, and their maximum photosynthetic rate is low. The Forest Service calls this an "inevitable trade-off", and notes the consequence that when a gap opens overhead, the leaves of the trees that were waiting in the shade are not well adapted to the light they have been waiting for. The same source sorts the trees of that forest into tolerance classes by the light each one needs, and the spread is the thing to take away: | Tolerance class | Typical light availability | |---|---| | Very tolerant | 1 to 3 percent of full sunlight | | Mid-tolerant | 5 to 25 percent | | Intolerant | 25 to 50 percent | | Very intolerant | more than 50 percent | Say what that means. Two trees standing in the same forest can differ by a factor of fifty in the light they need to make a living. Say what it does not mean. These are the tree species of the Hubbard Brook Ecosystem Study, a northern hardwood forest, and the numbers are about them. **Do not carry them to a vegetable.** Carry the shape: species differ enormously in where they break even, and a species that breaks even very low pays for it by being unable to use bright light when it arrives. ### What the budget predicts **Why a bright-looking windowsill can still be starving a plant.** Look again at the light table. NC State's guidance for indoor plants splits each category in two, and the split is the compensation point wearing gardening clothes: a low-light plant needs 25 to 74 foot-candles "to maintain growth" and 75 to 300 "to promote growth". A medium-light plant needs 75 to 149 to maintain and 150 to 1,500 to promote. There is a band where a plant persists and does not grow. That band is where most unhappy houseplants live, and no amount of water or fertiliser will move them out of it, because the missing input is light. And it is why the geometry in the opening matters so much. Three feet from a south window against nine feet from it is the difference between NC State's high-light class and its low-light class. Moving a plant across a room is a real intervention, not fussing. **Why a February seedling on a sunny sill comes out pale and stretched.** It is short of light twice over: the sill is a fraction of outdoor light, and February's day is short. Silverdale, the canonical locale for this project at about 47.65 degrees north, gets 8.4 hours of daylight in midwinter against 16.0 at midsummer; [The Growing Calendar](/library#the-growing-calendar) has the month-by-month table and the sourcing for it. University of Minnesota Extension recommends 16 to 18 hours a day of light for seedlings under lights, which tells you what growers think seedlings actually need. Starting too early is the classic beginner's mistake and [Starting Seeds](/library#starting-seeds) says so; the budget is why. **Why a warm dark room is worse than a cold dark one.** Respiration is metabolism, and refrigeration slows it, which is the reason NC State gives for refrigerating produce. Anything with no light income and a warm room has a higher bill against no earnings. That is also the whole principle of a root cellar: a stored potato is still alive and still spending, and cold is how you make it spend slowly. [Keeping What You Grew](/library#keeping-what-you-grew) covers the practice. **Why "more sun is always better" is wrong as stated.** The Forest Service defines the light saturation point as "the light level above which light no longer limits photosynthesis". Past that point, extra light adds no extra sugar, and a shade-adapted species reaches it early. Meanwhile the hot bright afternoon that delivered the surplus light is exactly the condition USGS names as driving transpiration up, so a plant past saturation is paying more water for no extra sugar. That is Part 2's problem, and it is why full sun is a requirement for some species and a stress for others. --- ## Part 2: Water, and the door it leaves by ### Ninety percent NC State Extension gives the number plainly: "Approximately 90% of the water taken up by a plant is lost through transpiration. The other 10% of the water is used in chemical reactions and in plant tissues." Say what that means. Nearly all the water you put on a garden does not end up in the plant. It passes through it and evaporates. Say what it does not mean. It is not waste. NC State lists what the flow does on its way through: it carries minerals up from the soil, it cools the tissue, it moves sugars and hormones around, and it holds the plant up. A plant without turgor pressure is a limp plant, which is what wilting is. And it is not optional, which is the real point. ### One door, two directions Transpiration is, as NC State puts it, "the process by which a plant loses water, primarily through its stomata, pulling more water up the xylem." Stomata are the pores on the leaf. Each one, NC State says, is bordered by two guard cells, and "the bending of the two guard cells regulates the passage of water, oxygen, and carbon dioxide." Read that list of three gases again. The pore that lets water vapour out is the same pore that lets carbon dioxide in. There is no version of this where the plant gets the carbon without paying the water. The leaf is waterproofed everywhere else: NC State describes the cuticle as a thin waxy layer over the epidermis, which is exactly a raincoat. The stomata are the deliberate holes in the raincoat, and they exist because the factory needs an air intake. So the plant has one lever, and it is a bad lever. Open the stomata and photosynthesise and lose water. Close them and keep the water and stop photosynthesising. NC State: "The stomata generally close during drought or high temperature stress, thus reducing further water loss." Everything in this part follows from that single trade-off. ### How much water, really USGS puts numbers on transpiration at field scale. An acre of corn gives off about 3,000 to 4,000 gallons of water each day, which USGS also gives as 11,400 to 15,100 litres. A large oak tree can transpire 40,000 gallons in a year. And over a growing season, a single leaf will transpire many times its own weight in water. The corn figure is worth converting, because it lands somewhere familiar. An acre is 43,560 square feet. An inch of water over an acre is 43,560 divided by 12, which is 3,630 cubic feet, and at 7.48052 gallons to the cubic foot that is 27,154 gallons. So: - 3,000 gallons a day is 21,000 gallons a week, and 21,000 / 27,154 = 0.77 inch a week. - 4,000 gallons a day is 28,000 gallons a week, and 28,000 / 27,154 = 1.03 inches a week. Which is to say a full corn canopy in the growing season transpires roughly three quarters of an inch to an inch of water per week, and that is where the familiar "an inch of water a week" gardening rule lives. Treat the agreement as a sanity check, not a derivation: the USGS figure is a closed corn canopy at peak, and your lettuce bed in May is not that. If you want the unit arithmetic worked slowly, [Units and Converting Them](/library#units-and-converting-them) has it. ### What drives the loss USGS names the drivers, and each one is a lever you either have or do not have: - **Temperature.** "Transpiration rates go up as the temperature goes up, especially during the growing season." - **Humidity.** "As the relative humidity of the air surrounding the plant rises the transpiration rate falls." - **Wind and air movement.** "Increased movement of the air around a plant will result in a higher transpiration rate", and USGS gives the mechanism in the next sentence: "Wind will move the air around, with the result that the more saturated air close to the leaf is replaced by drier air." - **Plant type.** Desert plants such as cacti and succulents transpire less, which is a whole different budget with a whole different set of compromises. - **Soil type and saturation.** When water is short, plants can begin to senesce and transpire less, which is the plant giving up leaf area rather than an efficiency gain. Put the wind and humidity bullets side by side, because together they are one idea. USGS's reason for the humidity effect is that "It is easier for water to evaporate into dryer air than into more saturated air", and its reason for the wind effect is that wind replaces the saturated air at the leaf with drier air. So wind does not dry a plant by force. It dries a plant by continuously taking away the small pocket of humid air the leaf had just made for itself. ### What the water budget predicts **Why a wilted transplant recovers overnight but not at noon.** This is the flagship example, and it is entirely mechanical. Wilting means loss is running ahead of uptake. Midday is when two of the drivers USGS names are both at their worst: temperature is at its highest and relative humidity at its lowest. At night both reverse, and the plant keeps absorbing through roots that never stopped. The deficit closes and by morning the plant is rigid again. So the plant standing up at 7am has not been cured. It has been refilled, and it will be back in deficit by 1pm, every day, until its roots can supply as fast as its leaves spend. **Why a wilted plant at noon is not necessarily a thirsty plant.** Because the stomata close under heat stress anyway, a plant can wilt at midday with damp soil underneath it. Before you water a midday-wilted plant, put a finger in the soil. If the soil is wet and the plant is wilting, adding water addresses nothing and starts the problem in Part 3. Check again in the evening: a plant that is still flat at dusk has a real supply problem, and one that has recovered had a delivery-rate problem. **Why cuttings root better with the leaves cut in half.** A cutting is a plant with a full set of transpiring leaves and no roots at all. Demand is normal, supply is zero, and the cutting has only its own stored water. So you attack the demand side twice. NC State's propagation guidance does both: "On large-leafed plants, the remaining leaves may be cut in half perpendicular to the midvein to reduce moisture loss", and "Maintain high humidity by covering the cuttings with a bottomless milk jug or by placing the container into a clear plastic bag." Halving the leaf halves the evaporating area. The bag raises humidity, which USGS tells us directly lowers the transpiration rate. You keep enough leaf to pay for root construction, and no more. That is the entire logic of a propagation setup, and once you see it you can improvise one out of anything. **Why wind matters more than gardeners expect.** A windbreak is a water conservation device. A plant on an exposed corner is on a different water budget from one six feet away in shelter, at the same air temperature, in the same soil. **Why humidity appears as a column in the crop data.** We will come back to this in Part 9, but `humidity_min` and `humidity_max` in `data/plants.csv` are describing where on this trade-off a species is comfortable, not how much it likes to be damp. --- ## Part 3: Roots, and the half that suffocates ### Where absorption actually happens Dig up a seedling gently and you will see a root system. What you will not see is the part that does the work. NC State describes the root tip as a sequence: the zone of cell division including the root cap, "which protects the interior cells as the root pushes through the soil", then elongation, then a zone of maturation where "root hairs begin to emerge... developing as outgrowths of the epidermal cells." And then the sentence that matters: "The majority of the water and nutrients absorbed by the plant enter through the root hairs." Root hairs are single-cell projections, effectively invisible, and they are not permanent. NC State: "Most plants produce root hairs that live only a few days or a few weeks. New root hairs form as roots continue to grow through the soil." So the absorbing surface of a plant is a thin moving band just behind each growing root tip. It is not the thick roots you can see. Those are plumbing and anchorage. ### What that predicts about where you put things NC State draws the practical conclusion itself: "Watering and fertilizing close to the trunk of a plant are of little use to the plant... It is much more effective to apply water and fertilizer at the dripline of the plant where root hairs are most prolific." The dripline is the circle on the ground under the outer edge of the canopy. Water poured at the trunk of an established tree lands on plumbing. This is one of the highest-value sentences in this whole guide, because almost everyone does it wrong and it costs nothing to fix. ### And what it predicts about transplanting Penn State Extension states the problem in one line: "Most plants experience a certain amount of shock from transplanting, when roots are disturbed and unable to absorb enough water." Combine that with the budget. Lift a plant out of the ground and you keep the leaves, which is the entire demand, and you lose an unknown fraction of the fine absorbing surface, which is the entire supply. That is why a transplant wilts even in wet soil, and why it wilts worst in the middle of the day. The specific claim you will hear, that lifting a plant strips off its root hairs, is the standard explanation, and it is consistent with everything above. It is not stated in those words on any page cited here. What is sourced is the outcome: roots disturbed, water uptake insufficient. Every piece of transplanting advice now becomes obvious: - **Transplant in the evening or under cloud.** Penn State: "While cloudy conditions are best for transplanting, it is also acceptable to plant in late afternoon or early evening, when temperatures are cooler and the sun is less intense." You are handing the plant a whole night of low demand to rebuild with. - **Water before you lift, not just after.** Penn State recommends watering within an hour before transplanting, to keep root balls moist and intact during handling. A dry root ball crumbles, and crumbling is the damage. - **Support the root ball, do not pull the stem.** Penn State says to support the top of the root ball with your fingers, and to "gently tease" crowded seedlings apart rather than forcing them. - **Container-grown plants barely notice.** Nothing was disturbed. The one deliberate exception is a pot-bound plant. Utah State Extension: "If roots have formed a thick circular mat around the root ball, it is often beneficial to disrupt the roots by making several shallow, vertical cuts in the root ball with a knife or gently breaking up the roots with your hands." You accept a short-term supply hit to stop roots from circling permanently. ### The partnership most plants are in Roots are not the whole absorbing system. The US Forest Service describes mycorrhizae as "a mutual partnership between certain soil fungi and fine root tips" that "contribute to tree growth and vigor by increasing both water and nutrient uptake, especially nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P)." The deal is explicit: "The fungal hyphae increase root surface contact with the soil, while the fungi are supplied with a reliable source of carbon." The plant pays in sugar, the fungus pays in reach. There are two main kinds. Endomycorrhizae, also called vesicular arbuscular mycorrhizae, colonise the majority of plants including many trees. Ectomycorrhizae, which are mostly the mushroom-forming fungi, are "almost exclusively limited to woody species". Some plants host both. Three USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service documents were tried for the rest of it, the hyphal length figures and the list of plant families that opt out of the partnership, and none of them would load. So the partnership is sourced here and the arithmetic of it is not, and the widely repeated claim about which vegetable families are non-mycorrhizal is left out rather than repeated on trust. The Sources section says which documents failed. The useful implication that does follow: a large part of your plant's nutrient supply is being run by an organism that lives on your plant's sugar, in your soil, and that organism is part of what [What Soil Is](/library#what-soil-is) means when it says soil is alive. ### Roots need air, and this is what kills most houseplants [What Soil Is](/library#what-soil-is) already establishes that about half of good soil by volume is pore space, and that water and air share it in direct competition. Go and read that section; the numbers are there and there is no point repeating them here. What it means for the plant is this. Roots respire. They burn sugar and they need oxygen to do it, all day and all night, exactly like the leaves. University of Minnesota Extension states the consequence directly: "Water covering the soil reduces the supply of oxygen to tree roots. Roots must have oxygen to survive and grow." Waterlogging does not drown a plant in the sense of filling it with water. It suffocates it, by filling the air space its roots were breathing from. And the soil then turns actively hostile: UMN notes that "the high concentrations of ethanol and hydrogen sulfide that are produced in waterlogged soil can damage tree roots", and that the main end products of organic matter decomposition in flooded soil are carbon dioxide, methane and humic materials. That is anaerobic chemistry, and the smell of it is the smell of a pot that has been overwatered for a month. The timescales are worth knowing because they are shorter than people expect: - **Young corn.** UMN reports that for corn younger than the six-leaf stage, "Only 3 to 4 days of being submerged in floodwater can be fatal to these young plants." - **Soybean.** UMN reports photosynthesis reduced by a third with 48 hours of flooding. Not dead, just running a third of an income. - **Trees, dormant.** "Most tree species can withstand one to four months of flooding during the dormant season." - **Trees, growing.** "One to two weeks of flooding can cause major, long-term damage to sensitive trees and shrubs, even death with some species", while tolerant species "can survive as long as three to five months in flooded situations." Those last two figures are not about the same set of species, so do not read them as a clean ratio. The shape is still unmistakable: a tree stands in water for months in winter and dies in it in weeks in summer. That is the same mechanism as everything else in this guide. A dormant tree has a low metabolic rate and therefore a low oxygen demand. A tree in full leaf in July is running hot. ### What this predicts **Why overwatering kills.** It is not that the plant gets too much water. It is that the water evicted the air. This is why a pot with no drainage hole kills reliably, why a saucer left full of water kills slowly, and why the failure looks like underwatering: roots that have died of suffocation cannot absorb, so the plant wilts, so a well-meaning person waters it again. **Why a bed that floods in January is a different problem from one that floods in July.** Same water, two different plants. **Why garden soil fails in a pot.** NC State is blunt: field soils "often retain too much water, have too little pore space (for oxygen), are too heavy, and potentially harbor harmful diseases, insects, and weeds." [Your First Tomato](/library#your-first-tomato) covers the practical side of this. **Why gravel in the bottom of a pot makes drainage worse, not better.** NC State: "Never put a layer of gravel or rocks in the bottom beneath potting mix... water will collect in potting mix just above the gravel." The water does not fall into the gravel; it hangs in the fine material above it. You have not added drainage, you have raised the waterlogged zone into the root ball. **Why compacted ground produces symptoms that look like everything else.** Same cause, less dramatic. [What Soil Is](/library#what-soil-is) covers bulk density and what compaction does to structure. --- ## Part 4: Nutrients, and the single most useful diagnostic in gardening ### Seventeen elements, and where they come from NC State Extension says plants need "17 essential nutrients, each in varying amounts." Three of them, carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, come from air and water. The other fourteen come from the soil. The fourteen are split into macronutrients and micronutrients, and NC State is careful about why: micronutrients are so called because "they are needed in much smaller amounts than the macronutrients." Say what that does not mean. It does not mean micronutrients are optional or less important. A plant short of boron is as stopped as a plant short of nitrogen. The word describes the quantity on the delivery note, nothing else. ### Presence is not availability This is the sentence to take away from the whole of soil fertility, and NC State states it in one line: "For a plant to absorb an element, it must be in a chemical form used by the plant and dissolved in the soil water." Two conditions, both of which can fail while the element is sitting right there in the soil. It must be in a usable chemical form, and it must be in solution. This is why pH matters so much, and why it matters as a control on availability rather than on supply. [What Soil Is](/library#what-soil-is) carries the pH scale, the class names, and NC State's warning that below about 5.5 manganese, zinc, copper, iron and aluminium can reach levels that damage plants. The other end of the scale does the opposite: University of Georgia Extension states that "High pH in the soil (over 7.0) is the most common cause of iron deficiency", and that manganese deficiency "typically occurs in soils that have a high pH (alkaline soils)." So a soil test that says you have plenty of iron and a plant that is clearly short of iron are not in conflict. They are describing the two different conditions in that sentence. Missouri Extension's diagnostic guide makes the same point about the physical side, listing water stress, anaerobic soil conditions, and "issues with compaction, crusting, drainage, or waterlogging" among the things to ask about before concluding that a nutrient is absent. ### Mobility: where the symptom appears tells you more than what colour it is Here is the diagnostic. It is simple, it is free, and most gardeners have never been told it. Some nutrients can be moved around inside the plant after they have been installed. Some cannot. NC State: nitrogen is "mobile in plant, moving to new growth", so "symptoms appear first on older growth". Phosphorus behaves the same way. Calcium has "limited mobility in plant", so its symptoms show on younger growth. University of Georgia Extension gives the same split with more detail. Of nitrogen: it "is mobile in the plant and when deficient, will quickly be moved to new growth, depleting the amount in mature foliage." Deficiency symptoms of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium "typically occur first on the older, lower leaves." Magnesium shows "interveinal yellowing in the older, lower foliage first." Iron and sulfur show on the newer leaves near the top. So the rule: **Symptoms starting on the OLD leaves, at the bottom: a mobile nutrient.** The plant is rationing. It is dismantling its old leaves to build new ones, which is a sensible thing for a plant to do and a clear signal that supply is short. Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, magnesium. **Symptoms starting on the NEW leaves, at the top: an immobile nutrient.** The plant cannot rob the old leaves even though the element is sitting in them. So the new growth gets whatever is arriving right now, and if nothing is arriving, the new growth fails while the old leaves stay perfectly green. Calcium, iron, sulfur, and boron, whose symptom is at the growing tip itself.
