That second case is the informative one, because an immobile-nutrient symptom very often means a delivery problem rather than an absence. The element may be in the soil in quantity and simply not reaching the plant, because of pH, or because of water, or because the root system is too small or too cold. The specific symptoms, from University of Georgia Extension except where the note says otherwise: | Nutrient | Where it shows | What it looks like | |---|---|---| | Nitrogen | Older, lower leaves | Yellowing of mature foliage on the lower limbs | | Phosphorus | Older leaves | Puckering and purple colour through the leaf | | Potassium | Older leaves | Brown outer margin on the leaf; fruit underdeveloped with yellow areas | | Magnesium | Older, lower leaves | Yellowing between the veins | | Calcium | New growth (location from NC State, not UGA) | Overall yellowing and cupping; blossom end rot on fruit | | Sulfur | New growth | Pale green, yellowish leaves | | Iron | New growth | Yellowing between the veins, veins staying green | | Boron | Growing tip | Distorted growing tip, which can lead to tip death; brittle foliage | That one parenthesis is not pedantry. University of Georgia describes the calcium symptoms without saying where on the plant they appear. NC State is the source for calcium having limited mobility in the plant and for its symptoms showing on younger growth. The conclusion is the same either way, and splitting it across two sources changes nothing about what you should do. It is simply worth being able to say which page each half of a claim came from, because a reader who checks one source and cannot find the other half has no way to tell a misattribution from a mistake. Note that magnesium and iron produce the same picture, yellow between green veins, and the only thing separating them is which end of the plant it started at. That one observation is the difference between buying the right thing and the wrong thing. ### Blossom end rot, worked The black leathery patch on the bottom of a tomato is the worked example, because it is a calcium symptom, and calcium is the nutrient NC State singles out as having limited mobility in the plant. University of Georgia Extension says "Either a lack of calcium in the soil or poor irrigation practices can lead to deficiency", describes blossom end rot as an indicator of calcium deficiency appearing as "a black, leathery lesion", and advises monitoring irrigation "to keep soil evenly moist." Note that both causes are on the table, and note which one the advice addresses. The commonly given mechanism, that calcium travels in the transpiration stream and is therefore delivered unevenly when watering is uneven, is the conventional account and is not stated on the page read here. What is stated is the pair of causes and the instruction to keep soil evenly moist, and those are enough to act on: if your watering has been erratic, fix that before you buy calcium for a soil that may already have plenty. ### Why the same fertiliser does nothing in cold soil Three separate mechanisms stack up, and every one of them is physical rather than chemical. Iowa State University Extension: "With cold soil, root growth is slowed, the capacity to absorb nutrients is reduced, and the diffusion of nutrients through soil towards the root surface is slowed." Penn State Extension: "Cold, wet soils cause reduced root growth rate, nutrient mobility, and nutrient mineralization." And: "Even though a soil may have high fertility, a seedling's root system may not be able to obtain the necessary nutrients due to lack of size and density within the soil." So: 1. **The root system is small and growing slowly**, so there is less absorbing surface in contact with less soil. 2. **The nutrients are not moving to the root**, because diffusion through soil water is slower when it is cold. 3. **Less nutrient is being released at all**, because mineralisation, the biological breakdown of organic matter into plant-usable forms, is done by soil organisms that are also cold. [What Soil Is](/library#what-soil-is) covers what organic matter releases in a year; that whole process runs on biology, and biology slows down in the cold. Phosphorus takes this worst, because it barely moves in soil to begin with. Penn State: "Phosphorus compounds are bound and do not readily move within the soil." Iowa State adds that phosphorus is "less mobile in soil than K, and much less than mineral N forms", and that "P is very critical for plants during very early growth, and an early P deficiency seldom can be fully corrected after crop emergence." ### What this predicts **Why your March fertiliser application seemed to do nothing and your May one worked.** Nothing was wrong with the fertiliser. **Why a purple cast on seedlings in a cold spring is ambiguous.** Purple is the phosphorus symptom in University of Georgia's list. But everything above says a cold soil can produce a phosphorus symptom without a phosphorus shortage, so the same purple has two possible causes and they call for opposite responses. If the cause is temperature, the mechanism says the symptom should ease as the soil warms and the root system grows, and that follows from the sources rather than being stated by them. If the shortage is real, Iowa State's warning applies: early phosphorus deficiency "seldom can be fully corrected after crop emergence". Which is an argument for knowing your soil's phosphorus level before the season rather than diagnosing from a leaf colour during it. **Why "feed the soil, not the plant" is not just a slogan.** Two of those three mechanisms are about the soil's biology and physical structure rather than about how much nutrient you added. **Why a soil test is worth more than a fertiliser purchase.** Everything above says the same thing: you cannot see availability, and guessing costs more than measuring. [Your Soil, Specifically](/library#your-soil-specifically) covers where to get it done. --- ## Part 5: Form, or why a plant is the shape it is ### The tip suppresses the rest Every shoot has a terminal bud at its end and lateral buds along its sides; NC State names them exactly that way. What you cannot see is that they are in a chemical argument, and the tip is winning. University of Georgia Extension: "Auxin moves downward in the shoot (toward the Earth's center) from the shoot apex and inhibits the growth and development of lateral buds." That is apical dominance. The tip is not simply growing faster than the buds below it, it is actively holding them back, and that is why a shrub left entirely alone tends to run upward and get bare at the bottom. Which means every cut you make is a message. ### What pinching actually does Remove the tip and you remove the source of the inhibition. The buds below it are released, and they grow. University of Georgia distinguishes the two cuts: - A **heading cut** "removes the terminal portion of shoots or limbs" and is highly stimulating, producing dense regrowth near the cut. "Vigorous shoot growth will usually occur within 6 to 8 in. of the pruning cut." - A **thinning cut** "removes an entire shoot or limb to its point of origin", which maintains apical dominance on the tips that remain and gives less vigorous, more natural growth. So the two cuts do opposite things, and the difference is not about how much you remove. Pinching the growing tip out of a basil plant is a heading cut: you have removed the source of the inhibition, the buds below are released, and you get branching where you had a single stem. That is why pinching makes a bushy plant. Shearing the outside of a shrub is a very large number of heading cuts at once. Each one produces dense regrowth within a few inches of itself, so what you build over several years is a solid green shell. And once that shell is dense, Part 1 finishes the job: the interior is below its compensation point, and it goes bare. Neither half of that is stated on the pruning page, but both halves are, and the shrub is the evidence. ### Pruning does not make plants smaller This one is counter-intuitive and it is worth stating flatly. University of Georgia describes pruning as reducing "the size of the above-ground portion of the plant in relation to the root system", which stimulates compensatory regrowth. It is invigorating, not dwarfing. Cut a vigorous shrub back hard and it will come back harder, because you have not touched the root system that supplies it, and you have removed the buds that were suppressing the rest. The plant that was too big for its spot in year one is more too big in year three. The answer to a plant that is too big is a different plant, not an annual fight. ### Branch angle is a dial University of Georgia: apical dominance is strongest in vertical shoots, because auxin moves downward. Horizontal branches lose it entirely, which produces the vigorous vertical shoots called water sprouts. Limbs held at 45 to 60 degrees from vertical reduce vigour near the apex and increase lateral growth further down the limb, and their regrowth after a cut appears further from the cut. So the angle you train a limb to is a dial on how vigorously it grows and where. Straight up is maximum dominance and maximum growth at the tip. Flat is no dominance and a row of water sprouts. The 45 to 60 degree band that University of Georgia names is the setting that spreads growth along the limb instead of concentrating it, which is what you want on anything you intend to pick fruit from. ### Stretching toward the light, and what it costs NC State: "Too little light causes a long internode and a spindly stem, an occurrence known as stretching or etiolation." University of Minnesota describes the same plant from outside: stems become "long and thin and appear to be reaching toward the source of light", leaves go "pale green to yellow to white" for lack of chlorophyll, and plants may drop leaves, especially older ones. And Utah State Extension states the structural consequence: "Poor light intensity is often the cause of tall, skinny plants that have difficulty staying upright." Go back to Part 1 and this is a budget decision. The plant has a limited sugar income and it is spending it on length instead of girth. In a forest that is a rational gamble: grow tall fast, reach the light, then thicken. On a windowsill in February it is a losing bet, because the light is not going to arrive, and the plant has spent its capital on a stem that cannot hold itself up. The fix has two parts, and the second one surprises people. **More light.** Which means closer, brighter, and longer, and "closer" is closer than most people think. The published numbers do not fully agree, and it is worth seeing the spread rather than one figure presented as settled: | Source | Distance above the plants | Hours per day | |---|---|---| | Utah State, seedling culture | 2 to 3 inches | 12 to 14 or more | | Minnesota, starting seeds indoors | no more than 4 inches, 2 ideal | 12 to 16 | | Minnesota, lighting for indoor plants | 4 to 6 inches for seedlings | 16 to 18 for seedlings | Two of those rows are the same extension service on two different pages, which is a useful reminder that "extension says" is not a single voice. What they agree on is the shape: a few inches, not a few feet, and most of the waking day, not a couple of hours. Nobody in that group is describing a plant on a windowsill. [Starting Seeds](/library#starting-seeds) works from the seed-starting page of that table and gives the practical routine. **Air movement.** Utah State: "Very light, intermittent, direct airflow on your seedlings can be beneficial", applied "one to several times a day for a short duration (5 to 10 minutes or more)", and a small fan at plant level "can help lower humidity and increase stem strength." Read that last phrase again, because it is doing real work. A fan is not there to dry the surface or discourage mould, though it does both. It is there because a stem that is pushed around builds itself stronger, and a seedling raised in perfectly still air has never been given the signal to do so. Then you put it outdoors. Which is the other half of hardening off. Penn State describes gradually acclimating seedlings over 10 to 14 days before transplanting to prevent "damage from sudden changes in light intensity and temperature." Utah State says the process should "minimally begin about two weeks before transplanting", starting with a few hours, starting in shade, increasing daily. The important thing about those numbers is that they are measured in days rather than minutes. The plant is not being psychologically toughened. It is making physical changes to itself, and physical changes take physical time, which is why hardening off cannot be compressed into an afternoon no matter how the week has gone. [Starting Seeds](/library#starting-seeds) covers the routine. --- ## Part 6: Making more of itself ### The parts, and why you care NC State names the structures: - The **stamen** is the male organ. It has an **anther**, containing the pollen-producing chambers, on a stalk called the **filament**. - The **pistil** is the female structure in the centre, made of a **stigma** at the top which is "the site of pollination", a **style**, and an **ovary** at the base. A flower with sepals, petals, stamens and pistils is a **complete** flower; one missing any of those is **incomplete**. A flower with both male and female parts is **perfect**; one with only one sex is **imperfect**. And the arrangement across the plant has two names worth knowing. NC State: plants with separate male and female flowers on the same plant are **monoecious**; species where the sexes are on separate plants are **dioecious**. ### What that predicts **Why squash fruit shrivels when it is the size of your thumb.** The hand-pollination method in [Saving Your Own Seeds](/library#saving-your-own-seeds) works by moving pollen from a male flower to a female flower with a paintbrush. That instruction only makes sense because of a structural fact: squash carries its two sexes in separate flowers on the same plant, which is the monoecious arrangement, so every single fruit depends on something physically carrying pollen between two flowers. Which means a squash plant covered in flowers and setting nothing is not hungry. It is unvisited. Adding fertiliser to it does nothing at all, and that is a genuinely common and expensive mistake. **Why buying one plant is sometimes buying nothing.** If a species is dioecious, the sexes are on separate plants, so one plant cannot fruit on its own no matter how well you grow it. Find out which arrangement a species uses before you buy a single specimen of it. **Why "fruit" and "vegetable" do not mean what you think.** In botany a fruit is the matured ovary of a flower, which is a definition rather than a claim about any particular plant, and it puts tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers and squash in the same category as apples. There is no corresponding botanical definition of "vegetable" at all; it is a kitchen word. We will meet the consequences of that in the data file in Part 9. **Why whether saved seed comes true depends on the flower, not on the plant.** Whether pollen reaches a stigma from the same flower or from a different plant decides whether the seed is a near-copy or a cross. [Saving Your Own Seeds](/library#saving-your-own-seeds) has the sourced crop-by-crop lists, the traps, and the isolation distances, and they are not repeated here. The mechanism is the only thing this guide adds: a plant that fertilises itself before anything else can reach it is genetically conservative, and a plant that relies on a bee has handed the choice of the other parent to the bee. --- ## Part 7: The switch, and why things bolt ### Three life strategies NC State: - **Annuals** "complete their entire life cycle, from seed germination to seed production, and die in one growing season." - **Biennials** "complete their life cycles in two growing seasons." - **Perennials** "live for more than two growth seasons, up to several years, decades, or even centuries." The strategy is the plant's answer to a scheduling problem. An annual bets everything on one season and must flower. A biennial spends year one building a store, usually the root or the bulb or the head we happen to eat, and year two spending that store on flowers and seed. A perennial amortises the cost of a body over many seasons. ### The switch from growing to flowering Somewhere in every plant's life there is a switch from vegetative growth to reproductive growth. After it, the plant is building flowers. The leaves stop getting bigger and the sugar goes somewhere else. For a gardener this switch is the single most consequential event in the season, because for many crops we eat the plant before the switch. After the switch a lettuce is bitter and a broccoli has bolted and a basil has gone woody. Two environmental signals control it in most temperate crops: day length and cold. ### Day length, which the plant measures as night length NC State defines photoperiod as "the amount of time that a plant is exposed to sunlight", and then gives the two classes in a way that repays close reading: - "Short-day plants produce flowers only when the period of darkness exceeds a critical minimum." - "Long-day plants form flowers only when the period of darkness is less than the critical night length." Both definitions are stated in terms of DARKNESS. The plant is measuring the night, not the day. The names are historical and slightly misleading. The onion is the cleanest example a gardener meets. University of Illinois Extension: "Onions start bulb formation when the day length is of the proper duration and different varieties of onions require different day lengths to initiate bulbing." Most varieties are long-day, for northern latitudes, or short-day, for southern. And the consequence, in Illinois's words: "onion varieties that are grown in the South are not adaptable to the North and vice versa." That is a very strong statement for an extension service to make. Not "performs less well". Not adaptable. The reason usually given is that a variety which bulbs at a shorter day receives its signal earlier in the season, before the plant has built enough leaf to fill a bulb with, which is the mechanism you would predict from the definitions above. The Illinois page does not spell that out, so treat the conclusion as sourced and the reasoning as inference. What matters either way is that the failure is in the seed catalogue, not in the garden, and no amount of good growing recovers from it. No page could be opened for this guide that gives the specific hour thresholds for the short-day, intermediate-day and long-day classes, so no numbers are stated for them here. Buy by the latitude class printed on the packet, and if the packet does not say, buy elsewhere. One further implication of the definitions, which was likewise not found stated on any page opened for this guide: because the plant is measuring the dark period rather than the light one, a night interrupted by light is not a long night. A security light or a streetlamp over a bed is, to a short-day plant, a shorter night than the calendar says. ### Cold, which is the trigger people blame on heat The second switch is vernalization: a requirement for a period of cold before the plant will flower. The obvious function, though this is an interpretation rather than something quoted from a source, is that it works as a calendar. A biennial that has been through a winter can tell spring from autumn, which a thermometer alone cannot. University of Minnesota Extension, on cool-season vegetables: "Bolting refers to premature flowering. It occurs at any point after a plant has shifted into its reproductive stage." And then the crucial sentence: "Since bolting is partially triggered by the accumulation of cold, these strategies can reduce exposure to cold temperatures for young plants." And on what happens after: "After this shift, high heat and longer days will speed up flowering." **Read those two in order, because between them they overturn the most common garden diagnosis there is.** The June heat wave did not make your spinach bolt. The cold snap in April made the decision. The heat wave carried out a decision that had already been taken. University of Minnesota gives the related failure in broccoli and cauliflower, called buttoning: "Leafy biomass is what allows a plant to photosynthesize and create energy for itself, and so it's important for plants to put on plenty of leaves before transitioning to head formation. But when spring weather is quite cool, plants can experience vernalization early, and the result is buttoning up." A tiny head on a small plant, because the switch was thrown before the factory was built. University of Illinois notes the same effect in onions from sets: large sets "may 'bolt' and form flower stalks", and "extremely cold weather during early season growth also may condition onions from sets to flower." Plants that throw a flower stalk "do not produce good bulbs for dry storage." And the quality consequence, from Minnesota: "Once a plant flowers, the heads are no longer marketable, and the taste of the foliage often becomes bitter. This is especially true for spinach and lettuce, which both become extremely bitter after flowering." ### What this predicts **Why sowing a biennial too early in spring backfires.** You are handing it the cold it needs to decide to flower, at a stage when it has no reserves to flower well from. Later sowings into warmer soil often overtake early sowings and do not bolt. **Why the crop you eat determines when bolting matters.** For lettuce, spinach, broccoli and cabbage, bolting ends the harvest. For a crop where you want the seed, the switch is the goal. And for a biennial whose seed you want to save, you must deliberately get it through a winter, which is why [Saving Your Own Seeds](/library#saving-your-own-seeds) puts carrots, beets, onions, parsnips and cabbage in the second-year category and tells you to store the roots over winter. **Why cilantro seems to bolt out of spite.** It is a fast annual; its whole strategy is to flower. The data file even encodes this: cilantro is the one row in `data/plants.csv` whose growth stage list contains an explicit `bolt` stage. **Why "grow it in a cooler spot" and "grow it in a shadier spot" are different advice.** Shade changes the light budget. Cool changes the switch and the transpiration rate. They are not interchangeable. --- ## Part 8: Starting from zero ### Why a seed does not just grow A seed that germinated the moment it was wet would germinate in the first warm rain of autumn and die in the first frost. So many of them do not. The US Forest Service's Woody Plant Seed Manual gives the definition, and it is a good one: dormancy is "a physiological state in which a seed disposed to germinate does not, even in the presence of favorable environmental conditions." That is a seed refusing to grow in conditions that would work. It is a timer, not a failure. The manual puts the purpose plainly: "survival of the species requires that they germinate at a time and place favorable for growth and survival of the seedlings", and in many species "germination at unfavorable times is prevented by a mechanism that is commonly described as dormancy." Note the source before you carry any of this to a carrot. The Woody Plant Seed Manual is about trees and shrubs, and deep dormancy is normal there in a way it is not in a packet of radish seed. Penn State covers the same mechanisms for garden seed and treats them as something occasional to be broken rather than the default condition. So read this part as the full range of what a seed can do, not as a description of your vegetable packets. ### Two places a seed can lock itself The Forest Service divides dormancy by where the lock is. **Seedcoat, or external, dormancy.** In the most common mode "the seedcoats (or other covering structures) are impermeable to the entry of moisture or gases." The legume family is the classic case, and people who handle seed call it hardseededness. A second mode is purely mechanical: the coat physically resists the swelling of the embryo. A third possibility is germination inhibitors sitting in the coat itself. **Embryo, or internal, dormancy.** This "arises from a condition within the embryo itself", most likely from germination inhibitors in the embryo or in its food storage tissue, with abscisic acid the most common one identified. For germination to happen "these inhibitors must be metabolically inactivated, or their effect must be overcome by germination-promoting substances." Penn State Extension gives the same two in garden language: physical dormancy is a "hard or thick seed coat" broken "by soaking or scarifying (scratching the surface) the seed", and chemical dormancy is governed by "plant hormones, notably, abscisic acid, which inhibits germination, and gibberellin, which ends seed dormancy", with cold stratification helping to break it. ### Picking the lock: scarification Scarification is any treatment that breaches the seed coat. The Forest Service lists the methods in order of increasing severity, and gives the operating principle, which applies to everything in this guide: "there are risks to seed viability inherent in all of them. In selecting a scarification treatment, the most gentle method should be tested first; then increasingly severe treatments until the desired effect is obtained." - **Cold water soak.** Where the coat is not completely impermeable, "soaking such seeds in water at room temperature for 24 to 48 hours may be sufficient." - **Hot water soak.** Seeds are put into very hot or boiling water and left there as the water cools. "The hot water softens the seedcoats or causes them to crack, and imbibition occurs as the water cools." The manual says numerous leguminous species can be treated this way, naming acacia, albizia and prosopis, all of them woody. - **Hot wire.** A heated needle or an electric woodburning tool burns small holes through the coats. - **Acid treatment.** Concentrated sulfuric acid, 15 to 60 minutes depending on species and seedlot, then washed thoroughly in running water. - **Mechanical.** For small samples, "seedcoats can be scarified by hand with knives, files, clippers, sandpaper, etc." **Do not do the acid method at home.** Concentrated sulfuric acid is a professional reagent handled with dedicated protective equipment and a plan for the waste and for a spill on a person. It is on that list because the manual is written for production nurseries. For a gardener, sandpaper or a nail file does the same job to the same seed, and the only thing you risk is the seed. The hot water method deserves respect too: boiling water into a container is an ordinary scald hazard, and it is worth doing at the sink rather than over your lap. ### Picking the other lock: stratification Internal dormancy is usually broken by imitating winter. The Forest Service: "For temperate species, this is usually a moist, chilling period, commonly called stratification, because it was formerly done by alternating layers of seeds and sand or peat in a pit in the ground." The procedure: "refrigerate fully imbibed seeds at 1 to 5 degrees C for 1 to 6 months." That is about 34 to 41 degrees F, which is refrigerator territory, and the seed must be moist, not dry, because the chemistry is happening. What happens during it, again from the manual: enzyme systems are activated, stored foods are changed to soluble forms, and the balance between inhibitors and promoters shifts. The seed is not waiting. It is working. Two practical notes the manual supplies. The optimum length "varies greatly among species and among different seedlots of the same species", so treat published durations as starting points. And there is a bonus: stratification gives nurseries "an increased uniformity of emergence", because chilling holds back the seeds that would otherwise have raced ahead. ### What germination actually requires Penn State gives four conditions for garden seed: "Temperature, moisture, air, and light conditions must be correct for seeds to germinate." Taking them in turn with the Forest Service's detail: **Water.** Penn State describes the first step, imbibition: "The seed rapidly takes up water and the seed coat swells and softens." The Forest Service describes three phases, a rapid initial uptake, a lag, and then a second rapid uptake just before germination. The first phase "is a physical process of moisture moving from a substance with high water potential (soil) to one with a low water potential (dry seed)", and it happens in dead seeds as well as live ones. A seed swelling proves nothing about whether it is alive. **Oxygen.** Penn State: "Seeds respire just like any other living organism. They need oxygen and produce carbon dioxide." The Forest Service says insufficient oxygen is not usually a barrier "except when seeds are buried too deeply in the soil or are submerged in water", and adds a detail that explains a lot of failed seed trays: "Moisture will actually form a film around seeds and inhibit the entry of oxygen." **Temperature.** Seeds of temperate woody plants germinate from a minimum of 2 or 3 degrees C to a maximum of about 45 degrees C, and "the major effect of temperature on germination, however, is on rate rather than total germination." Natural seedbeds swing between night and day, and many temperate woody species germinate most rapidly at about 20 degrees C at night and 30 in the day, that is about 68 and 86 degrees F; work with thermogradient plates suggests "an amplitude of change between day and night of 10 to 12 degrees C may be more important than the cardinal points." For vegetable crops, use the sourced soil-temperature table in [The Growing Calendar](/library#the-growing-calendar) rather than any of those woody-plant numbers. **Light.** Penn State: "Not all seeds have the same light requirements. Most seeds germinate best under dark conditions", while some require light. The Forest Service explains the machinery: a pigment called phytochrome exists in two forms, one absorbing red light at 660 nm and one absorbing far-red at 730 nm, and "red light converts Pr to Pfr in imbibed seeds, which is associated with overcoming dormancy", while far-red light drives it back "accompanied by a partial return of dormancy." So a seed can measure not just how much light there is, but what colour it is. That is a depth sensor and a canopy sensor in one, and it explains why seed on the surface behaves differently from seed an inch down. ### What this predicts **Why sowing depth matters twice over.** A seed has a finite food reserve. Penn State: after the shoot emerges "the seedling grows slowly while the storage tissue of the seed diminishes", until true leaves appear, and those leaves, "unlike cotyledons, photosynthesize light into energy." So too deep means the reserve runs out before the first leaf reaches the light. And too deep also means less oxygen. Two independent reasons for one rule. [Starting Seeds](/library#starting-seeds) has the practical depth rule. **Why a few kinds of seed must be surface-sown.** If a species needs light to germinate, burying it is a permanent instruction to stay dormant. The packet will say so. **Why a waterlogged seed tray rots instead of sprouting.** A film of water excludes oxygen, and a seed that has imbibed and cannot respire is a nutrient parcel sitting in warm damp soil. **Why weeds appear every time you dig.** The Forest Service notes that dry dormant seeds normally do not germinate in the dark. Buried seed therefore sits in the one condition that keeps it waiting, and turning the soil hands some of it the signal it has been waiting years for. That last step is an implication of the sourced mechanism rather than something stated on a page opened here, but the pattern in the garden is not in any doubt. **Why a packet of tree seed behaves nothing like a packet of radish.** Because it has a lock on it, and the lock has a key, and the key is somewhere between one and six months of damp cold. --- ## Part 9: Reading data/plants.csv The simulation behind this project reads its crops from a single file, `data/plants.csv`, which as of this writing holds 189 plant definitions in 26 columns. It is worth learning to read, partly because it drives what happens when you plant something in the game, and mostly because a row is a compact statement of everything in this guide. ### What the columns are, in groups **Identity.** `id`, `name`, `description`, `type`, and `harvest_item`, which names the item in the inventory that a harvest turns into. **The clock.** `growth_days` is total days to first harvest. `growth_stages` is the ordered list of named stages the plant passes through, colon-separated. `seasons` is the seasons it is grown in. **The inputs.** `water_liters_per_day` is the water demand per plant per day, which is Part 2 in one number. `nutrient_n`, `nutrient_p` and `nutrient_k` are relative demands for the three macronutrients most often limiting, which is Part 4. **The tolerance windows.** `ph_min` and `ph_max` are the preferred soil or reservoir pH band, which is Part 4's availability point and not a statement about how much nutrient is present. `temp_min_c` and `temp_max_c` are the temperature window. `humidity_min` and `humidity_max` are the relative humidity window, from 0 to 1, which is Part 2's transpiration trade-off. **The output.** `yield_min` and `yield_max`, in units of produce per plant. These are stored as fractional numbers on purpose: some crops genuinely yield less than one unit per plant, saffron being the example the file's own code comments give. **The game layer.** `seed_value`, `harvest_value`, `skill_required`, `seed_source`. **The ecology layer.** `companion_plants` and `adverse_plants`, as colon-separated lists of other ids. ### Reading one row Take the tomato row: tomato,Tomato,...,fruit,70,1.5,0.15,0.05,0.20,6.0,6.8,18,30, 0.50,0.80,2,8,seed:sprout:vegetative:flower:fruit:ripe, spring:summer,5,15,1,store:trade,basil:carrot:parsley,fennel,... Now read it as biology rather than as numbers. `70` days is a trap unless you read the file's header, which says so explicitly: eight rows count their days FROM TRANSPLANT rather than from seed, "because that is the basis every extension service publishes for them", and tomato is one of them. The others are pepper, eggplant, broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, celery and leek. The header notes that direct-sowing those adds roughly 30 to 45 days. [The Growing Calendar](/library#the-growing-calendar) covers this same trap from the seed packet's side, with the sourced numbers. `1.5` litres a day is a transpiration budget. Compare it to carrot at 0.3 and radish at 0.15. A tomato is a large plant carrying large fruit in the hottest part of the year with its stomata open; a radish is a small plant in cool weather that is finished in 25 days. `0.15, 0.05, 0.20` is nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium. Note that potassium is the largest of the three here, which is consistent with a fruiting crop: University of Georgia's deficiency descriptions are the only place in this guide's sources where a nutrient shortage is described as showing up in the fruit itself, and that nutrient is potassium. `6.0` to `6.8` pH is the availability window from Part 4. Two rows in the whole file have a window that closes in the acid range, blueberry at 4.5 to 5.5 and cranberry at 4.0 to 5.5, and those are the two famous acid-soil crops. Meanwhile 134 of the 189 rows keep their entire window inside 5.5 to 7.5. That distribution is the real shape of crop pH preference, and [What Soil Is](/library#what-soil-is) covers why it sits there. `18` to `30` degrees C is the temperature window, and it is worth reading as a growth window rather than a survival window, because a tomato does not die at 17 degrees. Twelve of the real-world rows carry a `temp_min_c` below zero, which is where frost tolerance is actually encoded: mache at minus 15 is the hardiest in the file, then kale, collard and chicory at minus 8, then spinach, brussels sprout and bok choy at minus 7. `seed:sprout:vegetative:flower:fruit:ripe` is the life cycle from Part 7, made explicit. Compare beet, whose stages run `seed:sprout:leaf_growth:root_swell:mature`, with no flowering stage at all, because we harvest a biennial before the switch. Compare cilantro, whose stage list contains `bolt` outright. ### What the perennials tell you Look at `growth_days` across the file and one thing jumps out. Asparagus is 730. Cranberry is 1095. Apple is 1460. Redwood is 7300. The header explains the convention: unless noted, the number counts from the propagule the plant is actually started from, clove for garlic, slip for sweet potato, crown for asparagus, cutting for the berry shrubs, through to the FIRST harvest. "Perennials therefore carry the establishment years... not the length of one fruiting season." That is an honest and unusual modelling choice, and it teaches the real lesson about perennials: the cost is paid up front. Two years of asparagus bed before a single spear is cut is the actual deal, and the file says so rather than hiding it. ### What the file cannot say, which is the more interesting half A data schema is a theory about what matters. Reading what is missing tells you where the simulation is simpler than the biology. **There is no light column.** Nothing in a row expresses light requirement, shade tolerance, or a compensation point. Part 1 of this guide, the budget that governs everything else, has no field at all. A row cannot distinguish a lettuce that will grow in partial shade from a tomato that will not. **There is no photoperiod field and no vernalization field.** So Part 7, the switch, cannot be expressed. The `seasons` column is doing the work of both, and it is a label rather than a mechanism: it says when a crop is grown, not what makes it flower. Bolting cannot emerge from this data, it can only be scripted. **There is no pollination field.** Nothing says whether a species is self-pollinating, insect-pollinated, wind-pollinated, monoecious or dioecious, which is exactly the information that [Saving Your Own Seeds](/library#saving-your-own-seeds) turns on. **There is no rooting depth and no root type.** So the interaction between a crop and a shallow soil over a restrictive layer, which is the single most important fact about a great deal of ground in the Puget lowland, cannot be modelled. [Your Soil, Specifically](/library#your-soil-specifically) covers depth to a restrictive layer, and it matters enormously. **There is no soil-oxygen or drainage field.** `humidity_min` and `humidity_max` are about air, not about soil pores. Part 3's suffocation failure has no column. **There is no mycorrhizal status.** None of that is a complaint. It is what a schema is: a decision about which of the infinite properties of a real thing the simulation is going to carry. Knowing which ones were left out is knowing where your own judgement has to fill in. ### Two things to notice in the file itself **The documented category list is shorter than the file.** The comment block at the top defines `type` as "Category: fruit, vegetable, grain, legume, herb, fiber", which is six values. The file actually contains ten: those six plus `tree`, `medicinal`, `decorative` and `alien`. If you are reading the header to understand the data, that will mislead you. The same comment block documents every column from `id` through `adverse_plants` but does not mention `harvest_item`, which is a real column in the data. **Some of the rows are not plants.** Three real-world rows, `oyster_mushroom`, `shiitake` and `button_mushroom`, are fungi. Their stage lists say so plainly: `spore:mycelium:pinning:fruiting:mature`. All three carry `type` = `vegetable`. Two more, `shadow_fungi` and `phase_mushroom`, are the science-fiction equivalents and carry `type` = `alien`. Fungi are not plants. They have no chloroplasts, no leaves and no stomata, they do not photosynthesise at all, and they get their carbon by digesting material that something else built. So the entire budget of Part 1 simply does not apply to them, which means the columns in those rows do not mean what they mean elsewhere. A `water_liters_per_day` for a mushroom is not a transpiration demand, because there is nothing transpiring. A `ph_min` is about a growing substrate rather than a soil solution feeding a root. Nothing is broken, but you are reading a different organism through a schema designed for a plant. It is worth noticing rather than fixing, because the same confusion runs through ordinary language. A mushroom sits next to the vegetables in a shop for culinary reasons, not biological ones. If you are foraging, that is more than a technicality: [Identifying Wild Plants](/library#identifying-wild-plants) treats fungi as a separate discipline with a separate risk profile, and it is right to. --- ## The habit this leaves you with A plant runs four budgets at once, and everything above is one of them: 1. **Sugar**, earned from light, spent every hour of the day and night. 2. **Water**, which can only be earned through the same pore that spends it. 3. **Oxygen at the roots**, which shares its space with water and loses. 4. **Fourteen elements from the soil**, only useful when they are in a usable form, dissolved, and physically reaching a root. When something looks wrong, the useful move is not to identify the symptom. It is to work out which budget is short, and then which of the two or three possible reasons is causing the shortfall. A yellow leaf is not a diagnosis. A yellow OLD leaf with green new growth, three weeks after a cold wet spell, on a plant that has not been repotted, is nearly one. That habit also tells you when to stop guessing. Three of the four budgets are invisible: you cannot see foot-candles, you cannot see soil air, and you cannot see availability. That is what a light meter, a spade and a soil test are for, and it is why they are worth more than anything you can buy in a bag. ## Where to go next - [What Soil Is](/library#what-soil-is) for the medium every one of these mechanisms happens in. - [Your Soil, Specifically](/library#your-soil-specifically) to find out what is actually under your feet. - [The Growing Calendar Where You Live](/library#the-growing-calendar) for frost dates, soil temperatures and day length with real numbers. - [Starting Seeds](/library#starting-seeds) to put Parts 1, 5 and 8 into practice on a windowsill. - [Your First Tomato](/library#your-first-tomato) for one plant, start to finish. - [Saving Your Own Seeds](/library#saving-your-own-seeds) for Part 6 done properly. - [Growing Food You Can Live On](/library#growing-food-you-can-live-on) for the arithmetic of calories, which is a different and harder problem than growing something. - [Your First Compost](/library#your-first-compost) for the return leg of Part 4. - [How an Ecosystem Holds Together](/library#how-an-ecosystem-holds-together) for what all of this looks like at the scale of a watershed, including nitrogen fixation, which this guide has deliberately not tried to cover. - [Identifying Wild Plants](/library#identifying-wild-plants) before you eat anything you did not plant. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. United States government publications are listed first because they are public domain and can be redistributed with this guide; the rest cannot, and everything taken from them has been restated here in our own words with the source named. ### United States government (public domain) - United States Geological Survey, Water Science School. Evapotranspiration and the Water Cycle (transpiration rates for an acre of corn and a large oak; a leaf transpiring many times its own weight in a season; the effects of temperature, relative humidity, wind and air movement, plant type, and soil type and saturation on transpiration rate; and the mechanism given for two of those, that it is easier for water to evaporate into drier air, and that wind replaces the more saturated air close to the leaf with drier air). https://www.usgs.gov/special-topics/water-science-school/science/evapotranspiration-and-water-cycle - USDA Forest Service. The Woody Plant Seed Manual, Agriculture Handbook 727, Chapter 1: Seed Biology, by Franklin T. Bonner (the definition of dormancy; seedcoat and embryo dormancy; the scarification methods in order of severity, including the cold water soak at 24 to 48 hours and the acid treatment at 15 to 60 minutes; stratification at 1 to 5 degrees C for 1 to 6 months and what happens during it; the three phases of moisture uptake; the temperature range and the importance of day-night amplitude; the aeration section and the water film that excludes oxygen; the phytochrome red and far-red system). https://www.fs.usda.gov/nsl/Wpsm%202008/Chapter%201.pdf - USDA Forest Service. The Woody Plant Seed Manual, Chapter 7: Nursery Practices. Downloaded and opened, but used only to confirm that the detailed pretreatment procedures live there; no fact in this guide is taken from it. https://www.fs.usda.gov/nsl/Wpsm%202008/Chapter%207.pdf - USDA Forest Service, Research and Development. Mycorrhizae (the definition of the partnership; the exchange of soil contact for carbon; ectomycorrhizae and endomycorrhizae, and which plants form which). https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/9995 - USDA Forest Service, Northern Research Station. Forest Physiology and Phenology, in the Hubbard Brook Ecosystem Study synthesis, by T. J. Fahey and others (the definition of the photosynthetic light compensation point; the definition of the light saturation point; light beneath a closed northern hardwood canopy as less than 1 or 2 percent of full sunlight; shade-tolerant species achieving a compensation point below 5 percent by thin single-mesophyll-layer leaves; the trade-off with low light saturation and low maximum photosynthetic rate; and Table 1, the tolerance classes of Hubbard Brook trees with their typical light availability limits of 1 to 3 percent, 5 to 25 percent, 25 to 50 percent and more than 50 percent of full sunlight). The document names Hubbard Brook throughout and this guide does not state a location beyond that, because the pages read did not give one. https://www.fs.usda.gov/nrs/pubs/jrnl/2019/nrs_2019_fahey_001.pdf ### University extension (copyrighted; cited as the authority, restated here in our own words) - NC State Extension. Extension Gardener Handbook, Chapter 3: Botany (the photosynthesis reaction and that leaves are the main site; respiration in all cells and continuing after harvest; transpiration and that approximately 90 percent of water taken up is lost through it; stomata, guard cells and the cuticle; root cap, zone of maturation, root hairs as the site of most absorption, their lifespan of days to weeks, and the dripline advice; terminal and lateral buds; xylem, phloem and vascular cambium; etiolation; annual, biennial and perennial; stamen, anther, filament, pistil, stigma, style and ovary; complete and incomplete, perfect and imperfect flowers; monoecious and dioecious; short-day and long-day plants defined by length of darkness; monocots and dicots). https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/extension-gardener-handbook/3-botany - NC State Extension. Extension Gardener Handbook, Chapter 1: Soils and Plant Nutrients (17 essential nutrients; carbon, hydrogen and oxygen from air and water; macronutrients and micronutrients named by amount needed; the requirement that an element be in a usable form and dissolved in soil water; cation exchange capacity; nitrogen and phosphorus mobile with symptoms on older growth, calcium of limited mobility with symptoms on younger growth). https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/extension-gardener-handbook/1-soils-and-plant-nutrients - NC State Extension. Extension Gardener Handbook, Chapter 18: Plants Grown in Containers (foot-candle values for full sun, overcast, an office and a library; the maintain-versus-promote light bands for low, medium and high light plants; distance from windows, including that the high-light class is within 4 feet of large windows facing south, east or west; symptoms of light below optimum; why field soil fails in a container; why a gravel layer makes drainage worse). https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/extension-gardener-handbook/18-plants-grown-in-containers - NC State Extension. Extension Gardener Handbook, Chapter 13: Propagation (removing leaves from the lower third to half of a cutting; cutting remaining leaves in half perpendicular to the midvein to reduce moisture loss; maintaining high humidity with a bag or a bottomless jug; what rooting compounds do). https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/extension-gardener-handbook/13-propagation - University of Georgia Extension. Basic Principles of Pruning Woody Plants, Bulletin 949 (auxin moving downward from the shoot apex and inhibiting lateral buds; heading cuts versus thinning cuts; vigorous regrowth within 6 to 8 inches of the cut; branch angle and vigour, including the 45 to 60 degree guidance and water sprouts on horizontal limbs; pruning as invigorating rather than dwarfing). https://fieldreport.caes.uga.edu/publications/B949/ - University of Georgia Extension. Nutritional Deficiencies in Vegetables, Bulletin 1569 (nitrogen mobile and moved to new growth; nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium symptoms first on older lower leaves; magnesium interveinal yellowing on older foliage; iron and sulfur on newer growth; the specific symptom descriptions for each nutrient; high pH over 7.0 as the most common cause of iron deficiency and manganese deficiency in alkaline soils; blossom end rot and the role of irrigation). Note that this page gives the calcium symptoms without saying where on the plant they appear; the "new growth" location in the table in Part 4 comes from NC State, and the table says so. https://fieldreport.caes.uga.edu/publications/B1569/ - University of Minnesota Extension. Lighting for Indoor Plants and Starting Seeds (photosynthetic photon flux and foot-candle bands for low, medium and high light; loss of chlorophyll and pale to yellow to white leaves; legginess; leaf drop starting with older leaves; 16 to 18 hours a day for seedlings; 4 to 6 inches between light and seedlings). https://extension.umn.edu/planting-and-growing-guides/lighting-indoor-plants - University of Minnesota Extension. Starting Seeds Indoors ("Keep lights no more than 4 inches above the tops of your seedlings: as close as 2 inches is ideal" and "Plants need 12 to 16 hours of light daily"). Opened specifically to check the table in Part 5, because these figures differ from the same extension service's indoor lighting page above. Both are quoted rather than averaged. https://extension.umn.edu/planting-and-growing-guides/starting-seeds-indoors - University of Minnesota Extension. Non-Pest Issues of Cool-Season Crops (bolting defined as premature flowering after the shift to reproductive growth; heat and longer days speeding flowering after the shift; the accumulation of cold as a partial trigger; spinach and lettuce becoming extremely bitter; buttoning in broccoli and cauliflower caused by early vernalization). https://extension.umn.edu/planting-and-growing-guides/non-pest-issues-cool-season-crops - University of Minnesota Extension. How to Manage Flood Damage to Trees (water covering soil reducing oxygen supply; roots requiring oxygen; ethanol and hydrogen sulfide in waterlogged soil; the end products of decomposition in flooded soil; one to four months of dormant-season flooding tolerated; one to two weeks in the growing season causing major damage to sensitive species; three to five months for tolerant species; leaf chlorosis and loss). https://extension.umn.edu/planting-and-growing-guides/how-manage-flood-damage-trees - University of Minnesota Extension, Northwest Crops blog. How Long Can Crop Plants Survive Saturated or Flooded Soils? (3 to 4 days of submersion fatal to corn younger than the six-leaf stage; soybean photosynthesis reduced by a third with 48 hours of flooding; flooded soils quickly becoming devoid of oxygen). https://blog-nwcrops.extension.umn.edu/2024/06/how-long-can-crop-plants-survive.html - Penn State Extension. Transplanting Annuals into the Garden (shock from transplanting when roots are disturbed and the plant cannot absorb enough water; watering within an hour before transplanting; cloudy conditions or late afternoon and early evening; supporting the root ball and teasing crowded seedlings apart; 10 to 14 days of hardening off preventing damage from sudden changes in light intensity and temperature). https://extension.psu.edu/transplanting-annuals-into-the-garden - Penn State Extension. Seed and Seedling Biology (the embryo, food reserves and seed coat; radicle, cotyledons, hypocotyl and epicotyl; imbibition; the four requirements of water, oxygen, temperature and light; most seeds germinating best in the dark; physical dormancy broken by soaking or scarifying; chemical dormancy, abscisic acid and gibberellin; epigeous and hypogeous emergence; the seedling living on storage tissue until true leaves photosynthesise). https://extension.psu.edu/seed-and-seedling-biology - Penn State Extension. Starter Fertilizer (cold, wet soils reducing root growth rate, nutrient mobility and mineralization; phosphorus compounds bound and not readily moving in soil; a seedling's root system unable to obtain nutrients for lack of size and density even in a fertile soil). https://extension.psu.edu/starter-fertilizer - Iowa State University Extension and Outreach, Integrated Crop Management. Fertilization Can Help with Cool Soils and Late Planting Dates (cold soil slowing root growth, reducing absorption capacity, and slowing diffusion of nutrients toward the root surface; phosphorus less mobile than potassium and far less than mineral nitrogen; early phosphorus deficiency seldom fully corrected after emergence). https://crops.extension.iastate.edu/cropnews/2018/04/fertilization-can-help-cool-soils-and-late-planting-dates - Utah State University Extension. Starting Vegetable Seeds Indoors, IV: Seedling Culture and Transplanting (poor light intensity causing tall skinny plants that have difficulty staying upright; hanging lights 2 to 3 inches above the growing plants; 12 to 14 or more hours of light a day; light intermittent airflow for 5 to 10 minutes one to several times a day and a fan at plant level increasing stem strength; hardening off beginning about two weeks before transplanting; cutting or breaking up a circling root ball). https://extension.usu.edu/yardandgarden/research/starting-vegetable-seeds-indoors-seeding-culture-and-transplanting - University of Illinois Extension. Onion, Home Vegetable Gardening (bulb formation beginning when day length is of the proper duration; different varieties requiring different day lengths; long-day for northern and short-day for southern latitudes; southern varieties not adaptable to the north and vice versa; large sets bolting; extremely cold weather during early growth conditioning onions from sets to flower; bolted plants not producing good storage bulbs). https://extension.illinois.edu/gardening/onion - University of Missouri Extension. Questions to Diagnose Crop Nutrient Deficiencies, G9074 (asking where symptoms appear first in order to distinguish mobile from immobile nutrient deficiencies; pH extremes limiting availability, particularly micronutrients at high pH; compaction, crusting, drainage, waterlogging and water stress as causes). https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g9074 ### Opened and could not be used Recorded here because the alternative to admitting a gap is filling it with a guess. - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Soil Health guides for educators: Soil Fungi, and Soil Biology. Both timed out repeatedly through the fetching tool, and a direct download returned an HTML error page rather than the document. Nothing in this guide is taken from either. The consequence is that the numbers usually quoted for mycorrhizal hyphal length, and the list of plant families that do not form mycorrhizae, are absent from Part 3 rather than sourced elsewhere. - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Florida Plant Materials technical note on mycorrhiza. Download blocked. - Oregon State University Extension, How Hormones and Growth Regulators Affect Your Plants, and Winter Vegetable Production West of the Cascades (PNW 548), and University of Minnesota Extension, Growing Cool-Season Vegetables in Minnesota. All returned HTTP 403. The auxin material in Part 5 comes from University of Georgia instead; the vernalization material in Part 7 comes from University of Minnesota's cool-season disorders page instead. - Michigan State University Extension, Bolting in Spring Vegetables, and Vernalization Part 1. Both returned an empty page body. No vernalization temperatures or durations are stated in this guide as a result. - Utah State University Extension, Onion Health Management and Production. The file exceeded the fetching tool's size limit, which is why Part 7 gives the day-length principle for onions but no hour thresholds for the short-day, intermediate and long-day classes. ### Stated in the text as reasoning rather than as sourced fact - The claim that lifting a plant strips off its root hairs. The outcome, that a disturbed root system cannot absorb enough water, is sourced to Penn State; the specific mechanism is labelled in Part 3 as the standard explanation rather than a sourced one. - The implication that an interrupted night is not a long night to a short-day plant, and the implication that turning soil triggers weed germination by ending the darkness that was holding buried seed dormant. Both follow from mechanisms that are sourced; neither consequence was found stated on a page opened for this guide, and both are labelled in the text. - The explanation of why a southern onion variety fails at a northern latitude, that it receives its bulbing signal before it has built enough leaf. The conclusion, that the varieties are not interchangeable, is University of Illinois; the reasoning is inference from the photoperiod definitions and is labelled in Part 7. - The statement that vernalization functions as a calendar. The requirement itself is sourced; the account of what it is for is an interpretation, and Part 7 says so. - The arithmetic converting USGS's 3,000 to 4,000 gallons per acre per day into 0.77 to 1.03 inches per week. The gallons are USGS; the conversion is done here and shown so it can be checked. - The observation that a `water_liters_per_day` figure means something different for the three mushroom rows in `data/plants.csv` than for a plant row. The biology is standard, and the point is about how to read the schema rather than a claim about any source. ### Inside this project - `data/plants.csv`, the crop definition file described in Part 9, read at 189 rows and 26 columns, including its header comment block and its `growth_days` convention note. - `src/systems/farming/mod.rs`, the `PlantDef` structure that the file is loaded into, read to confirm what each column is used for.
