docs.text: # Identifying Wild Plants Read this part before anything else. **This document cannot teach you to identify a plant, and nothing in it should be used as permission to eat one.** It teaches the method and the discipline: what identification actually is, what it is not, which parts of a plant carry the answer, and how to know when you do not have one. It contains no key, no species list, and no field marks you could act on tonight. That is deliberate, and it is not caution for its own sake. The failure mode in this subject is death, not disappointment. USDA's own words for the worst plant in this guide's home region: water hemlock is the most violently toxic plant that grows in North America, and only a small amount of its toxin is needed to produce poisoning in humans. Nobody eats it on purpose. People die from it because they believed it was something else. The way people actually learn this is in person, from somebody who already knows, one species at a time, over years. A book, a website and a phone app can all help that process along. None of them replaces it. If you read this whole document carefully and stop here, you have lost nothing. Its companion, [The Species Where You Live](/library#the-species-where-you-live), covers the four questions to ask about any living thing, why a common name is not an answer and a binomial is, and which authorities answer which question. Read that one first. This document does not repeat it, and it assumes you have it. ## The positive identification rule This is the spine of everything below, so it goes first. **You do not identify a plant by ruling out what it is not. You identify it by matching every diagnostic character of the thing you believe it is, and if one character does not match, or you cannot check it, you stop.** The failure this rule exists to prevent has a specific shape, and it feels like competence while it is happening. You look at a plant, you look at a description, and you tick features off. Leaf shape, yes. Flower colour, yes. Habitat, yes. Height, about right. Each tick makes you more confident. That process is confirmation, not identification, and confidence built that way is worth nothing, because **a plant with nine matching features and one deadly twin is not nine tenths safe.** The twin shares those nine features. That is what makes it a twin. So identification has two halves, and both must complete: 1. **Every diagnostic character of the species you believe it is, checked, on this individual plant, now.** Not most of them. Not the ones that were easy to see. Every one. A character you could not check because the plant is the wrong age, or the light was bad, or it would have meant cutting something you should not cut, is a character that did not match. 2. **Every dangerous species it could otherwise be, eliminated by name.** Not "I have never seen that here". Eliminated, one at a time, by a character you actually checked. If either half is incomplete, you have not identified the plant. You have a guess. Guesses are fine. Eating them is not. The phrase to be afraid of is **"it looks like"**. Not because looking is useless, but because looking is where the whole error lives. FDA, writing about mushrooms but describing the same human being, records that many cases of poisoning have happened in people who were using field guides, had a lot of experience, and were sure they had picked the right kind. The same page notes that poisonings are almost always caused by wild specimens collected by nonspecialists, and then adds, in parentheses, that specialists also have been poisoned. ## The fourth question, worked three times The companion guide gives four questions, and says the fourth one is the one that hurts: not "does this match" but **"what else could this be"**. Here is what that question looks like when you actually run it, using three real pairs from the species file that ships with this project, `data/locales/silverdale_wa/species.json`. Read these as demonstrations of a method. They are not instructions for telling these plants apart, and each one ends by saying so. ### Wet ground: water parsnip and water parsley against water hemlock Three plants in the same marsh. All three are in the carrot family. All three have divided leaves and small white flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters. Two of them, hemlock waterparsnip (*Sium suave*) and water parsley (*Oenanthe sarmentosa*), are native here and are treated as food in foraging literature. The third, western water hemlock (*Cicuta douglasii*), is the one USDA calls the most violently toxic plant on the continent. Notice the name first. USDA's own common name for the edible one is **hemlock** waterparsnip. A person who has carefully learned "avoid hemlock" has learned something that will not save them, because the word is on both plants. There are two real characters, and both come from USDA. On water hemlock, the side veins of the leaves lead to notches rather than to tips at the outer margin. And the thick rootstalk contains small chambers holding a highly poisonous brown or straw-coloured liquid, released when the stem is broken or cut. Now look at what those characters cost you. The vein character needs a single leaflet held up to good light and an eye that has done it before. The root character requires you to have already cut into a plant that poisons people by being cut; USDA is explicit that the liquid is released when the stem is broken, so cutting, mowing, pulling or clearing it is itself an exposure. The shipped record does the thing a book almost never does, and says the honest thing outright: **a beginner cannot reliably tell these two apart in the field, and experienced foragers have died getting it wrong.** Its working rule is to eat no carrot-family plant gathered from wet ground at all. One more thing from that record, because it is the part that generalises furthest. Water hemlock's lookalike list includes broadleaf cattail, which looks nothing like it. Cattail is on the list because cattail rhizomes are dug from the same marsh mud in autumn and winter, when the standing plants are gone and nothing above ground says which plant a root came from. That is not a visual confusion. It is the actual route by which a person meets the poison. So the question is not only "what looks like this", it is **"what would I be doing when I met this"**. ### Roadside: wild carrot against poison hemlock Poison hemlock (*Conium maculatum*) is deadly in every part. USDA states that all parts, leaves, stem, fruit and root, are poisonous. Wild carrot (*Daucus carota*), Queen Anne's lace, is the ancestor of the garden carrot and grows on the same road verges and field edges. Here there is a genuinely useful check, and this time it is a state authority rather than a federal one, so the fact is Washington's and the sentence is ours. Washington's noxious weed board describes poison hemlock as a very tall biennial, up to about 12 feet, with hollow, hairless stems carrying noticeable purple blotches; it describes wild carrot as smaller, covered all over with coarse stiff hairs, and without purple blotches on the stems. So a hairy stem points at wild carrot, and a hairless stem with purple blotches points at poison hemlock. Then run the test backwards and watch it fail. **Finding hairs is worth something. Not finding purple spots is worth nothing.** The spots develop as poison hemlock bolts, and a first-year poison hemlock is a low rosette with no stem to check at all. That rosette stage runs through autumn, winter and early spring, which is exactly the season you would be digging a first-year carrot root. This asymmetry is general and it is worth carrying out of this document as a habit. A field character usually works in one direction only. It can condemn, or it can support, rarely both. Before you lean on one, ask which direction it runs in, and what its absence actually proves. The same pattern appears in the shipped record for nodding onion. Onions smell of onion and death camas does not, so **no onion smell means do not eat it, full stop**. But smelling onion does not prove that the bulb in your hand is an onion, because a bulb picks up the smell from your fingers, your knife, or a crushed onion lying beside it in the basket. Hence the procedure: smell every bulb separately, with clean hands, before it joins the others. Note also that the shipped record labels this onion-smell test honestly, as something no public-domain federal source states in so many words. The half of it that is sourced is the dangerous half: USDA records that death camas is mistaken for wild onion. And the honest end of this pair, as the records give it: at the rosette stage a beginner cannot separate wild carrot from poison hemlock, and people better qualified than a beginner have died making exactly that call. There is no field character on offer here that closes that gap, because there is not one that works. ### Meadow: common camas against meadow death camas This is the most instructive pair in the whole subject, because the lesson it teaches is not about looking at all. Common camas (*Camassia quamash*) and meadow death camas (*Zigadenus venenosus*) share wet spring meadows, both are grass-leaved, both grow from a bulb, and both are dug for that bulb. USDA's plant guide for death camas states that the common name refers to the toxicity of the plant and its similarity in appearance to camas, and that it has been mistaken for other edible bulbous plants such as wild onion, sego lily and camas, **especially when flowers are lacking**. The same guide gives the number that matters: eating one or two death camas bulbs is enough to cause severe illness in children, and four or five can cause death. In bloom, there is a check anyone can make from standing height. The Forest Service describes common camas flowers as blue to bluish-violet, with tepals 12 to 35 millimetres long. USDA describes death camas petals as creamy white, about a quarter inch long, with a large gland at the base. Blue against creamy white, at arm's length. That is as easy as identification in this subject ever gets. Out of bloom there is no reliable field character at all, and the bulbs cannot be told apart safely by a beginner. So the answer is not a better field mark. **The answer is a calendar.** The identification happens in May, when the meadow is in flower. The harvest happens months later. Those are two different events, and the only thing that can carry the identification from the first to the second is a physical marker left on the individual plant, not your memory of where you walked. Walk the meadow in bloom, mark the individual plants you want, come back later, and dig only the plants you marked, one at a time, never working through a patch. If you arrive at a meadow with no flowers and no marks, you have no way to do this safely, and the correct action is to leave and come back in May. ## The parts you must look at, and the parts people look at instead Beginners identify plants by their leaves. Leaves are what is there for most of the year, they are what a photograph captures, and they are what a phone app is looking at. That is a rule of thumb rather than a measured finding, but the consequence of it is visible in every pair above, and the consequence is sourced. Look at where the answer actually sat in each case: - Water hemlock against water parsnip: leaf **venation** at a fine scale, and the **rootstalk**, underground. - Poison hemlock against wild carrot: the **stem**, hairs and blotches. Both plants have fern-like, finely divided leaves. USDA describes poison hemlock's leaves as delicate, like parsley, which is to say the leaves are the source of the confusion rather than the solution to it. - Camas against death camas: the **flower**, colour and size. Both have grass-like leaves. Three lethal pairs, three separators, and not one of them is a leaf outline. The answer sat in the flower, the fruit, the root, the stem cross-section and the smell. Those are the parts that carry the identification, and it is not an accident: they are the parts that vary least within a species and most between species. There is a fourth pair worth adding here, because it makes the same point about the part people actually reach for. Red baneberry (*Actaea rubra*) is a knee-high woodland herb whose berries the Forest Service describes as showy, poisonous, red or occasionally white, with a poisonous essential oil or glycoside found in all parts but most concentrated in the berries and the root, and the National Park Service states that the berries are poisonous and will often send the heart into cardiac arrest. It grows in the same moist shaded forest as claspleaf twistedstalk, whose red berries are eaten; the Forest Service describes twistedstalk as carrying only one flower on each flower stalk, hanging downward, giving rise to a single elliptic yellow or red berry which is edible. **The colour of the berry tells you nothing**, since baneberry's own fruit is red or white and both are poisonous. What separates the two is the architecture of the plant holding them: twistedstalk hangs one berry per stalk, dangling under an arching stem, while baneberry bunches its berries on one upright stalk held above the leaves. So the answer is not in the fruit you want to eat. It is in the plant the fruit is attached to, which is the part a person picking berries never looks at. And even that pair ends where all the others do. The Forest Service, writing about twistedstalk itself, warns that it can be mistaken for the poisonous *Veratrum* and says that perhaps it is better left unsampled. Two consequences follow, and the second is the dangerous one. **First, a description you cannot check is a character that did not match.** If a key asks about the stem and there is no stem yet, you are not most of the way there. You are stopped. **Second, the parts that carry the answer are the parts that are absent for most of the year.** A flower is present for a few weeks. A fruit for a few more. A first-year rosette has no stem. A root requires digging, and in one of the three cases above, cutting the root is itself the exposure. So the reliable characters and the convenient characters are almost exactly opposite sets, and a person working from leaves in September is working from the weakest evidence at the worst time. That mismatch is the whole reason the next section exists. ## The year is part of the identification Identification and harvest are two separate events, and for the dangerous cases they happen months apart. The camas pair is the clean demonstration, but the pattern repeats. Poison hemlock's purple-blotched stem exists only after it bolts; its rosette sits there all winter with nothing to check. Water hemlock's tuberous root, which USDA identifies as where the toxin is principally found, is in the ground year round, including the months when nothing above ground marks the spot. Japanese knotweed, in the shipped records, gets the same treatment from the other end: identify the stand in full summer growth, mark it, and return to that marked stand in spring, rather than deciding what a young shoot is on the day you want to eat it. The general form: **identify the individual plant when it is showing you the most, mark it physically, and let the marker carry the identification forward to the day you harvest.** Your memory of a location is not a marker. A photograph with a date is evidence about a plant, not about the plant now in your hand. This is also why a species list without a calendar beside it is missing the dimension that makes half of it usable. The month-by-month calendar for this project's worked locale is in [Where You Are: Silverdale, Washington](/library#silverdale-wa). ## The carrot family, and why you leave all of it alone Apiaceae, the carrot or parsley family, is the one family a beginner should treat as a single closed door. Look at what is inside it. Water hemlock, which USDA calls the most violently toxic plant in North America, whose toxin cicutoxin acts directly on the central nervous system as a violent convulsant. Poison hemlock, poisonous in every part, whose piperidine alkaloids cause progressive paralysis, and which USDA records has killed children through whistles made from its hollow stems. And then, in the same family: parsnip, parsley, anise, carrot, celery, dill, fennel. Those are not two lists that happen to be adjacent. They are the same list. USDA's account of how people are poisoned by poison hemlock names three confusions, and every one of them is with a food: hemlock **root** for wild parsnips, hemlock **leaves** for parsley, hemlock **seed** for anise. Three different organs of the plant, three different foods, three routes into a kitchen. To a beginner, the whole family presents the same silhouette: finely divided leaves and small white flowers in flat or domed umbrella-shaped clusters. That silhouette is not an identification. It is a family resemblance covering a group that contains staple foods alongside the plant USDA calls the most violently toxic in North America and another that is poisonous in every one of its parts. So the instruction here is blunt and it is the shipped data's own: **leave the entire carrot family alone until somebody has taught you, in person, in front of the plant.** Not until you have read more. Not until you are confident. Until a competent person has stood next to you and shown you. The shipped records build this in deliberately. Water hemlock's lookalike list does not only name specific twins; it carries a catch-all entry for wild carrot-family plants generally, and the record says outright that the catch-all is the part that actually protects people, because it never designates any white-umbel plant as safe. Copy that habit into any list you build yourself. A list that names three safe plants in a dangerous family is more dangerous than a list that names none. ## Mushrooms are a different discipline This section is short on purpose, because mushrooms are not a harder version of this subject. They are a different subject with a different failure mode and a much shorter margin, and they deserve their own treatment rather than a paragraph in a plant document. What you need to know before you go near them: **Identification often cannot be done by looking at all.** The Forest Service's field guide to macrofungi states plainly that many mushrooms can be identified only by examining the colour of spore prints or by examining spores and tissues under a microscope. The same guide notes that the cup at the base of an *Amanita* is often below the soil surface, which is why mushrooms should always be dug rather than picked, and it repeats one line at the foot of every page: do not eat any mushroom unless you are absolutely certain of its identity. **Some of the deadliest species cannot be separated from each other even by an expert without a microscope.** That same guide records that *Amanita virosa*, *A. verna* and *A. bisporigera* can only be distinguished from one another by their spore characteristics, and that collectively they cause 95 percent of fatal mushroom poisonings. **There is no rule of thumb, and cooking does not help.** FDA states that for individuals who are not trained experts there are generally no easily recognizable differences between poisonous and nonpoisonous species, that folklore notwithstanding there is no reliable rule of thumb for distinguishing edible mushrooms from poisonous ones, and that most mushrooms that cause human poisoning cannot be made nontoxic by cooking, canning, freezing or any other means of processing. FDA records poisonings from mushrooms that were raw, stir-fried, home-canned, blanched and frozen, and cooked in tomato sauce, which can render the sauce itself toxic even when no mushroom is eaten. **The margin is the real difference.** Amatoxins are the toxin family in the death cap and its relatives, and the shipped record for the death cap identifies that species as responsible for most deaths following ingestion of foraged mushrooms worldwide. FDA describes their latent period as ranging from 6 to 48 hours, averaging 6 to 15, **during which the patient shows no symptoms at all**. CDC's account of a 2016 California cluster describes three phases: delayed gastroenteritis 6 to 24 hours after eating, then symptomatic recovery at 24 to 36 hours when the patient feels better, then liver and multiorgan failure typically 3 to 5 days in. CDC notes that patients evaluated early may be discharged home only to return later in liver failure. Of the 14 cases in that cluster, three needed liver transplants, and one child was left with permanent neurologic impairment. The National Park Service at Mount Rainier states that identifying wild mushrooms can be extremely difficult and consuming them can be deadly, that its own species descriptions are intentionally brief and are not sufficient to positively identify edible mushrooms, and that you should not collect or eat any mushroom unless you are 100 percent confident of its identification. A federal agency writing its own species descriptions, telling you its own descriptions are not enough, is the clearest possible statement of what reading can and cannot do here. If you want to see what real records for this look like, the shipped species file carries four fungi worth reading and none worth acting on: `death_cap`, `funeral_bell`, `fly_agaric` and, on the other side, `pacific_golden_chanterelle`, whose record spends most of its length on the ways a chanterelle is got wrong. Read them as a picture of the discipline. Do not read them as a key. ## The universal edibility test does not work Survival literature carries a procedure, usually called the universal edibility test, for deciding whether an unknown plant is safe. In its common form it runs roughly like this: fast for some hours; separate the plant into its parts and test one part at a time; hold a piece against your skin, then your lip, then your tongue, waiting between each; chew a small amount and hold it without swallowing; then swallow a small amount and wait several hours before eating more. **A sourcing note, stated plainly.** That description is of the procedure as it commonly circulates. This document could not open a primary government copy of it with readable text, so it is not quoted from one here, and no source opened for this document endorses it as a safety procedure. What follows is not an argument against a text. It is what the toxicology actually says about the plants and fungi this document has already described. **It is defeated by delay.** The test is built on the assumption that a dangerous plant will tell you within hours. Several of the ones that matter most do not. FDA describes the amatoxin latent period as 6 to 48 hours with no symptoms at all. The National Park Service, writing for visitors rather than for veterinarians, puts the effects of death camas at 1 to 8 hours after eating the plant. Any waiting period short enough to be practical sits inside those windows, and a waiting period long enough to clear them is not a field procedure. Be careful with onset times generally, including the ones in this document's own sources. Most published poisoning timings for wild plants come from livestock work, because that is who the research was funded to protect. The shipped water hemlock record flags this explicitly: the onset figures usually quoted for it are USDA's livestock figures, no human-specific window was found in a public-domain source, and none should be invented. A procedure that depends on knowing how long to wait is resting on numbers that mostly are not about you. **It is defeated by dose.** The test's later steps involve deliberately swallowing a small amount. For the plants in this document, a small amount is the lethal unit. USDA states that only a small amount of the toxic substance in water hemlock is needed to produce poisoning in humans, and that one or two death camas bulbs is enough to cause severe illness in a child while four or five can cause death. There is no sub-toxic tasting dose to work with. **It is defeated by preparation.** Cooking, drying and processing do not rescue you. FDA states that most mushrooms causing human poisoning cannot be made nontoxic by cooking, canning, freezing or any other means of processing, and the amatoxin literature at NIH describes the toxin as heat stable, toxic whether eaten raw or cooked. Washington's noxious weed board records that poison hemlock's toxins remain potent in dried plant material, so a wilted scrap is still lethal, and the Forest Service records that dried meadow death camas remains toxic for at least 20 years. **It is defeated by accumulation.** Some toxins do not act on the meal that contains them. The shipped chanterelle record, citing the Forest Service, describes Paxillus syndrome, in which the toxins accumulate in susceptible eaters over long periods with little effect and then the next meal can cause sudden illness or death. Against a mechanism like that, "I ate some and I was fine" is not evidence about anything. **It is a folk method, and FDA names folk methods as a cause of poisoning.** In its account of how mushroom poisonings happen, FDA records that intoxication has occurred when people relied on folk methods of distinguishing between poisonous and safe species. **And it inverts the one instruction every poisoning authority gives.** MedlinePlus, in its poisoning first aid guidance, lists among its do-not instructions: do not wait for symptoms to develop if you suspect that someone has been poisoned. The universal edibility test is, structurally, an instruction to deliberately poison yourself a little and wait for symptoms. That is the opposite procedure. The test also fails the positive identification rule on its own terms. It is a way of trying to prove a negative, by observing that nothing bad happened yet. Nothing bad happening yet is not a character you checked. It is the absence of evidence, on a clock too short to produce any. There is one thing in the vicinity that is genuinely sound, and it belongs to correctly identified food rather than to unknown plants: when you eat a species for the first time, even one you have identified with certainty, cook it properly and start with a small amount, because individual people react badly to things that are perfectly safe for everyone else. That is a rule about your own body, applied to a known plant. It is not a way to find out what the plant is. ## Tools, in the order to trust them None of these identifies a plant. You identify the plant. These are what you identify it with, and they are listed worst-last on purpose. | Tool | What it is actually good for | Where it stops | |---|---|---| | **A person who knows, standing next to the plant** | Everything. This is how the skill is transmitted, and there is no substitute for it | Finding one takes effort. The companion guide's section on cooperative extension is where to start | | **A key in a regional flora** | Forcing you through the diagnostic characters in a fixed order, and stopping you at the one you cannot answer | Assumes flowers or fruit, and a vocabulary you have to learn. A key you fudge your way through gives a confident wrong answer | | **A field guide** | Learning what to look at, and generating candidates | It identifies; it does not know your county, your month, or your legal status. See the companion guide | | **A local species list with lookalikes** | The "what else could this be" half, which is the half guides leave out | Only as good as its sources, and its blanks mean nobody looked, not that nothing is there | | **A photo identification app** | A first guess. A name to go and check properly | Measurably unreliable, including in exactly the way that hurts. See below | | **Your own memory of a plant you saw once** | Nothing | It is not evidence about the plant in your hand | On apps, there is a real measurement rather than an opinion. Long and colleagues, publishing in *Clinical Toxicology* in 2023, tested four common plant identification applications against 16 species chosen for local availability and potential for misidentification. Overall accuracy at genus level was 76 percent and at species level 58 percent, with a range across apps from 94 percent down to 34 percent. The finding that matters is not the average: **five of eleven potentially toxic species were identified as an edible species by at least one application.** The authors' conclusion is that the apps cannot be used to safely identify edible plants, and that foragers need adequate botanical knowledge to harvest wild plants safely. Read that failure mode carefully. It is not that the apps are vague. It is that they are confidently wrong in the direction that kills you, and they are wrong while displaying a name and a percentage. An app's output is a candidate to go and verify. It is never an answer, and a high confidence number is not a second opinion. **What the data shipped with this project can and cannot do.** The file `data/locales/silverdale_wa/species.json` is a local species list of the kind in the fourth row above: 122 records for one real place, each carrying legal status, edibility with its conditions, toxicity, and a lookalike list with a danger rating and a paragraph on telling them apart. It is a reference, and it is honest about its own gaps. The other file this topic names, `data/plants.csv`, is a **cultivation** database: growth days, water, nutrients, pH and yields for crops you plant on purpose. It carries no identification characters, no lookalikes and no toxicity, and nothing in it should be used to decide what a wild plant is. ## What competence actually looks like, over years Nobody becomes safe at this by reading harder. The habits below are practice rather than sourced findings, so treat them as a rule of thumb; but they are the shape of what the people who are genuinely good at this did. **Learn ten plants completely instead of a hundred approximately.** Ten species you know in every season, at every stage, with every dangerous lookalike eliminated by name, is a real skill. A hundred you could recognise in a photograph is a hazard with a large vocabulary. The shipped records are built for the first kind of knowledge, which is why a single record runs to several paragraphs. **Walk the same ground.** The same route, repeatedly, through the year. The value is not coverage, it is repetition: you meet the same individual plants at every stage, and you see the transitions that a guide can only describe. The rosette in February and the bolted stem in June being the same plant is a fact you learn by watching, not by reading. **Photograph the same individuals through the season.** Date and location, and the parts that matter: whole plant, stem, leaf underside, flower, fruit. This is the mechanism that makes the camas rule work at scale. A photo file that runs from flower to seed head to winter rosette is an identification you can still use in November. **Write down what you could not determine.** "I could not check the stem because there was not one" is more useful, a year later, than a confident name. A record that only contains your successes is a record that has hidden every place you were guessing. **Get your determinations checked by a person, out loud, in front of the plant.** Being told you are wrong is the entire point, and it is the one thing no document can do for you. ## If somebody has eaten something unknown Act on this immediately. Do not wait to be sure. 1. **Call Poison Control. In the United States, 1-800-222-1222.** It is run by America's Poison Centers, it reaches your local poison centre from anywhere in the country, and it is free, confidential and staffed around the clock. You do not need to be sure anything is wrong to call. If the person is unconscious, having seizures, or having trouble breathing, call emergency services first. 2. **Keep a sample of the plant, and keep it separate.** Poison control will ask what the plant was and which part was eaten. A physical sample, or the rest of what was picked, is often the only way to answer that. Where somebody has already vomited, MedlinePlus advises saving it, because it can help experts identify what medicine will help. 3. **Do not induce vomiting.** MedlinePlus is explicit: do not induce vomiting unless told to by poison control or a health care provider. Nor should you try to neutralise the poison with lemon juice, vinegar or anything else, or use any cure-all antidote, or give anything by mouth to somebody who is unconscious. 4. **Do not wait to see how it goes.** This is the one that costs lives, and it is on MedlinePlus's do-not list in those words: do not wait for symptoms to develop if you suspect somebody has been poisoned. **Feeling fine proves nothing, and here is the arithmetic behind that.** Several of the worst toxins have a symptom-free interval by design. FDA gives the amatoxin latent period as 6 to 48 hours with no symptoms, and CDC describes a second phase, 24 to 36 hours in, when the patient appears to recover, before liver failure arrives on day three to five. The cost of believing that second phase is measurable: FDA's figures put mortality at about 10 percent for patients given aggressive support almost immediately, against 50 to 90 percent for those admitted 60 or more hours after eating. **The time you spend waiting to see whether you feel ill is the single largest thing you control about the outcome.** For plants, USDA's own instruction in cases of water hemlock poisoning is the same: contact a poison control centre and obtain emergency medical assistance as quickly as possible. This is also why none of the above depends on knowing what was eaten. You do not need an identification to make the call. The call is how you get one. ## What this guide does not qualify you to do It does not qualify you to eat anything. It was not trying to. What it should have left you with: - **Identification is a positive match on every diagnostic character, plus the named elimination of every dangerous twin.** Anything less is a guess, and "it looks like" is how people die. - **A field character usually runs in one direction only.** Before you lean on one, know what its absence proves, which is often nothing. - **The parts that carry the answer are the flower, the fruit, the root, the stem and the smell, not the leaf**, and those parts are absent for most of the year, which is why identification and harvest are separate events joined by a physical marker. - **The carrot family stays shut** until somebody has taught you in person. - **Mushrooms are a different discipline** with a shorter margin and a symptom-free window, and belong to their own guide. - **No test you can run in the field tells you whether an unknown plant is safe**, and the tests that claim to are defeated by delay, by dose, by preparation and by accumulation. - **If in doubt, the answer is always the same, and it is free.** Leave it. There is no meal on the other side of this that is worth the other outcome. The two topics that come next, what is edible where you live and what will hurt you there, are separate guides for a reason. Go to them from the beginning and let them teach it properly, and let a person teach you the rest. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. Poison hemlock: a very tall biennial up to about 12 feet, hollow hairless stems with noticeable purple blotches, fern-like toothed finely divided leaves with a strong odour when crushed, toxins remaining potent in dried plant material, its resemblance to wild carrot, and its Class B listing. https://www.nwcb.wa.gov/weeds/poison-hemlock - Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board. Wild carrot: that it may be confused with poison hemlock although it is smaller and lacks purple blotches on the stems, that the whole plant is covered with coarse stiff hairs, its height of 1 to 4 feet, its flat-topped umbels 2 to 4 inches across often with purple or pinkish flowers in the centre, and its Class C listing. https://www.nwcb.wa.gov/weeds/wild-carrot - America's Poison Centers. Poison Help. The 1-800-222-1222 number, that it reaches the caller's local poison centre from anywhere in the United States, and that the service is free, confidential and available at all hours. https://www.poisonhelp.org/ ### Could not be opened for this guide Listed so nobody assumes they were consulted. - US Army Field Manual FM 21-76, the usual attribution for the universal edibility test. The archived scan located for this document has no text layer, so the procedure is described above as it commonly circulates rather than quoted, and the description is labelled as such in the text. - USDA Forest Service, Pacific Northwest Research Station, the Pacific Northwest chanterelle report (PNW-GTR-576). Its text could not be extracted from the PDF in this session, so the Paxillus syndrome accumulation point above is attributed to the shipped species record that cites it, not quoted from the report directly. https://www.fs.usda.gov/pnw/pubs/pnw_gtr576.pdf ### The locale data this guide's worked examples rest on The three worked pairs, the catch-all lookalike pattern, the onion-smell asymmetry, the knotweed mark-and-return rule and the honest "a beginner cannot reliably do this" verdicts all come from `data/locales/silverdale_wa/species.json`, which records its own source URLs per record and its own licence at the top of the file. Its provenance is US federal sources plus Washington State agencies restated in our own words, with nothing taken from GBIF, iNaturalist, Wikipedia or OpenStreetMap. The record shape is defined in `schemas/locale.toml`. `data/plants.csv` is a cultivation database and carries no identification or toxicity data; it is named here only to say what it is not. ### Companion guides in this collection - [The Species Where You Live](/library#the-species-where-you-live) - [The Hazards Your Place Actually Has](/library#the-hazards-where-you-live) - [Where You Are: Silverdale, Washington](/library#silverdale-wa) - [The Growing Calendar](/library#the-growing-calendar)

docs.text: # The Year of Wild Food A wild food calendar is not a table you memorise. It is a rhythm you learn by watching one place for a year. That distinction sounds like a nicety and it is not. A table tells you that salmonberry ripens in late June. The rhythm tells you that salmonberry ripens about a month after it flowers, that it flowers when the hummingbirds arrive, and that both of those happen earlier in a warm open clearing than in the shaded creek bottom two hundred metres away. The table is wrong somewhere every year. The rhythm is never wrong, because it is a relationship between things you can see rather than a promise about a date. This guide is about **when**, and only about when. It is not about what is edible, not about how to identify anything, and not about whether you should put it in your mouth. Those are separate topics and they are separate on purpose. See the last two sections before you go outside. The worked example throughout is one real place: `data/locales/silverdale_wa/phenology.json`, which ships with this project and holds the year at Silverdale, Washington as sixty-eight dated events across twelve months. The reading copy of it, month by month, is [Where You Are: Silverdale, Washington](/library#silverdale-wa). This document does not repeat that calendar. It teaches you how to read one, how to tell a strong entry from a weak one, and how to build your own wherever you live. ## Phenology is a real word for a real thing The study of when living things do what they do has a name. Phenology, which the National Park Service defines as the study of seasonal life-history stages in plants and animals: leaf-out, flowering, fruiting, nesting, migration, the falling of leaves. The useful part is what the science found out about the mechanism, because it explains why your calendar keeps being slightly wrong. **Plants do not read the calendar. They count warmth.** The standard measure is accumulated growing degree days. Take the amount by which each day's mean temperature exceeds a base temperature below which the organism does nothing, and add those amounts up across the season. A plant does not open its buds on 3 April. It opens them when the running total reaches a threshold, and the calendar date that happens on is simply whatever date the weather delivered that year. **Warmth alone does not explain it either.** Two other things are in the mechanism. The first is chilling. A Forest Service study of a young Douglas-fir plantation in western Washington found the terminal buds needed roughly 1,200 hours between 0 and 5 C before they would respond to warmth at all, and only then did temperatures above 5 C force bud burst by accumulating heat. A mild winter can therefore delay spring rather than advance it, which is not what anyone expects. The second is day length. Forest Service work on coast Douglas-fir found that in the warm parts of the species range, growth cessation in autumn is driven mainly by short photoperiods rather than by cold, so a warmer climate extends the season only slightly. Day length is the one input that no weather can change. February has February's light no matter how warm the afternoon is, which is the same fact that governs the vegetable garden and is worked through in [The Growing Calendar Where You Live](/library#the-growing-calendar). Here is the finding from that Douglas-fir plantation that should permanently cure you of trusting a date. In two of the three years studied, trees on the **cooler** microsites broke bud two to four days **earlier** than trees on the warmer ones. Not later. Earlier. Within one plantation, on one hillside, in the same year. The authors concluded that simple models of bud burst are inaccurate and that you need chilling, heat forcing, photoperiod and spring freeze events together to predict the sequence. If a research plantation with instruments cannot get this right from temperature alone, your notebook will not get it right from a date. ## Key off what you can see, not off the day of the month The practical conclusion is that you should learn **indicators**: the visible events that tell you where the year actually is, as opposed to where the calendar says it is. An indicator is any observable thing that reliably comes before, with, or after the thing you want. It works because it integrates the whole winter you actually had. It does not need to know the temperature record, because it has already lived through it. At Silverdale the best one is Indian plum. The Forest Service records that it flushes light green leaves and white flowers much earlier than the other plants it grows among, and explains why it does that: it gathers light for fruit set before the deciduous shrubs around it leaf out and shade it. The consequence for you is that when a bare grey thicket suddenly shows pale green, spring has started here. That is a better signal than any date, because a cold year moves the leaves and does not move March. The whole first half of the year has that structure, and the calendar file marks the sequence for you: - Hazel catkins on bare branches, the earliest flowering shrub here, through January to March. Nothing else is doing anything yet. - Indian plum leaves, the first green in the understory, February into March. - Skunk cabbage lighting up the wet ground, before most other growth. Where it grows, the water table is at or near the surface, which makes it a map as well as a clock. - Red alder flowering. In Snohomish County, a Puget Sound lowland county close enough in latitude and elevation to read across, flowering begins 29 March and the flowers have all fallen by 12 April. - Alder leaf bud burst on 3 April in that same record, fully leafed out by 2 May. This is the canopy closing over the creek bottoms, which changes the light on the ground for the rest of the summer. Three kinds of indicator are worth learning deliberately. **What is in leaf.** Leaf-out is the strongest single marker of where spring is, because it is unambiguous and it happens once. First green in the understory, then the shrub layer, then the canopy. **What is in flower.** Flowering is what tells you a fruit is coming and roughly how long you have. Salmonberry ripens 30 to 36 days after pollination, so the bloom is a countdown you can actually read. Flowers also carry other information: the Forest Service notes that salmonberry flowering aligns with rufous hummingbird migration, so the bloom tells you the birds have arrived as well. **What the ground is doing.** Saturated, drying, cracked, frozen, or soft after the first rain. This is the indicator that governs autumn here, because the mushroom season and the salmon runs are both triggered by rain rather than by date. One caution about indicators that a beginner will hit within a season. An indicator tells you the year has reached a stage. It does not tell you that a particular plant three valleys away has reached that same stage. Indicators travel badly across distance, elevation and aspect, which is why the answer is always the same: watch your own ground. ## The shape of the year in a marine climate Before any of the sequences make sense you need the shape of the year they sit inside, because the shape is what makes this place different from the one the field guide was written for. **There is a wet half and a dry half, and the split is extreme.** At Silverdale, October through March delivers 1,154 mm of the annual 1,446 mm. That is 79.8 percent of the year's water falling in the six cold, dark months, which is closer to four fifths than to three quarters. December alone brings 252 mm, nearly as much as April through September put together, which manage 294 mm across six months. The dry half is genuinely dry. July gets 21 mm and August 28 mm, against a July mean high of 24.7 C. People who move here are surprised by this in both directions: surprised that they have to irrigate in a place famous for rain, and surprised that anything ripens at all in a place that is bone dry through the whole ripening season. **The frost window is wide and the average date is a trap.** The last spring frost falls on 29 March on average, which means that in half of all years it falls later than that. It comes as early as 5 March and as late as 24 April. The first autumn frost averages 14 November, ranging from 26 October to 1 December. Between them sits a median of 227 frost-free days. Those six dates are the backbone of the whole calendar, and they are the only kind of entry on it that is measured rather than estimated. More on that below, because it matters more than it sounds. **Light collapses faster than temperature does.** Silverdale runs from 8.4 hours of daylight in December to 16.0 in June. September still averages 22.2 C for a high and it is already down to 12.6 hours of light. That gap between a warm month and a dark one is why autumn here feels like it should have more growing in it than it does. Put those three together and you get the local shape: a long, mild, generous season at both ends, pinched hard in the middle by drought, and pinched at the shoulders by light rather than by cold. ## Spring: the tightest window and the one people miss Spring at Silverdale carries very little food and it carries it very briefly. Counting every entry that carries food, whether fruit, seed or harvest window, the calendar file lists two in March, five in April and seven in May. Compare that with twelve in each of August and September and you can see the shape of the problem: the spring window is thin, it is early, and by the time most people start thinking about foraging it has closed. The sequence runs roughly like this. Nettle shoots reach cutting size around March and stay worth taking into May. Bracken croziers uncoil between March and early May. Knotweed pushes its reddish shoots up in April. Cattail shoots follow into May. Camas comes into bloom from late May. **Why a shoot is only worth taking for a short time.** This is the part that a table cannot convey, and it is the central idea of spring. A shoot is a plant spending stored energy to build new tissue fast. For those few weeks it is tender, low in fibre, and concentrated. Then the plant switches from growing to defending and reproducing, and the same tissue becomes tough, fibrous, bitter, or actively unpleasant. Nettle is the clean example. The calendar's rule is to cut the top few inches while the plant is still under about knee height, and to stop once it flowers. Older nettle develops gritty mineral deposits that irritate the urinary tract, so this is not a matter of the leaves merely getting tough. The plant stops being food. That transition is driven by the plant's development, which means it is driven by accumulated warmth, which means it does not happen on a date. It happens when the plant gets there. You have to be watching. Note also how the calendar handles the honest limits of its own evidence. The nettle entry is labelled local consensus rather than published range, and it says why: the Forest Service gives flowering from late May to October but publishes no shoot emergence date, so the start of that window is a regional generalisation rather than a measurement. The file will not dress it up. **One spring entry is a warning rather than a harvest.** The calendar lists bracken croziers, and its entry is explicit that the Forest Service records western brackenfern as mutagenic and carcinogenic in rats and mice, with all parts including the spores implicated, to the point that face masks are recommended for people working in dense stands. It is widely eaten as a fiddlehead and, on that evidence, it should not be. Its value on this calendar is as an indicator instead: croziers in the open are often killed by late spring frost, so a frosted bracken patch is telling you that ground is a frost pocket. That is not foraging advice and this guide is not the place you learn it. It is here because a spring section that listed the shoots and quietly left that one out would be teaching you something false by omission. **And one spring event is the most important timing lesson in the whole dataset.** Common camas blooms from late May, and that bloom is the only few weeks in the year when it can be told apart from meadow death camas, which grows in the same ground and whose bulbs are indistinguishable. Once the leaves die back and the seed disperses, nothing above ground marks which is which. The lesson is not about camas. It is about the structure: **the identification and the harvest do not have to happen on the same day, and for the dangerous cases they must not.** You walk the ground when the plant is identifiable, you mark what you found, and you come back later and take only what you marked. The calendar is what carries an identification forward across the months when identification is impossible. How you actually tell those two plants apart is not taught here. It is taught in the identification guides, and the reasoning behind that split is set out in [The Species Where You Live](/library#the-species-where-you-live). ## Summer: the berry sequence Summer is when a calendar is easiest and most fun, because the events are conspicuous and they arrive in a reliable order even though they arrive on unreliable dates. The order at Silverdale, from the calendar file: - **Indian plum** disperses first, beginning around May and nearly finished by July. Most people never see it because it is over before they start looking. Only the female plants fruit. - **Salmonberry** is the first fruit anyone notices, June into July. The calendar's practical note is worth more than its dates: colour is not ripeness. Salmonberries run yellow through orange to deep red and all of those can be ripe, so you judge by how easily the fruit lifts off. Because a patch ripens over several weeks rather than all at once, the patch yields for far longer than any single plant does. - **Trailing blackberry**, the native one, June through August. Small, seedy, far more strongly flavoured than the invasive Himalayan, and it trails along the ground on thin wiry stems rather than making thickets, so it is easy to walk straight over. Worth looking down for in July. - **Thimbleberry** through mid to late summer. A ten-year study recorded earliest ripe fruit on 30 June and latest on 3 September, which is a two-month spread for one species, recorded by people who were watching on purpose. - **Red huckleberry**, roughly July through September, often growing straight out of a rotting stump. - **Himalayan blackberry**, August into September. It ripens about a month after its native cousin and bears far more heavily. - **Salal**, August through October, and it hangs on the plant long after ripening, so its window is unusually forgiving. - **Blue elderberry** from about late August. - **Evergreen huckleberry** last of all, ripening July to September and often still hanging into October. Two things to take from that list, neither of which is a date. **The sequence is more reliable than the calendar.** Trailing blackberry before Himalayan, salmonberry before thimbleberry, everything before evergreen huckleberry. In a cold year the whole sequence shifts later together. In a warm one it shifts earlier together. The order holds. So if you know where you are in the sequence, you know what is coming next without knowing today's date at all. **The overlap is the resource, not any single species.** Look at the count of ripe fruit entries per month rather than at the species: one in May, four in June, eight in July, ten in August, nine in September, five in October. The abundance is not one plant bearing heavily. It is many plants overlapping, which is also why a single failed species barely registers, and why the season is far longer than any one shrub's. Note the honest disagreement the file preserves rather than smooths over. The red huckleberry entry records that the Forest Service table gives August to September for Washington while the local record says July through September, and concludes that late July is the early edge rather than a reliable start. A calendar that reported one number and hid the other would look more confident and be worth less. ## Autumn: the richest and most crowded part of the year Autumn here is not a winding down. It is the busiest stretch on the calendar by a clear margin, and everything arrives at once. September carries twelve food entries, four salmon runs and five hazard entries at the same time. October carries nine food entries, four runs and six hazards. Nothing else in the year is close to that density. Four things converge. **Fruiting shifts from berries to keepers.** Salal, evergreen huckleberry and blue elderberry come on late, hold longer, and dry and cook better than the soft summer fruit. The nuts land in the same weeks: hazelnuts through September, acorns falling around October. The calendar notes the practical problem with hazelnuts, which is that squirrels and jays strip them within days of ripeness, so the answer is to watch the husks from August and pick slightly early, then cure them, rather than waiting for a clean drop that never comes. **The fungi arrive, on rain rather than on a date.** The National Park Service records for Olympic National Park, directly across Hood Canal, that mushrooms can be found nearly year round but the peak season runs from the start of the fall rains until the first major frosts. That is a season with two moving ends: it opens whenever the first sustained rain after the summer drought happens to fall, and it closes at the first hard frost, which the climate normals put anywhere from 26 October to 1 December. In a year when the rain returns in early September the season starts a month earlier than in a year when it holds off. **The salmon come in.** Chum run late October into December, peaking in November, and they spawn in the lowest and most accessible reaches of the local creeks. Coho run September into December, and the calendar file flags them as the one run to watch the weather forecast for rather than the calendar: they hold at the creek mouths and wait for the first heavy rain to raise the water, so a dry October delays them and a big early storm brings them in days. **The first frost lands somewhere in the middle of all of it.** Ten percent of years have frozen by 26 October. Half by 14 November. Two consequences follow from that pile-up and they pull in opposite directions. Autumn is when a year's worth of storable food is available and it is also when you have the least time and light to process it, because September is already down to 12.6 hours of daylight and October brings 131 mm of rain. What you do with a glut you cannot eat is the subject of [Keeping What You Grew](/library#keeping-what-you-grew). Two more things share the season and are worth knowing about even though neither is food. Black bears feed hardest in September and October, in the same weeks and often on the same fruit. And the autumn mushroom flush brings the dangerous species up in the same woods, on the same rain, as the good ones, which is exactly why mushrooms are a separate discipline with its own guide and not a paragraph in this one. ## Winter, which is not empty People assume the calendar goes blank. At Silverdale it does not. The file lists seventeen events in January and twenty in December, and several of them are food. **What is still standing.** Madrone berries ripen from early autumn through December or January, which makes them one of very few fruits left when the year closes and disproportionately important to birds. Salal fruit persists on the stem until December. Oregon grape is evergreen, so the plants are findable in every month even when they are not bearing, and marking a good stand in winter costs nothing. Bigleaf maple seed disperses from October all the way into January, with some still hanging in March. **The one harvest unique to deep winter.** Bigleaf maple sap runs. Washington State University Extension records that Pacific Northwest maples are tapped December to February, when freeze and thaw events drive the flow, and that collection is generally limited to a three to four week window. It needs nights below freezing and days above, which here means a hard clear snap rather than a typical grey wet January week. So the usable window inside the season is short and unannounced, and you have to be ready to take it when it comes. Flow stops at bud break. **What the tide does, and why it is the most useful winter fact here.** This one is genuinely counter-intuitive. Dyes Inlet gets roughly the same number of deep minus tides every month of the year. In the summer half they fall around midday. In the winter half they fall in the middle of the night, between roughly 22:00 and 02:00 from November through February. The tide table will show you winter lows as deep as any in June and they are entirely real, but they are in the dark and in the cold. The lowest tide of 2026 is 3.7 feet below datum at 23:51 on 24 December. Across a whole year there are only about 22 to 26 daylight minus tides at or below 2.0 feet below datum, and they cluster in runs of four to six days around the new and full moon between about mid April and mid August. That is the sort of fact worth marking on a calendar a year ahead. The tide side of all this is worked through properly in [Reading the Tide](/library#reading-the-tide). **What the low light costs you.** December gives 8.4 hours of daylight and 252 mm of rain; January 8.9 hours and 236 mm. That is not just unpleasant. It is a hard limit on how far you can walk, how long you can work outside, how much you can see, and how quickly conditions change on you. A winter trip that would be trivial in July is a different undertaking in December, and the deep tides being at midnight is the sharpest example: the calendar file's own advice is to treat a winter minus tide as an expert trip rather than a family one. **And the hazards do not sleep.** The calendar carries more hazard entries in November and December than in any summer month. Water hemlock keeps its tuberous root in the ground all twelve months, with nothing above ground in winter to show where it is. Poison hemlock stands as a green rosette through winter, at the exact time of year when a field edge has little else green in it. Poison oak drops its leaves and keeps its oil on the bare stems, which removes the only identification character most people know, in the same season people gather firewood. Winter is not the empty part of the calendar. It is the part where the calendar stops helping you identify anything. ## Confidence: the best idea in the file This is the part to steal for anything you build yourself. Every one of the sixty-eight events carries a label saying **what kind of claim it is making**. The file's own definitions: - **measured**: computed from raw observations or predictions, or taken from a NOAA normal that was itself computed from observations. - **published_range**: a named source states this range, though usually for a region larger than Silverdale. - **local_consensus**: the species record and regional sources agree, but no single publication gives the date. - **estimated**: a regional generalisation applied here with no local source, and the event says so. The file states the principle plainly: nothing in it dresses an estimate as a measurement, and where the honest answer is that the timing varies too much to pin down, the event says that instead of giving a date. Now look at how those sixty-eight actually break down. Eight are measured. Forty-one are published ranges. Eighteen are local consensus. One is an estimate. And here is the finding that should change how you read every calendar you are ever handed. **All eight measured entries are weather or water.** The frost dates, the growing season length, the wet season, the summer drought, and the three tide entries. Every single biological event on this calendar, every leaf-out, every bloom, every berry, every salmon run, is a published range or a local consensus. Not one of them is measured here. That is not a defect in the file. It is an accurate report of the state of the evidence. NOAA has run a weather station here for decades and publishes tide predictions for this inlet, so the physical year is measured. Nobody has run a thirty-year phenology study in Kitsap County, so the biological year is borrowed from regional publications and neighbouring counties and read across. You can see the seams if you look. The alder dates are unusually precise, 29 March for first flower and 3 April for bud burst, because they come from a Snohomish County record close enough in latitude and elevation to use directly. The Indian plum bloom is given as January to May because that is the Forest Service range across the whole species distribution, and the file narrows it to February through April here and says that it is doing so. Twenty-four of the sixty-eight events carry no source URL at all, and those are the ones assembled from agreement rather than from a publication. **So the question to ask of any calendar, including one printed in a beautiful book, is: which kind of claim is this?** A date computed from thirty years of observations at this station and a regional generalisation borrowed from four hundred miles away are not the same claim, and they should not be printed in the same typeface without a label. Most calendars do not tell you. That silence is the thing to notice. ## The three things this calendar refuses to say The file names three things a reader might expect and will not find, and each refusal teaches something real. Quoted from the file: **"no month-by-month biotoxin season: closures have no season and the calendar must not imply the tide answers that question."** Marine biotoxins come from algal blooms, which the state health department tests for continuously, and a closure can appear in any month. The water looks clear during a toxic bloom, and cooking and freezing do not destroy the toxin because it is in the meat. The lesson is about the structure of the question: a good tide tells you the water will be low. It tells you nothing whatsoever about whether the shellfish are safe, and a calendar that printed both side by side would invite exactly that inference. **A separate authority answers a separate question, and it has to be checked live, on the day.** **"no mushroom dates: fruiting here is triggered by rain, not by the calendar, so a date would be a fabrication."** This is the difference between an event that is scheduled and an event that is triggered. Leaf-out is scheduled, loosely, by accumulated warmth and light, which vary within a range. Fungal fruiting here is triggered by a specific weather event whose arrival varies by a month or more. A date is the wrong shape of answer for a triggered event. The right answer is the trigger, which is why the file gives you the trigger and the frost window that ends it, and no month. **"no fixed shellfish beach seasons: those are set beach by beach and annually, and reprinting last year's would be worse than silence."** Worse than silence is the key phrase. A stale rule that looks current is more dangerous than no rule at all, because it removes the prompt to go and check. Anything set annually by an agency belongs in a live lookup, never in a document that ships. Those three refusals generalise into one question you can put to any calendar: **what is this document quietly implying it can answer, that it cannot?** The honest ones tell you. Most do not. ## Keep your own Everything above is preparation for the only thing that actually works. **Walk the same route, in the same week, for one year, and write down what you see.** That is the whole method. It is unglamorous and there is no shortcut, and at the end of it you will know more about the timing of your own ground than any published source can tell you, because no published source is about your ground. How to do it so it is worth having: **Pick one route and do not change it.** Twenty minutes is plenty. It should include several habitats if you can manage it: some woodland edge, some open ground, some wet ground, some shoreline if you have one. The value comes from repetition, so a short route you actually walk weekly beats an ambitious one you walk four times. **Go on a schedule, not on inspiration.** Weekly is the useful interval for spring, when things change in days. Fortnightly is enough for midsummer and midwinter. The trap is that you naturally go out when the weather is nice, which quietly biases your record toward the mild weeks and away from exactly the conditions that move the dates. **Record the stage, not the impression.** Write "first open flowers on three plants" rather than "flowering". Standard stages are easy and worth using: first green leaf tip, leaves unfolding, first open flower, full flower, first ripe fruit, most fruit ripe, leaf fall. The point is that a stage is comparable between years and an impression is not. **Record the date and the place precisely,** and record the absences too. "Checked, not yet" on 12 March is a data point. A gap in the notebook is not. **Note what was happening at the same time.** This is what turns a list of dates into a rhythm. If you write down that the alder was in flower in the same week the nettle reached cutting height, you have learned a relationship that will still be true in a year when both are three weeks late. **Expect the second year to be the useful one, and the third to be better.** One year gives you dates. Two give you a spread. Three start to give you a sense of what a normal year even looks like, and the honest answer will be that there is not really a normal one. **Then check your record against the published ranges rather than the other way round.** If your ground runs consistently earlier or later than the regional source, that offset is real information about your site, and it is more valuable than the published number was. If you want your observations to be worth something beyond your own notebook, the USA National Phenology Network runs Nature's Notebook, which is the national programme for exactly this and has been collecting standardised observations since 2008. A note about why this project does not use its data, because the reason is instructive rather than critical: USA-NPN releases its data under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence, which is genuinely open but is not the public domain. An attribution condition attaches to every copy of anything it is bundled into, so this project checked the terms and then deliberately did not use it, and the phenology file says so on its face. That constraint is ours and not yours. You have no release bundle to keep clean, so for your own notebook the network is a good place to send your observations and a good place to see what your neighbours are recording. ## What this guide does not qualify you to do It does not qualify you to eat anything. Not one thing. Everything above is about **when**. It says nothing about **what**, and nothing at all about **whether**. Those are different questions with different failure modes, and the failure mode for this one is mild while the failure mode for those is not. Being wrong about a date costs you a wasted walk. Being wrong about an identification can kill you. The separation is deliberate and it runs through this whole collection. Identifying a plant to species, knowing what is reliably edible where you live, recognising the poisonous ones, mushrooms as their own higher-stakes discipline, harvesting without ruining the resource, and shoreline and shellfish harvest are each a topic of its own with its own hazards. Go to them from the beginning and let them teach it properly. Nothing here is a substitute for any of them, and knowing that salmonberry ripens in late June is not permission to pick something red in late June. Two things in particular that this guide has deliberately left alone: - **How to tell camas from death camas.** This guide told you that the bloom is the only window in which the question can be answered and that you must mark the plants and come back. It did not tell you what to look at, because that belongs to the identification topic. - **Which mushrooms.** This guide told you that fruiting is triggered by rain and gave you no dates. It said nothing about species, because fungi are a higher-stakes discipline than plants and are taught separately for that reason. Three things to carry out of here instead: - **A calendar is a rhythm, not a timetable.** Learn the sequence and the indicators and you will be right in a year that no table predicted. - **Ask any calendar what kind of claim each entry is making.** Measured, published range, local consensus, estimate. If it will not tell you, that is your answer. - **Some questions a calendar cannot answer at all,** and a good one says so out loud instead of filling the gap with a plausible month. The foundations under all of that are in [The Species Where You Live](/library#the-species-where-you-live), which is the guide to learning the living things around you, and which is likewise not a foraging guide. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. Government publications are listed first because they are public domain and can be redistributed with this guide; the rest cannot. ### United States government (public domain) - National Park Service. Phenology and Climate Change: Understanding Nature's Language through Data and Community Science (the definition of phenology as the study of seasonal life-history stages; accumulated growing degree days as the number of degrees the mean daily temperature exceeds a base temperature below which an organism remains developmentally inactive; temperature and precipitation as the climate drivers analysed). https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/ips-phenology-and-climate-change.htm - National Park Service, Olympic National Park. Fungi (mushrooms findable nearly year round, with the peak season running from the start of the fall rains until the first major frosts). This is the nearest federal statement of the rain trigger, directly across Hood Canal from Silverdale. https://www.nps.gov/olym/learn/nature/fungi.htm - USDA Forest Service, Pacific Northwest Research Station. Bailey, J.D. and Harrington, C.A., 2006. Temperature regulation of bud-burst phenology within and among years in a young Douglas-fir (*Pseudotsuga menziesii*) plantation in western Washington, USA. Tree Physiology 26: 421-430 (the chilling requirement of about 1,200 hours at 0 to 5 C; heat unit accumulation above 5 C; freeze events resetting the accumulation; cooler microsites breaking bud 2 to 4 days earlier than warmer ones in two of three years; the conclusion that simple models are inaccurate and that chilling, heat forcing, photoperiod and spring freeze events are all needed). https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/24576 - USDA Forest Service. Ford, K.R., Harrington, C.A. and St. Clair, J.B., 2017. Photoperiod cues and patterns of genetic variation limit phenological responses to climate change in warm parts of species' range: Modeling diameter-growth cessation in coast Douglas-fir. Global Change Biology 23(8): 3348-3362 (growth cessation in the warm parts of the range induced primarily by short photoperiods in autumn, so warming extends the growing season only slightly). https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/54549 - USDA Forest Service, Fire Effects Information System. The species reviews behind the leaf-out, bloom and fruiting windows quoted above: red alder (the Snohomish County observations of flowering beginning 29 March, flowers fallen by 12 April, leaf bud burst 3 April, fully leafed out 2 May, and the October leaf fall), salmonberry (flowering March to June, first leaves by 21 March in western Washington, fruit June to July, alignment with rufous hummingbird migration), thimbleberry (the ten-year study recording earliest ripe fruit 30 June and latest 3 September), red huckleberry, evergreen huckleberry, salal, trailing blackberry, Himalayan blackberry, red and blue elderberry, bigleaf maple, California hazelnut, stinging nettle and western brackenfern. Each is cited per event in the phenology data file, which records the individual URLs. https://research.fs.usda.gov/feis - USDA Forest Service, National Seed Laboratory. Woody Plant Seed Manual, *Oemleria cerasiformis* (Indian plum flowering January to May concurrent with leaf development, leaves and flowers flushing much earlier than other plant associates, fruit dispersal beginning in May and nearly finished by July). https://www.fs.usda.gov/nsl/Wpsm/Oemleria.pdf - NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. 1991-2020 Climate Normals, station USC00450872 (the frost percentile dates, the growing season length, and the monthly precipitation and temperature figures quoted throughout). https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/normals-annualseasonal/1991-2020/access/USC00450872.csv and https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/normals-monthly/1991-2020/access/USC00450872.csv - NOAA Center for Operational Oceanographic Products and Services. Tide predictions, station 9445901 Tracyton, Dyes Inlet, on MLLW (the daylight and night-time minus tide analysis, the count of daylight minus tides per year, and the 24 December 2026 low). https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/ ### State agencies and universities (cited as the authority; text ours) State agencies and universities are not covered by the federal public-domain rule, so these are cited for the fact and the sentences are ours. - Washington State University Extension, forest farming. Bigleaf maple syrup: tapping in the winter months December to February on freeze and thaw events, with a three to four week collection window. https://extension.wsu.edu/wrlp/forestfarming/crops/maplesyrup/ - Washington State Department of Health, Marine Biotoxins. That closures have no season, that the toxin is in the meat so cooking and freezing do not destroy it, and that the status must be checked live. https://doh.wa.gov/community-and-environment/shellfish/recreational-shellfish/illnesses/biotoxins - Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife. That shellfish beach seasons are set beach by beach and annually, and the salmon run and viewing information behind the autumn section. https://wdfw.wa.gov/places-to-go/shellfish-beaches and https://wdfw.wa.gov/places-to-go/salmon-viewing ### Openly licensed, checked and deliberately not used - USA National Phenology Network, terms of use. Its data is released under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence, with a required acknowledgement that data were provided by the USA National Phenology Network and the many participants who contribute to its Nature's Notebook program, plus a dataset citation. That is open, and it is not the public domain: the attribution condition would travel with every copy of this project's release bundle, so the phenology data file checked these terms and then did not use the data. The network is not in `data/sources/registry.json` for the same reason. Recommended to individual readers for their own observations, where no such constraint applies. http://www.usanpn.org/about/terms ### Inside this project - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/phenology.json`, the source of every Silverdale date, sequence and count in this guide. Sixty-eight events across twelve months, each carrying its own confidence label and its own source URLs, plus the file's own statement of what it deliberately leaves out. - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/species.json`, which says what the events refer to: 125 plants, fungi, mammals, birds, fish and shellfish with their legal status here, edibility, toxicity and lookalikes. - [Where You Are: Silverdale, Washington](/library#silverdale-wa), the generated month-by-month reading copy of that calendar. This guide teaches how to read it; that document is the calendar itself. - [The Species Where You Live](/library#the-species-where-you-live) for the four questions, why a binomial beats a common name, and how to read a species record honestly. - [The Growing Calendar Where You Live](/library#the-growing-calendar) for the cultivated side of the same year: frost dates, soil temperature, day length and succession planting. - [Reading the Tide](/library#reading-the-tide) for the tide side of the shoreline entries. - [The Hazards Your Place Actually Has](/library#the-hazards-where-you-live) for the seasonal hazards this guide only names in passing. - [Keeping What You Grew](/library#keeping-what-you-grew) for what to do with an autumn glut. ### Labelled in the text as rules of thumb, not sourced - That indicators travel badly across distance, elevation and aspect. The underlying variation is documented in the Forest Service sources above; the practical warning is a generalisation from them. - That weekly observation is the right interval in spring and fortnightly in midsummer and midwinter, and that the second and third years of a notebook are the useful ones. These are ordinary observing-practice advice, not measured findings. - That a shoot is tender and worth taking because the plant is spending stored energy quickly, and becomes tough when it switches to reproduction. The specific nettle consequence is from the phenology file's own entry; the general principle is a rule of thumb.
