docs.text: # Taking Without Ruining It Kneel on the gravel at a minus tide, push a garden fork in past the tines, and lever up. A clam comes out with the gravel, squirting, about two inches across, oval, ribbed, a purple stain inside the shell at the siphon end. You know what it is. It is a Manila clam. It is excellent food. Nothing about it is poisonous today. You may still be committing a crime by putting it in your bucket. Not because you were wrong about the clam. Because of who owns the ground under your knees, what month it is, whether you bought a piece of paper in January, how big that clam is, how many are already in the bucket, and whether the state health department has this particular beach open for biotoxins today. Six questions, none of them answerable by looking at the clam, all of them independent, and any one of them can make the answer no. That is what this guide is about. The Library already has a guide on identifying what you find, and it opens by refusing to be a field guide, which is the right refusal. [Identifying Wild Plants](/library#identifying-wild-plants) covers the question "what is this and will it hurt me". This one covers the other half: **you were right, it is edible, and there are still reasons not to take it.** Most of those reasons are not obvious, several of them carry legal penalties, and a few of them are about damage you will never see because it happens after you leave. ## What this guide will and will not do It will not tell you the rule for the ground you are standing on. It cannot. The rule depends on the parcel, and the parcel changes every few hundred yards along a shoreline, and the number attached to it changes by year and sometimes by emergency order mid-season. What it will do is teach you the **shape** of the question, so that you know how many separate answers you need and where each one lives. That is a transferable skill. The specific numbers in here are worked examples for one place, Silverdale, on Dyes Inlet in Kitsap County, Washington, and every one of them was read on a real page on 15 September 2026. Some of them will be wrong by the time you read this. The structure will not be. Three honest warnings before anything else. **This is not legal advice and nothing here is a permission.** Where a number appears, it appears with the body that published it, so you can go and check. Checking is the skill; reading this is not a substitute for it. **The consequences are not symmetric.** Mistaking something you may take for something you may not is an offence, and in the case of a federally listed species it is a serious one. Mistaking something you may take for something you may not costs you a handful of berries. When you cannot resolve the question, the cheap error is available and you should take it. **Moralising is not the point here.** There is a whole genre of writing about foraging ethics that tells you to be respectful and gives you nothing you can check. Being told to "take only what you need" does not tell you that a geoduck limit is one clam and a horse clam limit is seven, and it does not tell you which of those two is in your hole. Where a checkable rule exists, this guide gives you the rule. Where none exists, it says so in those words rather than inventing a comforting one. ## The first question is whose land it is Beginners skip this one. It is the question with legal teeth, and it is the one that most often turns an innocent afternoon into a citation. **Permission is the default requirement, not the exception.** In Washington, entering or staying on someone else's property without permission is criminal trespass: second degree on premises, a misdemeanour, and first degree in a building, a gross misdemeanour. Ignoring a posted sign or a request to leave is enough. The project's own law layer carries this as rule `wa-criminal-trespass`, citing RCW 9A.52.070 and 9A.52.080. Note what that means for harvesting: the trespass is complete when you are standing there. Taking something is a separate matter on top of it. There is no general right to forage on land you do not own. Some countries have one. This one does not. ### The tideland trap This is the one that catches people here, and it catches them because the ground genuinely looks public. Washington sold most of its tidelands. The Department of Ecology's page on the public trust doctrine puts it plainly: the state sold 60 percent of tidelands before 1971. That land was sold as property, and it is still property. A stretch of gravel that is underwater twice a day, that has no fence because a fence would not survive, that you reached by walking along the water from a public access point, can be somebody's parcel with a deed and a tax bill. The Department of Fish and Wildlife says something about this that is easy to misread. Its shellfish beaches page states that in Washington, most state recreational harvest regulations do not extend to shellfish harvest on private tidelands for personal use. Read carefully, that is not a permission. It means the state's seasons and bag limits are not the rule that governs a private beach. **The rule that governs a private beach is the owner's.** The owner may harvest their own shellfish under different constraints than you face on a public beach; you may not harvest there at all without their permission. And the public trust doctrine, which people reach for at this point, does not rescue you. Ecology is candid that the doctrine protects commerce, navigation and fisheries, and that the state Supreme Court extended it to incidental recreational rights on the water. But on the specific question of walking on a private beach, Ecology's own page says no Washington court has ruled whether walking on the beach or wading in the water on privately owned beaches, streambanks and tidelands is a right under the doctrine. That is an unresolved question of law, stated as unresolved by the state agency that would know. **So: you can float over a private tideland in a boat. Whether you may stand on it is not settled, and taking shellfish off it without permission is not in doubt at all.** Use the state's public beach list and confirm the beach is on it. ### The public land ladder, and why the rungs disagree Once you are on public land, the next surprise is that "public land" is not one thing. Five categories of public land near Silverdale have five different harvest rules, and they do not vary in the direction you would guess. **A national park is the most restrictive by default.** The federal regulation for the National Park System, 36 CFR 2.1, prohibits possessing, destroying or removing plants or their parts. Gathering is not a right you have and then lose; it is prohibited unless somebody specifically turned it on. The exception reads: "The superintendent may designate certain fruits, berries, nuts, or unoccupied seashells which may be gathered by hand for personal use or consumption upon a written determination that the gathering or consumption will not adversely affect park wildlife, the reproductive potential of a plant species, or otherwise adversely affect park resources." Every clause in that sentence is doing work. **By hand**, so no tools. **Fruits, berries, nuts, or unoccupied seashells**, so not roots, not bark, not a live shell with an animal in it. **Upon a written determination**, so the default is no and somebody has to have written down a yes for that park. Where a superintendent has written one, the numbers are specific. Olympic National Park states that you can legally collect one quart per person, per day of mushrooms. Mount Rainier National Park allows one gallon of edible fungi per person per day for personal use or consumption. Two national parks, same state, same agency, and a four-fold difference. There is no national park rule. There is a rule for the park you are standing in. **A national forest is a different agency with different law, and it is not the same thing as a national park.** This confuses people constantly here because the two nearest units share a name. Olympic National Forest states that no permit is required for incidental gathering of mushrooms for personal use, and that you may collect up to one gallon per species per year, and that you may not sell or trade mushrooms. For berries the same forest allows one gallon per day, three gallons per year, with commercial use prohibited. Fiddleheads are one pound per person per day. Campers may collect downed dead wood for immediate use without a permit, and a free personal use permit covers up to six cords of firewood per calendar year. Put those two side by side, because the comparison is the lesson. Olympic National Park, the more protected designation, allows a quart of mushrooms **per day**. Olympic National Forest, the working forest, allows a gallon per species **per year**. A gallon is four quarts, so **four days of legal picking in the park equals the forest's entire annual allowance for one species.** Assume the park is the stricter of the two, pick accordingly, and you are over the forest's limit in the first week of the season. **Washington state parks have their own rule and it is the most generous of the lot.** WAC 352-28-030 allows recreational harvest, possession or transport of edible plants and edible fruiting bodies including, but not limited to, mushrooms, berries and nuts, up to two gallons per person per day unless otherwise posted, and the two gallons may be made up of one or more species. That is eight quarts a day, eight times Olympic National Park's daily limit. It applies in recreation, resource recreation, natural, natural forest and heritage areas and in parks not yet classified. It does **not** apply in a natural area preserve, where no harvest of edible plants or fruiting bodies is allowed at all. Harvest techniques involving raking, or other techniques with the potential to degrade park natural or cultural resources, are prohibited. Commercial harvest of edibles is not allowed on park lands. And the rule contains a clause worth noticing, which we will come back to: it does not limit federally reserved tribal rights, including treaty rights. **Department of Natural Resources land has yet another set of numbers.** DNR allows personal use harvest from some of its managed lands: mushrooms limited to three gallons of a single species per day, not to exceed nine gallons plus one mushroom per year; berries limited to three gallons of a single species per day, not to exceed nine gallons per year; brush and ferns limited to root ball removal of not more than two plants per person per day and not more than four plants per person per year. No reselling. Harvesting any forest products from DNR campgrounds and picnic sites, natural area preserves or natural resources conservation areas is prohibited unless the harvest is specifically included in the site's management plan. The "nine gallons plus one mushroom" is not a typo and it is not a joke. It exists so that a single enormous mushroom that tips you over nine gallons does not make you a criminal. Somebody thought about that. Note the arithmetic in DNR's pair of numbers: three gallons a day against nine gallons a year means **three good days exhaust your year**, for that species. The daily limit is not the one that will catch you. The annual one is, and nobody is counting it for you. **County parks may prohibit it outright.** Kitsap County Code section 10.12.050 makes it unlawful to remove, destroy, mutilate or deface any tree, shrub, flower or other plant, or any rock, cliff or other natural feature, in a county park. "Park" is defined broadly at 10.12.020(1) to include any park, playground, beach or recreation centre owned or used by the county under the park director's supervision. A violation is a misdemeanour under 10.12.190. So the default on county ground is stricter than on state park ground, and a county **beach** is inside that definition. There is a carve-out, and I could not read it. Kitsap County Parks' rules page refers to a separate document called "Mushroom Harvest Policies", and a 2014 county resolution exists under that name, but neither the resolution PDF nor the stewardship plan that quotes it would render as readable text for me today. So I can tell you a county mushroom policy exists and that the general prohibition in 10.12.050 would otherwise cover mushrooms, and I cannot tell you what the policy says. Call Kitsap County Parks on 360.337.5350 before picking in a county park. That is the number on their own rules page. ### The comparison, in one place Mushrooms, because they are the one product with a number in every jurisdiction: | Land | Mushroom limit for personal use | |---|---| | Olympic National Park | 1 quart per person per day | | Mount Rainier National Park | 1 gallon per person per day | | Olympic National Forest | 1 gallon per species per calendar year, no permit | | Washington state parks | part of 2 gallons per person per day of all edibles, none in a natural area preserve | | Washington DNR land | 3 gallons of one species per day, max 9 gallons plus one per year | | Kitsap County parks | general prohibition at KCC 10.12.050, separate mushroom policy I could not read | | Private land | whatever the owner says | Five different numeric limits, one flat prohibition, and no way to derive any of them from any other. The spread between the tightest daily figure and the loosest is twelvefold: Olympic National Park allows a quart a day, DNR land allows three gallons of one species a day, and three gallons is twelve quarts. The only safe generalisation is that **there is no general rule**, and the question "how much may I pick" has no answer until you have answered "where am I". ### A pass is not a permission A Discover Pass costs 45 dollars a year or 10 dollars for a day and covers parking at recreation lands managed by Washington State Parks, the Department of Fish and Wildlife and the Department of Natural Resources. Note what it is: **parking.** It buys you the right to leave your car there. It carries no harvest right whatsoever, and the harvest rules on those three agencies' lands differ from each other, as above. A shellfish licence is a separate purchase. A specialized forest products permit is a third. People conflate them because they are all pieces of paper bought from the state. ## Tribal treaty rights, which are law and not courtesy Silverdale sits inside the usual and accustomed areas of treaty tribes, and the Suquamish Tribe is the local nation. This is not a cultural footnote to a harvesting guide. It is a live legal framework that determines who may take what from the beach you are standing on, and it is older than the state of Washington. **The source is a treaty, and a treaty is federal law.** The Treaty of Point Elliott was signed on 22 January 1855 by the Dwamish, Suquamish and some twenty other named tribes and bands. Because it is a federal instrument it is public domain, and Article 5 is short enough to give whole: > The right of taking fish at usual and accustomed grounds and stations > is further secured to said Indians in common with all citizens of the > Territory, and of erecting temporary houses for the purpose of curing, > together with the privilege of hunting and gathering roots and berries > on open and unclaimed lands. Provided, however, That they shall not > take shell-fish from any beds staked or cultivated by citizens. Read the verbs. The right is **secured**, not granted: the tribes reserved it, they did not receive it. It runs to **usual and accustomed grounds and stations**, which are specific places, not a general licence. And it is held **in common with all citizens**, three words that the later litigation had to work out the meaning of. **The courts quantified it.** In 1994 the federal district court took up shellfish specifically, in the proceeding usually named for Judge Rafeedie. As the Northwest Indian Fisheries Commission describes the outcome, the tribes hold harvest rights to half of all shellfish from all of the usual and accustomed places; all public and private tidelands within the case area are subject to treaty harvest, with an exception for artificially created beds and places specifically set aside for non-tribal shellfish cultivation, which is the modern reading of the treaty's "staked or cultivated" proviso; and tribal harvest on private beaches is subject to extensive time, place and manner restrictions. The Supreme Court declined to hear the case in 1999. **Read that sentence about private tidelands again, because it is the one that surprises people.** A private beach in Puget Sound is private against you. It is not private against a treaty right that predates the deed. **Co-management is real and current, not historical.** The Suquamish Tribe describes itself as one of 24 treaty tribes in the Puget Sound area that co-manage shellfish resources with the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, surveys beaches within its usual and accustomed area, and manages half of the total allowable catch on private and public beaches as the Treaty Share, with the state managing the other half, excepting tidelands identified as staked and cultivated under the Shellfish Growers Settlement. So when you read a WDFW beach season, you are reading the state's management of the state's half of a jointly managed resource. The number is not the whole of what the beach can give; it is the part of it allocated to you. Washington's own rules acknowledge this in their text. WAC 352-28-030, the state parks harvest rule, carries an explicit clause that it does not limit federally reserved tribal rights including treaty rights. A state rule cannot reach them, and it says so. **What this means for you, practically.** Three things, none of them onerous. Treaty harvest you may see happening on a beach, including one you thought was closed or one that is privately owned, is very likely lawful under a framework that does not run through the rules you were reading. It is not poaching and it is not your business to police. The Suquamish Tribe is a government with a fisheries department, not an interest group. If a question is about shellfish management around Dyes Inlet, they are one of the two co-managers holding the answer. And the treaty's own words are worth carrying: hunting and gathering roots and berries on **open and unclaimed lands.** In 1855 that phrase described most of this peninsula. The reason so little of it is open and unclaimed now is the same reason your own harvest question keeps coming back to who owns the ground. ## What "protected" means, as a verb "Protected" is a word people nod at without knowing what it prohibits. It is worth knowing, because the prohibited acts are broader than most people assume and they differ sharply between animals and plants. The Library's companion guide, [The Species Where You Live](/library#the-species-where-you-live), carries the inventory: which species here are listed, what each listing is, and why a blank field is not a clearance. That guide is the list. This section is the verbs. ### The federal layer **The Endangered Species Act defines "take" very broadly.** At 16 U.S.C. 1532(19), take means "to harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect, or to attempt to engage in any such conduct." Harass and harm are in there alongside kill. Attempting counts. For a listed animal, you do not have to catch it or hurt it to have taken it. **But the Act treats plants completely differently, and almost nobody knows this.** Section 1538(a)(1) prohibits taking listed fish or wildlife within the United States. Section 1538(a)(2), the plant provision, prohibits something much narrower: to "remove and reduce to possession any such species from areas under Federal jurisdiction; maliciously damage or destroy any such species on any such area; or remove, cut, dig up, or damage or destroy any such species on any other area in knowing violation of any law or regulation of any State or in the course of any violation of a State criminal trespass law." Parse the third clause. Off federal land, digging up a federally endangered plant is a federal offence **only if** you were also breaking a state law or trespassing. A listed animal on private land is protected by the Act. A listed plant on private land, absent some other violation, largely is not. That asymmetry is in the statute, it is deliberate, and it is the single most surprising thing in federal conservation law for somebody coming to it from the animal side. **The Migratory Bird Treaty Act covers parts, nests and eggs, which is why the feather on the trail is a problem.** 16 U.S.C. 703(a) makes it unlawful, unless permitted by regulation, "at any time, by any means or in any manner, to pursue, hunt, take, capture, kill, attempt to take, capture, or kill, possess, offer for sale, sell..." and continues through barter, purchase, ship, export, import, transport and carry. The protection extends to "any part, nest, or egg of any such bird" and to any product composed in whole or part of a bird, part, nest or egg. **Possess** is on that list, and **any part** covers feathers. A handsome flight feather picked up off the ground is a part of a protected bird, and possessing it is inside the literal prohibition. Whether anyone will ever bother you about one is a separate question from whether it is lawful, and the honest answer to the first is usually no and to the second is no as well. An empty nest is likewise named in the statute. If you want a feather in your house, buy one from a species the Act does not cover. **Marine mammals are protected by a third statute with its own definition.** Under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, take means to harass, hunt, capture, or kill, or attempt any of those, and the Act distinguishes Level A harassment, which injures, from Level B harassment, which disturbs behaviour patterns including migration, breathing, nursing, breeding, feeding or sheltering. NOAA Fisheries administers it for whales, dolphins, porpoises, seals and sea lions; the Fish and Wildlife Service for walrus, manatees, sea otters and polar bears. Level B harassment is the one that catches ordinary people. **Making an animal change what it was doing is take.** The shipped species data carries the local distances: NOAA guidance to observe seals and sea lions from at least 50 yards and to limit observation to 30 minutes or less (record `harbor_seal`); and for Southern Resident killer whales, a federal prohibition on approaching within 200 yards or positioning a vessel in their path within 400 yards, with Washington requiring boaters to stay 1,000 yards away since 1 January 2025, a state rule that applies to kayaks and paddleboards as much as to motorboats (record `killer_whale`). Where two rules apply, the stricter binds. A seal pup alone on a beach is not abandoned and is not yours to help. Approaching it is the take. ### The state layer Washington's protected wildlife rule, WAC 220-200-100, is titled with its own operative sentence: wildlife classified as protected shall not be hunted or fished. It has three buckets, threatened, sensitive and other, and the "other" bucket is enormous. It sweeps in all birds not classified as game birds, predatory birds or endangered species, mammals of the orders Cetacea and Pinnipedia, all bats except those in or near occupied buildings, and named species like the painted turtle and the California mountain kingsnake. Washington's predatory birds are only six species. Everything else with feathers that is not a game bird is protected wildlife, with no season, no licence and no bag limit, which means no lawful way to take one. The companion species guide works this through with the Steller's jay and the Douglas squirrel, and it is worth reading there rather than repeating here. **And here is the plant asymmetry again, at state level.** Washington's rare plant list is maintained by the Natural Heritage Program inside the Department of Natural Resources, which assigns plants a state conservation status of Endangered, Threatened, Sensitive or Possibly Extinct or Extirpated, and tracks nearly 400 plants and nonvascular species with conservation status, twelve of which are also listed under the federal Endangered Species Act. The same page states that legal responsibility for managing fish and wildlife species in the state is held by the Department of Fish and Wildlife. Notice what that division implies and be careful about what it does not prove. The agency that holds the enforcement power over wildlife is not the agency that holds the rare plant list. I could not open a page today that states in terms whether Washington generally prohibits taking a rare plant, so **I am not going to tell you it does or that it does not.** What I can tell you is that a state Endangered listing for a plant and a state protected classification for an animal are issued by different agencies under different authorities and should not be assumed to carry the same consequences. If you are about to dig something that appears on the Natural Heritage list, ask the Natural Heritage Program what the status means before you do, rather than guessing in either direction. ### Protection you would never guess from rarity Two of Washington's harvest rules have nothing to do with a species being scarce, and they bite ordinary people. **Specialized forest products.** RCW 76.48 sets thresholds above which picking becomes a regulated activity needing both a specialized forest products permit and the landowner's permission. More than 20 pounds of cut or picked evergreen foliage, which the statute defines to include evergreen boughs, huckleberry foliage, salal, fern, Oregon grape, rhododendron, mosses and bear grass. More than 5 pounds of cascara bark. More than 5 gallons of wild edible mushrooms. More than 5 Christmas trees. More than 5 native ornamental trees or shrubs, meaning ones lifted with the roots intact. Cones, berries and seeds are excluded from the foliage definition. None of those species is rare. The law exists because brush picking is a real industry on this peninsula and the permit system is how landowners and enforcement tell a picker from a thief. But it means a cheerful afternoon cutting salal for a wreath business crosses a legal line at 20 pounds, and it means the 5 gallon mushroom threshold sits underneath every one of those agency limits in the table above as a second, independent constraint. **Forest practices.** Significant timber harvest is regulated under RCW 76.09 and generally needs an approved forest practices application; cutting a few trees on a residential lot usually falls to county clearing and critical areas rules instead. The project's law layer carries this as `wa-commercial-forest-cutting-follows-forest-practices-rules`. If what you want is a tree rather than what grows on one, this is the regime you are in. ## Licences, seasons and limits, worked on shellfish Shellfish is the live case here, because Dyes Inlet is on the doorstep and because the rules stack in a way that teaches the general shape better than anything else does. **Three independent authorities must all say yes, and a fourth question sits underneath them.** You need a licence. The Department of Fish and Wildlife must have that specific beach open, within its size and bag limits. And the Department of Health's biotoxin status for that beach must be open on the day you go. WDFW puts the first two together bluntly: to harvest shellfish for human consumption safely and legally, both the health status and the WDFW season for a public beach must be open. Underneath all three sits the ownership question from the top of this guide, because most tideland here is private. **The biotoxin question belongs to a different guide and you should go and read it.** [Reading the Tide](/library#reading-the-tide) covers it properly, including why cooking and freezing do not help and why a toxic clam looks, smells and tastes normal. The one thing to carry over here is that the tide is what makes digging possible and has nothing whatsoever to do with whether the animal is safe to eat. Two independent questions. The hotline is 1-800-562-5632 and the answer expires daily. **The licence.** Washington requires a licence to fish or shellfish regardless of residency, and everyone aged 16 and over needs one. A resident shellfish and seaweed licence is 21.58 dollars; non-resident 47.39; resident senior aged 70 and over, 13.99. The annual combination licence, which covers freshwater and saltwater fishing as well, is 74.37 for a resident aged 16 to 69, 28.83 for a resident senior, 12.89 for a resident with a disability, and 170.00 for a non-resident. WDFW states that prices shown include all applicable fees and that buying multiple items in one transaction may reduce the cost. The step from shellfish-only to the full combination is 52.79 dollars. ### Why this guide will not restate the limits The shipped species data at `data/locales/silverdale_wa/species.json` already carries sourced WDFW limits for every shellfish here, with the URL each one came from, in the `protected` and `season` fields. The record ids are: `manila_clam`, `pacific_littleneck_clam`, `butter_clam`, `basket_cockle`, `varnish_clam`, `eastern_softshell_clam`, `fat_gaper_horse_clam`, `geoduck`, `pacific_oyster`, `olympia_oyster`, `bay_mussel`, `dungeness_crab`, `red_rock_crab`, `spot_shrimp`. Go there for the numbers rather than trusting the ones in a document like this, and here is the concrete reason why. The basket cockle's minimum size was raised to 2.5 inches in 2026, larger than the 1.5 inch minimum that applies to other clams, and WDFW gave its reasons as heat sensitivity, harmful algal blooms and a newly identified bivalve disease. That is a rule that changed inside the last year for biological reasons that were not known a few years ago. **A limit is a living number and a document is a fossil.** Any guide that hard-codes a bag limit into prose is wrong on a schedule. What is worth learning is the **shape** of the limits, because the shape is stable even when the numbers move: **Limits come in incompatible kinds.** A combined limit across many species, with exclusions: no more than 40 clams and not more than 10 pounds in the shell, excluding horse clams and geoducks. A first-dug limit, where you keep what comes up whether you like it or not: the first 1 geoduck, the first 7 horse clams, regardless of size or condition. A per-species count: 18 oysters. A sex-and-size limit: five male Dungeness crab at 6.25 inches carapace width, everything soft, female or undersized released. Four different mental models, all in force on the same beach on the same afternoon. **Two caps on the same limit means one of them binds first.** Forty clams and ten pounds works out to four ounces a clam. If the clams on your beach average more than four ounces in the shell, **you will hit ten pounds well before forty clams**, and the count is not the number to be watching. Work out which cap binds for the animals actually in front of you rather than counting to the headline number. **A first-dug limit removes your judgement on purpose.** You do not get to dig ten geoducks and keep the best one. The first one is yours and that is the end of the day's geoduck. The rule is written that way precisely to stop the sorting behaviour, because sorting means digging up and discarding nine animals that are unlikely to survive being dug. **Some species have no minimum size, which is not a licence to take small ones.** Softshell clams and varnish clams have no minimum. The varnish clam is an established invasive, so the reasoning there is obvious. The absence of a number is not an endorsement. **And some limits are pure conservation and pure closure.** The Olympia oyster, Washington's only native oyster, is not open for recreational or commercial harvest of wild stock, and the record `olympia_oyster` notes that by 2012 only about 5 percent of its historical bed habitat remained. The 2.5 inch minimum for oysters does most of the practical protecting, because almost no Olympia oyster ever reaches it. Which gives you the one rule worth memorising for this beach: **if an oyster is under 2.5 inches, leave it, whichever species you think it is.** **Where the data admits it does not know, it says so, and so should you.** The `bay_mussel` record states outright that the daily limit and minimum size for mussels could not be confirmed from a citable WDFW page, and tells you to look it up in the current sport fishing rules rather than assume it matches the 40 clam limit. That is the correct behaviour from a dataset and it is also the correct behaviour from you. ### The rules that are about the beach rather than the animal Buried in the shellfish rules is a second category people miss entirely, because they scan for numbers and these have none. They are not bag limits. They are instructions about leaving the habitat functional. **Refill your holes.** WDFW requires clam harvesters to refill the holes they dig, and advises pushing undersized or discarded clams into the refilled hole to reduce mortality. A clam left lying on the surface of a gravel flat does not walk back down. It dies, or a gull has it. The hole itself is also a problem: it changes drainage and it buries the neighbours. **Shuck oysters on the beach and leave the shells.** This one has no equivalent in the clam rules and people break it without realising. The WDFW rule, as carried in the shipped record `pacific_oyster` with its source URL, is that oysters must be shucked on the beach and the shells left on the same tideland at the same tide height where they were taken. The reason the same record gives is structural: the shell is the hard surface the next generation settles on, so removing it removes the reef. **The shell is the reef.** Carry a bucket of shells home and you have not just taken the oysters, you have removed the surface the next generation needed, from the exact tide height where it needed to be. WDFW's March 2026 season release repeated it: leave oyster shells on the beach and refill dig holes, to avoid damaging habitat and killing clams. **Oysters you eat on the beach count against your limit.** Obvious once stated, routinely ignored. **Each harvester needs their own container and must actually be harvesting.** The point of that rule is to stop one person filling several limits under other people's licences. **Spread out.** WDFW's own advice is to visit less popular beaches to spread harvest pressure, and separately not to park unsafely or illegally along busy roadways, which is how a good beach becomes a closed one. ## Harvest that does not destroy the population Now the part where honesty is harder, because the law runs out and the science is uneven. Some of what follows is well established. Some of it is reasoning from mechanism. Some of it is custom wearing a lab coat, and I will say which is which. ### What part you take changes everything The single most useful distinction in harvesting is not which species it is. It is **which part of the individual you are taking, and what that part was for.** **Fruit is the plant's reproductive surplus, and taking it is usually cheap.** A berry exists to be eaten; that is the entire strategy. The plant has already spent the energy, the seeds are already made, and being eaten is how they travel. Taking fruit does not remove the individual, does not remove next year's growing points, and in the normal case costs the plant the dispersal it wanted rather than the plant itself. This is why fruits, berries and nuts are the category that even the national parks rule is willing to designate for gathering: 36 CFR 2.1 names precisely "fruits, berries, nuts, or unoccupied seashells" and nothing else. That said, the fruit was not only for you. On this peninsula, berries are a food supply for birds and mammals at the exact moment they need to put on mass. Taking all of a small patch is not a plant conservation problem; it is an ecosystem one, which [How an Ecosystem Holds Together](/library#how-an-ecosystem-holds-together) treats properly. **A leaf is a cost the plant actually pays.** Leaves are the photosynthetic machinery. Stripping them removes the plant's ability to make the sugar it needs to refill its roots before winter, and the cost compounds if you come back to the same individual repeatedly in a season. A plant can lose some leaf area routinely, because being browsed is normal; it cannot lose most of it repeatedly without drawing down reserves it will need. **A root or a bulb is the whole individual, and that is not a metaphor.** This is where harvesting stops being a tax and becomes a removal. The clearest sourced statement of it comes from the Fish and Wildlife Service on American ginseng, whose harvest is regulated precisely because of this: "The harvest of a ginseng root kills the plant, that is why it's important never to harvest underage or undersize plants." Ginseng is worth understanding even though it does not grow here, because it is the best-documented case in the country of a root harvest that needed rules. It was placed in Appendix II of CITES in 1975, so an export permit is required. All wild and wild-simulated roots for export must come from plants five years of age or older, which is read off the rhizome as four or more stem scars; most states that permit harvest require five years and three compound leaves, called prongs. In all 19 states that allow it, the season starts in September, which is when seeds are ripe and can be planted back. And the international shipment must not be harmful to the survival of the species. Look at what that rule set is doing. It is not limiting how many roots you take. It is **requiring that every individual you kill has already reproduced several times**, and timing the season so the seeds go back in the ground. That is a fundamentally different design from a bag limit, and it is the design that root harvests need. Locally, the same logic applies to anything taken as a bulb or a tuber, common camas being the obvious one here. **Bark is often fatal, and the geometry is the whole story.** Bark carries the living tissue that moves sugar from the leaves down to the roots. Take a strip and the tree routes around it. Take a complete ring and there is no route. Be careful about what is cited here and what is not. I could not open a primary federal page today stating that mechanism in terms; the Forest Service documents on girdling that I tried are scanned or encoded and would not render as text. **Treat the mechanism as reported rather than cited by me.** What I **can** cite is the other side of it. Forest Service research on bark-peeled ponderosa pines in the Bitterroot Mountains dated the peelings from the mid-1600s until the early 1900s, found the scars on living as well as dead trees, and dated them by dendrochronology precisely enough to read off who was there and when. The study concludes those trees should be recognised as ecologically and culturally valuable features of old pine forests. Note carefully what that does and does not establish. It establishes that partially peeled trees carry dateable scars and are found alive, over a span of roughly 300 years of harvesting. It does not, by itself, quantify how often a peeled tree dies, and the study I opened does not address that. So the defensible statement is the narrow one: **partial bark removal leaves trees that go on living, and the geometry is what differs between taking a strip and taking a ring.** Washington has already put a number on the commercial end of it: more than five pounds of cascara bark makes you a specialized forest products harvester needing a permit and the landowner's permission. ### Perennial and annual are not the same animal An annual plant lives one season and reproduces once. Take it before it seeds and you have removed it and its entire contribution to next year's population in one act. Take it after it has seeded and you have taken a corpse. A perennial carries over. Its reserves are in a root, a rhizome, a bulb or a woody frame, and the harvest question becomes whether you took a part it can rebuild from stored energy or the store itself. That is why the part-taken distinction above matters more for perennials, and why the timing question matters more for annuals. This is mechanism, not a cited finding, and it is the kind of reasoning that should change what you do rather than being a fact you memorise. Before taking anything, ask: does this individual get another season, and did I just take the thing it needed to have one? ### Why the patch tells you nothing about the recovery Here is the problem that makes foraging harder than it looks, and no amount of care on the day solves it. **A patch that regrows in one year and a patch that regrows in twenty look identical on the day you harvest.** They are both green, both abundant, both apparently fine. The difference is in growth rate and reproductive age, which are invisible. You get exactly one observation, at one moment, and the variable you need is a rate. Which means the feedback loop that would normally teach you is broken. If you overharvest a fast-recovering patch, next year looks fine and you learn that you did no harm. If you overharvest a slow one, next year also looks roughly fine, because slow decline over twenty years is not visible year to year to a person who visits a few times a season. **You will get the same signal in both cases, and the signal will be reassuring in both cases.** The slow patch is the one you have to reason about rather than observe, and reasoning means knowing how old the individual has to be before it reproduces. Ginseng's five years is the worked example: a rule that exists because the observation on the day cannot tell you. ### Taking the biggest, and what I could not verify A thing that gets repeated, correctly in spirit, is that consistently taking the largest individuals selects against the population over generations, because the largest are disproportionately the reproducers and because size is heritable. The paper most often cited for it in plants is titled "Human-induced dwarfing of Himalayan snow lotus", which tells you its conclusion from the title alone. **I could not open that paper today.** The journal returned 403, PubMed returned a cookie wall, and the full text on PMC returned a security check. I do not restate a source I could not read, so: the claim exists, I could not verify it, and you should not take the numbers from me. What I **can** show you is that the regulators behave as though the underlying concern is real. That is weaker evidence, but it is checkable. Almost every harvest rule quoted in this guide is structured to protect individuals that have not yet reproduced, rather than to cap the total take: - Shellfish minimum sizes, so a clam spawns before it is legal. - Ginseng's five-year, four-stem-scar requirement for export. - The oyster minimum of 2.5 inches, which incidentally shelters the entire Olympia oyster population. - The cockle minimum raised to 2.5 inches in 2026 for stated sustainability reasons. Notice the direction. Every one of those says take the **older and larger** ones, which is the opposite of what selection pressure would recommend and the same as what population maintenance requires: leave the juveniles until they have bred. Both concerns point at the same practical behaviour for a harvester, which is to take the middle and leave both ends, and to leave the exceptional individual alone. I am labelling that as reasoning and as what the rules imply, not as a finding I sourced today. ### The rules of thumb, and which of them are just custom Now the direct answer to the question this section exists for. You will read, in foraging books, on blogs and in the mouths of otherwise careful people, that you should take no more than one third of what is present. You will also read one in ten. You will also read five percent. Sometimes the third is explained as one for you, one for the animals, one for the plant. **I went looking for a published basis and did not find one.** The rule appears in foraging guides and blog literature. I could not find it published by any wildlife agency, land management agency or peer reviewed source that I was able to open. So here is the honest label: **the one-third rule is custom, not a finding.** Presenting it as though it were an ecological law is the kind of error this project treats as a defect, because a reader who goes looking for the study will not find it and may throw out the good instinct along with the fake authority. There are three structural reasons to be suspicious of it beyond the missing citation, and they are worth understanding because they generalise. **The numbers do not agree with each other.** One third and one in ten differ by a factor of three, and five percent by a factor of six from the third. A genuine finding does not come in three mutually incompatible versions that nobody reconciles. **The denominator is never specified.** A third of what? Of the fruit on one plant? Of the plants in the patch you can see? Of the population, which you cannot see and could not count? Those are wildly different quantities and the rule is silent on which one it means, which is a reliable sign that it was never derived from anything. **It ignores the part-taken distinction entirely.** A third of the berries and a third of the bulbs are not remotely the same act. The first costs a population some dispersal. The second kills a third of the individuals. Any rule stated as a single fraction, applied identically to fruit, leaf, root and bark, is guaranteed to be either far too cautious for one of them or catastrophic for another. **So what should you do instead?** In order: 1. **Use the published limit where one exists.** In the great majority of situations near Silverdale, one does: an agency limit for the land you are on, a bag limit for the species, or both. The published limit is the answer and your rule of thumb is not needed. 2. **Where no limit is published, say so out loud and act on the part-taken logic.** Fruit, generous. Leaf, moderate and not from the same individual repeatedly. Root, bulb or bark, treat every one as a death and ask whether that individual had already reproduced. 3. **Take the middle and leave the extremes.** Leave the small because they have not bred. Leave the exceptional because it is the best breeder present. 4. **Move.** The single most effective conservation act available to a forager is not taking a smaller fraction of one patch. It is walking further and spreading the take across many. This is the same advice WDFW gives shellfish harvesters, which is to visit less popular beaches to spread out the pressure. 5. **And keep the honest version of the custom, which is worth keeping.** As a brake on human appetite, "don't clean it out" is good and probably ancient. It is a discipline, not a measurement. Use it as one. ## Mushrooms are a special case They are, but not quite for the reason people say. **The popular claim, stated accurately.** The National Park Service's page for Mount Rainier puts it this way: "Picking a mushroom is similar to picking a berry or apple in that the larger organism is usually not harmed." That is the claim, from a federal source, and note the word the source itself chose: **usually.** The reasoning behind it is sound and worth understanding. The mushroom you pick is a fruiting body. The organism is the mycelium, a network living in the soil or the wood, often considerably older and larger than the visible mushroom and unaffected by your knife. In that respect a chanterelle really is more like an apple than like a carrot, and picking it is closer to harvesting fruit than to killing an individual. On the four-part scheme above, mushrooms are in the cheap category. **What I could not establish.** The evidence usually cited for this is a long-term Swiss study of mushroom harvesting. I could not open it today: the journal page returned 403, the institutional repository would not render, and the abstract services refused or failed. I do not restate a paper I could not read, so I am not going to tell you what it tested, how long it ran or what it found, and you should not take any of that from me. What I have is the Park Service's sentence, which is sourced, hedged by its own author, and enough to act on. **What follows from the hedge.** "Usually not harmed" is not "never harmed", and the practical reading is that the act of picking is cheap while the **way** you go about it may not be. Two regulators at two different levels of government both wrote that into their rules, and neither of them capped the quantity to do it. The federal parks rule, 36 CFR 2.1, permits designated gathering only "by hand", which is a prohibition on tools rather than on amounts. Washington's state parks rule, WAC 352-28-030, prohibits harvest techniques involving raking or anything else with the potential to degrade park resources, while allowing a generous two gallons a day. **Both of them restricted the method and left the quantity alone**, which tells you which of the two they think does the damage. So: pick or cut the mushroom, whichever you prefer, and **do not rake the duff to find them.** The visible mushroom is cheap. The forest floor it came out of is not, which brings us to the last section. **And the national forest rules exist and are specific.** Personal use mushroom harvest on Olympic National Forest needs no permit and is capped at one gallon per species per year, with selling and trading prohibited. Commercial permits are separate and priced by volume: 50 dollars for 50 gallons on a 14-day permit, 80 dollars for 80 gallons on a 30-day permit, and 120 dollars for 120 gallons for a calendar year. A commercial use permit is required for anyone intending to sell, or harvesting more than the incidental use allowance. Underneath all of that sits the state threshold: more than five US gallons of wild edible mushrooms is a specialized forest product under RCW 76.48 regardless of whose land it came from, requiring a permit and the landowner's permission. On Olympic National Forest the federal personal-use cap of one gallon per species per year is the binding constraint long before the state threshold is reached; on DNR land, where nine gallons a year is allowed, the two regimes are closer together than they look. Check both. ## What you disturb besides the thing you take The take is the part you notice. It is frequently not the part that does the damage. **Trampling and compaction.** Feet compress soil. Compacted soil takes in less water, which means less moisture stored, fewer seeds germinating and fewer seedlings surviving, and more of the rain running off the surface instead, which erodes. The mechanism is slow, it is cumulative, and it is invisible on any single visit. What it looks like when it has run long enough is documented. The Park Service's account of a half-mile visitor-created trail at Cuyahoga Valley states that increased traffic there "has resulted in visible soil compaction, trampling of vegetation, soil erosion, and potentially even the spread of invasive plant species", and that "Large sections of the streamside plant community are now devoid of vegetation and rare plants have not been re-located." Read that last clause again. **The rare plants are not there any more, and nobody harvested them.** They were walked on. If you return to a productive spot repeatedly, you are building a trail whether you intended to or not, and your approach route will do more damage than your basket. The practical answers are dull and they work: vary your route in, do not walk the same line twice, stay on the durable surface where one exists, and accept that the fastest way to a patch is usually the way that kills it. **The intertidal, where everything you move is somebody's house.** A rock on a gravel beach is a habitat with two sides, and the underside is the good one: it is dark, damp at low tide, and sheltered. The Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary's tidepooling guidance is direct about all of it, and being federal it can be quoted: > If you want to peek under a rock, put it back the way you found it. > Never force an animal off its spot, you may tear off its feet, or > squeeze its organs. > Find footholds on bare rock, they are not as slippery and you will > avoid stepping on the animals and plants. > Intertidal animals should not be collected for bait. > Always obey fish and wildlife laws with respect to seasons, bag > limits, and sexes of animals taken for food. "Put it back the way you found it" is the whole rule and it is routinely half-done. A rock rolled aside and left with its underside up kills the community that was underneath, by sun and by drying, and kills the one that was on top, by burial. Turning it back over is not tidiness; it is the difference between looking and destroying. And "never force an animal off its spot" has a specific target: a limpet or a chiton prised off a rock usually does not reattach. The same logic drives the clam-hole rule from earlier. Refill the hole, and put the undersized animals back into it rather than leaving them on the surface. **Invasive seed, which travels on you.** The Park Service is specific about the mechanism: "Seeds can readily become lodged in our boots and stuck to our clothing." Equipment "can also house myriad plant parts, insect and aquatic species eggs and larvae, and microscopic critters." Vehicles carry "seeds and plant fragments becoming attached to dirty cars, boats, and trailers, or insects attaching their sticky egg masses to their surfaces." And firewood carries "wood-boring insects, insect eggs, and fungi". This is the damage most foragers never account for, because it happens at the next site rather than this one, and because a forager is precisely the person most likely to walk from a disturbed roadside verge into intact forest. **You are the vector, and you are going in the worst possible direction.** Knock your boots off and brush the seeds out before you leave a weedy site, not after you arrive at a clean one. Wash the vehicle after driving unpaved roads. Do not move firewood. Locally this connects to something the species guide raises: Himalayan blackberry is a designated noxious weed here, which means stands along roads, ditches and utility corridors may have been sprayed. Those same corridors are where you pick up the seed you then carry inland. **Litter and the beach you close behind you.** Washington's litter law scales penalties by volume, from a civil infraction for a cubic foot or less up to gross misdemeanour, with cleanup costs on top; the project's law layer carries it as `wa-littering-is-illegal-with-penalties-scaled-to-the-amount`. More practically, WDFW's own advice about parking includes not parking unsafely or illegally along busy roadways, and the reason that advice exists is that access to good beaches gets withdrawn over parking and rubbish far more often than over shellfish. ## What the shipped law data does and does not have This guide's declared data layer is `data/laws/laws.json`. Read its own disclaimer before you lean on it: it says in terms that it is a worked example rather than the law, that entries may be incomplete, out of date or simply wrong, that most have never been checked by a person, and that you should never act on it without reading the cited source. That is the right posture and it is also a limit you need to know about. **What it has that is relevant here.** Five entries carry real weight for a harvester: - `wa-criminal-trespass`, the permission-is-the-default rule, citing RCW 9A.52.070 and 9A.52.080. - `usa-don-t-harm-protected-species-or-their-habitat`, the Endangered Species Act entry, which correctly notes the take prohibition includes harm, harassment and significant habitat degradation, and that it applies on private land. - `wa-commercial-forest-cutting-follows-forest-practices-rules`, the RCW 76.09 entry, for anything at the scale of trees. - `kitsap-kitsap-requires-buffers-around-wetlands-and-streams` and `wa-critical-areas-on-your-property-are-protected-wetlands-strea`, which between them tell you that the wet ground and stream margins where a lot of the good plants are carry clearing restrictions even on land you own. Also relevant at the margins: `wa-shoreline-work-needs-a-permit-shoreline-management-act`, `kitsap-clearing-grading-and-filling-land-needs-a-county-permit`, `usa-filling-wetlands-or-waters-needs-a-federal-clean-water-act-p`, and `kitsap-gatherings-and-events-in-county-parks-need-permission`, which is the only entry in the whole file that cites the Kitsap park code. **What it does not have, and this is a real gap between the curriculum's promise and the data.** The topic `forage_ethics` promises to teach the reader to "know what is protected or illegal to take", and declares `data/laws/laws.json` as its data layer. Of the 170 rules in that file, **not one covers harvesting.** Specifically, the file has nothing on: - **Hunting, fishing or shellfish licences.** There is no rule in the file about needing a licence to take anything wild. There is a rule about licensing your dog. - **Seasons, bag limits or size limits** of any kind. - **The Migratory Bird Treaty Act.** The single most commonly violated wildlife statute in the country, and the one that surprises people most because it covers feathers and nests, does not appear. - **The Marine Mammal Protection Act**, on a county where marine mammals are visible from the shore most weeks of the year. - **Tribal treaty rights.** Nothing. No treaty, no usual and accustomed areas, no co-management, no Rafeedie. This is the largest omission in the file for this county, because it is the framework that determines who may take shellfish from every beach in it. - **Tideland ownership and the private-beach problem.** The file has fourteen entries under "Environment and land" and none of them mention tidelands. - **State protected wildlife.** WAC 220-200-100, the rule that makes nearly every native bird untakeable, is absent, as is any WDFW listing concept. - **RCW 76.48 specialized forest products**, the permit thresholds that turn brush picking into a regulated activity. - **Public land access categories.** Nothing on national parks, national forests, state parks, DNR land, the Discover Pass, or the fact that the rules differ between them. The category structure is not the problem; "Environment and land" is the obvious home for most of it. The content is simply not there. I am reporting this rather than fixing it, per the writing rules for this Library, so that the fix gets its own commit and its own reasoning. **A smaller observation about the species data**, which is much better populated. In `data/locales/silverdale_wa/species.json`, every mammal, fish and shellfish record carries a populated `protected` field, and 45 of the 66 plant records carry `null`. The companion species guide already documents what that null means, correctly, as "no protection was found, which is not the same as verified unprotected". So this is a known and honestly labelled gap rather than a defect. It is worth flagging here only because **a guide about what you may legally take is exactly the reader who will hit it**, and because the asymmetry is real and not merely an artefact of effort: as this guide's protection section sets out, plants genuinely are regulated by different agencies under different authorities than animals are, at both federal and state level. The empty field is partly a reflection of a genuinely thinner legal layer, which is itself the thing worth teaching. ## You own this when - You ask "whose land is this" **before** you ask "what is this", and you can name the five public land categories near Silverdale and say that their harvest rules are different without needing to remember which is which. - You know that most Washington tideland is private, that a private beach looks exactly like a public one, and that whether you may even stand on one is an unsettled question in Washington law. - You can state what the Treaty of Point Elliott reserved, in 1855, and you understand that treaty shellfish harvest reaches private tidelands and that the state manages half a jointly managed resource. - You know that "take" under the Endangered Species Act includes harm and harassment and attempts, that the Act protects listed plants far more narrowly than listed animals, and that the Migratory Bird Treaty Act reaches parts, nests and eggs, which means feathers. - You look up a bag limit in the current rules rather than repeating one you read somewhere, and you can say why: the cockle minimum changed in 2026. - You can say which cap binds first when a limit has two, and you understand what a first-dug limit is for. - You refill the hole, put the small ones back in it, shuck the oysters on the beach and leave the shells at the same tide height. - You can say, without hedging, that "leave a third" is custom rather than a published finding, and you can give the three structural reasons why a single fraction cannot be right for fruit, leaf, root and bark alike. - You treat a root or a bulb as the death of an individual, and you ask whether that individual had already reproduced. - You put the rock back the way you found it, every time, including the time when nobody is watching and you are already late. - You knock the seeds off your boots at the weedy roadside rather than at the trailhead of somewhere intact. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. Federal government publications are listed first because they are public domain and can be redistributed with this guide; the rest cannot, and their facts are restated here in our own words with the authority named. Every URL below was opened on 15 September 2026. ### United States government (public domain) - Office of the Law Revision Counsel, US House of Representatives. 16 U.S.C. 703, Migratory Bird Treaty Act (the prohibited acts; the extension to any part, nest or egg and to products made from them). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title16-section703&num=0&edition=prelim - Office of the Law Revision Counsel. 16 U.S.C. 1532, Endangered Species Act definitions (the definition of take at paragraph 19; endangered, threatened and person). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title16-section1532&num=0&edition=prelim - Office of the Law Revision Counsel. 16 U.S.C. 1538, Endangered Species Act prohibited acts (subsection (a)(1) for fish and wildlife and subsection (a)(2) for plants, which is the asymmetry this guide turns on). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title16-section1538&num=0&edition=prelim - US Government Publishing Office. 36 CFR 2.1, National Park System preservation of natural features (the general prohibition, and the superintendent designation exception for fruits, berries, nuts or unoccupied seashells gathered by hand). https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title36-vol1/xml/CFR-2024-title36-vol1-sec2-1.xml - US Fish and Wildlife Service. Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918 (the take prohibition in plain terms; 50 CFR 21 permits and exceptions). https://www.fws.gov/law/migratory-bird-treaty-act-1918 - US Fish and Wildlife Service, International Affairs. Ginseng (CITES Appendix II since 1975; five years of age and four or more stem scars for export; three prongs in most states; September season start in all 19 states; "The harvest of a ginseng root kills the plant"; the non-detriment requirement). https://www.fws.gov/international-affairs/permits/ginseng - NOAA Fisheries. Marine Mammal Protection Act (the moratorium on taking; take defined as harass, hunt, capture or kill or the attempt; Level A and Level B harassment; which agency administers which animals). https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/topic/laws-policies/marine-mammal-protection-act - Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary, NOAA. Tidepooling (put the rock back the way you found it; never force an animal off its spot; footholds on bare rock; no collecting intertidal animals for bait; obey seasons and bag limits). https://olympiccoast.noaa.gov/visitor/thingstodo/tidepooling.html - Office of National Marine Sanctuaries, NOAA. Tidepool Etiquette (step carefully, be gentle, leave animals, algae, rocks and shells where you find them, know the regulations). https://sanctuaries.noaa.gov/visit/tidepool/ - National Park Service, Olympic National Park. Fungi (one quart per person per day of mushrooms; the warning about poisonous species). https://www.nps.gov/olym/learn/nature/fungi.htm - National Park Service, Mount Rainier National Park. Mushroom Picking (one gallon of edible fungi per person per day for personal use; "Picking a mushroom is similar to picking a berry or apple in that the larger organism is usually not harmed"). https://www.nps.gov/mora/learn/nature/mushroom-picking.htm - National Park Service. How Invasive Species Spread (seeds lodged in boots and stuck to clothing; equipment; dirty cars, boats and trailers; firewood). https://www.nps.gov/subjects/invasive/how-invasive-species-spread.htm - National Park Service, Cuyahoga Valley National Park. The Columbia Sensitive Resource Zone (soil compaction, trampling, erosion and invasive spread along a social trail; streamside plant community devoid of vegetation and rare plants not re-located). https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/columbia-sensitive-resource-zone.htm - USDA Forest Service, Olympic National Forest. Mushrooms (no permit for incidental personal use; one gallon per species per year; no selling or trading; commercial permit tiers at 50, 80 and 120 dollars). https://www.fs.usda.gov/r06/olympic/forest-products/mushrooms - USDA Forest Service, Olympic National Forest. Special Forest Products (berries one gallon per day and three gallons per year with commercial use prohibited; fiddleheads one pound per person per day; downed dead wood for immediate use while camping; free personal use firewood permit up to six cords per calendar year; transplant permit up to five). https://www.fs.usda.gov/r06/olympic/forest-products/special-forest-products - USDA Forest Service Research and Development. Ancient barkpeeled trees in the Bitterroot Mountains, Montana (bark peelings dated from the mid-1600s to the early 1900s, on living and dead trees, dateable by dendrochronology; recognition of culturally modified trees as ecologically and culturally valuable). https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/40385 - USDA Forest Service Research and Development. Ecology and management of commercially harvested chanterelle mushrooms, PNW-GTR-576, Pilz, Norvell, Danell and Molina, 2003 (abstract only; see the note below on what would not open). https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/5298 - Treaty of Point Elliott, 22 January 1855, Article 5. A United States treaty and therefore a federal instrument. Read on the Washington Governor's Office of Indian Affairs copy. https://goia.wa.gov/resources/treaties/treaty-point-elliott-1855 ### State, county and tribal authorities (cited as the authority, facts restated here) - Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife. Clam, mussel and oyster harvest (most state recreational harvest regulations do not extend to shellfish harvest on private tidelands for personal use; both the health status and the WDFW season must be open; refill dig holes and push undersized clams back into them; each person needs a separate container and must be actively harvesting). https://wdfw.wa.gov/places-to-go/shellfish-beaches - Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife. News release, 23 March 2026, on shellfish season rules and sustainability (geoduck daily limit of one; cockle minimum size 2.5 inches; leave oyster shells on the beach and refill dig holes; a shellfish and seaweed or combination licence is required; spread out across less popular beaches; do not park unsafely along busy roadways). https://wdfw.wa.gov/newsroom/news-release/wdfw-urges-shellfish-harvesters-follow-rules-support-sustainability-state-clam-mussel-and-oyster - Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife. Fishing and shellfishing licences (a licence is required of residents and non-residents alike; all fishers aged 16 and over need one). https://wdfw.wa.gov/licenses/fishing - Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife. Fishing licence types and fees (shellfish and seaweed at 21.58 resident, 47.39 non-resident, 13.99 resident senior; annual combination at 74.37, 170.00, 28.83 and 12.89; prices include all applicable fees). https://wdfw.wa.gov/licenses/fishing/types-fees - Washington State Legislature. WAC 220-200-100, protected wildlife (protected wildlife shall not be hunted or fished; the threatened, sensitive and other categories; all birds not classified as game birds, predatory birds or endangered species; Cetacea and Pinnipedia; bats). https://app.leg.wa.gov/wac/default.aspx?cite=220-200-100 - Washington State Legislature. WAC 352-28-030, state park harvest of edible plants and fruiting bodies (two gallons per person per day of one or more species; the permitted park classifications; no harvest in a natural area preserve; raking and degrading techniques prohibited; no commercial harvest; does not limit federally reserved tribal rights including treaty rights). https://app.leg.wa.gov/wac/default.aspx?cite=352-28-030 - Washington State Legislature. WAC 352-28-010, removal of natural resources from state park lands (professional evaluation before removing significant trees; removal of other resources only under an approved conservation plan; consultation with WDFW and the Natural Heritage Program where endangered, threatened or sensitive species are present). https://app.leg.wa.gov/wac/default.aspx?cite=352-28-010 - Washington State Legislature. RCW 76.48, specialized forest products (the chapter's purpose and the requirement for both a permit and the landowner's permission). https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=76.48&full=true - Washington State Legislature. RCW 76.48.021, definitions (more than 5 Christmas trees; more than 5 native ornamental trees and shrubs removed with roots intact; more than 20 pounds of cut or picked evergreen foliage, defined to include boughs, huckleberry foliage, salal, fern, Oregon grape, rhododendron, mosses and bear grass; more than 5 pounds of cascara bark; more than 5 US gallons of wild edible mushrooms; cones, berries and seeds excluded from the foliage definition). https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=76.48.021 - Washington State Department of Ecology. Public Trust Doctrine (the state sold 60 percent of tidelands before 1971; the doctrine protects commerce, navigation and fisheries plus incidental recreational rights; no Washington court has ruled whether walking on the beach or wading on privately owned tidelands is a right under the doctrine). https://ecology.wa.gov/water-shorelines/shoreline-coastal-management/shoreline-coastal-planning/shoreline-laws-rules-and-cases/public-trust-doctrine - Washington State Department of Natural Resources. Where to go, what to do (personal use harvest limits on DNR-managed land: mushrooms three gallons of a single species per day and nine gallons plus one mushroom per year; berries three gallons per day and nine gallons per year; brush and ferns two plants per day and four per year by root ball; no reselling; harvest prohibited in campgrounds, picnic sites, natural area preserves and natural resources conservation areas unless in the site management plan). https://dnr.wa.gov/recreation/where-go-what-do - Washington State Department of Natural Resources, Natural Heritage Program. Rare Species (state conservation statuses of Endangered, Threatened, Sensitive or Possibly Extinct or Extirpated; nearly 400 plants and nonvascular species with conservation status, twelve also federally listed; legal responsibility for fish and wildlife held by WDFW). https://dnr.wa.gov/natural-heritage-program/rare-species - Washington State Parks. Discover Pass (annual 45 dollars, one-day 10 dollars; covers State Parks, WDFW and DNR recreation lands; it is a parking pass). https://parks.wa.gov/discover-pass - Kitsap County Code chapter 10.12, the Park Code (section 10.12.050, unlawful to remove, destroy, mutilate or deface any tree, shrub, flower or other plant, or any rock, cliff or other natural feature; the definition of park at 10.12.020(1); violation a misdemeanour under 10.12.190). https://dcd.kitsapgov.com/ordnances/kitsaphtml1110/Kitsap10/Kitsap1012.html - Kitsap County Parks. FAQs and rules (park hours, stay on designated trails, pack out trash; shellfish harvesting prohibited at Guillemot Cove Natural Preserve; the existence of a separate Mushroom Harvest Policies document; telephone 360.337.5350). https://www.kitsap.gov/parks/Pages/FAQRules.aspx - Northwest Indian Fisheries Commission. The Rafeedie Decision (half of all shellfish from all usual and accustomed places; all public and private tidelands in the case area subject to treaty harvest except artificially created beds and areas set aside for non-tribal cultivation; time, place and manner restrictions on harvest from private beaches; the Supreme Court declined review in 1999). https://nwifc.org/about-us/shellfish/rafeedie-decision/ - Northwest Indian Fisheries Commission. Shellfish (the treaty language and the history of tribes being excluded as tidelands passed into non-tribal ownership; joint state and tribal fisheries work). https://nwifc.org/about-us/shellfish/ - The Suquamish Tribe, Fisheries Department, Shellfish (one of 24 treaty tribes in the Puget Sound area co-managing shellfish with WDFW; surveys within the Tribe's usual and accustomed area; the Treaty Share is half the total allowable catch on private and public beaches, with tidelands identified as staked and cultivated under the Shellfish Growers Settlement excepted). https://suquamish.nsn.us/home/departments/fisheries/shellfish/ ### Project data - `data/laws/laws.json`. Read for this guide in full: 170 rules across six jurisdictions. The entries cited by id in the text are `wa-criminal-trespass`, `usa-don-t-harm-protected-species-or-their-habitat`, `wa-commercial-forest-cutting-follows-forest-practices-rules`, `wa-critical-areas-on-your-property-are-protected-wetlands-strea`, `kitsap-kitsap-requires-buffers-around-wetlands-and-streams`, `wa-shoreline-work-needs-a-permit-shoreline-management-act`, `kitsap-clearing-grading-and-filling-land-needs-a-county-permit`, `usa-filling-wetlands-or-waters-needs-a-federal-clean-water-act-p`, `kitsap-gatherings-and-events-in-county-parks-need-permission` and `wa-littering-is-illegal-with-penalties-scaled-to-the-amount`. The file's own disclaimer, that it is a worked example rather than the law and that most entries have never been checked by a person, is quoted in the text because it is load-bearing. What the file does not contain is set out in its own section above. - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/species.json`. The shellfish limits, protection statuses and approach distances in this guide are referenced by record id rather than restated, so that the sourced numbers live in one place: `manila_clam`, `pacific_littleneck_clam`, `butter_clam`, `basket_cockle`, `varnish_clam`, `eastern_softshell_clam`, `fat_gaper_horse_clam`, `geoduck`, `pacific_oyster`, `olympia_oyster`, `bay_mussel`, `dungeness_crab`, `harbor_seal`, `killer_whale`. - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/locale.json`. The place, and the `authorities` map that resolves the role `state-fish-wildlife` to the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife for this locale. ### Could not be sourced, and what was done instead - **The long-term Swiss mushroom harvesting study**, by Egli and colleagues. The publisher page returned 403, the institutional repository would not render, the abstract service returned 405 and the aggregator returned 403. Nothing about its design, duration or results is stated in this guide, because I could not read any of it. The guide rests instead on the National Park Service's own sentence, which is sourced and carries its own hedge. - **Human-induced dwarfing of Himalayan snow lotus** (Law and Salick, reported in PNAS 2005), the paper most often cited for size-selective harvest driving change in a plant population. The journal returned 403, PubMed returned a cookie wall and PMC returned a security check. Only its title is used in the text, and the text says so; no numbers or methods are given. The argument is carried instead by the observable structure of the regulations, which is checkable. - **The mechanism of girdling.** The Forest Service publications on girdling that were opened are scanned or use embedded subset fonts and would not render as text. The claim that a complete ring of bark removal kills a tree is therefore presented in the text as reported rather than cited. The sourced fact used in its place is the Bitterroot bark-peel study, which dates peelings across roughly 300 years and finds the scars on living as well as dead trees. The text says explicitly that this establishes that partially peeled trees go on living and does not quantify how often one dies. - **Kitsap County's Mushroom Harvest Policies.** The 2014 county resolution PDF and the stewardship plan that quotes it would not render as readable text. The existence of the policy is sourced to the county parks rules page, which references it; its contents are not stated here, and the guide gives the county parks telephone number instead. - **Washington seaweed harvest rules.** The detailed seaweed rules that appear in search results trace to a WDFW pamphlet from 2017-18, whose PDF would not render as text, and the current shellfishing regulations page is an index that does not carry them. **No seaweed rule of any kind is stated in this guide as a result**, including the daily limit, the tool restrictions and the state park closures. Seaweed harvest needs the same shellfish and seaweed licence, which is sourced above; everything else about it you must look up in the current sport fishing rules. - **The "leave a third" rule and its relatives.** Searched for deliberately and not found in any agency publication or peer-reviewed source that would open. Present in foraging guides and blog literature, in at least three mutually incompatible versions. Labelled in the text as custom rather than a finding, with the reasons. ### Companion guides in this collection - [Identifying Wild Plants](/library#identifying-wild-plants), which is the other half of this one: what it is, and whether it will hurt you. - [The Species Where You Live](/library#the-species-where-you-live), which carries the protection inventory this guide's verbs apply to, and the convention for reading a species record. - [The Year of Wild Food](/library#the-year-of-wild-food), for when things are available, which is the question that comes after may I take it. - [How an Ecosystem Holds Together](/library#how-an-ecosystem-holds-together), for who else was eating the thing you took. - [Reading the Tide](/library#reading-the-tide), for the minus tides that make shellfish digging possible and for the biotoxin question, which this guide deliberately does not duplicate. - [The Hazards Your Place Actually Has](/library#the-hazards-where-you-live), for the hazards of being out there at all.
