docs.text: # Testing Water The rest of the water run teaches you where water comes from, how to catch it, how to keep it, and how to treat it. Every one of those guides makes a decision for you, and every one of those decisions rests on an assumption about what is in the water. This guide is about replacing the assumption with a number. It matters more here than in most subjects, because the things that make water dangerous almost never announce themselves. A spring that runs clear, cold and sweet can carry nitrate from a field two miles uphill, arsenic out of the rock it flowed through, and the bacteria from a dead animal nobody found. Not one of those changes how it looks, smells or tastes. [Where Water Comes From](/library#where-water-comes-from) puts it as bluntly as it can be put: your senses are a one-way alarm. If they go off, believe them. If they stay quiet, you have learned almost nothing. A test is the instrument that answers the quiet case. This guide is about what that instrument actually measures, which is narrower than most people think, and how to use it so the answer means something. ## What a test is, and what it is not A drinking water test is a snapshot of one sample, drawn from one tap, on one day, analysed for the specific things you paid somebody to look for. Read that sentence again with each limit in mind, because all three are real and all three are routinely forgotten. **One sample, one day.** The result describes the water that came out of that tap at that moment. It does not describe last week's water and it does not promise anything about next month's. Contamination is not usually a steady trickle. EPA's account of nonpoint source pollution is explicitly an event mechanism: "NPS pollution is caused by rainfall or snowmelt moving over and through the ground. As the runoff moves, it picks up and carries away natural and human-made pollutants, finally depositing them into lakes, rivers, wetlands, coastal waters and ground waters." Water that is clean in August can be contaminated in November, by the same well, with nothing about the well having changed. **One tap.** Some of what a test finds was in the ground before you owned the place. Some of it was added by the pipe between the well and the glass. Those are different problems with different fixes, and which one you measured depends entirely on how you drew the sample. This is the single most misunderstood part of water testing and it gets its own section below. **One list.** A laboratory reports what it was asked to analyse. Nothing else. A sheet that says everything passed means everything on that sheet passed. If arsenic was not on the list, the sheet is silent about arsenic, and silence reads exactly like a pass to someone skimming it. The consequence worth carrying out of this section is that **when you sample is as much a decision as what you test for**, and most people never make it consciously. They test when it is convenient. Convenient is usually a dry week, because that is when you get around to errands, and a dry week is when a well is at its cleanest. ## When to sample Three kinds of timing, in order of how much they change the answer. **The routine one.** Once a year, as a habit, ideally at the same time each year so the results are comparable. Pick the part of the year when your water is most likely to be bad rather than least, which in a wet-winter climate means during or just after the wet season rather than in a dry August. That last point is a rule of thumb rather than an agency recommendation, but it follows directly from EPA's rainfall and snowmelt mechanism above. **The trigger ones.** CDC and EPA give nearly the same list, and every item on it is a day when nobody is thinking about their water. Test again, outside the annual cycle, when: - you are notified that there are problems with well water in your area; - there are problems near your well, such as flooding, land disturbances, or nearby waste disposal sites, or, in EPA's wording, new construction or industrial activity; - you replace or repair any part of your well system; - you notice a change in your water's taste, colour or smell; - you or someone you live with becomes pregnant; - a child starts living with you. Note what the last two have in common with the first four. Nothing about the water changed. What changed is who is drinking it, and for nitrate and lead that is the whole risk calculation. EPA adds the same thought for frequency: you may want to test more often if small children or elderly adults live in the house, or if someone is pregnant or nursing. **The after-something-happened one.** If the well has been flooded or disinfected, the timing is specific. CDC's guidance after a disaster is not to judge by eye: "After a disaster, it is safest to drink bottled water until you are certain that your water is free of contaminants and safe to drink." Sample "for total coliform and either *E. coli* or fecal coliform bacteria to confirm that the water is safe to drink." And if you have shock chlorinated the well, wait: "Wait at least 7 to 10 days to test the water after disinfection to ensure that the chlorine has been thoroughly flushed from the system." Testing a chlorinated well tells you the chlorine worked that afternoon. It tells you nothing about whether the contamination comes back. ## The annual test for a private well If you are on a public supply, most of this is being done for you and the results arrive in your Consumer Confidence Report once a year. If you are on a well, CDC's position is the whole story: "if you get your water from a private well, you are responsible for making sure it is safe to drink." Private systems, CDC says, are "not regulated or monitored by officials," and that covers rainwater collection systems too. USGS says the same thing about domestic wells: "The quality and safety of water from domestic wells are not regulated by the Federal Safe Drinking Water Act or, in most cases, by state laws. Instead, individual homeowners are responsible for maintaining their domestic well systems and for monitoring water" quality. CDC and EPA give an identical baseline, which is unusual and makes it easy to remember. CDC: "Test your well water at least once every year for total coliform bacteria, nitrates, total dissolved solids, and pH level." EPA: "Test your private well annually for total coliform bacteria, nitrates, total dissolved solids, and pH levels." Four things. Here is what each is actually for. | Test | What it answers | Why it is on the annual list | |---|---|---| | **Total coliform bacteria** | Is there a path from the surface into my water? | The cheapest early warning that the well's seal, casing or setting has been breached | | **Nitrate** | Is fertilizer, sewage or animal waste reaching the aquifer? | The one contaminant on this list that kills people, specifically infants, and it has no taste | | **Total dissolved solids** | How much dissolved mineral is in this water, in total? | A single number that moves when almost anything changes, including salt | | **pH** | Is this water acidic or alkaline? | Acidic water corrodes plumbing, which is how lead and copper get into it | Two of those are direct health questions and two are sentinels. TDS and pH rarely hurt anybody at the levels a household well produces; they are on the list because they change when something else changes, and they are cheap. That baseline is the floor, not the ceiling. CDC's own qualifier is the important half: "Contact your health department to find out what other germs or chemicals to test for based on where you live." The extras that come up most often are arsenic, lead, radon, volatile organic compounds, pesticides and herbicides, and which of them apply to you is a local geology and local land use question, not a general one. Your county or state health department can usually answer it in one phone call, and the answer is normally a short and surprising list. ## Coliform and E. coli: the indicator is not the pathogen This is the most misread result on a water report, in both directions. Total coliforms are a family of bacteria that are mostly harmless. EPA is explicit: "Total coliforms are a group of related bacteria that are (with few exceptions) not harmful to humans." They are measured because of what their presence implies. "Total coliforms are used to determine the adequacy of water treatment and the integrity of the distribution system," and "EPA considers total coliforms a useful indicator of other pathogens for drinking water." So a coliform positive is not a diagnosis. **It says a path exists between the outside world and your water. It does not say what came down that path.** Something got in; the test does not know whether that something was soil bacteria from a cracked well cap or sewage from a failed drainfield up the hill. *E. coli* narrows it considerably. EPA describes *E. coli* and fecal coliforms as "types of coliform bacteria that are directly associated with fresh feces." In a public system a positive *E. coli* result "can signify an acute MCL violation, which necessitates rapid state and public notification because it represents a direct health risk." Faecal matter has reached the water, recently. That is the result that means stop drinking it today, not at the weekend. EPA's health goal for both is zero. The MCLG, the level "below which there is no known or expected risk to health," is zero for total coliforms and zero for *E. coli*. The compliance number you may see quoted for public systems, an MCL of 5.0 percent of monthly samples positive, is a system-level standard for a utility taking dozens of samples a month. It is not a household allowance. For a single well with a single sample, read the result as present or absent. Two errors to avoid at this point. The first is treating a coliform positive as proof of illness, which it is not; the second, far more common and far worse, is treating a coliform negative as proof that the water is safe. A clean coliform result says nothing at all about nitrate, arsenic, lead, solvents or pesticides, because those are not organisms and the test was not looking for them. ## Nitrate: the one with a body count Nitrate deserves its own section because it is invisible, it is common wherever people farm or use septic systems, no home treatment in the companion guide touches it, and the people it kills cannot tell you they feel unwell. EPA's federal limit, the MCL, is **10 mg/L, measured as nitrogen**. The MCLG, the non-enforceable health goal, is also 10 mg/L, and the two matching is worth noticing. EPA sets an MCL "as close to MCLGs as feasible using the best available treatment technology and taking cost into consideration," so for many contaminants the enforceable limit lands above the health goal. Arsenic, in the next section, is the clear case: its goal is zero and its limit is not. For nitrate the two coincide, which means the legal line and the health line are the same line. EPA's stated health effect, in full: "Infants below the age of six months who drink water containing nitrate in excess of the MCL could become seriously ill and, if untreated, may die. Symptoms include shortness of breath and blue-baby syndrome." EPA's private well material gives the mechanism: nitrate is converted to nitrites in the body, producing methemoglobinemia, with "shortness of breath and blueness of the skin" in infants under six months. EPA gives nitrate's sources as "Runoff from fertilizer use; leaking from septic tanks, sewage; erosion of natural deposits." Read that list against your own upstream. Row crops, pasture, a neighbour's drainfield and your own drainfield are all on it. Nitrite, the related compound, has an MCL of 1 mg/L, also measured as nitrogen. **The units trap.** EPA's contaminant is named "Nitrate (measured as Nitrogen)," and that phrase is load-bearing. A laboratory may report nitrate on either of two bases: as nitrogen, or as the whole nitrate ion. The two numbers describe the same water and are not the same number. The federal limit of 10 is stated on the nitrogen basis. If your sheet does not say "as N" or "as nitrogen" next to the nitrate row, do not compare it to 10 until you have asked the laboratory which basis they used. This is the single most likely way to misread a water report in a direction that matters. **And the thing nitrate shares with arsenic and lead.** No taste, no smell, no colour. It is not removed by boiling, filtering through a camping filter, or chlorinating, and boiling actively concentrates it, because the water leaves as steam and the nitrate stays in the pot. [Making Water Safe to Drink](/library#making-water-safe-to-drink) has the full account of what home treatment does and does not reach; nitrate sits squarely in the category it calls chemicals, the one nothing in the household kit fixes. ## Arsenic, lead and the metals, and the question you are actually asking Metals split cleanly into two groups, and the split is not chemical. It is about where they joined the water. **What the ground handed you.** Arsenic is the archetype. USGS: "Arsenic occurs naturally as a trace component in many rocks and sediments," and it "can be released into groundwater as a result of human activities, such as mining, and from its various uses in industry, in animal feed, as a wood preservative, and as a pesticide." EPA's version of the same point lists arsenic's sources as "Erosion of natural deposits; runoff from orchards, runoff from glass and electronics production wastes." Arsenic's MCL is **0.010 mg/L**, in force since 2006. Its MCLG is **0**, meaning EPA names no level at which it expects no risk. The enforceable limit sits above that goal for the reason EPA gives in its own definition: an MCL is set "as close to MCLGs as feasible using the best available treatment technology and taking cost into consideration." So a result of 0.008 mg/L is legal and is not the same as safe, and the sheet will not say so. EPA's health effect is "Skin damage or problems with circulatory systems, and may have increased risk of getting cancer." How common is it? USGS found arsenic above the MCL in about **7 percent** of sampled drinking water wells nationwide, and about **16 percent** in the Southwest, with arsenic "detected more frequently and at higher concentrations in wells in the West than in the East." USGS estimates about **2.1 million people** drink from private wells with arsenic above the standard. Nobody is going to tell those households. Arsenic is not on the annual four, so it gets found only when somebody asks for it. **What your plumbing added.** Lead is the archetype on this side, and the distinction is stated by EPA directly: "Lead can enter drinking water when plumbing materials that contain lead corrode, especially where the water has high acidity or low mineral content that corrodes pipes and fixtures." And: "In homes with lead pipes that connect the home to the water main, also known as lead services lines, these pipes are typically the most significant source of lead in the water." That is why pH is on the annual list. Corrosive water is not itself a health problem; it is the mechanism that turns your own pipes into the contaminant. Lead's MCLG is **zero**. There is no MCL in the ordinary sense: lead is regulated by treatment technique, with an action level of **0.015 mg/L**, revised to **0.010 mg/L** effective 1 November 2027. An action level is a trigger for a water system to act, not a safety line for a household, and with an MCLG of zero there is no amount of lead that EPA describes as harmless. Three facts from EPA that people get wrong: - "Since you cannot see, taste, or smell lead dissolved in water, testing is the only sure way of telling whether there are harmful quantities of lead in your drinking water." - "Use only cold water for drinking, cooking and making baby formula. Remember, boiling water does not remove lead from water." - Testing "costs between $20 and $100," and "a list of certified laboratories are available from your state or local drinking water authority." EPA's other metals of concern in well water come with the same message that they arrive from both directions: household plumbing and service lines on one hand, and "mining, petroleum refineries, electronics manufacturers, municipal waste disposal, cement plants, natural mineral deposits" on the other, with health effects EPA summarizes as "acute and chronic toxicity, liver, kidney, and intestinal damage, anemia, and cancer." ### First draw versus flushed, which is the whole thing Here is the part that most people get wrong, and getting it wrong does not produce an error message. It produces a clean-looking result. **To find out what is in your source**, you flush the line first. EPA's general sampling procedure is to "Select a cold water faucet for sampling which is free of contaminating devices such as screens, aeration devices, hoses, purification devices or swiveled faucets," then "Open the faucet and thoroughly flush. Generally 2 to 3 minutes will suffice, however longer times may be needed, especially in the case of lead distribution lines. Typically the water temperature will stabilize which indicates flushing is completed." You are deliberately throwing away the water that sat in the pipes, because you want the aquifer's water, not the plumbing's. **To find out what your plumbing adds**, you do the exact opposite. EPA's instruction for lead and copper compliance samples: "If you are collecting a first-flush sample for lead/copper, allow the water to sit undisturbed for at least six hours. DO NOT intentionally flush the water line before the start of the 6 hour period. Place a wide-mouth 1 L bottle under the faucet. Open the faucet and collect the first water out of the tap." And, contrary to every other sample you will ever take: "DO NOT remove any screens or aeration devices." Same tap. Opposite procedures. Opposite questions. | | Source sample | First-draw lead sample | |---|---|---| | Question | What is in the aquifer or the main? | What is my plumbing putting in? | | Standing time | Irrelevant | At least 6 hours undisturbed | | Flush first | Yes, 2 to 3 minutes, until temperature stabilizes | No, and do not flush before the 6 hours either | | Aerator or screen | Remove it | Leave it on | | Bottle | As the laboratory supplies | Wide-mouth 1 litre | | What you collect | Water that has been moving | The very first water out | The failure mode is obvious once you see it and invisible otherwise. Somebody worried about lead runs the tap for two minutes because that is what you do before drawing water, fills the bottle, and gets a low number back. They have measured the water in the main, which was never the question. The lead is in the last few metres of pipe and the fixture, and they flushed it down the drain before sampling. Two further details from the same EPA guidance. Choose a tap "free from devices that are designed to change the water composition, such as water softeners or point of use filters," and "Use the bathroom tap if the kitchen tap has a water softener or point of use filter on it." And if you want to locate lead in a service line rather than just detect it, "8 to 10 sequential sample bottles (the number depends on how far the lead service line is from the tap) would be needed to see the profile of lead distribution." Each bottle is a slice of pipe; the one that spikes tells you which slice. ## Hardness, iron, manganese and the rest of the aesthetic list Everything above this point has a health number attached. This section does not, and being honest about that is the point of it. EPA publishes a second set of values called secondary maximum contaminant levels. They exist so that water is usable, not so that it is safe, and EPA says so twice over: "EPA does not enforce these 'secondary maximum contaminant levels' (SMCLs)," and "These contaminants are not considered to present a risk to human health at the SMCL." | Contaminant | SMCL | What you notice | |---|---|---| | Aluminum | 0.05 to 0.2 mg/L | | | Chloride | 250 mg/L | salty taste | | Color | 15 color units | | | Copper | 1.0 mg/L | | | Corrosivity | Non-corrosive | | | Fluoride | 2.0 mg/L | | | Foaming agents | 0.5 mg/L | | | Iron | 0.3 mg/L | rusty colour, sediment, metallic taste, reddish or orange staining | | Manganese | 0.05 mg/L | black to brown colour, black staining, bitter metallic taste | | Odor | 3 threshold odor number | | | pH | 6.5 to 8.5 | | | Silver | 0.1 mg/L | | | Sulfate | 250 mg/L | | | Total dissolved solids | 500 mg/L | hardness, deposits, coloured water, staining, salty taste | | Zinc | 5 mg/L | | Hardness is not on that list because it is not a contaminant at all. USGS: "The simple definition of water hardness is the amount of dissolved calcium and magnesium in the water," and "Hardness is a property of water that is not a health concern, but it can be a nuisance." The usual bands, in milligrams per litre as calcium carbonate: | Classification | Range | |---|---| | Soft | 0 to 60 mg/L | | Moderately hard | 61 to 120 mg/L | | Hard | 121 to 180 mg/L | | Very hard | above 180 mg/L | **Now the honest part, which cuts both ways.** A secondary exceedance is not a health finding and should not be treated as one. Orange staining in the bath is iron, and iron at 0.4 mg/L will not hurt anybody. Plenty of money gets spent on treatment systems because a number on a sheet was above a line, without anybody noticing that the line was an aesthetic one. But the aesthetic parameters are also the cheapest clues you will ever buy, because they move when the water changes. Three in particular: - **Corrosivity and pH** point at lead and copper, for the reason in the previous section. Water that eats plumbing is a metals risk even when the metals test is clean today. - **Chloride and TDS** point at salt, which on a coast means something specific. Next section. - **A change** in any of them, against last year's sheet, is a signal that something in the system or the aquifer is different, and that is exactly the situation CDC names as a reason to test outside the annual cycle. One more piece of vocabulary, since it appears on some reports. EPA also issues health advisories, which "identify the concentration of a contaminant in drinking water at which adverse health effects and/or aesthetic effects are not anticipated to occur over specific exposure durations." These are not standards: "HAs are not to be construed as legally enforceable federal standards and are subject to change as new information becomes available." So a report can carry three different kinds of line, and only one of them is an enforceable health limit. ## Chloride and conductivity: the coastal early warning If your well is anywhere near salt water, this is the section that matters most, and it is the cheapest testing in the whole guide. The mechanism is a pressure balance rather than a barrier. USGS: "Groundwater pumping can reduce freshwater flow toward coastal areas and cause saltwater to be drawn toward the freshwater zones of the aquifer." The boundary is not a line but "a diffuse zone where freshwater and saltwater mix," called the zone of dispersion or zone of transition. The reason to watch it with instruments rather than with your tongue is that chloride's secondary standard, 250 mg/L, is a **taste** threshold. By the time water tastes salty it has been changing for a long time, and [Where Water Goes](/library#where-water-goes) explains why that is a problem you only get to have once: salt is dissolved through a body of rock, not sitting in a spot, and turning the pump down stops it getting worse without making it better on any timescale a household plans around. USGS lists the outcome plainly: "Saltwater intrusion decreases freshwater storage in the aquifers, and, in extreme cases, can result in the abandonment of wells." So watch the trend, not the threshold. Washington's Department of Ecology specifies exactly what to watch for wells under its coastal monitoring conditions, and the specification is a good template anywhere on a coast: measure **chloride**, **conductivity** and **static water level**, twice a year, in April and September, with the chemical analysis done by a state-accredited laboratory. Ecology reports that some coastal wells in Washington are already unusable because of intrusion. Three parameters, and each does a different job. Chloride is the direct evidence of sea salt. Conductivity is the cheap proxy, because dissolved ions are what make water conduct at all, and USGS notes that "even a small amount of ions in a water solution makes it able to conduct electricity" and that "the most common dissolved substances are salts, common table salt (sodium chloride (NaCl)) is the one we know best." A conductivity meter therefore responds to salt without being able to name it, which is exactly what a screening instrument is for. Static water level is the cause rather than the symptom: it tells you whether you are drawing the aquifer down, which is what lets the salt move in the first place. April and September bracket the wet and dry ends of the year, so the pair of readings shows you the seasonal swing rather than a single ambiguous point. **Here, specifically.** The Kitsap Peninsula has no upstream river. USGS describes the hydrologic setting as similar to that of an island, and groundwater is the normal domestic source and the only one: every litre of fresh water on this peninsula fell on this peninsula. The most detailed federal study found no widespread seawater contamination of peninsula wells, and named the local areas where chloride in well water exceeds 25 mg/L: the southern Longbranch peninsula, Horsehead Bay, Point Evans, Sinclair Inlet, Eagle Harbor, Fletcher Bay, the north end of Bainbridge Island and the north tip of the Kitsap peninsula. Silverdale and Dyes Inlet are not on that list. Sinclair Inlet, about 11 km south, is. Two things about that reassurance. The first is its date: it rests on 1980 field data, which makes it 45 years old, so a shoreline well should be tested for chloride rather than assumed clean. The second is the number itself. Twenty-five milligrams per litre is one tenth of the SMCL, far below anything you could taste, and it was chosen as an indicator of intrusion precisely because it is low. Waiting for 250 is waiting for the answer to stop being useful. Local well depths give a sense of what you would be sampling: near Silverdale the median recorded depth is 98 feet, about 30 metres, with half of local wells between 41 and 255 feet. The shallow end sits in the unconfined surficial unit, which is the most exposed both to surface contamination and to seasonal decline. ## Home test kits, honestly The question everybody asks, so here is the answer without the hedging. **What a strip or a home kit actually resolves.** Colour-change chemistry is good at a small number of things that are present in large amounts and have a simple, distinctive reaction: pH, total hardness, free chlorine, occasionally iron, occasionally nitrate at coarse resolution. For those, a strip gives you a band rather than a number, and the band is usually enough, because the decisions those parameters drive are coarse decisions. Knowing your water is very hard rather than soft is useful. Knowing it is 190 rather than 185 mg/L is not. **What it cannot do**, and this is the part the packaging is quiet about. Every analytical method has a floor below which it cannot distinguish a real result from noise. The federal definition of that floor, the method detection limit, is "the minimum measured concentration of a substance that can be reported with 99% confidence that the measured concentration is distinguishable from method blank results." The health limits that matter most are very low numbers: arsenic at 0.010 mg/L, lead's action level at 0.015 mg/L falling to 0.010. A colour comparison against a printed chart is not a technique that resolves ten parts per billion, and no amount of careful squinting makes it one. The same applies to a coliform result, which is a culture with an incubation time and a controlled medium, not a dye reaction. **What the federal system requires instead.** EPA "protects drinking water by requiring that laboratories become certified to analyze drinking water samples and that they use analytical methods approved by EPA." Both halves matter: a certified laboratory and an approved method. CDC's instruction is one line, "Use a state-certified laboratory to test your water," and EPA's is "Only use laboratories that are certified to do drinking water testing." So the honest split is this, and the ranking within it is a rule of thumb rather than an agency recommendation: - **Use a home kit** for pH, hardness and chlorine, for checking a treatment system is still doing something, and for watching a trend between real tests. A conductivity meter belongs in this category too, and on a coastal well it is the most useful cheap instrument you can own, because it costs nothing to read weekly and it moves before anything tastes wrong. - **Use a certified laboratory** for every number you would act on: coliform and *E. coli*, nitrate, arsenic, lead and the other metals, volatile organic compounds, pesticides, radionuclides. Anything with a health limit attached, anything you would spend money to treat, and anything you would reassure a pregnant household member with. **How to find one.** Your state or local health department maintains the list. CDC: health and environmental departments "should have a list of the state-certified (licensed) laboratories in your area that test for different germs and chemicals." EPA points to your state's laboratory certification programme, and notes that your local health department "may provide private well testing for free." EPA itself will not do it: "Unfortunately, EPA is unable to test residential or commercial drinking water upon request." The federal Safe Drinking Water Hotline, 800-426-4791, can point you at sampling information and at your state's programme. ## How to take a sample A badly taken sample is worse than no sample, because it returns a number and the number is wrong in an unknown direction. Most of the ways to ruin one are invisible. **The rule that comes before all the others:** ask the laboratory first and use their bottles. EPA's own guidance opens with it. "Check with the laboratory before collecting samples to ensure that sampling equipment, preservatives, and procedures for sample collection are acceptable. It is best to obtain sampling supplies directly from the laboratory performing the analyses." A bacteriology bottle is sterile and may contain sodium thiosulfate; a metals bottle may already contain nitric acid. Neither can be improvised, and a rinsed-out jam jar is not a substitute for either. **The general procedure**, which applies to most chemistry: 1. Collect "in an area free of excessive dust, rain, snow or other sources of contamination." 2. "Select a cold water faucet for sampling which is free of contaminating devices such as screens, aeration devices, hoses, purification devices or swiveled faucets. Check the faucet to be sure it is clean. If the faucet is in a state of disrepair, select another sampling location." 3. Use a tap "high enough to put a bottle underneath, generally the bath tub or kitchen sink, without contacting the mouth of the container with the faucet." 4. "Open the faucet and thoroughly flush. Generally 2 to 3 minutes will suffice... Typically the water temperature will stabilize which indicates flushing is completed. Once the lines are flushed, adjust the flow so it does not splash." 5. Record the site, the sampler's name, the date and time of collection, the method, the analysis requested and any preservative used. 6. Deliver or ship so that holding times are met. "Holding time starts at sample collection and ends at preparation and/or analysis," so leave the laboratory time to process it. **For bacteria**, the rules tighten. Sterile 125 or 150 mL plastic bottles must be used. Then, in EPA's words: "Do not rinse the bottles. The bottles are sterile so care must be taken not to contaminate the bottle or cap. Once the distribution line is flushed and the flow reduced, quickly open the bottle (but do not set the cap down), hold the cap by its outside edges only, and fill the sample bottle to just above the 100 mL line leaving a one inch headspace. Cap the bottle immediately and place it into a cooler with ice for delivery or overnight shipment to the laboratory." EPA's short list of tips for coliform sampling is worth pinning above the sink: - remove any attachments on the faucet; - allow water to flow for 5 or 6 minutes before sampling; - do not rinse or overfill the container; - always collect cold water, never sample hot water; - do not touch the inside of the sample bottle or its cap. And the sampling sites EPA says to avoid for total coliform if possible: outdoor faucets; faucets connected to cisterns, softeners, pumps, pressure tanks or hot water heaters; new plumbing and fixtures or those repaired recently; faucets that hot and cold water come through; threaded taps; swing spouts; faucets positioned close to the sink or ground; and leaky faucets. Every item on that list is a place where something other than your water supply can contribute bacteria, and a positive from one of them tells you about the tap rather than about the well. **For metals**, the bottle is preserved with nitric acid to pH below 2, and if the preservative is already in the bottle, do not rinse it. Fill to within one to two inches of the top. **Holding times**, which are the constraint people plan around worst: | Analysis | Time from collection | |---|---| | Coliform and *E. coli*, drinking water | 30 hours | | Coliform, source water compliance samples | 8 hours | | Coliphage | 48 hours | | Metals, mercury | 28 days | | Metals, other | 6 months (acid preserved); received within 14 days if not preserved | | Nitrate, nitrite, chloride, conductivity, TDS and other unpreserved chemistry | short; deliver the same day or ship overnight, and check with the laboratory | The 30 hours is not a guideline, it is federal regulation: 40 CFR 141.21 states that "The time from sample collection to initiation of analysis may not exceed 30 hours." The practical consequence is that a bacteriology sample is a logistics problem before it is a chemistry problem. Do not draw one on a Friday afternoon. Do not draw one before a long drive. Get the ice ready before you get the bottle out, and know when the laboratory's courier runs. Keep the sample cold the whole way. EPA's preservative for biological samples is to cool below 10 C, and to cool unpreserved chemistry to about 4 C, in both cases without letting the sample freeze. ## Reading the result sheet A laboratory report is a list of numbers next to a list of limits, and the limits are not all the same kind of thing. Four kinds appear, and confusing them is the usual source of both false alarm and false comfort. | Term | What it means | Is it a health limit? | |---|---|---| | **MCLG** | "The level of a contaminant in drinking water below which there is no known or expected risk to health." They "allow for a margin of safety and are non-enforceable public health goals" | Yes, and it is the purely health-based one. Not enforceable | | **MCL** | "The highest level of a contaminant that is allowed in drinking water," set "as close to MCLGs as feasible using the best available treatment technology and taking cost into consideration" | Yes, enforceable, but it is a feasibility line as well as a health line | | **Action level / treatment technique** | An action level triggers a required response; a treatment technique is "a required process intended to reduce the level of a contaminant in drinking water" | Indirectly. Used where measuring at the tap is not a clean compliance test, as with lead | | **SMCL** | A secondary standard, for taste, odour, colour and staining | **No.** EPA does not enforce them and says the contaminants are "not considered to present a risk to human health at the SMCL" | Add health advisory values as a fifth category if your report carries them: informative, not enforceable. **Now the number that is most often misread: "not detected."** It does not mean zero. It means the laboratory's method, at its detection limit, could not distinguish this sample from a blank. The detection limit is defined federally as "the minimum measured concentration of a substance that can be reported with 99% confidence that the measured concentration is distinguishable from method blank results." Everything below that floor reports the same way, whether it is genuinely absent or sitting just beneath the floor. Which makes the detection limit itself a number you should read. A report that says arsenic was not detected, at a detection limit of 0.001 mg/L, has told you something useful: arsenic is at most a tenth of the MCL. A report that says arsenic was not detected, at a detection limit of 0.02 mg/L, has told you almost nothing, because the floor of the method is above the legal limit. Both sheets read "ND" in the same column and in the same typeface. The questions to ask of any sheet, in order: 1. **What was on the list?** Everything not analysed is unanswered, not passed. 2. **What kind of limit is each comparison against?** Health, aesthetic, or advisory. 3. **What are the units, and on what basis?** Milligrams per litre against micrograms per litre is a factor of a thousand. Nitrate as nitrogen against nitrate as the ion is a different scale again. 4. **What is the detection limit for each non-detect?** And is it well below the limit that matters? 5. **How was the sample drawn?** For any metal, first draw or flushed, and therefore which question did this answer. 6. **When was it drawn?** Wet season or dry, before or after an event. ## When a result comes back bad There is a correct order here, and the mistake is nearly always to start at step four. **1. Stop drinking it.** Immediately, before anything is diagnosed, and with particular urgency if the household includes an infant, a pregnancy, or anybody immunocompromised. CDC's post-disaster instruction generalizes well: drink bottled water "until you are certain that your water is free of contaminants and safe to drink." Water for washing floors, flushing and watering is a separate question with a much lower bar, and separating your uses by how clean they need to be takes the pressure off, as [Where Water Comes From](/library#where-water-comes-from) describes. **2. Confirm it.** One sample is one sample, and sampling error is real, particularly for bacteria where a contaminated tap or a warm bottle can manufacture a positive. Resample, properly, ideally from a different tap as well, and tell the laboratory what you found the first time. **3. Find the cause.** This is the step people skip and it is the one that decides everything after it. A coliform positive is a path, so go looking for the path: the well cap and its seal, the casing, the grouting, the surface grading around the wellhead, a nearby drainfield, a flooded depression, recent digging. A nitrate result points uphill at fertilizer, sewage or animal waste. A lead result points at your own pipes, and the first-draw versus flushed pair tells you whether it is the service line or the fixture. An arsenic result points at the rock, which means it is not going away and not caused by anything you did. **4. Fix the cause.** A cracked cap, a failed seal, a drainfield, an abandoned well nearby used as a shortcut for surface water. Where the cause can be fixed, fixing it is cheaper and permanent, and it fixes the contaminants you did not test for at the same time. **5. Only then, treat.** And treat for the specific thing you found, with the specific method that reaches it, which is what [Making Water Safe to Drink](/library#making-water-safe-to-drink) is for. Its central table exists because no single method covers everything: boiling handles every germ and no chemical; camping microfilters miss viruses; chlorine misses *Cryptosporidium*; nothing in the household kit removes nitrate or arsenic. If you disinfect a well, remember the timing above: wait 7 to 10 days after disinfection before retesting, so you are measuring the well rather than the chlorine. **Treating without finding the cause is the mistake.** It is popular because it is purchasable, and it fails in two specific ways. A treatment system sized for the contamination you measured does not know about the contamination you did not, and the path that let one thing in is still open. And every treatment system is a maintenance obligation: a filter past its service life is not neutral, it is a reservoir. Fix the hole, then filter what still gets through. ## Surface water and rainwater: what a test tells you there, and why it is less The sibling guides cover both sources in full. [Collecting Rainwater](/library#collecting-rainwater) is the build guide and treats barrel water as non-potable throughout; [Where Water Comes From](/library#where-water-comes-from) ranks streams, lakes and springs by risk. This section is only about what testing adds, which is less than it adds for a well, and for a reason worth understanding. A well draws from a body of water with a long residence time. It changes slowly, which is exactly what makes an annual snapshot meaningful: this year's result is a reasonable guide to next month's, absent an event. Surface water and roof runoff have no such stability. EPA's nonpoint source mechanism is a description of pulses: rainfall and snowmelt move over the ground, pick up pollutants, and deposit them. A creek sampled on a dry Tuesday and the same creek sampled two hours into the first storm after a dry spell are, in any practical sense, two different waters. A clean result from the dry Tuesday does not transfer. The sampling logistics say the same thing. EPA's national beach guidance for recreational water holds bacteriological samples at 1 to 4 C and says "Do not hold samples longer than 6 hours between collection and initiation of analysis," against 30 hours for drinking water. Short holding times exist because the population in the bottle is changing. So what is testing surface water or rainwater good for? - **Characterising a source you will use repeatedly**, by sampling several times across the year rather than once, specifically including during and just after rain. A single result is close to worthless; a set of six that brackets the seasons is a real description. - **Answering a chemical question**, which is the half that does not change hour to hour. Metals, nitrate and dissolved solids in a stream reflect the watershed and the rock, and those move slowly. This is where a test earns its money on surface water. - **Checking a roof system for what the roof itself contributes**, which is a fixed property of the materials rather than a weather event. - **It is not good for** certifying a batch as safe to drink. For that, the answer is treatment every time, matched to the pathogen classes, because the biological result you would need has already expired by the time it comes back. Two structural facts underneath all of that. CDC's line about private supplies, which explicitly covers rainwater collection systems as well as wells: "These private water systems are not regulated or monitored by officials." Nobody else is checking. And the natural filtration that makes groundwater the better bet, in CDC's careful phrasing, is conditional: ground water "is naturally filtered, which might remove some germs and chemicals. How much is filtered out depends on how far the water is below ground and the area's local geology." One footnote on bottled water, since it is what people fall back on while a well is under investigation. FDA regulates it rather than EPA, and requires producers to obtain water from an approved source and to "Sample and test both source water and the final product for contaminants." It is a tested product, which is exactly the property you want while your own supply is an open question. ## What can go wrong - **You tested once, five years ago, and it was fine.** A test is a snapshot. Wells fail silently, usually with something that has no taste, and the annual habit exists because the failure gives no other warning. - **You tested in August, when the well is at its cleanest.** Sample when the water is most likely to be bad, and at the same point in the year each time so the numbers compare. - **Your coliform test was clean, so you assumed the water was safe.** A coliform test looks for one thing: a path from the surface. It is silent on nitrate, arsenic, lead, solvents and pesticides. - **You got a coliform positive and concluded there was sewage in your water.** Maybe. The indicator says a path exists, not what used it. *E. coli* is the result that means faeces, and it is the one that means stop today. - **You ran the tap for two minutes before taking a lead sample.** You measured the main. The lead was in the water you flushed away. First-draw means six hours undisturbed, no flushing, aerator left on. - **You compared a nitrate number to 10 without checking the basis.** The federal limit is 10 mg/L measured as nitrogen. If the sheet reports the nitrate ion instead, the comparison is wrong. - **You saw "not detected" and read it as zero.** It means below the method's floor. Read the detection limit next to it, and check it sits well below the limit that matters. - **You spent money treating an aesthetic exceedance.** Secondary standards are for taste, colour and staining, and EPA neither enforces them nor treats them as health limits. - **You drew a bacteriology sample on a Friday afternoon.** Thirty hours is a federal limit, not a suggestion, and the clock starts when you fill the bottle. - **You rinsed the sterile bottle out first, because that is what you do with bottles.** You have just contaminated it. Do not rinse, do not overfill, do not touch the inside of the bottle or the cap. - **You bought a treatment system before finding the cause.** The path that let one contaminant in is still open, and the system only removes what it was sized for. - **You have a shoreline well and have never tested chloride.** Waiting for a salty taste means waiting for 250 mg/L, and intrusion is the one contamination in this guide that does not undo. ## How you know it worked - You have a laboratory result from within the last year, from a state-certified laboratory, covering at minimum total coliform bacteria, nitrate, total dissolved solids and pH. - You have asked your county or state health department what else your area specifically needs, and you have tested for whatever they named. - You can say, for each metal result you hold, whether it was a first-draw or a flushed sample, and therefore which question it answered. - You know which numbers on your sheet are health limits and which are aesthetic, and you have not confused a stained bath for a hazard. - For every non-detect you are relying on, you know the detection limit, and it is well below the limit that matters. - You know the date of every sample and what the weather had been doing. - If you are on a coast, you have a chloride and conductivity baseline, not an assumption, and you intend to repeat it at the wet and dry ends of the year. - If anything came back bad, you looked for the cause before you shopped for a filter. When those are true, the other four water guides stop being guesswork. You can choose a source knowing what is in it, treat for the thing that is actually there, store it without wondering what you sealed in, and say to somebody else, with a piece of paper behind it, that the water in this house is fit to drink. That last one is the part that is worth the fifty dollars. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. United States government publications are listed first because they are public domain and can be redistributed with this guide; the rest cannot, so every fact taken from them is restated here in our own words. ### United States government (public domain) - Environmental Protection Agency. National Primary Drinking Water Regulations (the definitions of MCL, MCLG, action level and treatment technique; the nitrate and nitrite MCLs measured as nitrogen; the arsenic MCL and MCLG; the lead MCLG, treatment technique and action level including the 2027 revision; copper; total coliform and *E. coli* goals; the health effects and sources of nitrate, arsenic and lead). https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/national-primary-drinking-water-regulations - Environmental Protection Agency. Secondary Drinking Water Standards: Guidance for Nuisance Chemicals (the full SMCL table with values, the noticeable effects for chloride, iron, manganese and total dissolved solids, and the statements that EPA does not enforce them and that they are not considered a health risk at the SMCL). https://www.epa.gov/sdwa/secondary-drinking-water-standards-guidance-nuisance-chemicals - Environmental Protection Agency. Revised Total Coliform Rule and Total Coliform Rule (total coliforms as a group that is largely not harmful to humans, their use as an indicator of treatment adequacy and distribution system integrity, and *E. coli* and fecal coliforms as types directly associated with fresh feces). https://www.epa.gov/dwreginfo/revised-total-coliform-rule-and-total-coliform-rule - Environmental Protection Agency. Protect Your Home's Water (the annual private well test list, testing more often for small children, elderly adults and pregnancy, the immediate-test triggers, and the instruction to use only certified laboratories). https://www.epa.gov/privatewells/protect-your-homes-water - Environmental Protection Agency. Potential Well Water Contaminants and Their Impacts (the six contaminant categories for well water, their sources, the nitrate-to-nitrite mechanism and blue baby syndrome, and the heavy metal sources and health effects). https://www.epa.gov/privatewells/potential-well-water-contaminants-and-their-impacts - Environmental Protection Agency. Basic Information about Lead in Drinking Water (corrosion of plumbing materials, lead service lines as typically the most significant source, that lead cannot be seen, tasted or smelled and testing is the only sure way, flushing, cold water only, that boiling does not remove lead, and the $20 to $100 testing cost). https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/basic-information-about-lead-drinking-water - Environmental Protection Agency, Region 8 Laboratory. Quick Guide to Drinking Water Sample Collection, second edition (the general sampling procedure; cold water faucet free of screens and aerators; the 2 to 3 minute flush to temperature stabilization; the lead and copper first-flush procedure with 6 hours undisturbed, no flushing, wide-mouth 1 L bottle and aerators left in place; sequential sampling of a lead service line; sterile 125 or 150 mL bacteriology bottles, not rinsing them, holding the cap by its outside edges, the 100 mL line and one inch headspace; the coliform sampling tips and the list of sites to avoid; nitric acid preservation for metals; and the holding times for biological, metals and unpreserved chemistry analytes). https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-11/documents/drinking_water_sample_collection.pdf - Environmental Protection Agency. Certification of Laboratories that Analyze Drinking Water Samples (the requirement that laboratories be certified and use analytical methods approved by EPA). https://www.epa.gov/dwlabcert - Environmental Protection Agency. Contact Information for Certification Programs and Certified Laboratories for Drinking Water (finding a certified laboratory through your state's certification programme, and that EPA is unable to test residential or commercial drinking water on request). https://www.epa.gov/dwlabcert/contact-information-certification-programs-and-certified-laboratories-drinking-water - Environmental Protection Agency. Drinking Water Health Advisories (what a health advisory value is, and that health advisories are not legally enforceable federal standards). https://www.epa.gov/sdwa/drinking-water-health-advisories-has - Environmental Protection Agency. Basic Information about Nonpoint Source Pollution (the rainfall and snowmelt mechanism by which runoff picks up and carries pollutants into ground and surface waters, and nonpoint source as the leading remaining cause of water quality problems). https://www.epa.gov/nps/basic-information-about-nonpoint-source-nps-pollution - Environmental Protection Agency. National Beach Guidance and Required Performance Criteria, Appendix 4B2, Sample Collection (not touching the inside of the bottle or cover, headspace for mixing, icing or refrigerating bacteriological samples at 1 to 4 C, and the 6 hour holding limit for recreational water samples). https://archive.epa.gov/water/archive/web/html/app4b2.html - Code of Federal Regulations, title 40 section 141.21, Coliform sampling (the requirement that the time from sample collection to initiation of analysis may not exceed 30 hours). https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2021-title40-vol25/xml/CFR-2021-title40-vol25-sec141-21.xml - Code of Federal Regulations, title 40 part 136 appendix B (the definition of the method detection limit as the minimum measured concentration reportable with 99 percent confidence that it is distinguishable from method blank results). https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2021-title40-vol25/xml/CFR-2021-title40-vol25-part136-appB.xml - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Guidelines for Testing Well Water (the annual test list, the events that should trigger an extra test, the instruction to use a state-certified laboratory, that the health department holds the list of certified laboratories, and the advice to ask the health department what else to test for locally). https://www.cdc.gov/drinking-water/safety/guidelines-for-testing-well-water.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. How to Disinfect Wells After an Emergency (drinking bottled water after a disaster until the water is known to be safe, sampling for total coliform and either *E. coli* or fecal coliform, the 7 to 10 day wait after disinfection before testing, and the Safe Drinking Water Hotline on 800-426-4791). https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/how-to-disinfect-wells-after-an-emergency.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Drinking Water Sources: An Overview (public systems being regulated and monitored while private systems including rainwater collection are not, and natural filtration of ground water depending on depth and local geology). https://www.cdc.gov/drinking-water/about/drinking-water-sources-an-overview.html - United States Geological Survey. Arsenic and Drinking Water (arsenic as a natural trace component of rocks and sediments and its human sources, higher frequency and concentration in western wells, about 7 percent of sampled drinking water wells nationwide and about 16 percent in the Southwest exceeding the MCL, about 2.1 million people on private wells above the standard, and domestic wells being unregulated with the homeowner responsible for monitoring). https://www.usgs.gov/mission-areas/water-resources/science/arsenic-and-drinking-water - United States Geological Survey, Water Science School. Hardness of Water (the definition of hardness, the soft, moderately hard, hard and very hard bands in mg/L as calcium carbonate, and that hardness is not a health concern but can be a nuisance). https://www.usgs.gov/special-topics/water-science-school/science/hardness-water - United States Geological Survey, Water Science School. Conductivity (Electrical Conductance) and Water (dissolved ions making water conductive, and salts, principally sodium chloride, being the most common dissolved substances). https://www.usgs.gov/water-science-school/science/conductivity-electrical-conductance-and-water - United States Geological Survey. Saltwater Intrusion (pumping reducing freshwater flow toward the coast and drawing saltwater into freshwater zones, the interface as a diffuse zone of dispersion, and intrusion decreasing freshwater storage and in extreme cases leading to the abandonment of wells). https://www.usgs.gov/mission-areas/water-resources/science/saltwater-intrusion - Food and Drug Administration. FDA Regulates the Safety of Bottled Water Beverages (the requirement that producers use an approved source and sample and test both source water and the final product for contaminants). https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/fda-regulates-safety-bottled-water-beverages-including-flavored-water-and-nutrient-added-water ### Washington State agencies (cited as the authority, restated in our own words) Washington is a state, not the federal government, so these publications are ordinary copyright. Their facts are used here; their wording is not. - Washington State Department of Ecology. Seawater Intrusion (sea level rise and over-pumping of wells near saltwater coastlines as the causes; the monitoring specification of chloride, conductivity and static water level measured in April and September with chemical analysis by a state-accredited laboratory; and that some coastal wells in Washington are now unusable). https://ecology.wa.gov/water-shorelines/water-supply/water-rights/seawater-intrusion ### Inside this project - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/water.json`, for the Kitsap Peninsula figures quoted here with their own provenance: the peninsula's hydrologic setting and groundwater as the only domestic source, and the well depth distribution near Silverdale, from USGS Scientific Investigations Report 2014-5106 (Welch, Frans and Olsen, 2014, https://pubs.usgs.gov/sir/2014/5106/); and the seawater intrusion findings, including the list of areas where chloride in well water exceeds 25 mg/L and the 1980 vintage of that finding, from USGS Open-File Report 80-1186 (Hansen and Bolke, 1980, https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/ofr801186). - [Where Water Comes From](/library#where-water-comes-from), for the sources themselves, their risks, the habit of looking upstream, and the point that your senses are a one-way alarm. - [Making Water Safe to Drink](/library#making-water-safe-to-drink), for the treatment that follows a bad result, the pathogen classes, and the contaminants no home treatment reaches. - [Storing Water Safely](/library#storing-water-safely), for keeping the result good once you have it. - [Collecting Rainwater](/library#collecting-rainwater), for roof catchment and why barrel water is treated as non-potable throughout. - [Where Water Goes](/library#where-water-goes), for the watershed above you, the septic and runoff mechanisms that put things in a well, and why seawater intrusion is a decision you get to make once. ### Labelled in the text as rules of thumb, not sourced - Sampling during or just after the wet season rather than in a dry late summer. It follows from EPA's rainfall and snowmelt mechanism, but no agency opened for this guide recommends a season. - The split between what a home kit is worth using for and what requires a certified laboratory. The certification requirement and the detection limit definition are sourced; the specific division of parameters between the two lists is ours. - The ranked order of response to a bad result: stop drinking, confirm, find the cause, fix the cause, then treat. Each individual step rests on sourced facts; the ordering is ours. - The reading that a conductivity meter is the most useful cheap instrument for a coastal well. Ecology's monitoring specification is sourced; calling it the best value for money is a judgement.

docs.text: # Water Chemistry Take the lid off a kettle that has been boiled every day for a year and look at the element. There is a hard pale crust on it. Scrape a bit off with a fingernail; it is gritty, like very fine stone. That is stone. It is the same mineral as chalk and limestone, and an hour before it landed on your element it was invisible, dissolved in water that looked exactly like water. Nobody added it. You boiled clean tap water and rock came out. This guide is about why that happens, and about the dozen other things that follow from the same handful of facts. ## What this guide is for, and what it cannot do Four guides in this Library already tell you where water comes from, where it goes, how to test it and how to make it safe. (There are others alongside them on catching rain, storing it and reusing it, but those four are the ones this guide sits underneath.) Every one of them hands you numbers: 10 mg/L, 0.3 mg/L, pH 6.5 to 8.5, 500 mg/L. They tell you which side of each line you want to be on. None of them tells you what those numbers physically are. So a reader finishes all four knowing which thresholds matter and still unable to predict anything. Why does one well stain the bath orange and the neighbour's does not? Why does a softener help the kettle and do nothing for the nitrate? Why does the county say run the tap before you drink, and then say do not run the tap before you sample? This guide is the layer underneath. Read it and those four stop being lists of thresholds. You should be able to look at an unfamiliar laboratory sheet, or an unfamiliar product on a shelf, and reason about it rather than look it up. **Two honest limits.** First, nothing here tells you what is in your water. Chemistry is not a substitute for a test, and [Testing Water](/library#testing-water) explains why your senses are very nearly useless for this. Second, this guide does not teach treatment procedure. [Making Water Safe to Drink](/library#making-water-safe-to-drink) is where boiling times, bleach doses and filter pore sizes live. What this guide adds is the reason each of those works on what it works on, which is the part that lets you evaluate a product nobody has reviewed. Where this guide leans on a number one of the others already carries, it points at that guide rather than reprinting it. The point is to complete them, not to duplicate them. ## The one idea underneath everything: water is a lopsided molecule Almost everything in this guide falls out of a single structural fact. USGS states it plainly: "Water molecules have a polar arrangement of oxygen and hydrogen atoms." The hydrogen side, USGS says, carries a positive electrical charge and the oxygen side a negative one. Water is not a neutral little ball. It is a molecule with a positive end and a negative end, and that makes it behave like an extremely weak magnet with respect to anything else that carries charge. Watch what that does to table salt. USGS again: "Water can become so heavily attracted to a different compound, like salt (NaCl), that it can disrupt the attractive forces that hold the sodium and chloride in the salt compound together." The mechanism is exactly what you would guess from the shape: "The positively-charged side of the water molecules are attracted to the negatively-charged chloride ions and the negatively-charged side of the water molecules are attracted to the positively-charged sodium ions," and so "Water molecules pull the sodium and chloride ions apart, breaking the ionic bond that held them together." That is dissolving. A crystal of salt is not destroyed or converted; it is taken apart piece by piece by billions of small electrical tugs, and the pieces are then surrounded by water molecules and carried away individually. The record `sodium_chloride` in `data/chemistry/compounds.csv` gives salt's solubility as 360 g/L, which is an enormous amount of rock to hide in a litre of something clear. This is why USGS calls water "the 'universal solvent'" and says it "is capable of dissolving more substances than any other liquid." And it is why the same page adds the qualifier that matters: "Of course it cannot dissolve everything." **The rule that predicts which is which.** Water dissolves things that carry charge, or that have their own lopsided positive and negative ends. It does very badly with things that are electrically bland all over. Chemists shorten this to "like dissolves like." Look down the `solubility_water` column in `compounds.csv` and the split is visible without knowing any chemistry. The salts and the acids and the small alcohols are soluble or miscible: `sodium_chloride` 360 g/L, `potassium_chloride` 340 g/L, `saltpeter` 316 g/L, `ethanol` miscible, `acetic_acid` miscible, `glucose` 909 g/L. The greasy hydrocarbons are not: `octane` insoluble, `kerosene` insoluble, `toluene` 0.52 g/L, `benzene` 1.79 g/L. Sugar and alcohol have oxygen and hydrogen sticking out with charge on them; petrol is carbon and hydrogen arranged so evenly that water has nothing to grab. A caveat about where that last explanation comes from, because it applies to a few other places in this guide as well. The polarity of water, the positive and negative ends, and the salt mechanism are all stated by USGS on the pages cited above. The generalisation to "like dissolves like," the hydrogen bond, which is the specific name for the attraction between the positive hydrogen of one water molecule and the negative oxygen of the next, and the structure of a soap molecule described below are standard chemistry but are **not** on any page opened for this guide. USGS describes the attraction without naming it. Treat that vocabulary as ordinary textbook material rather than as something a federal agency said. ### Four things that follow immediately **1. Hardness exists.** Rain falling through air picks up carbon dioxide, which makes it a weak acid, and weak acid dissolves carbonate rock. The National Park Service describes the process that carves caves: "precipitation, such as rainwater or snowmelt, mixes with carbon dioxide from air and decaying plants in soil and forms carbonic acid," and "Once the acidic water reaches carbonate rocks (e.g. marble, limestone, dolomite), it can seep into cracks and dissolve the rock to create rooms and passageways." A cave is a hole where the water took the rock away dissolved. The calcium is still in the water, downstream, and eventually in your kettle. **2. Salt wrecks soil.** Sodium dissolves completely and goes wherever the water goes, including into the spaces between clay particles, where it does structural damage that has nothing to do with toxicity. [Greywater](/library#greywater) carries that argument in full, with its own sources, including the sodium adsorption ratio and why softener brine is prohibited from greywater systems by name. It is the best worked example in the Library of a dissolved thing causing harm by physics rather than poisoning. **3. Oil does not rinse off.** Water has nothing to grip on a fat or a grease, so it beads and runs past. Soap works because a soap molecule is built as a compromise: a greasy tail that will bury itself in the oil and a charged head that water will accept. That is also why hard water ruins soap, which is the next section but one. **4. And the big one: a filter cannot remove something that is dissolved.** This is the single most useful consequence in the guide, so it gets its own section. ### Dissolved versus suspended, and why the difference decides everything Two things can be "in" water, and they are not the same kind of thing at all. **Suspended** means small solid pieces, floating or drifting, still themselves. Silt, clay, rust flakes, leaf fragments, bacteria, cysts. They are separate objects with edges. They will eventually settle if you leave the water alone. They scatter light, which is why water carrying them looks cloudy. **Dissolved** means taken apart and mixed in among the water molecules, one particle at a time, with no edges and nothing to settle. Salt, calcium, nitrate, lead, arsenic, sugar, oxygen. Dissolved things do not settle out, and they are very much smaller than anything a filter is built to catch. For scale: [Making Water Safe to Drink](/library#making-water-safe-to-drink) records CDC's figure of about 0.01 micron for the finest class of filter, the ultrafilter, and a dissolved ion is far below even that. Most dissolved substances are also invisible, which is the property that matters here, though that one has an exception worth naming. USGS's list of what makes water turbid includes dissolved coloured organic compounds, which are the kind of thing that stains a bog stream brown. So a few dissolved things do colour water. What none of them do is make it cloudy in the way suspended particles do, and the great majority of what this guide is about, every ion and every gas, is completely invisible at any concentration that matters. A filter is a sieve. It works by having holes smaller than the thing you want to keep out. [Making Water Safe to Drink](/library#making-water-safe-to-drink) gives CDC's ladder of pore sizes and which organism each catches, and the whole ladder lives in the suspended world. Nothing on it can sieve out a dissolved ion, because a dissolved ion is travelling in among the water molecules at roughly their own scale. Any hole big enough to let the water through is big enough to let the sodium through with it. You cannot separate them by size alone. So anything that removes a dissolved substance has to work by some principle other than sieving: sticking it to a surface, swapping it for a different ion, pushing water through a membrane and leaving it behind, or boiling the water away from it. Every one of those has a different blind spot, and that is what the treatment section at the end of this guide is about. Carry this one sentence out of here if nothing else: **clarity is mostly a statement about what is suspended, and it tells you almost nothing about what is dissolved.** [Where Water Comes From](/library#where-water-comes-from) makes the same point from the safety side and calls it the most expensive wrong belief about water. This is the physical reason it is true. ## pH pH is the measurement everybody has heard of and almost nobody can use, because two things about it are routinely skipped. USGS gives the definition: "pH is a measure of how acidic/basic water is." The scale "goes from 0 to 14, with 7 being neutral," with lower numbers acidic and higher numbers basic. ### It is logarithmic, and that is not a technicality USGS: "pH is reported in 'logarithmic units'. Each number represents a 10-fold change in the acidity/basicness of the water." Their example: "Water with a pH of five is ten times more acidic than water having a pH of six." People nod at this and then reason about pH as if it were a thermometer, where 6 and 7 are neighbours. They are not neighbours. They are a factor of ten apart. Work it through with numbers you will actually meet: - EPA's recommended range for drinking water runs from pH 6.5 to pH 8.5. That is two units, so the acceptable range spans a **hundredfold** difference in acidity from one end to the other. Two supplies can both be "in range" and be a hundred times apart. - USGS says "Normal rainfall has a pH of about 5.6", slightly acidic, and attributes that to carbon dioxide gas from the atmosphere. That is 1.4 units below neutral, so ordinary clean rain is about **25 times** more acidic than neutral water. Rain is not neutral anywhere, and it never was. - USGS's own example of coal mine drainage sits at pH 2, which is five units below neutral: a hundred thousand times. pH belongs to a family of scales that do not behave the way a ruler does, and the habit of checking which kind you are holding is worth having generally. [Units and Converting Them](/library#units-and-converting-them) works through the two other members you will meet: temperature, which has an offset as well as a scale factor, and area and volume, which go as the square and the cube of a length. It does not cover logarithmic scales, so pH is the third kind and this is the place it gets explained. ### What pH does not tell you, which is the amount Here is the part most popular writing omits entirely, and it is the reason a pond, a soil, or a body of water resists change. pH tells you the **intensity** of the acidity right now. It says nothing about **how much acid or base it would take to move it.** Those are different questions, and the second one has its own measurement. That measurement is **alkalinity**, and USGS defines it as exactly this: "The buffering capacity of a water body; a measure of the ability of the water body to neutralize acids and thus maintain a fairly stable pH level." Two things about alkalinity trip people up. **It is not a chemical.** USGS: alkalinity is "a property of water that is dependent on the presence of certain chemicals in the water, such as bicarbonates, carbonates, and hydroxides." You cannot buy a bottle of alkalinity. It is a capacity that a particular mixture of dissolved substances happens to have. **It is not the same word as "alkaline".** Alkaline means the pH is above 7. Alkalinity means the water has reserves that resist the pH moving at all, in either direction. Water can be slightly acidic and have high alkalinity; water can be slightly basic and have almost none. USGS measures it by titration: add acid in small increments while watching the pH. At first almost nothing happens, because the bicarbonate and carbonate are absorbing each addition. Then the reserves run out and the pH drops steeply. The volume of acid it took to reach that turn is the alkalinity. **Where it comes from is geology.** USGS notes that runoff from limestone country raises alkalinity, while granite country produces lower alkalinity. Limestone is calcium carbonate; it puts carbonate and bicarbonate into every drop that touches it. Granite does not. **The consequence.** USGS: water with high alkalinity "will experience less of a change in its own acidity when acidic water, such as acid rain or an acid spill, is introduced into the water body." Put that together with the geology above and you get the useful prediction: two lakes can take the same rainstorm, or the same spill, and respond completely differently, and the thing that decides which is which is the rock their water came off rather than anything about the lakes themselves. An analogy that holds up: pH is the reading on the thermometer; alkalinity is the size of the radiator. Knowing the temperature of a room tells you nothing about how fast it will cool when you open a window. That distinction is not an academic nicety. It comes back twice in this guide: it is half of what decides whether your plumbing dissolves into your water, and it is the reason a soil or a pond has a characteristic resistance to whatever you add to it. ### What a pH number is good for at home Low pH is the one that costs you money, and not by hurting you. EPA's secondary standard for pH is a range, 6.5 to 8.5, and EPA lists the noticeable effects on both sides: at low pH, "bitter metallic taste; corrosion"; at high pH, "slippery feel; soda taste; deposits." Neither of those is a health effect, and EPA says of the whole secondary list that "These contaminants are not considered to present a risk to human health at the SMCL." Acidic water is not a poison. It is a solvent that has been made slightly hungrier, and the thing it is going to dissolve is your plumbing. That is the corrosivity section below, and it is the reason pH earns its place on the annual well test that [Testing Water](/library#testing-water) describes. ## Hardness WHO's definition is the original one and it is the most useful, because it names the thing people actually notice. WHO describes hardness as the traditional way of measuring how much water reacts with soap, with hard water needing considerably more soap before it will lather at all. USGS gives the modern version: "The simple definition of water hardness is the amount of dissolved calcium and magnesium in the water." Both are right, and the gap between them is the story. Hardness was defined by laundry a long time before anybody could measure calcium. ### Where it comes from USGS: "As water moves through soil and rock it dissolves small amounts of naturally-occurring minerals and carries them into the groundwater supply." WHO names the rocks: calcium and magnesium occur in many sedimentary rocks, of which limestone and chalk are the commonest. So hardness is a map of the geology upstream of you, delivered in solution. Limestone and chalk country gives hard water. Granite country, which USGS names as the low-alkalinity case, gives soft water. The same rock that sets alkalinity sets hardness, which is why the two usually move together. The scale of this is easy to underestimate. USGS reports that "In the United States, about 40% of the groundwater used for drinking comes from karst aquifers," karst being terrain "created from the dissolution of soluble rocks, principally limestone and dolomite." Two fifths of the groundwater Americans drink comes out of rock that water has been eating. Note the qualifier: that figure is about drinking supply, not about all groundwater withdrawn for every purpose. USGS adds the reason groundwater is usually harder than surface water: "Because water is such an excellent solvent it can contain lots of dissolved chemicals. And since groundwater moves through rocks and subsurface soil, it has a lot of opportunity to dissolve substances as it moves. For that reason, groundwater will often have more dissolved substances than surface water will." Contact time is the variable. A creek touches rock for hours; an aquifer holds water against rock for years. WHO adds a detail worth knowing because it explains odd test results. No single substance causes hardness, WHO says. It comes from a range of dissolved metal ions carrying more than one positive charge, mostly calcium and magnesium, but with aluminium, barium, iron, manganese, strontium and zinc all contributing as well. So iron and manganese count toward hardness, which is one reason a high-iron well can report hardness that the calcium alone does not explain. ### The bands, and what they are not USGS and WHO agree on the classification, in milligrams per litre expressed as calcium carbonate: below about 60 is soft, 60 to 120 moderately hard, 120 to 180 hard, and above 180 very hard. [Testing Water](/library#testing-water) reprints the bands in the context of reading a laboratory sheet, which is where you will meet them. What the bands are not is a safety scale. USGS: "Hardness is a property of water that is not a health concern, but it can be a nuisance." Very hard water is not dangerous water. It is expensive water. You may also see hardness in **grains per gallon**, which is the unit the softener industry uses and the one printed on the dial of most equipment. Penn State Extension gives the conversion: one grain per gallon is about 17 mg/L. So the very-hard threshold of 180 mg/L is roughly 10.6 grains per gallon. Any time a salesman and a laboratory seem to disagree by a factor of about seventeen, this is why. ### Temporary and permanent hardness, and why a kettle furs up WHO notes that although hardness is caused by those positive ions, it can also be discussed in two parts: carbonate hardness, which it gives the older name of temporary hardness, and non-carbonate hardness, older name permanent. Those two old names describe genuinely different behaviour and they explain the crust you scraped off the element. **Carbonate hardness is the calcium and magnesium that arrived paired with carbonate and bicarbonate**, which is to say the part that came out of limestone, and it is the part that is also providing your alkalinity.
