docs.text: # Greywater Stand in the shower and count while the water warms up. However long that takes in your house, every second of it is water that was treated to drinking standard, that you paid for, and that went down the drain without touching you. Put a bucket there and you catch it. That part is easy. The bucket costs nothing and the water is clean. Now scale it up. The Washington State Department of Health puts the greywater a household produces at up to forty gallons per person each day, and calls it the largest single portion of a home's wastewater. For two people that is eighty gallons a day leaving the building, most of it barely dirty, at exactly the time of year the garden is thirsty. That is the appeal, and it is a real one. But the bucket is the honest beginning of this subject and it is worth noticing how far it is from the end of it. Everything difficult about greywater happens after you have caught it: where you are allowed to put it, how long you may keep it, what was dissolved in it before you caught it, and which of those things quietly ruins your soil two years from now while you are congratulating yourself on the water you saved. ## What this guide will and will not do It will tell you what greywater legally is in Washington, which is not what most writing on the subject says it is. It will give you the real numbers from the real rule, with the section they come from, so you can check every one. It will explain the failure modes and where each one bites. It will not tell you whether your system is legal. It cannot. In Washington the decision is made by a named official in your county, the local health officer, and that official is allowed to be stricter than the state and is allowed to decide your site is unsuitable. There is no way to read your way to that answer. The most useful thing this guide can do is make the phone call you eventually make a short one, because you will already know what you are asking about. It also will not help you build a system. Plumbing a house for greywater is work for a licensed designer in most of the cases the rule contemplates, and the rule says so explicitly. What this guide gives you is the ability to understand what that designer is doing and to notice when something is wrong. One more limit, stated here because it is the single most common error. **Greywater reuse never replaces a sewer connection or a septic system.** The Washington rule says this outright: using a greywater irrigation system does not serve as an alternative to an approved on-site sewage system or a connection to an approved public sewer, and that holds even for buildings with waterless toilets (WAC 246-274-005(3)). A greywater system in Washington is a seasonal side branch off a permanent wastewater system, with a valve so you can send the water back down the normal path whenever you need to. If you are imagining greywater as the way to avoid installing a septic system, stop here. That is not what this is. ## The definition, which is genuinely different depending on where you stand Here is a claim you will find stated confidently and without qualification all over the internet: kitchen sink water is not greywater. In Washington that is false. It is false in the statute and false in the rule, and the difference matters enough to change what you are allowed to build. **Washington.** The state defines greywater in statute at RCW 90.46.010(8) and repeats it in the rule at WAC 246-274-009(4). Both give the same list: domestic type flows from bathtubs, showers, bathroom sinks, washing machines, dishwashers, and kitchen or utility sinks. Greywater does not include flow from a toilet or urinal. That is the entire boundary. Kitchen sinks are in. Dishwashers are in. What Washington does instead of excluding the kitchen is split greywater into two grades, in the same definition: - **Light greywater** is flows from bathtubs, showers, bathroom sinks, washing machines, and laundry-utility sinks. - **Dark greywater** is flows from dishwashers, kitchen and nonlaundry utility sinks, either alone or mixed with light greywater. Read that second definition slowly, because it contains the trap. Dark greywater is the kitchen flows **alone or in combination with light greywater**. One kitchen sink plumbed into your shower line does not produce mostly-light greywater. It produces dark greywater, all of it, and dark greywater requires a treatment component and the most demanding tier of system (WAC 246-274-300(2)(a)). Mixing is a one-way door. **California.** The California definition, at Health and Safety Code section 17922.12, lists bathtubs, showers, bathroom washbasins, clothes washing machines and laundry tubs, and then says specifically that kitchen sinks and dishwashers are not included. The opposite of Washington, in the same country, on the same coast. **Oregon.** Oregon's Department of Environmental Quality includes showers and bathtubs, bathroom sinks, kitchen sinks and laundry, and excludes toilet discharge, garbage wastes from kitchen sinks fitted with garbage disposal units, and wastewater contaminated by soiled diapers. A third answer: the kitchen sink is in, but the grinder under it puts you out. Three neighbouring states, three different boundaries. So when you read a confident sentence online about what greywater "is", the useful question is not whether the writer is careless but which state they live in. Most of them are in California, which is why the kitchen exclusion is repeated so often as though it were physics. **The practical consequence for you.** If you are in Washington and you want the simplest legal system, you want light greywater only, and you want the kitchen nowhere near it. Not because kitchen water is not greywater here, but because it is the expensive kind. ## Blackwater is a word the Washington rule does not use You will notice something if you read the whole of chapter 246-274 WAC: the word blackwater never appears in it. Not once. That is not an oversight. Washington's statute defines domestic wastewater as wastewater from greywater, toilet, or urinal sources (RCW 90.46.010(7)), and defines greywater by listing fixtures and excluding toilets and urinals. The line is drawn by naming what is on each side, not by defining a second category. So the honest answer to "what is the regulatory definition of blackwater in Washington" is that there is not one in this chapter, and anybody who gives you a crisp Washington blackwater definition is importing it from somewhere else. This matters more than a terminology quibble, because the Department of Health's own literature review reached a conclusion that ought to be uncomfortable for anyone who thinks of greywater as obviously the clean half. Reviewing the published studies, the department concluded that the pollution level in a greywater stream that includes kitchen sinks, dishwashers and laundry machines used to wash dirty diapers can be equal to or greater than blackwater, and needs regulating consistently with on-site sewage rules. The same review puts it more bluntly elsewhere: a sink with a garbage grinder used for washing raw meat or dishes, and a washing machine used for soiled diapers, can carry more pollution than a toilet. The numbers behind that are worth carrying around. Biochemical oxygen demand, BOD5, is the standard measure of how much organic material is in water and therefore how hard it will be for an environment to digest it. The department's review reports these figures from the literature: | Water | BOD5 | |---|---| | Bathroom-only greywater, Danish apartment study | 26 to 130 mg/L | | Greywater including kitchen wastewater | 26 to 295 mg/L | | Raw sewage | about 300 mg/L | | Treated wastewater | under 10 mg/L | The top of the kitchen-inclusive greywater range, 295 mg/L, is indistinguishable from the raw sewage benchmark of about 300 mg/L. Not typical greywater, the top of its range. But a category whose range reaches raw sewage is not a category you can treat as harmless because of its name. ### The four things that stop being greywater Washington's general requirements (WAC 246-274-011(1)) put four kinds of water outside the system regardless of which fixture they came from. These are the lines that turn permitted reuse into an illegal discharge: **Diaper wash water.** The greywater may not contain water used to wash diapers or similarly soiled or infectious materials. This is the classic line and all three states draw it: Oregon excludes wastewater contaminated by soiled diapers, and California's definition excludes water affected by infectious, contaminated or unhealthy bodily wastes. The reason is direct. Diaper laundry is faecal material, and faecal material is the exact thing the whole regulatory structure exists to keep out of soil that people touch. If there is a baby in the house and the nappies go through the washing machine, that washing machine is not a greywater source while that is true. The department's review makes the same point from the other direction when it identifies the lowest-risk sources as bathroom fixtures and washing machines **in homes without children living in them**. **Toxic substances, cleaning chemicals and hazardous household products.** The rule names examples: waste from a water softener, cleaning car parts, washing greasy or oily rags or clothing, rinsing paint brushes, waste solutions from home photo labs or similar hobby or home-occupation activity, and home maintenance activities. Note the first one on that list. **Water softener regeneration waste is prohibited by name**, and that is the single most sodium-loaded thing a house produces. Come back to this when you reach the soil section; it is not an arbitrary exclusion. **Biomedical waste**, as that term is defined in chapter 70A.228 RCW. **Anything that is not domestic type flow.** The greywater has to have the consistency and strength typical of a household. A home business that generates something else does not get to route it through the garden because it happens to leave via a sink. ## Storage: the twenty four hour line, and what is happening on the other side of it There is a widely published short storage limit for untreated greywater, and in Washington it is real, it is written down, and it is twenty four hours. The exact form it takes depends on the tier: - **Tier 1 systems may not store greywater at all.** Not for a day, not at all. The rule says the greywater may not be stored and that it must be delivered by gravity, with no pumps (WAC 246-274-100(1)(f) and (g)). A Tier 1 system is a pipe, a slope and a garden. - **Tier 2 systems may store it for no more than twenty four hours** (WAC 246-274-200(1)(g)). - **Beyond twenty four hours you need a treatment component**, which by definition makes it a Tier 3 system (WAC 246-274-300(2)(b)). So the limit is not a rule of thumb somebody repeated. It is the boundary between two regulatory tiers, and crossing it changes what you are legally required to build. **Why the number exists.** The Department of Health's literature review gives the mechanism, and it is worth understanding rather than memorising. Greywater has a high BOD5, which means it contains a lot of organic material that bacteria want to eat. Bacteria eating it consume oxygen. In a closed tank the oxygen is a fixed and small supply, so it runs out quickly. What grows next is anaerobic bacteria, which do not need oxygen, and a characteristic product of anaerobic bacteria is hydrogen sulfide, which the review describes as an extremely odorous gas. That is the rotten egg smell, and it is the smell of a tank that has gone septic. The review concludes that storing untreated greywater longer than twenty four hours is not recommended. **The second reason, which is worse.** The same review reports that the warm wet conditions inside plumbing and storage tanks actually increase indicator organisms when greywater is held past twenty four hours. Stored greywater is not a container of a fixed number of germs slowly dying. It is a nutrient broth at room temperature. The review, citing the Water Environment Research Foundation, reports that indicator organisms can persist and even multiply in stored greywater because of the available nutrients and biofilm formation, and that pathogens seeded into greywater are capable of reproducing during storage. Specific findings it cites: Salmonella typhimurium and Shigella dysenteriae survived several days when seeded into greywater at pH 6.5 and 25 degrees C. A virus, poliovirus type 1, behaved differently and fell by 90 percent or more after six days under the same conditions. So the direction of travel depends on the organism. Some bacteria grow. Some viruses die off. A tank is not a disinfection step for either. **A number for pathogen load.** The review reports faecal coliform results in greywater samples ranging from about 1.8 x 10^4 to 7.9 x 10^6 per 100 mL. For scale, drinking water standards are written around zero. Greywater is not lightly contaminated water; it is contaminated water whose contamination is invisible because it is dissolved in something that looks like weak tea. **The honest caveat, because it is in the source.** The department's review also states plainly that despite the presence of faecal indicator organisms and pathogens, a consistent relationship between greywater reuse and illness rates is unknown at this time. That is a real and important qualification and it should not be sanded off. The hazard is established; the population-level illness rate attributable to domestic greywater reuse is not. Design as though the pathogens matter, because they are measurably there, but do not tell people greywater irrigation is a known cause of outbreaks, because the literature the state relied on does not say that. **What this means for a bucket.** If you are hand-carrying shower warm-up water to a shrub the same afternoon, the storage problem is not really yours; you have not stored it. If you are filling a drum in the basement to water the garden at the weekend, you have built the exact thing the twenty four hour rule exists to prevent, and by Monday it will smell like it. A drum of four day old greywater is a disposal problem, not a resource. One more thing about storage, because you will meet it. Some published greywater guidance from drier states suggests adding chlorine bleach to extend how long greywater can be held. A New Mexico State University extension publication says exactly that. Do not carry that advice into Washington. Bleach is a cleaning chemical, the Washington rule prohibits cleaning chemicals in greywater, bleach damages the plants you are irrigating, and the tier structure here answers the same problem with a treatment component instead. Advice written for one regulatory regime does not travel. ## Where it may go, and where it may not ### Subsurface, always, with no exceptions in this chapter The entire Washington chapter is named for this: greywater reuse for subsurface irrigation. The general requirements say the greywater must be used only for subsurface irrigation, and separately that it may not surface in any way, including by ponding or runoff, and must stay below the ground surface so that people and animals do not come into contact with it (WAC 246-274-011(1)(a) and (g)). Two separate requirements, which is deliberate. The first governs how you design it. The second governs what happens afterwards. A system that was designed subsurface but is now ponding in a low corner of the garden has violated the second even though it satisfied the first, and the rule treats surfacing greywater as a definition of failure (WAC 246-274-009(2)(a)). This rules out, in Washington, a set of things people do elsewhere and write about enthusiastically: sprinklers, surface drip lines lying on mulch, watering cans, hoses, spraying anything, and washing the car with it. The Department of Health's own review reaches the same conclusion from the risk side, finding that untreated greywater from any source is not suitable for uses involving direct exposure such as washing cars, toilet flushing and spray irrigation, but that subsurface irrigation can be an acceptable use. ### How deep For Tier 2 and Tier 3 systems the rule is specific (WAC 246-274-415(5)): the subsurface irrigation components go a minimum of four inches deep and no deeper than twelve inches below finished grade, and the four inch cover must be two inches of suitable soil plus two inches of mulch. For Tier 1 the requirement is at least four inches of appropriate cover, which may be suitable soil or mulch, humus or compost, topped up through the season as it settles (WAC 246-274-100(1)(k)). There is a reason for the upper bound as well as the lower one. Too shallow and the water surfaces, which is the exposure failure. Too deep and you are past the root zone, which means you are no longer irrigating plants, you are disposing of wastewater into the ground, which is a different activity with a different permit. ### How much soil has to be underneath This is the requirement that decides whether a site works, and it is the one most likely to stop you. For Tier 2 and Tier 3 systems there must be a minimum of **twenty four inches of suitable soil** between the irrigation components and any restrictive layer, or the highest water table during the growing season (WAC 246-274-415(6)). Be precise about which tier that binds. Twenty four inches is a Tier 2 and Tier 3 design requirement; the Tier 1 section does not state a separation distance. What Tier 1 has instead is the general requirement that applies to every tier: the system must be located in suitable soil (WAC 246-274-011(1)(j)). Since suitable soil is *defined* as unsaturated soil above the seasonally high water table and above any restrictive layer, shallow ground is still a problem for a Tier 1 system. It is just a problem with no published number attached, which means it is resolved by the local health officer's judgement rather than by a measurement you can take yourself and check. Suitable soil has a definition: unsaturated soil above the seasonally high water table and above any restrictive layer, in which water, air and root growth are sustained (WAC 246-274-009(22)). A restrictive layer is a stratum that impedes vertical movement of water, air and roots, and the rule names hardpan, claypan, fragipan, caliche, some compacted soils, bedrock and unstructured clay soils (WAC 246-274-009(19)). Do the stacking. If your irrigation line is at the shallowest allowed depth of four inches, you still need twenty four inches of suitable soil below it, so you need a soil column at least twenty eight inches deep before you hit anything restrictive. Twenty eight inches is about 71 cm. If you place the line at the deepest allowed twelve inches, you need thirty six inches, about 91 cm. Hold onto the 71 cm figure; it is about to matter locally. ### The setbacks, which are Washington's and only Washington's WAC 246-274-405, Table I, sets minimum horizontal setbacks. Two columns: one measured from the edge of the subsurface irrigation components, one from tanks and other system components. | From | Irrigation edge | Tanks and components | |---|---|---| | Building foundation, down-gradient | 10 ft | not applicable | | Building foundation, up-gradient | 2 ft | not applicable | | Property or easement line | 2 ft | 2 ft | | Pressurised water supply line or public water main | 10 ft | 10 ft | | Interceptor, curtain drain or drainage ditch, down-gradient | 30 ft | not applicable | | Interceptor, curtain drain or drainage ditch, up-gradient | 10 ft | not applicable | | In-ground swimming pool | 10 ft | 5 ft | | Spring or surface water, from the ordinary high-water mark | 100 ft | 50 ft | | Well or suction line | 100 ft | 50 ft | | Public drinking water well | 100 ft | 100 ft | | Public drinking water spring, from the ordinary high-water mark | 200 ft | 200 ft | | Decommissioned well | 10 ft | not applicable | | Down-gradient cut or bank, 5 ft or more undisturbed soil above a restrictive layer | 25 ft | not applicable | | Down-gradient cut or bank, under 5 ft undisturbed soil above a restrictive layer | 50 ft | not applicable | | On-site sewage system, primary and reserve areas | 10 ft | not applicable | **These are Washington's numbers. Do not carry them anywhere else.** Every state writes its own and they are not close to each other. If you are reading this outside Washington, the correct use of this table is as a list of the *kinds* of thing that get a setback, so you know what to ask your own regulator about. The distances are not transferable and using them elsewhere would be inventing a regulation. Two definitions the table depends on. Down-gradient means liquid will flow toward the thing when it hits a water table or restrictive layer; up-gradient means it will flow away. That is why the same feature gets two different numbers: a foundation uphill of your irrigation field is a much smaller problem than one downhill of it. And if surface water in the area is used as a public drinking water supply, the system has to sit outside that supply's source water protection area entirely, which is a different and larger constraint than any distance in the table. **The well setback deserves its own paragraph.** One hundred feet from a well, measured from the edge of the irrigated area. If you are on a private well, as much of rural Kitsap is, this is frequently the binding constraint on a small lot, and it interacts badly with the two foot property line setback: you must keep a hundred feet from *a* well, and your neighbour's well counts. The point of the setback is travel time through soil. Soil is the treatment step in a subsurface greywater system; there is no other one in Tier 1 or Tier 2. Distance is how you buy enough of it. The related guide [Testing Water](/library#testing-water) covers what you would actually test a well for and what coliform in a well result means, which is the other end of this same concern. ### The other siting rules Beyond the table, the general requirements add several conditions that each rule out real sites (WAC 246-274-011(1)): - The greywater must be used and contained within the property boundary of the building it came from, or on nearby property where you are legally allowed to use it. It may not run onto a neighbour. - The system may only be used during the growing season. - It must be in suitable soil, on land that is stable. - It may not be in an environmentally sensitive area, as determined by the local health officer. That determination is theirs, not yours. - Irrigation rates may not exceed the evapotranspiration rate of the field. You may not apply more water than the plants and evaporation can remove. - There must be a readily accessible, visibly labelled diversion valve that sends the greywater back to the sewer or septic system when needed: when soils are saturated or frozen, when something blocks or backs up, when you have hit the daily limit, or simply when you would rather not use it. - Pipes and above-ground tanks must be labelled: caution, nonpotable water, do not drink. - Mulch, if used, must be permeable enough to let greywater infiltrate quickly. For Tier 2 and Tier 3 there is also a slope limit: the irrigation field may only be on slopes of less than thirty percent, which the rule notes is about seventeen degrees (WAC 246-274-415(10)). ### Never letting it touch the drinking water This is the failure with the worst consequences and the least warning, and it deserves separating out from the rest. Everything above is about greywater reaching people slowly, through soil and plants. Cross-connection is greywater reaching people immediately, through a tap. A cross-connection is any point where a non-potable system can reach a potable one. The ways it happens in practice are mundane: a greywater line teed into a hose bib so the garden can be watered from either, a greywater tank topped up from the mains with a hose left dangling below the water line in the tank, a pump plumbed so it can draw from either source, or simply two similar-looking pipes in a crawlspace and a future owner who guesses wrong. The pressure in a household supply is not constant, and when it drops, water in a connected non-potable line can move the wrong way. The Washington greywater chapter carries several requirements that exist for this reason, and it is worth seeing them as one group rather than as scattered details: - **Labelling.** Pipes and above-ground tanks must carry the words: caution, nonpotable water, do not drink (WAC 246-274-011(1)(p)). This is not decoration. It is the control that protects the person who opens up your plumbing in fifteen years and has never heard of you. - **Separation from supply pipes.** Ten feet between the irrigation components and any pressurised water supply line or public water main, and ten feet from tanks and other system components (WAC 246-274-405, Table I). - **One hundred feet from a well or suction line**, and a hundred feet from a public drinking water well, two hundred from a public drinking water spring (same table). If area surface water is a public drinking supply, the system must sit outside its source water protection area entirely. - **Backflow from the sewer side.** Tanks must have an overflow pipe, at least as large as the inlet, flowing by gravity to the sewer or septic system, fitted with a check valve or backwater valve so that sewage cannot come back up it (WAC 246-274-410(2)(a)(vi)). Note the direction this one guards: it is protecting your greywater tank from your septic tank. - **Tamper-proof tanks.** Storage and pump tanks must be water-tight, anchored against overturning, and not susceptible to intrusion by humans or vectors (WAC 246-274-410(2)(a)). A tank a child can open is a tank a child can drink from. And the umbrella requirement: greywater reuse must comply with all applicable local codes and state rules including the Uniform Plumbing Code as adopted in chapters 51-56 and 51-57 WAC (WAC 246-274-005(1)). **What I could not check, said plainly.** Backflow prevention proper, which is to say the assemblies and air gaps that stop non-potable water entering a potable system, is governed by the plumbing code rather than by the greywater chapter, and I was not able to open the text of that plumbing code chapter. So this guide can tell you that the greywater rule points at the plumbing code and that cross-connection is the reason, and it cannot tell you what the plumbing code requires. That is a question for the person doing the plumbing, and it is a good test of whether they know this subject: a plumber who does not immediately talk about cross-connection when you say the word greywater is the wrong plumber. The one rule you can apply yourself without any of that: **never create a path, of any kind, by which greywater and drinking water can occupy the same pipe.** Not a temporary one, not a valved one, not one you promise to be careful with. Separate pipes, separate fittings that do not mate, everything labelled. [Storing Water Safely](/library#storing-water-safely) is the other half of this habit, and the contrast between the two guides is the lesson. Clean stored drinking water is rotated on something like a six month cycle. Untreated greywater is not storable for twenty four hours. Six months against one day: two liquids, both of them water, about a hundred and eighty times apart in how long they keep. If those two ever share a container or a pipe, the shorter number wins. And for Tier 2 and Tier 3 the designer must consider site sensitivity, for which the rule gives examples: shellfish growing areas, designated swimming areas, wellhead protection areas for Group A public water systems, and aquifer recharge areas critically important under the Growth Management Act (WAC 246-274-410(2)(d)(i)). If you live on Puget Sound, read that list again. The first item is the water you can see from the road. ## What this means on the ground in Silverdale The canonical place for these guides is Silverdale, at the head of Dyes Inlet in Kitsap County, at about 47.65 degrees north. Several of the requirements above land here in specific and checkable ways. ### The soil is probably the thing that stops you The soil survey for the Silverdale area (`data/locales/silverdale_wa/soil.json`, from the USDA NRCS SSURGO survey of Kitsap County) says the dominant series is **Alderwood**, at 49.9 percent of mapped land. Nearly half the ground here is one soil. Alderwood is a gravelly sandy loam over very gravelly sandy loam, sitting on dense glacial till. The record gives the representative depth to that restriction as **56 cm**, with a full mapped range of 50 to 102 cm. It also notes a seasonal perched water table as shallow as 65 cm, and rates the series very limited for septic tank absorption fields. Now put that against the rule. For a Tier 2 or Tier 3 system the shallowest legal placement of an irrigation line is four inches down, and it needs twenty four inches of suitable soil beneath it, so the minimum workable soil column is about 71 cm. The representative Alderwood profile gives 56 cm. That is about 15 cm short, and it is short at the most favourable possible placement of the line. So on the single most common soil in Silverdale, at its representative depth, **a Tier 2 or Tier 3 irrigation field does not have room to meet the state separation requirement.** The top of the mapped range, 102 cm, clearly does. Somewhere in between is a threshold, and which side of it your particular garden sits on is not something a soil survey can tell you. A Tier 1 system is not measured against that twenty four inch figure, as explained above, but it is not thereby in the clear: it still has to sit in suitable soil, and a densic layer at 56 cm with perched water above it is the definition of the thing suitable soil is defined against. The difference is that for Tier 1 you are asking the health officer a judgement question rather than failing an arithmetic test. Which is exactly why the rule does not let you decide this from a map. A Tier 2 or Tier 3 system requires a soil and site evaluation performed by a qualified professional or the local health officer, and only a soil scientist or those people may do it (WAC 246-274-420(1)). The survey number is a reason to expect a problem, not a finding. If you take one thing from this section, take this: **on Alderwood soil, have the separation checked before you spend money on anything else**, because it is the requirement most likely to end the project and the cheapest one to test first. The second most common series, Indianola at 10.3 percent, is loamy sand to sand with no recorded restriction and very high conductivity. That solves the separation problem and introduces the opposite one: the survey rates it very limited for septic absorption fields because of seepage and inadequate filtering. Soil is the treatment step. Soil that water races through is not doing the step. [Your Soil, Specifically](/library#your-soil-specifically) goes into what these series are and how to tell which one you are standing on. ### The rain is on your side here, which is unusual The Department of Health's guidance on irrigating plants with greywater recommends periodically flushing the soil where it is high in clay, or in areas receiving less than twenty inches of annual precipitation. The idea is that rain washes accumulated salts down past the root zone, and where there is not enough rain you have to irrigate deliberately with clean water to do the same job. Silverdale receives 1446 mm of precipitation a year (`data/locales/silverdale_wa/climate.json`). That is about 57 inches, nearly three times the twenty inch threshold, and it arrives mostly in winter, when the greywater system is required to be switched off anyway. December alone is 252 mm and January 236 mm. This is a genuine local advantage and it is worth saying plainly: the winter here does the salt flushing that a gardener in New Mexico has to do on purpose. It does not make sodium a non-problem, for reasons in the next section, but it does mean the accumulation story that dominates greywater writing from the southwest is weaker on the Kitsap Peninsula than the source material implies. ### The season you are allowed to use it is not the season you want it Greywater systems may only run during the growing season, defined as between the last frost of spring and the first frost of autumn, extendable by greenhouse if the plants keep growing (WAC 246-274-009(6) and 246-274-011(1)(i)). Locally the average last spring frost is March 29 and the average first autumn frost is November 14, with a growing season of 227 days in the locale climate record. So the legal window is roughly the start of April to the middle of November. But look at where the water shortage actually is. July receives 21 mm of rain and August 28 mm: 49 mm across the two months, under two inches. That is the dry season, and it is squarely inside the legal window, which is good news. The trouble is the shoulders. In April, May, October and November the ground here is already wet, evapotranspiration is low, and the rule caps your application at the evapotranspiration rate. Applying greywater to saturated Puget Sound soil in late October is how you get surfacing, and surfacing is a regulatory failure as well as an exposure one. The practical shape of that: in this climate the diversion valve is not an emergency device, it is the normal control you will use for most of the year. A Silverdale greywater system is a July and August appliance that happens to be legal for longer. ### Two local details that are easy to miss First, three separate provisions of the rule allow a resident owner of a single-family residence to do work that would otherwise need a professional, and all three carry the same qualifier: **not adjacent to a marine shoreline**. The owner may design the system (WAC 246-274-410(1)(a)), perform the soil and site evaluation (WAC 246-274-420(2)) and install it (WAC 246-274-430(2)), in each case only if the residence is not on a marine shoreline and the system reuses no more than 300 gallons per day. Silverdale sits at the head of Dyes Inlet. A waterfront property here loses the do-it-yourself route in all three places at once. Second, shellfish growing areas are the first example the rule gives of a sensitive site. Dyes Inlet drains through Port Washington Narrows into Sinclair Inlet and then the main basin of Puget Sound (`data/locales/silverdale_wa/water.json`). [Where Water Goes](/library#where-water-goes) follows that path in detail and explains why shellfish function as the receipt for what a watershed's households did. Greywater applied here is applied upstream of a shellfish resource, and the local health officer is entitled to weigh that. ### The comparison nobody makes, which in this climate they should The following is my reasoning from the numbers above rather than a position any regulator has published, and it is offered as such. Greywater is not the only non-potable water available for a garden. The other one is rain, and Silverdale gets about 57 inches of it a year. Set the two side by side honestly. Greywater's apparent advantage is that it arrives all year, including in summer when no rain falls. But Washington confines greywater irrigation to the growing season anyway, so the winter supply is unusable, and the twenty four hour limit means you cannot bank any of it for later. Greywater cannot be saved. Rainwater can: that is the entire point of a cistern, and it is legal, ordinary and uncontroversial. So in this specific climate the comparison comes out lopsided. To irrigate in July with greywater you need plumbing, a soil and site evaluation, in most cases a permit and a qualified designer, a diversion valve, ongoing records, an acceptance that you are putting detergent sodium and faecal indicator organisms into your soil, and a set of restrictions on what you may grow with it. To irrigate in July with rainwater you need a tank big enough to carry water from a winter that delivers 252 mm in December alone, and you need to have set it up before the rain stopped. Greywater earns its complexity where water is genuinely scarce across the whole year, which is why the best greywater literature comes from the southwest, and why the department's own list of suitable plants reads like a desert planting scheme. On the Kitsap Peninsula the scarcity is seasonal and the rain is abundant, which is a different problem with an easier answer. None of which makes greywater reuse wrong here. It makes it the second thing to try. [Collecting Rainwater](/library#collecting-rainwater) covers the first, including the same warning this guide has been making in a different key: that water is not for drinking either. ## Food crops: the distinction is the edible part, not the plant Washington's answer is one sentence and it is precise. Greywater may be used for subsurface irrigation of plants that produce food, but it must not come into contact with the edible portions of any plant (WAC 246-274-011(1)(b)). So the rule is not "no food crops". It is "no contact with the part you eat". That single distinction does most of the work, and it sorts real plants into groups that are not intuitive. **Generally compatible with the requirement.** Fruit and nut trees, cane fruit, grapes, and anything where the edible part is held well above the soil on a woody frame. The water goes into the root zone, the food is a metre or more away in the air, and the contact the rule prohibits does not occur in normal operation. This is where greywater irrigation makes the most sense anyway, because established trees and canes want deep infrequent water, which is what a subsurface line delivers. **The problem group: root crops.** Carrots, beetroot, potatoes, radishes, turnips, parsnips, onions. The edible portion of a root crop is, by definition, in the ground, in the wetted zone, in direct contact with the irrigation water. There is no way to subsurface-irrigate a carrot without the greywater touching the carrot. A New Mexico State University extension publication states the restriction in its sharpest form: root crops eaten uncooked should not be irrigated with greywater. Under the Washington requirement the concern is broader than eaten-uncooked, because the rule prohibits the contact itself rather than prohibiting the eating. **The other problem group: anything eaten raw and close to the ground.** Lettuce, spinach, salad leaves, strawberries, low herbs. The edible part is inches from the soil, the plants are usually harvested without cooking, and soil splash onto leaves is normal. A properly buried line does not splash, but a properly buried line that has begun to surface does, and surfacing is a failure mode you may not notice for weeks under a mulch layer. **The reasoning, which is worth having rather than just the rule.** Cooking kills the pathogens that make greywater a health question. Salmonella and Shigella do not survive a proper cook. So the hazard concentrates exactly where food goes from soil to mouth without a heat step. That is why the raw-eaten crops and the root crops are the ones that matter, and it is also why the tidy version of this rule that people remember, "no greywater on vegetables", is both too strict and too vague. An apple tree is fine. A radish is not. **Where the risk actually sits, and the honest ranking.** If you want one rule that survives contact with a real garden: put greywater on the perennials. Trees, shrubs, canes and ornamentals. Water the annual vegetable beds with clean water. You lose almost nothing, because the perennials are the thirsty deep-rooted things that benefit most from subsurface water anyway, and you remove the entire category of failure at once instead of managing it plant by plant. [Growing Food You Can Live On](/library#growing-food-you-can-live-on) covers what is worth growing here; [Handwashing and Personal Hygiene](/library#handwashing-and-hygiene) covers the step that actually breaks the transmission chain after you have been in the garden, which is the one people skip. ## What goes down the drain matters more than the plumbing This is the part of the subject that ruins gardens, and it is the part almost nobody thinks about when they are planning a system, because it feels like a detail about shopping rather than a detail about engineering. The Department of Health's review states the principle exactly: the amount of pollutants carried by greywater varies depending on what goes down the drain, and when people manage what goes down the drain, the amount of chemicals and pathogens can be reduced significantly. Your greywater system is a device that takes everything you pour into your sinks and puts it in your soil. That is the whole machine. ### Sodium, and why it is the one that actually gets you Laundry detergents contain salts, used as fillers and to improve cleaning. How much varies a great deal by brand, and the department notes that top loading machines designed to save water tend to produce higher concentrations of pollutants, because the same salt load arrives in less water. The measure that matters is the **sodium adsorption ratio**, SAR, which compares sodium against calcium and magnesium. The department's review, drawing on an Australian study of thirty wash samples from fifteen households, reports that irrigation waters with SAR above 6.0 are cause for concern, and that approximately **two-thirds of all the laundry water samples tested exceeded 6.0**. The review's conclusion from that study is that long-term application of such water to a single location, without adding calcium such as gypsum, could be expected to cause significant soil structural damage. Read that again: two thirds of ordinary household laundry water was above the threshold of concern. **Why sodium does this.** [What Soil Is](/library#what-soil-is) explains that soil is not just particles but particles arranged into aggregates, which USDA calls peds when they formed through soil development, and that the gaps between and inside those crumbs are what hold air and water and let roots through. It also explains that clay particles are small and plate-shaped. Both facts are the setup for this one. What holds clay plates together into a crumb is the cations sitting on their surfaces. Calcium and magnesium carry two positive charges each, so a single ion can bridge between two clay surfaces and pull them together. Sodium carries one. It cannot bridge, and it holds a larger shell of water around itself, so where sodium takes the place of calcium on those surfaces the plates stop being pulled together and start pushing apart. The crumbs come apart into individual plates. That is dispersion. The consequences follow from the geometry. The department's review describes them: soils low in electrical conductivity but high in sodium relative to other cations become unstable in water, hard surfaces form that make it difficult for plants to germinate or grow, infiltration rates are reduced, and waterlogging can result. Dispersed plates travel into the pores and block them, so the structure that made the soil drain is gone and the same soil now sheds water it used to absorb. The review quotes a researcher it cites, Amoozegar, to the effect that the adverse impact of sodium on soil hydraulic properties is well known, and reports that greywater including kitchen wastewater was found detrimental to plant growth and damaging to soil in testing. This is the failure mode that makes greywater worth taking seriously even if nobody ever gets sick from your system. It is slow, it is cumulative, it is invisible for a long time, and it is difficult to reverse. Reversing it means adding calcium, usually as gypsum, to displace the sodium, and then leaching the displaced sodium away, which takes water and time. And it connects back to a rule you have already read. **Water softener waste is prohibited in greywater by name** (WAC 246-274-011(1)(d)). A softener works by swapping calcium and magnesium out of your water and sodium in, then flushing the captured calcium away in a brine. Its waste stream is the highest-sodium, lowest-calcium water in the house: precisely the worst possible SAR. The rule is not being fussy. It is excluding the one appliance whose entire purpose produces the exact chemistry that destroys soil structure. **What to do about it.** The department's specific guidance is that liquid detergents generally contain less sodium than powdered detergents and are recommended when irrigating with greywater. Beyond that, the useful habits are: rotate which area receives greywater rather than always hitting one bed, and let the winter rain do the leaching, which in this climate it will. ### Boron, which is a narrower problem and a harder one Boron is a plant nutrient with an unusually narrow window between too little and too much. USDA Agricultural Research Service publishes crop tolerance categories based on boron concentration in soil water: | Category | Boron | |---|---| | Very sensitive | under 0.5 mg/L | | Sensitive | 0.5 to 1.0 mg/L | | Moderately sensitive | 1.0 to 2.0 mg/L | | Moderately tolerant | 2.0 to 4.0 mg/L | | Tolerant | 4.0 to 6.0 mg/L | | Very tolerant | 6.0 to 15.0 mg/L | ARS places citrus and stone fruits, along with onion and snap beans, in the sensitive range, and alfalfa, sugar beet, tomato, cotton and asparagus among the more tolerant. It also cautions that tolerances vary with climate, soil and variety. The household connection is borax and perborate bleaches, which are boron compounds and appear in laundry products. The New Mexico State University extension publication names sodium, bleach and borax together as things in greywater that can damage plants. **What I could not source, said plainly.** I could not find a measured boron concentration for household laundry greywater from any regulator whose page I was able to open. The Washington Department of Health's own literature review, which covers salts, pH, nitrogen, phosphorus, fats and oils and pathogens in detail, does not discuss boron at all. So the sourced position is: boron has a narrow tolerance band, published crop thresholds start below 0.5 mg/L for sensitive species, borax-containing laundry products put boron into greywater, and nobody in the sources I opened has published what concentration that produces in a typical household's wash water. Avoid borax-based products if you are irrigating with the result. Treat any specific number you see quoted for boron in greywater as unverified until you find its source. ### Bleach, and the rest of the cleaning cupboard The rule prohibits cleaning chemicals and hazardous household products generally. The department's review reinforces it from the other side, concluding that the lower-pollutant subset of greywater is lower-pollutant especially when people avoid cleaners containing harsh chemicals, bleaches, disinfectants or phosphates. There is a real conflict to be aware of here, and it is not a small one. Bleach and disinfectants exist to kill microorganisms. Soil function depends on microorganisms. A greywater system delivers your cleaning products directly to the living part of your soil, bypassing every treatment step that would otherwise degrade them. The same is true of a septic system, which is why EPA's septic guidance warns that pouring toxins down the drain can kill the organisms that treat your waste. A greywater system has even less buffer than a septic tank, because it has no tank. ### The rest of the chemistry, briefly From the department's review: - **pH** of greywater runs from 6.5 to 8.7. It is typically alkaline because of soaps and detergents. This is the mechanism behind the department's plant guidance discussed below. - **Nitrogen** is not a significant concern in greywater, because most of the nitrogen in household wastewater comes from urine and urine is not in greywater. - **Phosphorus** does matter, and its main source in greywater is dishwashing detergent. Phosphorus drives algal growth in fresh water. - **Fats, oils and grease** are highest in kitchen greywater; the review cites a study finding roughly a tenfold increase in oils and greases from kitchen waste over all other greywater sources. Grease is also what clogs a subsurface irrigation system, which is a maintenance failure before it is an environmental one. ### The plants that will not tolerate it, which is awkward here The Department of Health publishes a list of plants poorly suited to greywater irrigation, and the pattern is that shade-loving and acid-loving plants do badly, because they evolved in the acid forest soils and greywater is alkaline. The unsuitable list includes azaleas, begonias, bleeding hearts, crepe myrtle, deodar cedar, dogwood, ferns, foxgloves, gardenias, holly, hydrangeas, impatiens, magnolias, oxalis, primroses, redwoods, rhododendrons and violets. Read that list as a Pacific Northwest gardener and wince. Rhododendrons, ferns, dogwood, holly, hydrangeas, azaleas, primroses: that is not a list of exotics, that is a description of a Kitsap garden and a good deal of the surrounding forest understorey. The rhododendron is Washington's state flower. The better-suited list is drier-country planting: Austrian pine, bearded iris, big basin sage, burning bush, cottonwood, fringed sage, honeysuckle, Italian stone pine, junipers, mugo pine, many native desert plants, oaks, rabbit brush, roses, rosemary, Russian olive, sedum and sumac. So the uncomfortable local conclusion is that the plants greywater suits best are substantially not the plants that grow here by default, and the plants that define the local landscape are on the avoid list. That does not make greywater useless in western Washington. It does mean the fantasy version, where you quietly route the shower onto the existing shrubbery and everything is better, is the wrong picture. You would be irrigating rhododendrons with alkaline water. The department adds two warnings worth repeating exactly. Some harmful effects are not visible immediately and may take one or two years to appear. And if you see signs of stress in irrigated plants, stop using greywater on them. That first one is the reason this section is long. A system that is damaging your soil looks exactly like a system that is working, for about two growing seasons. ## Permits, tiers and who actually decides ### The three tiers, with the numbers | | Tier 1 | Tier 2 | Tier 3 | |---|---|---|---| | Greywater grade | Light only | Light only | Light or dark | | Flow limit | 60 gal/day | under 3,500 gal/day | under 3,500 gal/day | | Storage | None permitted | Up to 24 hours | Any, with treatment | | Distribution | Gravity, no pumps | Even, typically pressure | Even, typically pressure | | Treatment | None | None | Required | | Approval | Registration may be required | Permit required | Permit required | A treatment component becomes mandatory, moving you to Tier 3, in five situations (WAC 246-274-300(2)): dark greywater, storage beyond twenty four hours, irrigating a green roof, serving a high public exposure area such as a playground or sports field, or whenever the local health officer decides treatment is needed to protect public health or water quality. Where treatment is required for light greywater the product must meet NSF/ANSI Standard 350-1; for dark greywater, NSF/ANSI Standard 40 (WAC 246-274-400). ### Tier 1 in practice, and the arithmetic that decides whether it fits Tier 1 is the accessible option: light greywater, sixty gallons a day or less, from a single-family residence, through a single diversion point, by gravity, no storage, at least four inches of cover. You may install up to two separate Tier 1 systems from two diversion points, with combined flows of 120 gallons per day or less, and no single field may exceed sixty (WAC 246-274-100(2)). You must keep a record of the system showing where it is, which fixtures feed it, how the design meets the requirements, its maintenance needs and the irrigation area calculation, recorded on the department's Greywater System Checklist and Irrigation Area Estimation Tool. The local health officer may require you to register it by filing that record, and may require extra review if you install two systems or if your property is on an on-site sewage system with design flows under 3,500 gallons per day (WAC 246-274-100(1)(m), (n) and (3)). Does sixty gallons a day fit a real household? The rule itself gives you the numbers to check, in the fixture design flow table it provides for when actual flows are unknown (WAC 246-274-410(2)(b)(ii)): water-conserving washing machine 8 gallons per person per day, traditional 11; laundry sink 3; water-conserving bathroom sink 5.4, traditional 6; water-conserving shower 10, traditional 17; bathtub 24 gallons per bath; kitchen sink 6; dishwasher 1. Take a two person household and total the light greywater fixtures: - With water-conserving fixtures: 10 plus 5.4 plus 8 equals 23.4 gallons per person per day, so 46.8 gallons for two people. Inside the sixty gallon limit. - With traditional fixtures: 17 plus 6 plus 11 equals 34 gallons per person per day, so 68 gallons for two people. Over the limit. So Tier 1 fits a small, water-conserving household and does not fit a conventional one, and whether it fits yours turns on your shower head. Note also that these are the *totals available*; you do not have to route all of them. Diverting only the washing machine, which is the single most common approach, gives 16 gallons a day for two people on a conserving machine, comfortably inside Tier 1. For scale on the other side, the Department of Health puts household greywater at up to forty gallons per person each day, which is the largest single portion of a home's wastewater. Two people at that rate produce eighty gallons, more than one Tier 1 system can take. Greywater reuse at this tier captures a slice of your greywater, not all of it. ### Tier 2 and Tier 3, and the septic catch Both require a permit from the local health officer before installation (WAC 246-274-200(2) and 246-274-300(4)), a soil and site evaluation (WAC 246-274-420), design by a qualified professional in most cases (WAC 246-274-410(1)), installation only by someone the health officer has approved (WAC 246-274-430(1)), and inspection before the system is covered (WAC 246-274-435). Here is the catch that affects most rural Kitsap properties. Tier 2 and Tier 3 systems are written for buildings served by a public sewer or a *large* on-site sewage system, meaning one with design flows between 3,500 and 100,000 gallons per day. An ordinary house on an ordinary septic system is well under that. The route back in is a carve-out: if the building is served by an on-site sewage system with design flows under 3,500 gallons per day, the greywater must originate from a single-family residence and must not exceed **300 gallons per day** (WAC 246-274-200(1)(e) and 246-274-300(3)(e)). That 300 gallon figure is the one to remember, because it recurs. It is also the ceiling under which a resident owner may design, evaluate and install their own system, provided the residence is not adjacent to a marine shoreline, and the threshold under which the health officer may reduce permitting to registration when a qualified professional designed a Tier 2 system for a single-family residence (WAC 246-274-425(2)(d)). The rule also requires that diverting greywater must not adversely affect the functioning of the septic system it is diverted from (WAC 246-274-410(2)(c)), and separately that using a greywater system changes none of the design, capacity or reserve area requirements for that septic system (WAC 246-274-005(2)). You do not get a smaller septic system for having a greywater system. ### The question you have to ask before any of this Here is the part that is easy to miss and would waste the most of your time. **Chapter 246-274 WAC may not be in force in your county.** The rule took effect on July 31, 2011, and required local boards of health to implement it within three years. But it also provides that if a local board of health cannot adjust its resources to implement and enforce the chapter, the older on-site sewage rules in chapter 246-272A WAC continue to apply to greywater reuse for subsurface irrigation in that jurisdiction (WAC 246-274-007(1) and (2)). The Department of Health's own page tells readers to check with their local health jurisdiction to learn whether greywater reuse under chapter 246-274 WAC is allowed there, or to ask how to support that effort if it is not allowed yet. And local boards may adopt requirements more stringent than the state's (WAC 246-274-007(4)), with Tier 1 owners expressly required to comply with any more stringent local regulations including design and permitting (WAC 246-274-100(4)). So there are three possible answers to "can I do this here": yes under the tier system, yes but only as an on-site sewage system under the older chapter, or yes with additional local requirements on top. You cannot tell which from reading state law. ### For Kitsap County specifically The local health jurisdiction here is the **Kitsap Public Health District**. Their Drinking Water and Onsite Sewage program is at 345 6th Street, Suite 300, Bremerton, WA 98337, telephone 360-728-2235, open weekdays 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. **I could not find a greywater page on the Kitsap Public Health District site.** Their onsite sewage and drinking water pages cover septic permits, well records, building clearances and contractor requests, and nothing I opened mentioned greywater, graywater or reclaimed water. That absence is not evidence that greywater reuse is prohibited here, and I want to be careful not to imply it is. It means the answer is not published where I could find it, and the only way to get it is to ask them. Ask two questions: whether Kitsap implements chapter 246-274 WAC, and if so whether they require Tier 1 systems to be registered. The in-app law browser carries adjacent entries that are worth reading first for context: `kitsap-septic-systems-and-wells-need-health-district-approval` and `kitsap-septic-systems-must-be-permitted-maintained-and-inspected` for the health district's role, `wa-a-household-well-usually-doesn-t-need-a-water-right-permit-b` if you are on a well, and `kitsap-kitsap-requires-buffers-around-wetlands-and-streams` plus `kitsap-critical-areas-and-shoreline-rules-restrict-building-near-wa` if any part of your lot is near water or wet ground. None of those is a greywater rule; there is no greywater entry in that data at present. Treat them as pointers to the right office, and read the cited regulation rather than the summary. ### Ongoing obligations, once it exists For Tier 2 and Tier 3 (WAC 246-274-440), the owner must get approval before altering or expanding the system, protect it from surface drainage including footing and roof drains, ensure the greywater keeps coming from the correct fixtures, and either repair problems promptly or divert to the sewer or septic until repaired. At property transfer the owner must give the buyer the system record and any maintenance records, in addition to the seller disclosure statement Washington requires. If the system is abandoned or removed, the owner must notify the local health officer in writing. And if any system of any tier fails or is suspected of failing, the owner must immediately divert the greywater to the sewer or septic system, and nobody may use the greywater system until the failure is corrected (WAC 246-274-445). Note that standard: *suspected* of failing. You do not get to wait for confirmation. ## What can go wrong **Greywater surfacing.** The most common and most serious failure. Causes: application faster than the soil accepts, saturated ground, a blocked line forcing water back, settling that left the line too shallow, or a field sized for plants that have since died. Consequence: direct human and animal contact with water carrying faecal indicator organisms at the levels described earlier. Response is not optional, it is the rule: divert immediately, stop using the system, fix it before restarting. **A storage tank that has gone septic.** You will smell it, because hydrogen sulfide is unmistakable. It means the water went anaerobic, which means it was held too long. The fix is not deodoriser, it is not holding it that long. **Kitchen water sneaking in.** A plumber ties the kitchen sink into the greywater line because it was convenient, and your Tier 1 or Tier 2 system is now handling dark greywater, which is illegal without treatment and brings tenfold grease, the phosphorus load, and the sodium that was proven detrimental to plants in testing. This is the change most likely to happen without anyone thinking of it as a change. **A prohibited input entering routinely.** Somebody starts washing nappies, a water softener gets installed, a hobby moves into the utility sink, a car part gets degreased in the laundry tub. The plumbing did not change but the water did, and what is coming out of it is no longer legally greywater. **Slow sodium damage.** No symptom for a season or two, then poor infiltration, crusting, water sitting where it used to soak away, and plants doing worse each year on more water. Two thirds of laundry samples in the study the state relied on were above the SAR threshold of concern, so this is the default trajectory rather than an unlucky one. Rotating the irrigated area and letting winter rain leach it are the practical defences here; gypsum is the remedial one. **Irrigating the wrong plants.** Alkaline water onto rhododendrons, ferns, azaleas and the rest of the acid-loving list. Symptoms may take one to two years to appear. **Running it out of season.** October here is wet, evapotranspiration is low and the soil has no capacity. The rule confines use to the growing season, and the season ends before the calendar suggests. **Assuming greywater reduces your septic requirement.** It does not. The rule says so twice. **Building it before checking how much soil is actually under the field.** On Alderwood soil, which is about half of Silverdale, the representative profile does not have room for the twenty four inch separation a Tier 2 or Tier 3 system needs, and is marginal for the suitable-soil requirement every tier needs. This is the cheapest thing to check and the most likely to end the project. Check it first. ## How you know it worked - You can state, without looking it up, which fixtures feed the system, and the kitchen is not among them unless you have a treatment component. - The diversion valve is reachable without moving anything, is visibly labelled, and you have actually operated it. - Pipes and any above-ground tank carry the nonpotable water warning. - Nothing is wet on the surface anywhere over the field, in any weather, checked by walking it rather than by looking out of a window. - You know the separation distance between your irrigation line and the first restrictive layer beneath it, because somebody dug and looked. - The plants over the field are the same or better after two full seasons, not just after one. Water still soaks in at the same rate it did. - You have the system record, and it is current with what is actually buried out there rather than what was drawn. - You have spoken to the Kitsap Public Health District and know which rule applies to you here. - You have a season, each year, when the valve is turned to the sewer and stays there. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. United States federal government publications are public domain and can be redistributed with this guide. State agencies, universities and county bodies are not: 17 U.S.C. 105 covers federal works only, so every fact taken from those is restated here in our own words with the source named. ### Washington State law and rules (state, restated) - Washington Administrative Code, Chapter 246-274, Greywater Reuse for Subsurface Irrigation, read in full. The source of every tier, distance, depth, volume and prohibition in this guide, including: the definitions of greywater, light greywater and dark greywater and the absence of any definition of blackwater (246-274-009); the general requirements including subsurface-only use, the food crop contact rule, the diaper and water softener prohibitions, the no-surfacing rule, growing season limit, diversion valve and labelling (246-274-011); the Tier 1 rules including the 60 gallon limit, no storage, gravity distribution, two-system maximum, record keeping and more-stringent-local-rules clause (246-274-100); the Tier 2 rules including the 24 hour storage limit, the 300 gallon septic carve-out and the permit requirement (246-274-200); the Tier 3 rules and the five triggers for mandatory treatment (246-274-300); the NSF standards (246-274-400); the setback table (246-274-405); design requirements including the fixture design flow table, the not-adjacent-to-a-marine-shoreline owner exception, and the sensitive site examples including shellfish growing areas (246-274-410); irrigation field requirements including the 4 to 12 inch depth, the two inches of soil plus two inches of mulch cover, the 24 inch separation from a restrictive layer or water table, the soil loading table and the 30 percent slope limit (246-274-415); soil and site evaluation (246-274-420); installation permits (246-274-425); installers (246-274-430); inspection (246-274-435); operation, maintenance and property transfer (246-274-440); failures (246-274-445); local implementation, the three year deadline, the fallback to chapter 246-272A WAC and the authority to be more stringent (246-274-007); applicability and the exclusion of indoor reuse under the plumbing code (246-274-003); and the statement that greywater reuse is not an alternative to a sewer connection or on-site sewage system (246-274-005). https://app.leg.wa.gov/wac/default.aspx?cite=246-274&full=true - Revised Code of Washington 90.46.010, Definitions. The statutory definition of greywater at subsection (8), identical in scope to the rule's and explicitly including dishwashers and kitchen sinks, and the definition of domestic wastewater at subsection (7). https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=90.46.010 ### Washington State Department of Health (state agency, restated) - Greywater Reuse. The department's plain-language definition, the tier table, the statement that local health jurisdictions had three years to implement and that readers must check whether chapter 246-274 WAC is allowed in their jurisdiction, the figure of up to 40 gallons of greywater per person per day, the characteristics listed by source (including high pH and sodium from the dishwasher), the recommendation of liquid over powdered detergents, and the statement that greywater reuse is not an alternative to an approved on-site sewage system. https://doh.wa.gov/community-and-environment/wastewater-management/greywater-reuse - Irrigating Plants with Greywater. The lists of plants not suitable and more suited to greywater irrigation, the observation that shade-loving and acid-loving plants do badly, the recommendation to flush soils periodically where clay content is high or annual precipitation is under 20 inches, the note that sandy soils are less vulnerable than clay, and the warnings that harmful effects may take one to two years to appear and that irrigation should stop if plants show stress. https://doh.wa.gov/community-and-environment/wastewater-management/greywater-reuse/plant-irrigation - Greywater Reuse in Washington State, Rule Development Committee Issue Research Report, DOH 337-108, September 2025. The literature review behind the rule. Source of: the finding that greywater including kitchen, dishwasher and diaper-laundry flows can equal or exceed blackwater in pollution and that such a sink or washing machine can carry more pollution than a toilet; the BOD5 figures (bathroom-only 26 to 130 mg/L, kitchen-inclusive 26 to 295 mg/L, raw sewage about 300 mg/L, treated wastewater under 10 mg/L); the anaerobic mechanism behind the 24 hour limit and hydrogen sulfide; the finding that indicator organisms increase when greywater is stored past 24 hours and that seeded pathogens can reproduce during storage, with Salmonella typhimurium and Shigella dysenteriae surviving several days at pH 6.5 and 25 degrees C while poliovirus type 1 fell 90 percent or more after six days; faecal coliform ranging from about 1.8 x 10^4 to 7.9 x 10^6; the statement that a consistent relationship between greywater reuse and illness rates is unknown; the SAR discussion including the threshold above 6.0, the two-thirds of laundry samples exceeding it and the gypsum remedy, drawn from a Queensland study (Howard et al., 2005); the Amoozegar finding on kitchen greywater damaging soil and plants; greywater pH of 6.5 to 8.7; nitrogen being insignificant because urine is excluded; phosphorus coming mainly from dishwashing detergent; the tenfold increase in fats and oils from kitchen sources; and the conclusions that direct exposure routes should not be allowed while subsurface irrigation is acceptable. https://doh.wa.gov/sites/default/files/legacy/Documents/Pubs//337-108.pdf - Greywater Reuse, Recycling, and Water Conservation Links. Used to identify the department's guidance documents and the related rule chapters, including the plumbing code chapter governing indoor gray water systems. https://doh.wa.gov/community-and-environment/wastewater-management/greywater-reuse/greywater-links ### Other states, for the comparison only (state agencies, restated) - California Health and Safety Code section 17922.12. The California definition of graywater, listing bathtubs, showers, bathroom washbasins, clothes washing machines and laundry tubs, and stating that kitchen sinks and dishwashers are not included. https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=17922.12 - Oregon Department of Environmental Quality, Graywater. Oregon's definition including showers and bathtubs, bathroom sinks, kitchen sinks and laundry, and excluding toilet discharge, garbage wastes from kitchen sinks with garbage disposal units, and wastewater contaminated by soiled diapers; and the Type 1, 2 and 3 classification by treatment level. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/wq/programs/Pages/Water-Reuse-Graywater.aspx ### United States government (public domain) - US Environmental Protection Agency. How to Care for Your Septic System. The guidance that pouring toxins down the drain can kill the organisms that treat waste, the list of things never to put down a drain including grease, household chemicals, solvents and paint, the effect of concentrating laundry into one day, and the recommendation against garbage disposals to reduce fats, grease and solids. https://www.epa.gov/septic/how-care-your-septic-system - US Environmental Protection Agency. Onsite Non-Potable Water Reuse Research. EPA's quantitative microbial risk assessment work on onsite reuse, the reference pathogens studied (Norovirus, Rotavirus, Campylobacter jejuni, Cryptosporidium, and Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA), the use of risk-based log reduction targets by pathogen group and end use, and the finding of high and variable pathogen loads in these waters. https://www.epa.gov/water-research/onsite-non-potable-water-reuse-research - US Environmental Protection Agency. Basic Information about Water Reuse. The definition of water reuse and the principle that the amount of treatment needed depends on the risk to human health or the environment. https://www.epa.gov/waterreuse/basic-information-about-water-reuse - US Environmental Protection Agency. REUSExplorer. Confirmation that state regulations, not a federal rule, govern onsite non-potable reuse, and that EPA's summaries are not legally binding. https://www.epa.gov/waterreuse/regulations-and-end-use-specifications-explorer-reusexplorer - US Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service, Agricultural Water Efficiency and Salinity Research Unit. Boron Tolerance of Crops. The six tolerance categories and their concentration ranges, example sensitive crops (citrus, stone fruits, onion, snap beans) and tolerant crops (alfalfa, sugar beet, tomato, cotton, asparagus), and the caution that tolerances vary with climate, soil and variety. https://www.ars.usda.gov/pacific-west-area/riverside-ca/agricultural-water-efficiency-and-salinity-research-unit/docs/databases/boron-tolerance-of-crops/ ### University extension (copyrighted, restated) - New Mexico State University Extension, Safe Use of Household Greywater, publication M106. The guidance that untreated greywater should not be kept longer than one day and that high bacteria counts cause objectionable odours; that greywater containing sodium, bleach or borax can damage plants and that automatic dishwasher water should not be used for irrigation; that greywater should be dispersed over a large area and rotated with fresh water to avoid sodium build-up; that root crops eaten uncooked should not be irrigated with greywater; and the recommendation to avoid liquid fabric softeners and detergents containing softeners. Note that this publication also suggests adding chlorine bleach to extend storage, advice which conflicts with the Washington rule and is flagged as such in the text above. https://pubs.nmsu.edu/_m/M106/index.html ### Local data shipped with this guide - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/soil.json`. The Alderwood series at 49.9 percent of mapped land, its texture and drainage, representative depth to densic restriction of 56 cm with a mapped range of 50 to 102 cm, perched water table as shallow as 65 cm, and the very limited rating for septic absorption fields; and the Indianola series at 10.3 percent, loamy sand to sand, with its own very limited septic rating for seepage and inadequate filtering. Derived from USDA NRCS SSURGO, Kitsap County Area survey WA635. - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/climate.json`. Annual precipitation of 1446 mm, the monthly distribution including July at 21 mm and August at 28 mm, growing season of 227 days, average last spring frost of March 29 and first autumn frost of November 14. - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/water.json`. The drainage path from the Barker Creek-Frontal Dyes Inlet HUC12 through Port Orchard to the main basin of Puget Sound. - `data/laws/laws.json`. The adjacent Kitsap and Washington entries cited by id in the permits section. Note that this data contains no greywater, water reuse or greywater permitting entry. ### Could not be sourced - **A measured boron concentration in household greywater.** No regulator page I could open publishes one, and the Washington Department of Health's literature review, which covers salts, pH, nitrogen, phosphorus, fats and oils and pathogens in detail, does not address boron at all. The crop tolerance thresholds above are real and sourced; what a given household's wash water actually contains is not something I could establish. - **Whether Kitsap County implements chapter 246-274 WAC.** The Kitsap Public Health District publishes nothing about greywater that I could find. Their contact details above are from their Drinking Water and Onsite Sewage page. This must be established by asking them. - **Whether hand-carrying a bucket of greywater is regulated.** The Washington rule is written about greywater irrigation systems, defined as an integrated system of components that conveys greywater from the building and provides subsurface irrigation. I could not find any published statement about whether hand-carried water falls inside or outside that definition, so this guide does not tell you that it is exempt. Ask the health district. - **USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service technical material on sodicity.** Several NRCS documents on sodic soils and the sodium adsorption ratio were identified but would not load; the NRCS server timed out repeatedly. The sodium and soil structure material in this guide therefore rests on the Washington Department of Health's literature review and on the sourced material already in [What Soil Is](/library#what-soil-is), not on NRCS.
