docs.text: # Choosing Where to Build Almost everything about a building can be fixed later. A cold house can be insulated. A leaking roof can be replaced. A bad layout can be rearranged, a small house extended, an ugly one resurfaced, a damp one dried out. All of that costs money, and money is the only thing it costs. The site is different. You cannot move a house off a failing bluff. You cannot lift it out of a floodway. You cannot turn a north-facing slope to the south, or drain a spring that runs under the foundation, or make the county reclassify the ground. You can spend enormous sums making a bad site tolerable, and people do, and at the end of it they still have a bad site with an expensive house on it. That is the whole reason this guide exists. Siting is the one decision in building that is close to permanent, and it is usually made fastest, on the least information, by the person with the least expertise, under the most time pressure. It is made by whoever liked the view. So this is about slowing that decision down and putting it in order. **You may not have a choice.** Most people do not. You inherited the land, you bought the only lot you could afford, you rent, you are building on the corner of a family property, or the house is already there and has been for sixty years. If that is you, none of the following is wasted: it becomes the list of things to find out about ground you are already standing on. Knowing that the till is at two feet does not move your house, but it explains your wet crawlspace, tells you why the drainfield struggles, and stops you spending real money on the wrong fix. Read it as a diagnosis rather than a choice. The worked example throughout is Silverdale, Washington, at the head of Dyes Inlet on the Kitsap Peninsula, because there is real sourced data behind every number. The method is the part that transfers. ## Ask the questions in order of how permanent the answer is This ordering is a **rule of thumb**, not a standard anyone published. But the logic is hard to argue with: each question below is harder to undo than the one after it, so answering them out of order means you can fall in love with a site for a reason that does not survive contact with the reason above it. | # | Question | If the answer is bad | Reversible? | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Can the ground hold it? | The site is not a building site | No | | 2 | Will water reach it? | The site is not a building site | Almost never | | 3 | Can you get water, and get rid of waste? | Possibly unbuildable, certainly expensive | Sometimes, at real cost | | 4 | Can you get to it, in February? | Expensive forever, and a safety problem | Sometimes, at real cost | | 5 | Is it a pleasant place to live? | You will be a bit colder and a bit gloomier | Partly, with design | People do this in reverse. They start at 5, because 5 is what you can see from the road. The view, the trees, the quiet, the way the light falls in June. Those are real goods and they are the last thing to weigh, because a beautiful site that fails question 1 is not a compromise, it is a different kind of object entirely. Two of these questions have a specific character worth naming in advance. Questions 1 and 2 are answered by the ground and cannot be negotiated with. Questions 3, 4 and 5 are answered by money, and the honest form of each is not "can I?" but "how much, forever?" ## 1. Can the ground hold it? ### Slope, and the hazard that is actually here The famous geologic hazard on this coast is the Cascadia megathrust earthquake. The everyday one is the coastal bluff landslide, and for a siting decision the everyday one is the one that should move you. USGS puts a magnitude 9 on Cascadia at 10 to 15 percent in the next 50 years. Landslide-producing winters here recur on a scale of years. The numbers are from a USGS study that mapped landslides across Kitsap County using lidar. It found **231 landslides**, covering about **0.8 percent of the county's land area**, and the distribution is the part that matters for siting: **67 percent of the mapped landslide area lies within 500 metres of the present coastline**, and about **77 percent of mapped landslides involve Vashon advance outwash deposits**. Two mapped slides sit directly on the Dyes Inlet shoreline near Silverdale, one pair on the east shore and northern end of the inlet totalling about 32,000 square metres with possible evidence of recent activity, and one of about 9,000 square metres west of the inlet, north of Chico. This is not a theoretical hazard. In the winter of 1996 to 1997, coastal landslides in Kitsap County destroyed millions of dollars of public and private property and **killed a family of four on Bainbridge Island**. NOAA's storm record for the Kitsap Peninsula zones logs 10 debris-flow events since 1996, including a 2007 fatality and a December 2010 episode causing about a million dollars of damage. **The mechanism explains the map.** The Kitsap Peninsula is mantled by late Pleistocene glacial deposits. The critical arrangement is permeable advance outwash sand sitting on the low-permeability Lawton Clay. Rainwater sinks freely through the sand, reaches the clay, cannot get through it, and perches. Pore pressure builds through a sustained wet spell, and the bluff face lets go. Washington's Department of Ecology describes the same pattern in plain terms for property owners: most landslides happen after heavy rainfall or rapid snowmelt saturates the soil, and loose sand and gravel lying over dense silt and clay is one of the conditions that raises the risk. Three things follow, and all three are siting decisions. **The top of a bluff and the toe of a bluff are both hazardous, and for different reasons.** On top, the ground you are standing on is what leaves. Below, you are where it lands. Ecology's guidance for Puget Sound bluff owners is to build a prudent distance from the top or the bottom of a steep slope, and it declines to put a number on "prudent", which is the correct thing for a general document to do. **Nothing you do to the house changes the slope, but plenty of things you do to the site change the water.** Ecology is specific that drainage improvements are the most cost-effective way to reduce slide risk, that septic drainfields and irrigation systems placed between a house and the bluff edge make instability worse, that roof runoff should be piped away from the slope rather than discharged near it, that clearing upland vegetation creates excess runoff, and that native vegetation helps anchor soil and absorb water. Every one of those is a decision you make at siting time and live with afterward. **And the bluff stays dangerous after the shaking stops.** The April 1949 deep earthquake triggered a large landslide on 90-metre-high bluffs at the Tacoma Narrows **three days later**, and that slide generated its own local wave. Surviving the shaking is not the same as surviving the earthquake. ### What a map can and cannot tell you about a slope Two federal products are worth knowing apart, because people use one when they need the other. USGS says a **landslide hazard map** indicates the possibility of landslides occurring throughout a given area, and that a **landslide susceptibility map** describes the relative likelihood of future landsliding based solely on the intrinsic properties of a locale or site. Note "relative" and "solely on the intrinsic properties". A susceptibility map tells you that this kind of ground fails more often than that kind of ground. It does not tell you what your ground will do. USGS also notes that an ideal hazard map would show not only the chance that a landslide starts at a place, but the chance that it travels downslope a given distance. Most available maps do not show the second thing, which is exactly the thing that matters if you are at the toe. A **landslide inventory**, like the Kitsap study above, is different again and more useful: it is a record of failures somebody actually found and mapped. If your parcel is inside a mapped landslide polygon, that is not a probability, it is a history. ### The honest limit of this section A document cannot tell you whether a particular slope will hold a particular house. Neither can a map, a neighbour, a contractor, or the person selling you the land. Ready.gov's instruction is blunt and correct: seek advice from a geotechnical expert for evaluating landslide hazards or designing corrective techniques to reduce landslide risk. Ecology says the same for this coast specifically, and adds the qualifier that matters, which is to find an engineering geologist or geotechnical engineer familiar with **coastal slopes**. Bluff behaviour here is a specialism, not a general civil engineering question. A geotechnical investigation on a residential lot is not cheap. It is also, by a wide margin, the cheapest thing on this page relative to what it prevents, and it is the one expense in this guide that is unambiguously worth paying for if there is any slope in the picture at all. If the answer comes back ambiguous, that is an answer. ### The ground itself, apart from the slope Slope is not the only way ground fails to hold a building. The soil survey rates ground for exactly this, and [Your Soil, Specifically](/library#your-soil-specifically) is the guide to reading it. Three of its findings are siting findings rather than gardening findings. **Dense till at two feet is the character of this place.** About 64 percent of the mapped land around Silverdale is a thin gravelly mantle over dense glacial till. Alderwood alone is 49.9 percent of it, with its restriction at a representative 56 cm and a mapped range of 50 to 102 cm, and a seasonal perched water table as shallow as 65 cm. The survey rates Alderwood **Very limited** for dwellings with basements, for perched ground water at 75 to 180 cm plus slope on the steeper phases, and Very limited for shallow excavations for wetness and the dense layer itself. The binding constraint in Central Kitsap is not bedrock. Only one series in the whole area, Schneider at 0.3 percent, has a lithic contact at all. **Wet ground announces itself in the ratings and nowhere else on a sunny day.** Norma, 6.1 percent of the land, is a hydric soil with an apparent water table at the surface and winter ponding, rated Very limited for dwellings with and without basements, for local roads and streets, for septic, for small commercial buildings and for shallow excavations. It looks like the best ground on the property: dark, deep, 7.5 percent organic matter. In February it is a pond. **Some ground moves or disappears under you.** Shalcar is muck and Mukilteo is peat, and the survey rates both for more than 30 to 60 cm of total subsidence: drain them and the ground surface drops by half a metre as the organic material oxidises. Bellingham is a vertic silty clay that shrinks and swells, rated Very limited for dwellings for shrink-swell, wetness and ponding over four hours, and Somewhat limited to Very limited for local roads for low strength. Tacoma is tidally influenced low ground at the heads of the inlets that floods, ponds, runs pH 4.5 to 5.5 and carries sulfidic material. The locale data's grower note on Tacoma is three words long: leave it alone. And one category that means the survey is declining to answer. **Urban land** is not a soil. It is pavement, buildings and engineered fill, and the survey carries no interpretations for it, which is honesty rather than unhelpfulness. On any parcel that has been built on, graded or filled, assume the top layer is not what the survey describes and that the only way to find out is to dig. ## 2. Will water reach it? Water arrives from three directions, and a site can be fine in two of them and ruined by the third. Take them in order: what falls on it, what flows across it, and what sits under it. [Where Water Goes](/library#where-water-goes) is the full treatment of the mechanism; this is the siting subset. ### What falls on it Silverdale gets about 1,446 mm of rain a year at the nearest station with a full record, and the distribution is the design problem: December brings 252 mm, July brings 21 mm, and just under 80 percent of the year's water falls between October and March. County-wide the swing between years is nearly twofold, from 818.6 mm in 2013 to 1,544.6 mm in 1999. For siting, the useful consequence is that **every drainage question here is a winter question and every water-supply question is a summer question**, and a site visit in one season tells you nothing about the other. A lot inspected in August is a lot you have not seen. The other consequence is volume. A roof concentrates rain that used to fall over the whole footprint into a few discharge points, and where those points discharge is a siting decision made at the same moment as the building's position. On a bluff lot, it is the siting decision. ### What flows across it This is the one you can see, and only in the rain. Water arriving from uphill does not care about your property line. A site can be perfectly drained on its own and still receive the runoff of five acres above it, especially if the ground above was recently cleared or paved. Ecology names upland vegetation clearing as one of the conditions that raises landslide risk here, for exactly this reason. Look for: a swale or shallow channel crossing the lot, a culvert discharging above you, a road ditch that ends nowhere in particular, a neighbour's downspouts, bare scoured soil, silt fans at the bottom of a grade, and the line where grass changes species. All of that is a record of where water has been going, written in the ground. ### What sits under it The perched water table is the local signature. Over half the land here sits on dense till with water sitting on top of it through the wet season, at 46 to 75 cm depending on the series. A crawlspace or footing excavated to that depth in August is dry; the same hole in February is in the water table. There is also the water that arrives sideways underground and surfaces as a **seep or spring**. This is the classic ruinous surprise, because it is invisible for eight months of the year and it does not appear on any map. A spring under or above a building is not a drainage inconvenience, it is a permanent pressure source in the exact place you least want one, and on a bluff lot it is the mechanism of failure. Signs, in the wet season: rushes, sedges, skunk cabbage or willow in a line or a patch; ground that stays green in a dry August while everything around it browns off; a wet spot on a slope with no channel feeding it; water in a test hole that rises after you stop digging. **Rule of thumb:** if you can only visit a site once, visit it in the wettest week you can arrange, in the rain, on foot. Everything in this section is visible then and invisible in summer. ## The mapped flood zone, and the water that actually arrives These are two different things and conflating them is the single most common flood mistake. ### What the map says FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer is the starting point and it is free. For Silverdale it returns a clear picture: the waterfront at the head of Dyes Inlet is **Zone AE with a base flood elevation of 14 feet**, the Chico Creek mouth is AE with a BFE of 13 feet, the Barker Creek mouth is **AE FLOODWAY**, and the built-up upland, including the census-designated place centroid, Clear Creek at Silverdale Way, and Bucklin Hill, is **Zone X, minimal flood hazard**. The panels covering Silverdale are DFIRM 53035C at 1:6000, effective 2010-11-04 and 2017-02-03. The vocabulary is precise and worth learning. A **Special Flood Hazard Area** is, in FEMA's words, the area that will be inundated by the flood event having a 1-percent chance of being equaled or exceeded in any given year. **Shaded Zone X** is the band between the limit of that flood and the 0.2-percent-annual-chance flood. **Unshaded Zone X** is outside the SFHA and above the 0.2-percent flood elevation. "100-year flood" means the 1-percent zone and is a worse name for it, because it sounds like a timetable and it is an annual probability. **Floodway** is the sharpest word on the map. It is the part of the channel and adjacent land that has to stay clear to carry the flood. Barker Creek's mouth is in one. Building in a floodway is a different regulatory conversation from building in an AE zone, and the answer is usually no. ### What the map does not say FEMA states it plainly: **there is no such thing as a "no-risk zone"**, and heavy rains, poor drainage, and even nearby construction projects can put you at risk for flood damage. Ready.gov puts the same point the other way round: flooding does not follow lines on a map. Being outside the zone is not the same as being safe, it is the same as being unmapped. Three specific reasons the map understates a particular lot: **It maps the sources it studied.** Riverine and coastal flooding are studied. Local ponding behind a plugged culvert, sheet flow off a newly cleared hillside, a blocked roadside ditch and a failed detention pond generally are not. FEMA's own summary of what it cannot map for you is short and blunt: heavy rains, poor drainage and nearby construction projects can put you at risk. That gap is worth more attention here than in most places, because there is no large river on this peninsula, so the flooding the locale data records is localised rather than catastrophic. Concluding from that that the unmapped kind is the kind most houses here actually meet is our inference, not FEMA's. **It is a snapshot of a watershed that keeps changing.** FEMA says flood risk is always changing, and names nearby construction as one of the things that changes it. The Silverdale panels became effective in 2010 and 2017, and the study behind a panel predates the panel. A watershed that has been built on since is not the watershed the elevations were computed for, and the map does not update itself. **The zone boundary is a line on a 1:6000 map, and your lot is a point.** The same caution the soil survey prints about its own scale applies here. At the edge of a zone, the line is an interpretation, not a measurement of your ground. So use the map as the first gate, not the last word. If it puts you in a zone, that is dispositive and you should believe it. If it puts you out of one, you have learned that the studied sources do not reach you, and you still have to answer the local-drainage question yourself, in the rain, with your own eyes. ## The tide, for anything near the shoreline Two things make a shoreline site different from an ordinary low-lying one, and both are about reference levels. ### Which zero is your number measured from? An elevation is meaningless without its datum. NOAA distinguishes the two families you will meet: geodetic vertical datums are generally used to express land elevations, while water level datums are a slightly different vertical datum, used as the reference to which bathymetric soundings on nautical charts are referenced. A surveyor's elevation, a base flood elevation and a tide prediction may all be quoted in feet and none of them need share a zero. NOAA publishes a tool, VDatum, whose whole purpose is converting elevation data from various sources into a common reference system, and the fact that such a tool has to exist is the point. Practically: **before you compare any two elevations on a shoreline site, make somebody tell you the datum of each.** Ask the surveyor in writing. A half-metre error here is not a rounding problem, it is the difference between a finished floor above the base flood elevation and one below it. [Reading the Tide](/library#reading-the-tide) covers the datum ladder in full, including why mean lower low water is the United States chart zero and why predicted heights can legitimately be negative. ### The range here is large, and everything rides on top of it At the reference station for this inlet the **great diurnal range**, from mean higher high water to mean lower low water, is about **11.72 feet**, and the mean range of tide is **7.97 feet**. That is a large swing, and it means the same shoreline elevation is well underwater or well clear depending on the hour. Two local details that matter for a site near Dyes Inlet. **Your nearest tide station may not have published datums.** Dyes Inlet has its own NOAA station, 9445901 at Tracyton, but it is a subordinate station and NOAA publishes no datums for it. The datums above come from its reference station at Bremerton, in a different inlet. That is normal, and it means the numbers you are using for your shoreline have been transferred from somewhere else. **There is no seamless land-to-seabed elevation surface for this inlet.** The National Map returns zero topobathymetric lidar products here, and zero seamless 1-metre products. There is excellent 1-metre bare-earth lidar on the land, from the 2017 Olympic Peninsula survey, and it simply stops at the water. ### The tsunami rides on whatever the tide is doing This is the part people get wrong, and it is arithmetic rather than opinion. The Washington Geological Survey's modelled inundation for a large Seattle Fault earthquake reaches the head of Dyes Inlet, with a maximum amplitude of **5 feet at the Silverdale point and a modelled arrival time of 5 minutes**. Nearby modelled points run higher: Bremerton and Sinclair Inlet 9 feet, Agate Passage 11, Point White 16. The Cascadia megathrust case is smaller inside Puget Sound, about 2.5 feet at Bremerton, arriving in roughly 2 hours 40 minutes. Now put that 5-foot wave against an 11.72-foot tidal range. **The tide stage dominates the outcome**, and the locale hazard data says so outright. A 5-foot wave arriving at mean lower low water starts from nearly twelve feet below mean higher high water. The same wave at a high tide starts from the top of the range. The modelled amplitude is not the water level you will see; it is what gets added to whatever the water is already doing, and nobody gets to choose the hour. For siting, the conclusion is simple and unpopular: on a low shoreline parcel, the elevation that matters is not the one that keeps you dry on an ordinary winter storm tide. Five minutes of warning also means there is no evacuation plan that involves a vehicle. [The Hazards Your Place Actually Has](/library#the-hazards-where-you-live) covers what to do about that; this guide's contribution is that the decision is made when you pick the contour line. ## 3. Can you get water, and get rid of waste? On a peninsula these two questions are the same question, because the water you drink and the water your drainfield discharges into are the same body of groundwater. ### Water in The Kitsap Peninsula has no upstream river to divert from. USGS describes its hydrologic setting as similar to that of an island, and groundwater is the normal domestic water source and the only one. Every litre of fresh water on this peninsula fell on this peninsula. What that means for a specific parcel: **Drilling depth is knowable in advance.** From the recorded depths of 646 USGS-inventoried wells within about 6 km of Silverdale, the median is **98 feet, about 30 metres**, with the middle half falling between 41 and 255 feet and the deepest at 1,200 feet. That distribution is your budget range, and the spread between the 25th and 75th percentile is a factor of six. **How much you may legally take is not the statewide answer.** The Washington statewide groundwater permit exemption allows a domestic withdrawal of up to 5,000 gallons per day without a water right. But Silverdale is in WRIA 15, named in state law among the watersheds with a streamflow restoration requirement, and there a new domestic permit-exempt withdrawal is capped at an annual average of **950 gallons per day per connection**, dropping to **350 gallons per day, indoor use only**, under a drought emergency order. There is a $500 fee to the permitting authority, and a condition that the applicant manage stormwater on-site by maximising infiltration. Those are interim statutory measures that apply until rules say otherwise, and Ecology adopted the WRIA 15 watershed plan in December 2024 with rulemaking to follow, so confirm the current number before relying on it. **On a shoreline parcel, ask about chloride.** The most detailed federal study found no widespread seawater contamination of Kitsap Peninsula wells, and listed the local areas where chloride exceeds 25 mg/L: Silverdale and Dyes Inlet are not on that list, Sinclair Inlet about 11 km south is. The asterisk is that the finding rests on 1980 field data. Test rather than assume. [Where Water Goes](/library#where-water-goes) explains why this particular contamination does not undo. **If a well is not the plan, connection is a question with an address.** Whether a parcel can connect to a public water system, what the connection costs, and how far the main is from the property line are all answerable before you buy, by asking. They are frequently not asked. ### Waste out The drainfield is the part of a house that is most tightly coupled to the ground under it, which makes it the part most likely to decide whether a lot is buildable at all. [Where Water Goes](/library#where-water-goes) explains the mechanism: the tank settles solids, and the **soil** is the treatment plant. That is why the soil survey's septic ratings are a siting document. The survey's verdict for this area is unusual and worth knowing before you look at a single listing: **septic drainfields rate Very limited on essentially every major series here**, for opposite reasons depending on which ground you are standing on. Too slow on the till and lake-sediment soils, where the objection is wetness and restricted percolation. Too fast on the outwash sands, where the objection is seepage through the bottom layer and inadequate filtering in the 60 to 150 cm filter field zone, which is a groundwater contamination finding rather than a drainage failure. Indianola, the best-draining ground in the area, fails for the second reason. "Very limited" does not mean forbidden. In the survey's own vocabulary it means the limitation generally cannot be overcome without major soil reclamation, special design, or expensive installation, and that poor performance and high maintenance can be expected. In siting terms: this lot needs an engineered system, and you should find out what kind and what it costs before you commit, not after. Two regulatory facts turn all of that into numbers on a site plan. **Separation distances eat small lots.** Washington's on-site sewage rule sets minimum horizontal separations that include **100 feet from a nonpublic drinking water well**, **100 feet from nonpublic surface water** measured from the ordinary high water mark, **10 feet from a building foundation** and **5 feet from a property line**, and the local health officer may increase them where the contamination risk is higher. Draw those circles on a plan of a one-acre sloping waterfront lot with a well, a house, a driveway and a creek on it, and the buildable area is often much smaller than the lot. **Depth of usable soil sets the system type, and therefore the price.** The same rules set the required treatment level from the **vertical separation**, meaning the depth of original undisturbed soil below the bottom of the treatment component. The table runs in bands from 12 to 18 inches at the shallow end up to 60 inches or more at the deep end, and the shallower the separation the higher the treatment level demanded and the more likely the system has to distribute effluent under pressure with timed dosing rather than by gravity. Deep separation on a medium-textured soil is the one combination that gets you a plain gravity drainfield. Read that against the local geology and the shape of the problem is obvious. Alderwood's till sits at a representative 56 cm, which is about 22 inches from the surface, with a mapped range of roughly 20 to 40 inches. The trench bottom has to sit somewhere in that column, and whatever is left below it is your vertical separation. On half the land here, there is not much left. That is not a reason nothing can be built; it is the reason the system costs what it costs, and it is knowable before you buy. **Who actually decides** is the local health jurisdiction, not the state. In Kitsap County that is the Kitsap Public Health District, and the sequence is worth knowing because people get it backwards: the health district's building clearance, which checks the proposed project against the septic system and water supply, comes **before** the county issues a building permit. ## 4. Can you get to it, in February? Access is the question people underrate most reliably, because on the day you look at the property it is July and the road is fine. ### The road, and what it is made of The soil survey rates ground for **local roads and streets** in the same way it rates it for dwellings, and the ratings are instructive. Norma and McKenna rate Very limited for ponding and wetness. Shalcar and Mukilteo rate Very limited for ponding, wetness, subsidence and very low strength. Kitsap silt loam rates Somewhat limited for low strength by AASHTO group index, shrink-swell and wetness. Those are engineering statements about a road surface in the wet season, and they are free. A private road or long driveway on the wrong ground is a permanent running cost. It is also a shared one: if three houses use it, the question of who pays for rebuilding it is a social arrangement you are buying into, not a line in a contract. ### Grade, and the vehicles that have to come Every vehicle you will ever need has to arrive under its own power, in the conditions of the day it is needed. That list is longer than people expect: a fuel truck, a septic pump truck, a well drilling rig, a concrete mixer, a lumber delivery, a moving van, a propane tanker, an ambulance, a fire engine. This is a **rule of thumb** rather than a code citation, and it is worth more than most things in this guide: before you commit to a steep driveway, ask the local propane supplier and the local septic pumper whether they will come up it, and ask in writing. They know the answer immediately, they answer for free, and their answer is a real constraint on a real vehicle rather than a theoretical gradient. A driveway your car climbs easily in August can be one a loaded truck will not attempt in January. The same rule of thumb applies to turning. A vehicle that gets up your driveway and then cannot turn around has to reverse down it. ### The fire service question Ask the fire district that covers the parcel, before you buy, what they need in order to reach it: access width, surface, grade, turnaround, overhead clearance, bridge capacity if there is a bridge, and where the nearest water supply for firefighting is. In much of the United States these requirements come from a model code the county has adopted, so the authoritative answer is local and specific. There is also usually an insurance consequence attached to distance from a fire station and distance from a hydrant, which is a recurring cost you can find out in advance. Around Silverdale, the wildfire risk is genuinely low by Washington standards, and it is also the hazard most likely to be underestimated here, which is a combination worth holding in mind rather than resolving. There is no modern mapped fire perimeter within about 15 km; the only perimeters intersecting that area are three very large pre-settlement events dated 1308, 1508 and 1701. But the westside Douglas-fir regime is infrequent and stand-replacing, and the binding constraint in a fire here is not fire behaviour, it is getting off a peninsula reached by two bridges and ferries. ### The season that actually closes roads Wind and snow, not fire. In NOAA's record for the Kitsap Peninsula zones from 1996 to 2025, **24 of 30 years** had at least one high or strong wind event, 80 events in total, peaking at 77 mph in December 2000. On 15 November 2006 about 8,000 people in Kitsap County lost power, three roads were closed or partly blocked by downed trees and power lines, and the Hood Canal Bridge closed for several hours. The same record holds 48 heavy snow events, with heavy snow in 18 of the 30 years, and wet lowland snow near freezing is what brings limbs and lines down. So the siting question is not whether the road ever fails. It is how long you are prepared to be on the wrong side of a fallen tree, and how many houses are on your side of it to help clear it. A single-access road serving one house is a different proposition from a loop serving twenty. ## 5. Only now: is it a pleasant place to live? Everything above is a veto. This section is the part that decides whether the house is good, and in a marine climate at 47.6 degrees north it is not a matter of taste. It is a comfort and energy decision with numbers behind it. ### Aspect and solar access The Department of Energy's building science guidance is simple at the level that matters for siting: a home oriented north-south will optimise exposure to solar energy while minimising overheating from the low-angled east-west sun, and this requires proper placement of windows and overhangs, and careful placement of plants and trees so that shading falls where it does the most good. For anything intended to use passive solar heating or photovoltaics, DOE's guidance is to carry out a solar assessment and mark the proposed array location on the site plan, which is to say: settle it at siting time, not later. What makes that concrete here is the winter sun angle, and it is worse than people imagine. The following is **arithmetic, not a citation**. The sun's altitude at solar noon is 90 degrees minus your latitude, plus or minus the 23.44 degrees of the Earth's axial tilt depending on the season. At Silverdale, latitude 47.6445 north: | Date | Sun's altitude at solar noon | |---|---| | Winter solstice, about 21 December | **18.9 degrees** | | Equinoxes, about 20 March and 22 September | 42.4 degrees | | Summer solstice, about 21 June | 65.8 degrees | Nineteen degrees is very low. Three consequences follow, all of them arithmetic from that one number. **Shadows in midwinter are about 2.9 times the height of whatever casts them.** The multiplier is 1 divided by the tangent of 18.9 degrees. A 30-metre stand of second-growth conifer on your southern boundary throws a shadow roughly 87 metres long at noon on the shortest day. A two-storey neighbour throws about 20 metres. A tree line that is comfortably out of the way in June is across your whole building envelope in December. **A north-facing slope steeper than about 19 degrees receives no direct sun at all at midwinter noon.** Nineteen degrees is a 34 percent grade, which is not a cliff. For scale, the soil survey maps Kitsap silt loam on terrace escarpments around Dyes Inlet at slopes up to 70 percent, including an Indianola-Kitsap complex mapped at 45 to 70 percent, and 45 to 70 percent is about 24 to 35 degrees. A north-facing parcel on one of those escarpments is in its own shadow at noon in December, and that is before any trees. **The window is short even where the sun does reach you.** The US Naval Observatory gives sunrise at 07:56 and sunset at 16:22 for 21 December 2026 at Silverdale, with solar noon at 12:09: eight hours and twenty-six minutes of daylight, against sixteen hours at midsummer. Any ridge or tree line to the south cuts a real bite out of that eight and a half hours. **How to check it, on the ground, for nothing:** stand on the proposed building site at solar noon, face south, and look at the skyline. Hold your arm out and use your fist at arm's length, which subtends roughly ten degrees of sky. If the ridge, the trees or the neighbour's roof stand higher than about two fists above the horizon to the south, the midwinter sun does not clear them. The fist measure is a **rule of thumb** from field navigation, not a surveying instrument, but it answers the question well enough to change a decision. Do it in winter if you can, when the low sun will simply show you the answer. There is a second-order benefit worth naming. Every degree of comfort you win from aspect is a degree you do not have to buy fuel for, every year, forever. Western Washington is climate zone 4C, the marine zone, and its recommended insulation levels are as demanding as genuinely cold zones 5 and 6 because mild and long still adds up. See [Insulation and Heat Loss](/library#insulation-and-heat-loss). Siting is the only insulation decision you make for free. ### Wind, and the shelter that is worth having The prevailing damaging wind here comes with Pacific winter storms, and those are synoptic systems that arrive from the south and southwest. Exposure to that quarter is what costs you. The trade-off to think about explicitly is that the same trees that shelter a site from wind are the trees that shade it in winter and drop limbs on it in a storm. That is a genuine tension, and the resolution is usually geometric rather than binary: shelter to the south-west and north, open to the south for light, and nothing tall enough to reach the house standing where it would fall on it. ### Cold air drainage, and the frost pocket The bottom of a hollow is colder than the ground above it, and the mechanism is straightforward. The National Weather Service describes it directly: cold air will settle in the valleys since it is heavier than warm air, therefore frost conditions are more prone in these regions, and valleys also shelter the area from stronger winds, which enhances the potential for frost. The drainage itself is a named process: over the course of a clear night the denser, cooler air on higher ground sinks into the valley, which begins to fill from the bottom with cold layers of air. NWS calls this cold air drainage. The magnitude is not small. On a clear, calm night with strong radiational cooling, NWS notes that the super-cooled layer right at the surface can be up to 10 degrees Fahrenheit cooler than the air at the four to five feet where observations are normally taken. So the temperature in the hollow at plant height is not the temperature on the forecast, and it is not the temperature at the top of your own driveway. For siting this has three practical consequences. **A slight rise beats a hollow, even a small one.** A building site a few metres up the slope from a depression sits above the pooled cold air on exactly the nights when it matters. **Anything that dams the flow creates a pond of cold air behind it.** A solid fence, a dense hedge, a road embankment or a building across the slope will hold cold air upslope of it. This is a real effect on a garden and a mild one on a house. **The frost dates in the climate record are the station's, not yours.** [The Growing Calendar Where You Live](/library#the-growing-calendar) covers how to read them; the siting point is that a hollow runs colder than the published dates and a slope runs warmer. There is a local wrinkle that shows how fine-grained this gets. Silverdale sits on a hardiness zone boundary: the ZIP codes covering Silverdale, west Bremerton and Poulsbo are zone 8b, while two nearer the Bremerton waterfront are 9a. Shoreline sites here run about half a zone warmer than sites a few hundred metres inland or uphill, because the water moderates them. Half a zone is a real difference for a fruit tree, and it is decided by where you stand. ## Who to ask, before you commit This is a checklist of bodies to contact, not legal advice. Nothing here is a substitute for asking them, and the answers are specific to a parcel number. The pattern holds in most of the United States even though the names change; the Silverdale specifics are the worked example. **The county planning and permitting department.** In Kitsap County this is the Department of Community Development, which issues building, fire, stormwater and site development permits, and which administers the zoning code, the Critical Areas Ordinance and the county's Shoreline Master Program. Ask: what is this parcel zoned, is it a legal lot of record, what are the setbacks, what critical areas are mapped on it, and what studies will be required with an application. **The critical areas question specifically.** Washington's Growth Management Act requires counties to designate and protect critical areas, and defines them as wetlands, areas with a critical recharging effect on aquifers used for potable water, fish and wildlife habitat conservation areas, frequently flooded areas, and geologically hazardous areas. The statute defines geologically hazardous areas as areas that, because of their susceptibility to erosion, sliding, earthquake or other geological events, are not suited to the siting of commercial, residential or industrial development consistent with public health or safety concerns. Read that definition again: the state has written down, as a matter of law, that some ground is not a building site. A bluff parcel here is very likely to be mapped as one, and a mapped geologically hazardous area normally triggers a required geotechnical report and a buffer around the top and the toe. The size of that buffer is set by your county's ordinance, so get the number from the county rather than from any general document, this one included. **Shoreline rules, if you are anywhere near saltwater.** Washington's Shoreline Management Act reaches inland: shorelands extend landward 200 feet in all directions, measured on a horizontal plane from the ordinary high water mark, and the definition also picks up floodways, floodplain areas extending 200 feet from those floodways, and associated wetlands and river deltas. Two hundred feet is further than people assume, and a parcel can be entirely inside shoreline jurisdiction without touching the beach. **The local health jurisdiction, for septic and water supply.** Kitsap Public Health District. Ask whether the parcel has an existing approved system or a valid site evaluation, what soil type and vertical separation the site carries, what system type that implies, and where the reserve drainfield area is. Remember that its building clearance precedes the county building permit. **The state water agency, for what you may legally take.** Washington's Department of Ecology administers water rights, and WRIA 15 overrides the statewide permit-exempt allowance here. The locale's authorities map in `data/locales/silverdale_wa/locale.json` records the current contact for this and for the other state-level bodies below. **The fire district**, for access and water supply, as above. **The state geological survey**, for the mapped landslide, liquefaction and tsunami layers. Washington's is the Washington Geological Survey and its Geologic Information Portal. Every state has an equivalent and what each has mapped varies enormously. **Utilities**, for the boring and decisive question of what it costs to bring power, and whether there is any. A long service run is a large number and it is quotable in advance. **And the seller's own disclosures and the title.** Easements, access rights across someone else's land, shared well agreements, road maintenance agreements, and any recorded geotechnical report or condition. A shared well with no written agreement is a dispute waiting for a dry August. The locale file's `authorities` block holds the current bodies and URLs for the state extension service, the state water agency, the state fish and wildlife agency, the health department's biotoxin programme, the noxious weed board, the soil testing lab and the regional air agency. It is the place to look up who is who rather than trusting a name in a document that may be years old by the time you read it. ## How to survey a candidate site yourself, in a day None of this replaces a professional. All of it is free, takes one day, and will either raise a question worth paying a professional to answer or save you the fee entirely. **Before you go, one hour at a desk.** 1. Look up the parcel on FEMA's Flood Map Service Center. Write down the zone, and the base flood elevation if there is one. 2. Look it up on your state's geologic hazard portal. Write down whether any landslide, liquefaction or tsunami layer touches it. 3. Look it up in the soil survey, following [Your Soil, Specifically](/library#your-soil-specifically). Write down the map unit name and phase, the drainage class, the depth to any restrictive layer, and the ratings for dwellings, local roads and septic, **with the reason printed next to each rating**. 4. Find the 12-digit hydrologic unit it sits in and what is upstream of it, following [Where Water Goes](/library#where-water-goes). 5. Look at whatever aerial imagery you can get, at several dates if possible. Old imagery shows what used to be there: a pond, a pit, a barn, a logging road, a slide scar. You now have a hypothesis. The day out is for testing it. **What to walk.** Walk the whole parcel, the boundaries included, not just the pretty part. Walk the slope above you and the slope below you, and, if you can get permission, walk onto the neighbouring ground uphill, because that is where your water comes from. Walk the access from the public road to the building site, and back down. Then imagine a concrete truck doing it. **What to look at.** - The shape of the ground. Hummocky, irregular, stepped ground on a slope, with trees leaning at odd angles or curving at the base, is what old movement looks like. So is a bench or a scarp that does not belong to the general grade. - Ready.gov's list of slow landslide signs, which apply to any existing structure on the site: doors or windows that stick or jam; new cracks in plaster, tile, brick or foundations; slowly developing, widening cracks in the ground; and changes in the pattern of storm-water drainage on slopes. - Standing water, and the vegetation that indicates it. Rushes, sedges, skunk cabbage and willow are telling you about the water table. - The bluff edge, if there is one, from a safe distance, and the beach below it if you can reach it. Fresh raw soil, toppled trees, exposed roots and a fan of debris at the toe are a recent failure. - The skyline to the south, with the fist measure above. - The neighbours' houses. Where did people who have lived here a while choose to put their buildings, and what do their driveways, retaining walls and drainage look like? That is decades of accumulated local knowledge, sitting in plain view. **What to dig.** Dig at least three holes, well apart, in the parts of the site you actually intend to use. Not one. The point is to find out whether the ground is uniform, and one hole cannot answer that. Dig each one past the depth the soil survey gives for its restrictive layer, and look for: the horizon depths and colours against the published profile; where the gravel starts; where roots stop and turn sideways; whether the spade hits something it cannot get through, and at what depth; and whether water seeps into the hole and rises after you stop. A steel probe rod or a digging bar maps a hardpan across a site far faster than a spade, on a rough grid of points. That is a **rule of thumb**, not a published method, and it works. Watch for signs that the ground is fill rather than natural soil: an abrupt knife-sharp boundary between layers, mixed colours with no pattern down the profile, fragments of brick, concrete, asphalt, glass or plastic, a hard compacted layer at exactly the depth machinery would have tracked, and horizons out of order. **When to go.** Twice, if you possibly can: once in the wettest week of winter and once in late summer. If you only get one visit, make it the wet one. Almost everything that makes a site bad is visible in February and invisible in August. That timing advice is a **rule of thumb**; the underlying seasonality is in the climate data. **Who to talk to.** The neighbours, and this is not a courtesy, it is data collection. Nobody has published what they know and no map contains it. Ask, in these words or near enough: - How deep is your well, and has it ever run low in August? - Does your drainfield give you trouble, and what kind of system is it? - How often does the power go out, and for how long? - Has the road ever been impassable, and what closed it? - Has anything ever slid, anywhere along here? - Where does the water come out in a big storm? - Who owns the road, and who maintains it? People answer these questions generously and at length, because nobody usually asks. Half an hour on a doorstep routinely turns up something no agency knows. ## If you already own the site Then this stops being a choice and becomes a list of things to find out, which is still worth doing. Several of them cost money and are worth it. **Free, this week.** The flood zone, the state geologic hazard layers, the soil map unit and its ratings, the hydrologic unit and what is upstream, the parcel's zoning and mapped critical areas, and the walk in the rain with three test holes. That is most of the picture. **Worth paying for, roughly in order of what it prevents.** 1. **A geotechnical investigation**, if there is any slope, any bluff, any sign of past movement, or any intention to build or add. This is the one that prevents the outcome nothing else prevents. 2. **A current survey with the datum stated in writing**, if you are near a shoreline, a floodplain, or a boundary anyone could argue about. A surveyor's elevation whose datum nobody recorded is a number you cannot use. 3. **A septic inspection and a locate of the existing system and its reserve area**, if you are on septic and do not have the as-built. 4. **A water test**, including chloride if you are near saltwater, and the basic bacteriological and nitrate panel regardless. 5. **A lead test on the soil**, if the house is old or close to a road. [Your Soil, Specifically](/library#your-soil-specifically) covers why and against what number to read the result. **Free and permanent, whatever the above says.** Get the roof water away from the building and away from any slope, in pipes, discharging somewhere that can take it. Keep drainfields and irrigation off the ground between a house and a bluff edge. Keep native vegetation on a slope. Ecology's summary is that drainage improvements are the most cost-effective way to reduce slide risk, and drainage is the one part of this whole subject where a homeowner with no budget can genuinely change the outcome. ## What can go wrong - **You judged the site in summer.** The perched water table, the seep, the boggy corner, the road that fails and the way water crosses the lot are all February phenomena. A July inspection is a partial inspection and it is the one everybody does. - **You treated a flood map as a safety certificate.** Outside the zone means the studied sources do not reach you. FEMA says there is no such thing as a no-risk zone. - **You compared two elevations with different datums.** A survey elevation, a base flood elevation and a tide height need not share a zero. Ask for the datum in writing. - **You looked at the bluff top and forgot the toe.** Both are the hazard. So is the ground three days after an earthquake. - **You bought the view.** A view lot on this coast is very frequently a bluff lot, and the two facts are the same fact. - **You assumed "Very limited" meant "a bit awkward".** In the survey's own words it means major reclamation, special design or expensive installation, with poor performance and high maintenance expected. - **You checked whether a septic system was possible but not what type.** The type follows from the vertical separation, and the price follows from the type. - **You never drew the separation circles on the plan.** A hundred feet from the well, a hundred feet from surface water, plus setbacks, can leave a large lot with a small buildable area. - **You planned the driveway for your own car.** The pump truck, the fuel truck and the fire engine are the ones that decide. - **You did not ask the neighbours.** They know about the slide, the flood, the well that ran dry and the road that closes, and none of it is written down anywhere. - **You cleared the trees uphill.** That is named by Ecology as one of the conditions that raises landslide risk here, and it is a thing people do to improve a view. - **You assumed the fine-grained public data exists.** There is superb 1-metre lidar on this land and no topobathymetric coverage of the inlet at all. Check before relying on a dataset. ## How you know it worked - You can name, for your site, the soil map unit and phase, the depth to its restrictive layer, and what the survey rates it for dwellings, roads and septic, with the reason next to each rating. - You know its flood zone, and if it has a base flood elevation you know the number and the datum it is measured from. - You know whether any landslide, liquefaction or tsunami layer touches it, and if it is on or below a slope, a geotechnical engineer has looked at it rather than a document. - You have walked the site in heavy rain and can say where water enters it, crosses it and leaves it. - You have dug at least three holes and know what stops a spade, and at what depth. - You know what a well costs here and what you are legally allowed to draw, or you know what a connection costs and how far away the main is. - You know what septic system type the ground implies, and roughly what that costs, before you have committed to anything. - You have asked the fire district and the septic pumper whether they can reach the building site. - You have stood on the site at midwinter noon, or done the fist measure, and you know whether the sun reaches it in December. - You have talked to at least two neighbours about water, power and the road. When those are true, you are no longer choosing a site by how it looks. And if the answer is that this site is a poor one and you are going to build on it anyway, because it is the site you have, then you at least know exactly which problems you have bought, which is the difference between a budget and a surprise. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. Its provenance is USGS 3DEP, USGS GNIS, USGS NHD, NOAA CO-OPS and USGS Open-File Report 2008-1292. - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/hazards.json`, for the landslide inventory figures, the flood zones and base flood elevations, the tsunami model outputs, and the wind, snow and wildfire event records. Its provenance is USGS, FEMA, NOAA and the Washington Geological Survey. - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/soil.json`, for every soil series share, restrictive layer depth, drainage class and suitability rating quoted here, from the USDA NRCS SSURGO database for survey areas WA635 and WA778. - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/water.json`, for the precipitation figures, the well depth distribution, the WRIA 15 withdrawal limits and the seawater intrusion findings. - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/climate.json`, for the monthly normals, the daylight hours, the hardiness zone boundary detail and the winter design temperature. - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/locale.json`, whose `authorities` block holds the current name and URL for each state-level body a reader here has to contact. - [Your Soil, Specifically](/library#your-soil-specifically), for how to read a soil survey, what a restrictive layer is, what a drainage class means, and how to test the map against the ground with a spade. - [The Hazards Your Place Actually Has](/library#the-hazards-where-you-live), for the full hazard list sorted by warning time, and for what to do about the ones a siting decision cannot remove. - [Where Water Goes](/library#where-water-goes), for the watershed, the hydrologic soil groups, how a septic system actually treats wastewater, and why the two opposite drainfield failure modes look the same on a rating sheet. - [Where Water Comes From](/library#where-water-comes-from), for the sources a household actually has and what is wrong with each. - [Reading the Tide](/library#reading-the-tide), for the tidal datum ladder, why mean lower low water is the chart zero, and how to read a prediction. - [Insulation and Heat Loss](/library#insulation-and-heat-loss), for climate zone 4C and what the shell of a building has to do here. - [The Growing Calendar Where You Live](/library#the-growing-calendar), for the frost dates a frost pocket will beat. - [Collecting Rainwater](/library#collecting-rainwater), for storing what falls on the roof rather than only routing it away. - [Where You Are: Silverdale, Washington](/library#silverdale-wa), the generated gazetteer. ### Arithmetic rather than citation Three figures in this guide are geometry, not measurements, and are labelled as such in the text. The sun's altitude at solar noon is 90 degrees minus the latitude, plus or minus the Earth's axial tilt of 23.44 degrees. At 47.6445 degrees north that gives 18.9 degrees at the winter solstice, 42.4 at the equinoxes and 65.8 at the summer solstice. The USNO sunrise and sunset times above are the sourced cross-check that the December day really is that short. The midwinter shadow multiplier of about 2.9 is 1 divided by the tangent of 18.9 degrees, so a 30-metre tree casts roughly an 87-metre shadow at solar noon on the shortest day. A directly north-facing slope is in its own shadow at solar noon on the winter solstice once its angle exceeds the sun's altitude, so once it is steeper than about 18.9 degrees, which is a 34 percent grade. The 45 to 70 percent slope phases the soil survey maps on the Dyes Inlet terrace escarpments correspond to about 24 to 35 degrees. ### Labelled in the text as rules of thumb, not sourced - The ordering of the five siting questions by how permanent each answer is. Each individual constraint is sourced above; the ranking is ours. - Visiting a candidate site in the wettest week of winter, in the rain, and treating a summer-only inspection as a partial one. The seasonality is in the climate data; the advice to plan around it is ours. - Digging at least three test holes rather than one, and using a probe rod or digging bar on a grid to map a hardpan quickly. Standard field practice, published as a method by nobody. - Asking the propane supplier and the septic pumper, in writing, whether they will drive your driveway. No agency says this; it is simply the cheapest way to convert a gradient into an answer. - The fist-at-arm's-length measure of about ten degrees of sky, used to check whether a southern skyline blocks the midwinter sun. A field navigation convention, not an instrument. - The list of signs that a layer is fill rather than natural soil, and the list of vegetation and landform signs of old movement and of seasonal water. Each sign is ordinary field practice; the lists as given are not quoted from any single publication. - Interviewing the neighbours, and the specific questions to ask them.

docs.text: # Your First Solar Power If the power went out tonight, could you keep a phone alive, a light on, and the internet running? A small portable solar setup can do exactly that, and it is the safest way to learn how solar works. This guide covers plug-and-play gear only: a portable power station (a battery box with ordinary outlets) plus a folding solar panel, or an even smaller USB solar charger. You plug things together; you never touch wiring. One hard boundary before anything else: whole-house solar, rooftop panels, and anything that touches your home's electrical wiring is work for a licensed electrician, full stop. So is building your own battery bank from loose cells or car batteries. House wiring can kill, roof and ladder falls maim, and a badly built battery bank is a fire. This guide is the safe first rung of the ladder. Where a number matters, it comes from the US Department of Energy, the EPA, the US Fire Administration, or a university extension service. ## Watts and watt-hours, in kitchen language - A watt (W) is how hard electricity is flowing right now, like how far a faucet is open. - A watt-hour (Wh) is how much electricity flowed over time, like how much water ended up in the pot. A lamp makes it concrete. Wattage multiplied by hours of use gives watt-hours, and 1,000 watt-hours make one kilowatt-hour (kWh), the unit on your electric bill. Take an electric kettle rated at 1,500 watts, which is an ordinary rating for one: run it an hour and it has used 1,500 watt-hours, which is 1.5 kWh. For scale, the Energy Information Administration puts the average US residential customer at 10,791 kWh a year, about 899 kWh a month, which is roughly 30 kWh a day. A portable power station holds one or two. A power station's size is listed in watt-hours (how much the tank holds). Its output rating is in watts (how far the faucet can open at once). You need both numbers, and the troubleshooting section shows why. ## What you need (cheap first) - Cheapest rung: a small folding USB solar charger. No battery; it charges a phone or power bank directly in sunlight. Good for learning how much sun actually matters, for less than most gadgets cost. - The main event: a portable power station. Pick one with LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) battery cells; the chemistry section explains why. Around 250 to 500 watt-hours is a sensible first size. - A matching folding solar panel. Portable panels commonly range from 100 to 400 watts (University of Colorado Denver's emergency preparedness guidance). Buy the panel made for your station so the plugs simply fit. - The cords that came in the box. Use only those, nothing improvised. - Free but essential: the labels on your devices, and ten minutes of arithmetic. ## Step 1: Read a device label Every device has a nameplate: a sticker with its electrical ratings, usually on the bottom or on the power brick. It is there by law. OSHA's electrical standard, 29 CFR 1910.303(e)(1), says equipment may not be used unless it is marked with the manufacturer and with "markings giving voltage, current, wattage, or other ratings as necessary." So the numbers you need are on the thing itself. The amps-times-volts method and the appliance wattage table below are republished by Virginia Cooperative Extension: 1. If the label lists watts (W), that is the most the device draws. 2. If it only lists amps (A) and volts (V), multiply them: amps x volts = watts. A router brick marked 12V 1.5A can draw at most 12 x 1.5 = 18 watts. 3. The label is the most the device draws, so budgeting the label number is a safe overestimate, the direction you want to err in. ## Step 2: Add up a day, one worked example Say you want to run a phone, one LED lamp, and your internet router through a one-day outage. - Phone: the EPA's official figure is 0.019 kWh, about 19 watt-hours, for one full smartphone charge, counting charger losses. Two charges = 38 Wh. - LED lamp: a roughly 10-watt LED bulb matches an old 75-watt bulb (the Department of Energy lists 9.5 to 14 watts as the equivalent range). Five evening hours: 10 W x 5 h = 50 Wh. - Router: label says up to 18 watts, running all day: 18 W x 24 h = 432 Wh. Total: 38 + 50 + 432 = 520 watt-hours. Notice what happened: the always-on device ate the budget, not the phone. Turn the router off for 8 sleeping hours and you save 18 x 8 = 144 Wh, bringing the day to about 376 Wh. That is the most useful lesson in home energy: small loads that never stop cost more than big loads used briefly. For the trimmed 376 Wh day, a 500 watt-hour station covers you with margin; the full 520 Wh day needs a bigger one. And know that a station delivers roughly 10 to 15 percent less than its rated watt-hours through the AC outlets (the conversion electronics take their cut), so buy above your budget number, never right at it. ## Step 3: Why panels rarely give their rated watts A "100-watt" panel almost never delivers 100 watts, and that is not a scam; it is how the rating works. Panels are rated under a standard test of 1,000 watts of sunlight per square meter: bright, direct, noon sun. University of Maryland Extension calls one hour of that a "peak sun hour," and most places get only a few per day: Maryland averages about 3.92 peak sun hours daily in its west and 5.06 near the Chesapeake. Clouds, haze, season, and sun angle are already averaged into those numbers. On top of that, Maryland Extension applies a standard derate factor of 86 percent (14 percent lost to wiring, dirt, aging, temperature, and similar real-world friction). Colorado's emergency-preparedness guidance saw the same thing at the product level: a 400-watt portable panel typically produces 350 to 360 watts even in optimal conditions. Shade is worse still: full shade produces nothing, and even a small shadow across the panel causes a significant loss. So the honest recharge math for a 100-watt panel in a 4-peak-sun-hour location is: 100 W x 4 h x 0.86 = about 344 watt-hours per day. That does not fully refill the 520 Wh untrimmed day computed above; a 200-watt panel (about 688 Wh per day) does. It very nearly covers the 376 Wh trimmed day, which is the better argument for trimming. Size the panel to the day, not to the brochure. ## Step 4: One honest paragraph about battery chemistry Portable stations use two main lithium chemistries. Older-style lithium-ion (NMC, the laptop kind) stores more energy per pound. LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate, LFP) is heavier but lasts far longer and resists overheating. The Department of Energy's grid-storage cost assessments have used about 2,000 full charge cycles for LFP versus about 1,200 for NMC at 80 percent depth of discharge (the 2022 update raised both); makers now commonly advertise 3,000-plus cycles for LFP. Even at the conservative 2,000, that is a full drain and refill every day for over five years. For a box that will be cycled for years, LiFePO4 is worth its extra weight and cost. ## Step 5: Place and angle the panel 1. Ground level only. Never put a portable panel on a roof; roof and ladder work is where this hobby injures people. Nothing up there is worth it at this scale. 2. Face it south (in the northern hemisphere). Maryland Extension: due south is best; southeast or southwest costs about 5 percent. 3. Tilt it toward the sun instead of laying it flat. The extension rule of thumb is a tilt near your latitude (30 to 45 degrees across the mid US); Colorado's guidance suggests about 30 degrees if you want one number. Folding panels have kickstand legs for exactly this. 4. Chase the shade away. Recheck every hour or two; a shadow creeping over one corner quietly ruins the whole panel's output. 5. Keep the station itself out of the sun while charging, in shade or indoors with the cable running out. Heat is the battery's enemy. ## Step 6: Charging discipline and storage The US Fire Administration and university safety offices agree on these: - Charge only between 32 F and 105 F (0 C to 40 C). Charging a lithium battery below freezing damages it; charging it in high heat is a fire risk. - Never leave it in direct sunlight or a hot car; both are a fire risk. - When wall-charging, plug the station straight into a wall outlet, never into a power strip, and use only the cord that came with it. - Do not keep charging after it is full, and do not charge while asleep. - Store it at room temperature, away from anything that can burn. - Stop using any battery that gives off an odor, changes color or shape, swells, leaks, gets unusually hot, or makes odd noises. If you safely can, move it away from anything that can catch fire (outdoors on bare ground is ideal), and do not charge it again. If a battery ever smokes or flames, get out and call 911. There is no beginner-level response to a lithium fire. ## What a realistic budget buys (2026 prices, will drift) Ballpark only, and prices move constantly: in 2026, small portable stations (a few hundred watt-hours) start around $150 to $300, mid-size units around 1,000 watt-hours commonly sell in the $400 to $700 range, and the 1,500 to 2,500 Wh class runs roughly $700 to $2,000. Folding panels add money on top, from well under $100 for small ones upward. The honest way to compare is dollars per watt-hour of capacity: divide the price by the rated Wh and prefer the lower number at a given size, favoring LiFePO4 chemistry for its longer life. A $200 station you understand beats a $2,000 one bought blind. ## What can go wrong (honest troubleshooting) - It charges much slower than the panel rating. Normal; reread Step 3. A 100-watt panel giving 50 to 70 watts under a hazy sky at a lazy angle is physics, not a defect. Fix the angle, chase the shade, and expect the rating only in cloudless noon sun. Near zero in full sun? Check every cable connector first. - It will not run my heater, kettle, or toaster. Also physics. Heating appliances draw 1,000 to 1,500 watts continuously (a typical electric kettle is rated 1,500 W), and a small station's output may top out at 300 to 600 watts, so it shuts off to protect itself. Motors (fridges, pumps) are sneakier: they briefly surge far above their running watts at startup, so a station can fail to start a fridge it could otherwise run. Match appliance labels to the station's continuous and surge ratings before the outage. Heat is the job small solar does worst; plan blankets, not electric heaters. - Winter output collapses. Expected. Peak sun hours are annual averages; winter days sit well below them, and the effect grows with latitude: the University of Alaska Fairbanks extension's solar manual puts Fairbanks' maximum midwinter sunlight near 100 W per square meter versus about 970 in June, roughly a tenth. Plan winter around the wall charger, top up before storms, and treat winter solar as a bonus. - It sat in the closet a year and the level dropped. Batteries self-drain slowly. Top it up on a calendar reminder every few months, the same habit as rotating stored water. Your first afternoon will probably include a shaded panel, a surprise shutdown, and slow charging. That is cheap tuition; every failure here teaches you before the day it matters. ## How you know it worked - You can read any device label and say what it draws, in watts. - You have a written watt-hour budget for your outage day, and your station's capacity covers it. - Your panel has real sun on it, angled and unshaded, and you have watched the input watts change as you moved it. - The station lives indoors at room temperature, charged, away from anything that burns, and you know the temperature rules by heart. - You know exactly where this rung ends: the day you want solar on a roof or in your house wiring, you call a licensed electrician. When all five are true, you own working backup power, and you understand it. That understanding is what scales: sizing loads in watt-hours, derating panels, respecting battery chemistry, and knowing your limits are exactly the skills a professional whole-house install is built on. ## Sources - https://www.pubs.ext.vt.edu/2901/2901-9014/2901-9014.html - https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.303 - https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=97&t=3 - https://www.epa.gov/energy/greenhouse-gas-equivalencies-calculator-calculations-and-references - https://extension.umd.edu/resource/working-solar-design-and-system-sizing-fs-2023-0655 - https://www.energy.gov/cmei/femp/purchasing-energy-efficient-light-bulbs - https://ehs.washington.edu/system/files/resources/lithium-battery-safety.pdf - https://www.ucdenver.edu/center-for-innovative-design-and-engineering/community-engagement/emergency-preparedness-services-new/surviving-in-place/backup-power-options/charge-your-battery-system - https://www.usfa.fema.gov/prevention/home-fires/prevent-fires/batteries/ - https://www.energy.gov/eere/analysis/2022-grid-energy-storage-technology-cost-and-performance-assessment - https://www.uaf.edu/ces/publications/database/energy/solar-energy-manual.php
