docs.text: # Insulation and Heat Loss A heated room costs money every hour it stays warm. Insulation is the only thing you can buy once that keeps lowering that cost for the rest of the building's life. Everything else in the heating bill is a running expense: the fuel, the electricity, the filters, the service calls. The shell of the building is the one part you pay for once. That is why this comes before the guide on heating. If you size a heater for a leaky, uninsulated room, you buy a bigger heater and then feed it forever. Fix the room first and the heater gets smaller, the fuel bill gets smaller, and the room stops having a cold side. It also comes before the guide on ventilation, for a less obvious reason. A tighter, better insulated building traps moisture as readily as it traps heat, and trapped moisture rots timber and grows mould. That is the caution in this topic, and it has its own section below. Where a number matters here, it comes from a US government publication: the EPA's ENERGY STAR programme, the Department of Energy's Building America research, the Forest Products Laboratory, or the parts of federal regulation that set what insulation has to do. Where a figure is a rule of thumb rather than something an agency measured, it says so in the text. ## The three ways heat moves, in things you can feel You do not need equations for this. You need to recognise three different sensations, because each one is stopped by a different thing. **Conduction** is heat travelling through solid material. It is the cold you feel when you put a bare hand on a window pane or a concrete floor. The Forest Products Laboratory defines the property behind it plainly: thermal conductivity is the rate of heat flow through one unit thickness of a material with a temperature difference across it. Some materials pass heat greedily and some grudgingly, and the spread is far wider than most people expect. This is what insulation thickness fights. **Convection** is heat carried by moving air. It is the draught across your ankles, and it is also the reason an unheated upstairs somehow stays warmer than a heated downstairs. ENERGY STAR describes the whole building version of it: in cold weather, warm air rises in your house just like it does in a chimney, escapes into the attic, and sucks cold air in all around the house to replace it. Insulation does almost nothing about this. Sealing does. **Radiation** is heat crossing open space as invisible light, the way you feel a wood stove across a room without touching it. It is the weakest of the three in an ordinary heated room, but it is the reason foil-faced products exist. The FTC's insulation rule is precise about how they work: the test for reflective insulation measures the emittance of the reflective surface, meaning its power to radiate heat, and the resulting R-value depends on the emittance, the air space next to it, and the direction the heat is flowing. A foil product with no air space beside it is just a thin sheet. Most of the money in an ordinary house is lost to the first two, and most people spend their effort on the first one only. ## What R-value and U-value actually mean R-value is resistance to heat flow. ENERGY STAR's definition is the plain one: R-value is a measure of insulation's ability to resist heat traveling through it, and the higher the R-value, the better the thermal performance. U-value, or U-factor, is the same fact stated backwards. It is the rate of heat transmission, so lower is better. They are reciprocals of each other, which is worth internalising because insulation is sold in R-values and windows are sold in U-factors, and you cannot compare them until you flip one of them over. A window rated U-0.25 is resisting heat about as well as R-4 of anything else. **R-values add.** Stack R-13 of batt and R-10 of exterior board and you have R-23 through that path. This is the one piece of arithmetic in the whole subject, and it is why ENERGY STAR's retrofit guidance is written as "add R5 to R10 insulative wall sheathing beneath the new siding" rather than as a replacement value. You are adding to what is there. Two honest complications follow immediately. The first is that the addition only holds along a single path through the wall. It does not hold for the wall as a whole, because the wall has studs in it. That is the thermal bridging section below, and it is the single biggest reason a finished wall underperforms the number on the bag. The second is that R-value per inch is not a constant. The FTC actually forbids advertising it. Under 16 CFR 460.20, a manufacturer may not give the R-value for one inch or the R-value per inch of a product, and in the narrow case where test results allow a range, the label must carry the sentence: "The R-value per inch of this insulation varies with thickness. The thicker the insulation, the lower the R-value per inch." So treat every per-inch figure in this guide, including the ones below, as a rough comparison between material families rather than a number you can multiply out. ## Where a building actually loses heat Here is the honest state of the evidence. There is no single federal pie chart that says a typical house loses some exact percentage through the roof, some through the walls, and some through the floor. The proportions depend on the building's shape, its age, and where it is. Anyone who quotes you crisp percentages for that breakdown is quoting a rule of thumb, whatever it looks like. What the agencies do say, and what actually decides where your money goes, is this. Space heating and cooling dominate the bill. The Energy Information Administration reports that more than half, 52 percent in 2020, of a household's annual energy consumption goes to just two end uses: space heating and air conditioning. The leaks that matter are not the ones you feel. ENERGY STAR is blunt about it: people notice draughts around windows and doors and assume those are the major source of wasted energy, but in most homes the most significant air leaks are hidden in the attic and basement, and those are the leaks that significantly raise your energy bill. They put the total in an image worth keeping: if you added up all the leaks, holes and gaps in a typical home's envelope, it would be the equivalent of having a window open every day of the year. Air leakage is not a rounding error next to insulation. You can put a number on this using two parts of the same federal standard, HUD's Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards. Take a single wide home, 14 feet by 66 feet, as a worked example; the dimensions are mine, the coefficients are HUD's. - 24 CFR 3280.509(a) gives the default for air leakage: infiltration heat loss equals 0.7 multiplied by the temperature difference, multiplied by the feet of perimeter, in Btu per hour. The perimeter is 160 feet. On a night when it is 0 F outside and 70 F inside, that is 0.7 x 70 x 160, which is about 7,800 Btu per hour. - 24 CFR 3280.506(b) caps the whole insulated shell in the coldest of its three zones at a heat transmission coefficient of 0.079 Btu per hour per square foot per degree F. The envelope of that home is about 3,128 square feet, so the shell loses about 0.079 x 3,128 x 70, which is about 17,300 Btu per hour. Leakage is therefore roughly 31 percent of the total loss, and close to half as much as everything the insulation is doing. And note what the regulation says about its own number: the shell coefficient explicitly **excludes infiltration, ventilation, and condensation control**. The code figure for the shell does not count the air leaking through it at all. That is the whole argument for the next section. ## Seal first, insulate second This order is not a preference. It is the order that gets you the most comfort per dollar, and doing it backwards wastes both. Insulation slows conduction. It does not stop air. Blown insulation laid over an unsealed attic floor lets warm air keep pouring up through the gaps, and now the gaps are buried where you cannot find them. ENERGY STAR's guide tells you to look for dirty insulation in the attic, because dirt is where air has been filtering through it. That dirt is a photograph of the money leaving. ENERGY STAR estimates that homeowners can save an average of 15 percent on heating and cooling costs, or an average of 11 percent on total energy costs, by air sealing their homes and adding insulation. Their own methodology describes the target as sealing leaks to the attic space, through the foundation, and around windows and doors to achieve a 25 percent reduction in total air infiltration. The sequence that follows from the chimney effect is attic, then basement. ENERGY STAR describes the mechanism: warm air generated by the furnace rises through the house and out through attic leaks, and cold outside air gets drawn in through basement leaks to replace it. Seal the top first, then seal the bottom to stop the draw. Practical notes from the same guide: - Plug the big holes first. Their words: do not worry about finding and sealing all the little holes; your biggest savings come from plugging the large ones. Look where inner and outer walls meet the attic floor, at dropped soffits, and behind attic kneewalls. - Caulk handles gaps of 1/4 inch or less. Spray foam handles 1/4 inch up to about 3 inches. - The rim joist, the framing where the floor joists land on top of the foundation, is a row of open cavities all the way around the building. Seal the top and bottom of each one. - Weatherstrip the attic hatch. It is a hole in your ceiling. - If ducts run through the attic, seal them with mastic or foil tape, never household duct tape. ENERGY STAR says sealing and insulating ducts can increase heating and cooling system efficiency by 20 percent. Three cautions that belong with the work, not after it: - Keep all insulation 3 inches away from recessed can lights unless they are rated IC, meaning rated for insulation contact. - Knob and tube wiring, found in houses built before about 1930, can be a fire hazard when it is in contact with insulation. If you find it, stop and get an electrician. - Never cover soffit vents. Blocking airflow at the eaves is, in ENERGY STAR's words, the most common mistake homeowners make when installing insulation. - After you tighten a house, have a technician check that the gas or oil furnace, water heater and dryer are still venting properly. A tighter house raises the chance of carbon monoxide building up indoors. This one is not optional. ## What insulation is made of, and the honest trade-offs Start with why insulation works at all. The Forest Products Laboratory publishes thermal conductivities for common building materials in the same units, which makes the comparison honest. In US units, R-value per inch is simply one divided by the conductivity, so the right hand column below is arithmetic on the left hand column, not a separate claim. | Material | Conductivity, Btu in/(h ft2 F) | R per inch | |---|---|---| | Mineral wool | 0.25 | about 4 | | Softwood lumber at 12 percent moisture | 0.7 to 1.0 | about 1.0 to 1.4 | | Plaster | 5 | about 0.2 | | Concrete | 6 | about 0.17 | | Glass | 7 | about 0.14 | | Steel | 310 | about 0.003 | | Aluminium | 1,500 | about 0.0007 | The Department of Energy's Building America programme gives the same picture from the other direction, as a working range for designers: insulation products run about R-3 to R-7 per inch, wood about R-1 per inch, concrete about R-0.1 per inch, and steel about R-0.003 per inch. Two independent federal sources agreeing on steel at R-0.003 per inch is worth noticing, and we will come back to it. For what you would actually buy for an attic, ENERGY STAR's figure is the practical one: R-38 is about 10 to 14 inches deep, depending on insulation type. That works out to somewhere around R-2.7 to R-3.8 per inch for the ordinary batts and blown materials, which is the honest middle of the Building America range. Now the trade-offs, which are mostly about fire and water. **Fire behaviour.** There is a real dividing line here, and federal regulation draws it cleanly. Under HUD's standard at 24 CFR 3280.207, ordinary thermal insulation must have a flame spread index of 25 or less and a smoke developed index of 450 or less, and insulation left exposed on an attic floor must additionally have a critical radiant flux of not less than 0.12 watts per square centimetre. Fibrous insulation meets that and can simply sit there. Foam plastic cannot. Under 24 CFR 3280.208, foam plastic insulation may not be used inside wall or ceiling cavities or left exposed to the interior unless it is protected by an interior finish of 5/16 inch gypsum board or equivalent, or used as sheathing no more than 3/8 inch thick with a flame spread rating of 75 or less and separated from the inside of the home by at least 2 inches of mineral fibre or an equivalent thermal barrier. That is the trade you are making when you buy the higher R per inch: foam needs a fire barrier between it and the room, and fibrous insulation does not. **Cellulose** has its own federal safety standard, 16 CFR 1209, and it tells you exactly what the regulator was worried about. Cellulose must have a critical radiant flux of at least 0.12 watts per square centimetre, and in the smouldering combustion test it must show no evidence of flaming combustion and lose 15 percent or less of its initial weight. It must also pass a corrosiveness test, in which six metal coupons are examined over a light bulb and must show no perforations. A standard does not get a corrosion clause by accident: treat contact between damp cellulose and metal as a known concern, which in practice means keeping it dry. **Moisture behaviour, and ageing.** Two things the FTC rule reveals about products you will be sold: - For polyurethane, polyisocyanurate, and extruded polystyrene, R-value tests must be run on samples that fully reflect the effect of ageing on the product's R-value. Those three foams lose R-value over their life, and the rule exists so the label accounts for it. - For loose-fill cellulose, tests must be done at the settled density. It settles. Blow it deeper than the finished depth you want. And one that matters more than any product choice: **compressed insulation loses R-value, badly.** HUD publishes a table for exactly this at 24 CFR 3280.509(c). Squash a batt uniformly to half its intended thickness and it retains 61 percent of its rated R-value. Blown insulation restricted to half its depth retains 72 percent. An R-30 batt crammed into a space meant for R-19 is not R-30, and paying for the higher number and then crushing it is one of the commonest ways money is wasted in this trade. ## Thermal bridging, or why the wall is worse than the bag Every stud in a wall is a path for heat that goes around the insulation. Building America's definition is the useful one: thermal bridging happens whenever framing members or attachment devices span through an assembly from inside the conditioned space to outside the thermal envelope. How much of the wall is stud? HUD's default assumption, used when nobody has measured the actual building, is that framing is 15 percent of wall area excluding windows and doors, and 10 percent of ceiling and floor area. So roughly a seventh of your wall is not insulated at all; it is wood, at about R-1 per inch. Now put steel in place of the wood. Steel conducts heat several hundred times better than softwood does, on both federal sources above. A steel stud is not a slightly worse stud. It is a metal fin running from the warm side of the wall to the cold side, and it shorts out the insulation between studs so effectively that a steel framed wall with R-13 in the cavities performs nowhere near R-13 overall. This is why you should never compare a steel framed building to a wood framed one on cavity insulation alone. Fasteners do it too, at a smaller scale that adds up. Building America notes that cladding attachments can be a significant source of heat transfer, and that metal Z-bar connectors through exterior insulation can lose over 50 percent of the thermal resistance of that continuous insulation layer. The fix, in every case, is **continuous insulation**: a layer of board on the outside of the framing, unbroken by studs, so every path through the wall has to cross it. This is exactly what ENERGY STAR's retrofit guidance is describing when it says to add R5 to R10 of insulative wall sheathing beneath new siding in zones 4 through 8. The continuous layer is worth more per R than the same R added inside the cavity, because it is the only part of the wall the studs cannot bypass. Federal practice takes this seriously enough to require it in the arithmetic. Under 24 CFR 3280.508(c), the effect of framing must be included in the heat loss calculation, and other low resistance paths, which the regulation calls thermal shorts, must be explicitly accounted for once they add up to more than 1 percent of the exterior surface area. A thermal short is defined there as any path that separates heated from unheated space and is insulated to less than half the level of the material around it. ## The dew point, and how insulation rots a building This is the caution in this topic, and it deserves your full attention because the failure is invisible for years and then expensive. Air holds water vapour, and warm air holds more of it than cold air. Cool a parcel of air enough and it cannot hold what it has any more, so the water comes out as liquid. The temperature where that happens is the dew point. EPA's mould course states the everyday version: when warm, humid air contacts a cold surface, condensation may form, the way it forms on a cold bottle taken out of a refrigerator. Here is why insulation is implicated. Insulation works by creating a temperature difference across itself. That is its entire function. So by definition, the far side of your insulation is colder than the room, and the better the insulation, the colder that surface gets. If warm indoor air can reach that cold surface, it will condense there, inside the wall or the roof, where nothing dries and nobody looks. What grows next is not in doubt. EPA is clear that mould grows on virtually any organic material as long as moisture and oxygen are present, and that wet building materials must be dried within 24 to 48 hours to avoid mould growth. A wall cavity that condenses every cold night is never dry for 24 hours. EPA's recommendation for the air in the room is to keep indoor relative humidity below 60 percent, ideally between 30 and 50 percent. The building science answer is to stop the moist air getting in, and to let whatever does get in dry out in one direction. HUD's standard at 24 CFR 3280.504 is the clearest short statement of it in federal regulation. Ceilings in its two colder zones must have a vapor retarder of not more than 1 perm installed **on the living space side** of the roof cavity. Exterior walls must use one of several methods: a vapor barrier of not more than 1 perm on the living space side; or unvented cavities with exterior covering and sheathing whose combined permeance is **not less than** 5.0 perms, so the cavity can dry outward; or cavities ventilated so condensation can dissipate. Then read the part that catches people out. For homes built for humid climates, the same regulation puts the vapor retarder on the **exterior** side of the wall insulation instead, and requires the interior finish to be at least 5.0 perms so the wall can dry inward. The rule to take away is this: a vapor retarder goes on the warm side, and which side is warm depends on your climate. A layer that is correct in a cold climate is a moisture trap in a hot humid one. If you are unsure which situation you are in, the answer is to ask someone local who knows, not to guess, and not to install two of them on opposite faces of the same wall, which guarantees that anything that gets in can never leave. Three practical signs that you have this problem already, from ENERGY STAR's list of things to fix before you insulate anything: - Wet or damp insulation, which means a leaking roof. - Mouldy or rotted rafters or floor joists. - Kitchen, bathroom or dryer vents exhausting moist air into the attic instead of outdoors. This is common, it is easy to check, and it is pumping a household's worth of water vapour into the coldest part of the building. A history of ice dams belongs on that list too. ENERGY STAR treats it as an indication of serious air leaks: heat escaping into the attic melts snow on the roof, the water runs down and refreezes at the cold eaves, and the resulting dam backs water up under the shingles. Their counterintuitive but correct guidance is that a well insulated attic should also be well ventilated, so it stays cold in winter. ## Windows Windows are usually the worst surface in the room, and the reason is not the frame or the seals. It is that glass is not an insulator. The Forest Products Laboratory puts glass at a thermal conductivity of 7 Btu in/(h ft2 F). Invert that and a solid inch of glass is about R-0.14. An ordinary pane is an eighth of an inch thick, so the glass in a single glazed window contributes something in the region of R-0.02. Effectively nothing. Compare that against an attic that ENERGY STAR wants at R-49 to R-60 and you can see the scale of the mismatch. Whatever a window does achieve comes from the air or gas trapped between panes, the low emissivity coatings on the glass surfaces, and the frame, not from the glass. That is why glazing count and coatings matter so much and why the industry sells windows on U-factor. The federal standard for manufactured homes simply requires it: under 24 CFR 3280.506(d), homes built for the coldest of its three zones must be factory equipped with storm windows or insulating glass. ENERGY STAR's practical guidance, for when you are buying: - Certified windows, doors and skylights can shrink energy bills by an average of up to 13 percent on heating and cooling costs nationwide, compared with non certified products. - For north facing windows, which get little direct sun, buy the lowest U-factor you can afford, because heat loss is all that is happening there. - In a cold climate, a south facing window ideally has a higher solar heat gain coefficient, so it collects free sun, together with a low U-factor so it does not give the heat back at night. - East and west windows should have a low solar heat gain coefficient or be shaded, especially west facing ones, which take the summer sun at the hottest part of the day. - Even certified windows can suffer condensation in cold weather. If yours run with water, that is the dew point section above, showing up on the coldest surface in the room. It is information, not a defect. If you cannot replace windows, and most people cannot, that is what the next section is for. ## How much insulation you need depends on where you live There is no universal right answer, and anyone who gives you one without asking where you live is guessing. The United States is divided into eight climate zones by temperature, each subdivided into three moisture regimes labelled A for moist, B for dry and C for marine. That map was built for the Department of Energy by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory from analysis of 4,775 US weather sites, first adopted in the 2004 IECC supplement, and adopted by ENERGY STAR for Homes in 2006. The zones follow county boundaries specifically so that you can look yours up by name. **To find your zone**, use the Department of Energy's Building America county guide listed in the sources below. It names every county in the United States and gives its region. ENERGY STAR's R-value page carries the same map with the recommended levels next to it. ENERGY STAR's recommendations for retrofitting existing wood framed buildings, which follow the 2021 IECC Residential Provisions Table R402.1.3, run like this: | Zone | Attic if uninsulated | Attic if 3 to 4 inches already | Floor | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | R30 | R25 | R13 | | 2 | R49 | R38 | R13 | | 3 | R49 | R38 | R19 | | 4A and 4B | R60 | R49 | R19 | | 4C, 5 and 6 | R60 | R49 | R30 | | 7 and 8 | R60 | R49 | R38 | **For the Pacific Northwest**, meaning western Washington and the western side of Oregon, the zone is 4C, the marine zone. Building America's county table puts King, Kitsap, Pierce, Snohomish, Thurston, Whatcom, Skagit, Clallam, Jefferson, Mason, Grays Harbor, Pacific, Lewis, Cowlitz, Wahkiakum and Clark counties in the marine region, while the counties east of the Cascades are classed as cold. A marine climate is defined there by a coldest month averaging between 27 F and 65 F, a warmest month averaging under 72 F, at least four months averaging above 50 F, and a dry summer, specifically that the wettest month of the cold season gets at least three times the rain of the driest month of the rest of the year. If that sounds like where you live, you are in 4C. So for a house in western Washington, the targets are: - **Attic:** R60 if it is currently uninsulated, R49 if it already has 3 to 4 inches. - **Floor:** R30. - **Basement or crawlspace wall:** R15 of insulative wall sheathing, or an R19 batt. - **Above grade walls, when the siding comes off anyway:** blow the empty cavity full, and add R5 to R10 of insulative sheathing beneath the new siding. If the wall is already an insulated 2x4 wall, add R10 of sheathing. Notice that the marine zone gets the same attic target as genuinely cold zones 5 and 6 and the same floor target, even though its winters are mild. Mild and long still adds up, and the wet part of a marine climate is exactly the condition that makes the moisture section above matter most. ## If you have very little money In rough order of value returned per dollar. This ordering is a rule of thumb built from what the sources below prioritise, not a measured ranking. 1. **Find the big attic holes and plug them.** Cost is a few tubes of caulk and a couple of cans of foam. Chasing the large openings where walls meet the attic floor, at dropped soffits and behind kneewalls, is the highest return work in the entire subject. 2. **Weatherstrip the attic hatch and the exterior doors.** Hours, not days, and very little money. 3. **Seal the rim joist in the basement or crawlspace.** This stops the cold air being drawn in at the bottom to replace what left at the top. 4. **Check that the bathroom and dryer vents actually go outside.** Free to check. If they do not, fixing it protects the building itself, not just the bill. 5. **Plastic film over the worst windows for the winter.** ENERGY STAR publishes this as a do it yourself project for a reason: it is the cheapest thing that measurably helps the worst surface in the room, and the trapped air layer is doing the same job a second pane of glass would. 6. **Then add attic insulation,** once the air sealing is done. It is the easiest place in the house to add insulation and the one where depth is cheapest. 7. **Seal and insulate any ducts running through unheated space,** worth up to 20 percent of system efficiency on ENERGY STAR's figure. 8. **Walls and windows last,** because they cost the most per unit of improvement and, in the case of walls, are best done when the siding is coming off anyway for another reason. Everything from 1 to 5 is achievable in a weekend for the price of a tank of fuel. Nothing on that list requires a contractor, and nothing on it can be undone by moving house, because by then it has already paid you back. ## What can go wrong - **You insulated and the bill barely moved.** Almost always air sealing that was never done, or done after the insulation buried the holes. Insulation slows conduction; it does not stop air. - **One room is still cold.** Look for a bypass rather than thin insulation: a dropped ceiling, a kneewall with an open back, a cantilevered floor over outside air, or ducts running through an unheated attic. - **The windows stream with water now.** You tightened the house, so the moisture that used to leak away is staying in. Manage it with ventilation and humidity, not by reopening the leaks. Keep indoor relative humidity below 60 percent, ideally 30 to 50, per EPA. - **There is mould in a corner that was never mouldy before.** Same cause. Cold corners behind furniture are one of the places EPA specifically names, because the furniture blocks the room's warm air from reaching the wall and drops that surface below the dew point. Pull the furniture off the wall and fix the humidity. - **Ice dams appeared or got worse.** Heat is still escaping into the attic and the attic is too warm. This is an air sealing problem showing up on the roof, and it can also mean your soffit vents got covered. - **The new insulation looks dirty already.** Air is still moving through it. Find the hole. - **You bought the highest R per inch product and the wall still tests poorly.** Check the studs. A continuous exterior layer usually beats a premium cavity material, because it is the only layer the framing cannot bypass. - **The batts are bulging or crammed.** Compressed batts lose R-value on a published federal curve: half thickness means 61 percent of the rating. Cut them to fit rather than forcing them. - **The furnace or water heater smells or the CO alarm goes off after the work.** Stop and call someone qualified now. A tighter house changes how combustion appliances vent, and this is the one failure mode in this guide that can kill you the same night. ## How you know it worked - You can say which of the three heat paths you were addressing with each thing you did, and you did not try to fix air movement with insulation. - The air sealing happened before the insulating, and you plugged the large openings rather than chasing every small one. - You know your climate zone by name, you looked it up by county, and your targets came from the table for that zone rather than from a general recommendation. - Nothing is compressed, nothing covers a soffit vent, and nothing sits against a non-IC recessed light. - You know which side of your walls the vapor retarder belongs on and why, and there is not a second one on the opposite face. - The bathroom and dryer vents discharge outdoors. - Your combustion appliances have been checked since the house got tighter. - The house is warmer at the same thermostat setting, and the cold side of the room is gone. When those are all true you have not just lowered a bill. You have changed what the building costs to run for the rest of its life, and you understand the mechanism well enough to judge the next quote you are given. Recognising a thermal short, knowing that a surface below the dew point will wet itself, and understanding that a sealed envelope needs deliberate ventilation are the same three ideas behind every building science decision you will ever be asked to make. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. Government publications are listed first because they are public domain and can be redistributed with this guide. ### United States government (public domain) - Environmental Protection Agency, ENERGY STAR. A Do-It-Yourself Guide to Sealing and Insulating with ENERGY STAR, EPA 430-F-04-024, July 2016 (hidden attic and basement leaks, the chimney effect, plugging large holes first, caulk and foam gap sizes, rim joists, attic hatch, duct sealing at 20 percent, R-38 at 10 to 14 inches, attic ventilation and ice dams, can light clearance, knob and tube wiring, combustion safety after tightening). https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/asset/document/DIY_Guide_2016.pdf - Environmental Protection Agency, ENERGY STAR. Recommended Home Insulation R-Values (the definition of R-value, the recommended levels by climate zone for attic, floor, wall and basement, and the note that the guidance follows the 2021 IECC Residential Provisions Table R402.1.3). https://www.energystar.gov/saveathome/seal_insulate/identify-problems-you-want-fix/diy-checks-inspections/insulation-r-values - Environmental Protection Agency, ENERGY STAR. Methodology for Estimated Energy Savings from Cost-Effective Air Sealing and Insulating (the 15 percent and 11 percent savings figures, and the 25 percent infiltration reduction target). https://www.energystar.gov/saveathome/seal_insulate/methodology - Environmental Protection Agency, ENERGY STAR. Why Seal and Insulate? (the equivalent of a window open every day of the year). https://www.energystar.gov/saveathome/seal_insulate/why-seal-and-insulate - Environmental Protection Agency, ENERGY STAR. Residential Windows, Doors and Skylights (13 percent average savings, condensation on certified windows). https://www.energystar.gov/products/res_windows_doors_skylights - Environmental Protection Agency, ENERGY STAR. Independently Tested and Certified Energy Performance (U-factor and solar heat gain coefficient by orientation, buy the lowest U-factor you can afford). https://www.energystar.gov/products/building_products/residential_windows_doors_and_skylights/independently_tested_certified_energy_performance - Environmental Protection Agency. Mold Course, Chapter 2: Why and Where Mold Grows (condensation on cold surfaces, the 24 to 48 hour drying window, relative humidity below 60 percent and ideally 30 to 50, cold corners behind furniture). https://www.epa.gov/mold/mold-course-chapter-2 - Department of Energy, Building America Solution Center, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. Reducing Thermal Bridging in Mass and Steel-Framed Multifamily Buildings (the definition of thermal bridging, R per inch by material family, Z-bar connector losses, continuous exterior insulation as the fix). https://basc.pnnl.gov/resource-guides/reducing-thermal-bridging-mass-and-steel-framed-multifamily-buildings - Department of Energy, Building America. Building America Best Practices Series Volume 7.1: Guide to Determining Climate Regions by County (the definition of a marine climate, and the county by county region table used for the western Washington list). https://www.eere.energy.gov/buildings/publications/pdfs/building_america/ba_climateguide_7_1.pdf - Department of Energy, Building America. Building Science Climate Maps, Top Innovation profile (the eight temperature zones and three moisture regimes, the 4,775 weather sites, adoption in the 2004 IECC supplement and by ENERGY STAR for Homes in 2006). https://www1.eere.energy.gov/buildings/publications/pdfs/building_america/4_3a_ba_innov_buildingscienceclimatemaps_011713.pdf - USDA Forest Service, Forest Products Laboratory. Wood Handbook, FPL-GTR-113, Chapter 3, Physical Properties and Moisture Relations of Wood (the definition of thermal conductivity and the comparative conductivities for wood, aluminium, steel, concrete, glass, plaster and mineral wool). https://www.fpl.fs.usda.gov/documnts/fplgtr/fplgtr113/ch03.pdf - Federal Trade Commission. 16 CFR Part 460, Labeling and Advertising of Home Insulation (the definition of home insulation, the ban on R-value per inch claims at 460.20 and its required disclosure, the ageing requirement for polyurethane, polyisocyanurate and extruded polystyrene and the settled density requirement for loose-fill cellulose at 460.5, and the emittance basis for reflective insulation). https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title16-vol1/xml/CFR-2024-title16-vol1-part460.xml - Consumer Product Safety Commission. 16 CFR Part 1209, Interim Safety Standard for Cellulose Insulation (the noncorrosiveness requirement and its metal coupon test, the critical radiant flux of 0.12 watts per square centimetre, and the smouldering combustion criteria of no flaming combustion and 15 percent or less weight loss). https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title16-vol2/xml/CFR-2024-title16-vol2-part1209.xml - Department of Housing and Urban Development. 24 CFR Part 3280, Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards (3280.207 flame spread and critical radiant flux for insulation; 3280.208 the fire barrier required over foam plastic; 3280.504 vapor retarder placement and permeance, including the reversal for humid climates; 3280.505 air infiltration; 3280.506 the maximum heat transmission coefficients by zone and the storm window requirement; 3280.508 framing and thermal shorts in the calculation; 3280.509 the infiltration formula, the default framing percentages, and the insulation compression table). https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title24-vol5/xml/CFR-2024-title24-vol5-part3280.xml - Energy Information Administration. Use of Energy Explained: Energy Use in Homes (52 percent of household energy consumption for space heating and air conditioning, 2020). https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/use-of-energy/homes.php ### A note on what is not sourced here No federal publication gives a single reliable percentage breakdown of heat loss by building surface, so this guide does not quote one. The ordering in the section on what to do with very little money is a rule of thumb assembled from the priorities in the sources above, not a measured ranking. The worked example comparing air leakage to shell loss uses dimensions chosen for illustration; both coefficients in it are HUD's.
