Labelled as rules of thumb in the text, and not sourced
docs.text: # Handwashing and Personal Hygiene Almost everyone reading this already washes their hands and is confident they do it properly. That confidence is the problem this guide exists to address, because handwashing is one of those skills where the gap between "I do that" and "I do that correctly" is wide, invisible from the inside, and paid for in illness. It is worth the twenty minutes it takes to read, for three reasons. The first is size of effect. Very little else you can do for your health is this cheap and returns this much, and the numbers further down are specific enough to check. The second is that this is the one link in the sanitation chain that holds when everything else fails. Your water treatment can fail, your toilet can fail, your refrigeration can fail, the supply chain that brings you clean anything can fail. Soap and twenty seconds still works. It works in a flood, in an outage, on a homestead with no plumbing, and in a house where the tap runs fine. That is exactly the property you want from the thing you rely on most. The third is that the common beliefs about it are wrong in specific, correctable places. Most people believe hand sanitiser is a slightly less convenient equal of soap. It is not, and the section on that is the one most likely to change what you actually do. A boundary before anything else: this guide is about not getting sick and not making other people sick. It is not medical advice, and it does not replace a clinician. If someone in your household has persistent diarrhoea, a fever, or a wound that is getting worse rather than better, that is a doctor's problem and not a hygiene problem. ## How big the effect actually is Every figure in this section comes from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which publishes the pooled results of the handwashing literature. They are theirs, not ours. CDC reports that handwashing reduces the number of people who get sick with diarrhoea by 23 to 40 percent, and "reduces diarrheal illness in people with weakened immune systems by 58%." It reduces respiratory illnesses such as colds in the general population by 16 to 21 percent, and reduces absenteeism due to gastrointestinal illness in schoolchildren by 29 to 57 percent. (Those three ranges are CDC's figures, restated here without its dashes rather than quoted.) Stated the other way round, CDC says handwashing "can prevent about 30% of diarrhea-related sicknesses" and "about 20% of respiratory infections." The global picture is where the size becomes hard to argue with. CDC states that "about 1.8 million children under the age of 5 die each year from diarrheal diseases and pneumonia," and that handwashing with soap "could protect about 1 out of every 3 young children who get sick with diarrhea, and almost 1 out of 5 young children with respiratory infections." Against that, CDC puts "estimated global rates of handwashing after using the toilet" at "only 19%." The World Health Organization looks at the same behaviour inside hospitals and reports that hand hygiene improvement programmes can prevent up to half of avoidable infections acquired during health care, and return on average sixteen times what they cost to run. WHO also reports that compliance among health workers themselves averaged just under 60 percent in intensive care units, splitting sharply between higher-income and lower-income countries. (WHO material is copyrighted, so it is restated here rather than quoted.) Read those two paragraphs together. Even the professionals who are trained, audited and reminded do it a little over half the time. This is not a skill people fail at because it is hard. They fail at it because it is boring and invisible, and nothing makes the failure obvious until somebody is ill. ## Where the germs come from Two routes account for nearly all of it. The first is faecal. CDC's framing of the scale is worth keeping in your head: a single gram of human faeces, which CDC notes is "about the weight of a paper clip," "can contain one trillion germs." That gets onto hands after using the toilet, after changing a nappy, after handling animals or animal waste, and less obviously after handling raw meat, which carries the gut organisms of the animal it came from. The second is respiratory. Coughing, sneezing and nose-blowing put organisms on your hands, and touching a surface someone else coughed on puts them there too. Neither route makes you ill by being on your skin. Skin is a good barrier. CDC names the step that completes the journey: you get ill when you "touch your eyes, nose, and mouth with unwashed hands," or "prepare or eat food and drinks with unwashed hands." So hands are not the destination. Hands are the bridge. Washing them is how you take the bridge down. ## The five moments that matter most CDC publishes eleven key times to wash. They group naturally into five moments, and the grouping is not arbitrary: it follows the two routes above rather than following habit. Habit says wash when your hands look dirty. The evidence says wash when your hands have just crossed one of these boundaries, whether or not anything is visible. **1. After the toilet, and after anyone else's.** CDC: "After using the toilet," and "After changing diapers or cleaning up a child who has used the toilet." This is the moment with the largest single effect and the one the 19 percent figure is about. **2. Before food touches your hands or your mouth.** CDC: "Before, during, and after preparing food," and "Before and after eating food." Note *during*. The moment you put down raw meat and pick up the salad is a moment, and it is the one people skip because they are in the middle of something. **3. After coughing, sneezing or blowing your nose.** CDC: "After blowing your nose, coughing, or sneezing." This is the whole of the respiratory 16 to 21 percent, and it is the moment people most reliably forget because nothing on the hands looks different afterwards. **4. Around illness and around wounds.** CDC: "Before and after caring for someone at home who is sick with vomiting or diarrhea," and "Before and after treating a cut or wound." Both directions matter. Before protects the wound or the patient from you; after protects you and everyone else from them. **5. After the dirty jobs you do not think of as dirty.** CDC: "After touching an animal, animal feed, or animal waste," "After handling pet food or pet treats," and "After touching garbage." If you only fix one thing after reading this guide, fix number 3. It is the cheapest correction on the list and the one almost nobody makes. ## The technique, and why each part is there CDC's five steps: "Wet your hands with clean, running water (warm or cold), turn off the tap, and apply soap." Then "Lather your hands by rubbing them together with the soap." Then "Scrub your hands for at least 20 seconds." Then "Rinse your hands well under clean, running water." Then "Dry your hands using a clean towel or an air dryer." That is the whole procedure. What follows is why each step is in it, because the reasons are what let you adapt the procedure when conditions are not ideal. **Soap removes, it does not kill.** This is the single most useful thing to understand. Soap and water lift dirt, grease and organisms off the skin so the rinse can carry them away. CDC draws the contrast plainly against sanitiser, which works by killing. Removal is why soap handles things that resist killing, and it is why the rinse is not an optional tidy-up at the end. If you lather and then wipe rather than rinse, you have loosened everything and left it on your hands. **Friction is the working part.** The soap does the chemistry; your hands do the mechanics. Lather is evidence that soap and water are properly mixed on the skin, not an end in itself. **Twenty seconds is a duration, not a gesture.** CDC: "Scientific studies show that you need to scrub for 20 seconds to remove harmful germs and chemicals from your hands." Time yourself once, honestly, against a clock. Most people are at five to eight seconds and are genuinely surprised. CDC suggests humming "Happy Birthday" twice as a timer, which sounds childish and works. **Cover the whole hand, including the parts the standard motion misses.** CDC: "Make sure to scrub all areas of your hands, including your palms, backs of your hands, between your fingers, and under your fingernails." Palm-to-palm rubbing, which is what most people actually do, touches almost none of that. The thumb is the clearest example. Wrap one hand around the other thumb and rotate; that motion does not occur naturally in any part of ordinary handwashing, which is why the thumb gets skipped. CDC names the pattern directly in its hand hygiene guidance: "Remember to clean your thumbs, finger tips, and in between the fingers," because "these areas are commonly missed when cleaning hands with alcohol-based hand sanitizer." The same geometry applies to soap. **Water temperature does not matter.** CDC: "Warm and cold water remove the same number of germs from your hands." Hot water buys you nothing except a greater chance of damaging your skin, which is its own problem later in this guide. Wash in whatever is comfortable. **Antibacterial soap buys nothing either.** CDC: "Use plain soap and water to wash your hands. Studies have not found any added health benefit from using antibacterial soap." Plain soap is cheaper, gentler and equally good. This matters practically, because plain soap is the one you can store in bulk, improvise, or eventually make. **Drying is part of the wash, not the cleanup afterwards.** This is the step people treat as optional and it is not. CDC puts it simply: "Germs spread more easily when hands are wet, so make sure to dry your hands completely, whatever method you use." The measurement behind that statement is worth knowing, because it is much larger than people expect. Patrick, Findon and Miller, writing in *Epidemiology and Infection* in 1997, had subjects touch surfaces with washed but undried hands and counted what transferred: roughly 68,000 organisms onto skin, 31,000 onto food, and 1,900 onto utensils. After drying, the same contacts transferred 140, 655 and 28. That is a reduction of about 99.8, 94 and 99 percent respectively, achieved by nothing more than a towel. CDC cites this study in its own evidence listing for hand hygiene. So a careful twenty-second wash followed by wiping your hands on your jeans undoes a large part of what you just did. Dry on something clean, and dry completely. ## Soap versus alcohol sanitiser This is the section most likely to correct something you believe. Sanitiser is genuinely useful. It is fast, it needs no water, and in settings where the alternative is not washing at all it is clearly better than nothing. But it is not a substitute for soap and water, and the ways it fails are specific and predictable. **It does not kill everything.** CDC, naming names: "Soap and water are more effective than hand sanitizers at removing certain kinds of germs like norovirus, Cryptosporidium, and Clostridioides difficile." Those three are not obscure. They are, respectively, the most common cause of outbreak vomiting illness, a water-borne parasite with a tough outer shell that also shrugs off chlorine, and a gut organism that forms spores. CDC states each case separately elsewhere: "Hand sanitizer does not work well against norovirus." "Alcohol-based hand sanitizers are not effective against Crypto." "Alcohol-based hand sanitizer doesn't kill *C. difficile*." Note what those three have in common. Each survives in a form that resists chemical attack. Soap does not care, because soap is not attacking them. It is lifting them off and washing them down the drain. **It does not remove chemicals.** CDC: "Hand sanitizers might not remove harmful chemicals, such as pesticides, and heavy metals like lead." If you have been handling fuel, paint, garden chemicals or old paint dust, sanitiser is the wrong tool entirely. **It fails on dirty or greasy hands.** CDC: "Hand sanitizers may not be as effective when hands are visibly dirty or greasy." Its instruction is blunter than that: "Don't use hand sanitizer if your hands are visibly dirty or greasy," and the examples it gives are "after gardening, playing outdoors, fishing, or camping." This one matters enormously for the homesteading reader, because it describes essentially every task you will do outdoors. A film of soil or oil physically shields organisms from the alcohol. Sanitiser on muddy hands is theatre. **The concentration is a hard threshold.** CDC: "use a hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol to clean your hands." Below that it does not reliably work, and plenty of products on shelves are below it. CDC's healthcare guidance also gives a ceiling: alcohol content "must not exceed 95% alcohol content by volume," because alcohol needs some water present to denature proteins. Read the label; the percentage is the only thing on it that matters. **The technique is different too.** CDC: "Apply the gel product to the palm of one hand," "Cover all surfaces of hands," "Rub your hands and fingers together until they are dry. This should take around 20 seconds." If it dries in four seconds you did not use enough. And the same missed spots apply, which is the context CDC's thumbs-and-fingertips warning was written for. **One safety note.** CDC: "Supervise young children when they use hand sanitizer to prevent swallowing alcohol, especially in schools and childcare facilities." The honest summary: sanitiser is the tool for clean-looking hands away from a sink. Soap and water is the tool for everything else, and the only tool for the moments that matter most. CDC's own line is the one to remember: "Washing hands with soap and water is the best way to get rid of germs in most situations." ## Washing when water is scarce This is the homesteading case and the emergency case, and it is where the skill stops being automatic. **The water for washing does not have to be drinking water.** This surprises people and it is the fact that makes handwashing possible when your drinking supply is short. CDC states that during "a boil water advisory or 'do not drink water' advisory, it may be safe to wash hands with tap water," and adds the conditional upgrade: "Wash your hands with soap and water that has been boiled or disinfected if local authorities or your doctor recommend extra caution." There is a hard floor under that, though. Washing water must not be sewage-contaminated. CDC's companion guidance on bathing draws the line explicitly: "Do not bathe in water that may be contaminated with sewage or toxic chemicals," and "Do not bathe in rivers, streams, or lakes that are contaminated by flood water, human sewage, or animal waste." It also warns that "open wounds and rashes that have been exposed to contaminated water can become infected." Water that would merely give you an upset stomach if you drank it is acceptable for washing. Water carrying sewage is not, at any point in the chain. **Running water beats a basin, and you can improvise running water.** Washing in a shared bowl recontaminates everyone's hands from the same water. The fix is a container that pours. CDC's own emergency instruction is the simplest version: "If clean tap water is not available, create a temporary handwashing station by using a large water jug." A jug with a small hole near the base, or a bottle with a pinhole punched in the cap and the cap loosened to let air in, gives you a thin controllable stream. The rule is that your hands never touch the container or the water supply, only the stream. **The tippy tap is the developed version of that idea**, and CDC publishes build instructions for it in several languages. A systematic review of tippy taps by Mbakaya, Kalembo and Zgambo in *BMC Public Health* in 2020 describes the design as a three or five litre jerry can of water hung from a wooden frame, with a string from the neck of the can down to a stick at ground level. Press the stick with your foot, the can tips, and a small hole releases a stream. Soap hangs from the frame alongside. Nothing you touch with dirty hands is something you touch again with clean ones. The same review reports the number that makes it worth building: a good hand wash at a tippy tap can use about 50 mL of water, against up to 500 mL at a tap. A ten to one saving is the difference between handwashing being affordable on a hauled water supply and not. The review also reports school programmes where handwashing rose from a few percent to near-universal after tippy taps were installed, alongside large falls in reported stomach complaints. **Soap stretches too.** CDC's global WASH materials note that "a soapy water handwashing solution can be made by mixing water with liquid or powdered soap," which turns a small amount of soap into many washes. **Greywater discipline.** The water that has run over your hands is now greywater, and where it goes is part of the same problem. Put the catch basin where the runoff cannot reach a well head, a spring, a stream, or the surface of anything you are going to eat raw. Site the whole station downhill and well away from your drinking water source. This is a topic in its own right and it is flagged again at the end of this guide. ## Soap without buying soap Soap is simpler than it sounds and more dangerous to make than it sounds. The FDA, which has to define soap precisely for regulatory purposes, puts it plainly: "Ordinary soap is made by combining fats or oils and an alkali, such as lye." What you get is "alkali salts of fatty acids," a molecule with one end that mixes with water and one that mixes with fat. That double nature is the whole trick, and it is why soap lifts grease and the organisms riding in it off your skin. FDA adds the reassuring part: "When made properly, no lye remains in the finished product." It also notes that most modern cleansers are not soap at all: "Most body cleansers, both liquid and solid, are synthetic detergent products." For handwashing purposes this does not matter. Both work. **Now the part that does matter.** The alkali is lye, and lye is one of the more dangerous substances a household will ever handle. NIOSH lists sodium hydroxide under the synonyms "caustic soda, lye, soda lye, sodium hydrate," names the target organs as "eyes, skin, respiratory system," and lists the effects as "irritation eyes, skin, mucous membrane; pneumonitis; eye, skin burns." The first aid entries are the tell: "Eye: irrigate immediately. Skin: water flush immediately." NIOSH sets the recommended exposure limit at a ceiling of 2 mg per cubic metre and considers 10 mg per cubic metre immediately dangerous to life and health. In plain terms: lye burns skin on contact, blinds on contact with eyes, and the reaction of lye with water releases enough heat to matter. So this guide is not going to teach soapmaking in a paragraph, because a paragraph is exactly the amount of instruction that gets someone hurt. Soapmaking is a real, learnable, worthwhile skill with its own protective equipment, its own procedure and its own mistakes. Learn it from a source that treats it as such. What belongs here is only this: you can make soap, it is not mysterious, and the danger is entirely in the lye rather than in the soap. ## Nails, hair, clothing and bedding Briefly, because these matter less than the twenty seconds but are not nothing. **Nails.** CDC: "Dirt and germs can live under fingernails and contribute to the spread of some infections, such as pinworms," and "more dirt and bacteria can gather under long nails than short nails." The instructions are short: "Keep nails short and trim them often," and "scrub the underside of nails with soap and water (or a nail brush) every time you wash your hands." CDC also says not to bite or chew nails, and not to cut cuticles, since they "prevent infection." On artificial nails, CDC's healthcare guidance is unambiguous, and it is the strongest statement it makes on any of this: "germs can live under artificial fingernails both before and after using an alcohol-based hand sanitizer and handwashing." **Hair, clothing and bedding.** Keep hair out of food and off wounds, and wash it regularly. Change and wash clothing that has been in contact with soil, animals, or anyone's illness before wearing it again. Wash bedding regularly, and wash it promptly after any illness involving vomiting or diarrhoea. None of this needs a schedule you will not keep. The principle is that fabric which has touched a contaminated thing is now a contaminated thing, and it stays that way until it is washed. ## Hand care, because cracked skin is an infection route This is the failure mode created by doing everything else right. Washing strips the skin's natural oils. Do it often enough and the skin cracks, and cracked skin is worse than a nuisance. CDC's assessment in *Emerging Infectious Diseases* is blunt: "damaged skin more often harbors increased numbers of pathogens. Moreover, washing damaged skin is less effective at reducing numbers of bacteria than washing normal skin." The same review notes that "soaps and detergents have been described as the most damaging of all substances routinely applied to skin," and that "more washing and scrubbing are unlikely to be better and may, in fact, be worse." So the damage is self-reinforcing. Broken skin carries more organisms and is harder to clean, which invites more washing, which breaks it further. CDC's occupational guidance gives thresholds. Hand dermatitis "is made worse by wet work: when hands are wet for more than 2 hours per day, hand washing more than 20 times per day, or wearing gloves for more than 2 hours per day." It presents as "redness, dry skin, itching, burning, blisters, and crusts," and in 2020 it was "the second most common nonfatal occupational illness." That is not a rare complaint. What to do about it: - **Moisturise deliberately, not occasionally.** CDC: "Keep hands well moisturized with thick creams and ointments like plain petrolatum or petroleum." Thick and boring beats pleasant and thin. - **Choose fragrance-free.** CDC recommends a product with few ingredients and no fragrance "to reduce the risk of irritation," and suggests looking for "ingredients like dimethicone or glycerin to help protect the skin." - **Use sanitiser as the gentler option when hands are already clean.** This is counterintuitive and it is CDC's position: "Compared to soap and water, alcohol-based sanitizers remove fewer natural protective oils and cause less drying and damage." When there is nothing to remove, the gentler tool is the right one. - **Treat stinging as information.** CDC: "If alcohol-based sanitizer burns, this is because the skin is already cracked and damaged." That is a signal to increase moisturising, not to stop cleaning your hands. Two things make this worse that are not sourced here, so take them as **rules of thumb**: cold dry weather, and harsh or strongly scented soap. Both are consistent with the mechanism CDC does describe, which is loss of the skin's protective oils, but neither number is one we can point at. If your hands crack every winter, moisturise ahead of the season rather than in response to it. ## The rest of the chain Handwashing is one link. Three others carry most of the remaining risk, and each is a topic in its own right that is not written yet. Here is what each one is, and why it is not covered here. **Human waste.** Everything in the faecal route above starts somewhere, and that somewhere is a toilet, a latrine or a hole in the ground. Getting this wrong contaminates groundwater and surface water for everyone downhill of you, which is a larger and slower failure than a dirty hand. CDC's emergency sanitation guidance makes one point that belongs in both topics: "install handwashing stations at every sanitation facility, regardless of the type of sanitation facility installed." The two topics are physically joined, and the handwashing station is part of the toilet, not a separate amenity. Siting, depth, distance from water, composting and pathogen die-off times all belong to that guide. **Greywater.** Washing water, laundry water and shower water are not sewage, but they are not clean either. The EPA's research on onsite non-potable reuse treats greywater as a stream that can be reused for non-drinking purposes given appropriate treatment, and the pathogens it tracks in that work include norovirus, rotavirus, *Campylobacter jejuni* and *Cryptosporidium*. EPA points out that there is no single national rule for this: it has produced a guidebook for state and local jurisdictions to write their own. So greywater is simultaneously a public health question and a legal one whose answer changes by state, which is exactly why it needs its own guide rather than a paragraph. **The pathogens that matter.** Everything above is written in terms of "germs," which is a useful simplification and a limiting one. The organisms behave differently: some are killed by chlorine and some are not, some survive on surfaces for hours and some for months, some need a thousand cells to make you ill and some need ten. Knowing the specific short list is what lets you reason about a situation this guide did not anticipate. That is a guide of its own. Two related guides are already written and worth reading alongside this one: **Making Water Safe to Drink**, for what to do about a source you do not trust, and **Storing Water Safely**, for keeping a supply that stays drinkable. Neither is repeated here. ## What can go wrong - **You wash thoroughly and then dry on your trousers.** The most common way to waste a good wash. Wet hands transfer organisms by orders of magnitude more than dry ones, and a dirty towel is a fresh source. Dry completely, on something clean. - **You use sanitiser after gardening, butchering or working on an engine.** Soil and grease shield organisms from alcohol. Wash. - **You use sanitiser during a vomiting illness in the house.** This is the norovirus case, and it is precisely where sanitiser is weakest. Soap and water, every time, for everyone. - **Your sanitiser is under 60 percent alcohol.** Check the label. Many scented and novelty products are. - **Everyone washes in the same basin of water.** The second person is washing in the first person's runoff. Pour instead: a jug, a bottle with a hole, a tippy tap. - **You wash constantly and your hands crack.** You have created a new infection route. Moisturise heavily, switch to sanitiser when hands are merely routine rather than visibly soiled, and do not reduce washing at the five key moments. - **You washed your hands but not the tap.** If you turned the tap on with contaminated hands you will turn it off with clean ones. Use a towel or your wrist, or fit a lever tap. This is a real route and it is why CDC's first step includes turning off the tap before lathering. - **You are relying on antibacterial soap to make up for a short wash.** It does not. Twenty seconds of plain soap beats five seconds of anything. - **Handwashing facilities exist but nobody uses them.** The most common failure at the household scale, and it is a placement problem rather than a willpower problem. A station beside the toilet and beside the kitchen gets used; one across the yard does not. ## How you know it worked - You can name the five moments without looking, and moment 3, after coughing or sneezing, is one of them. - You have actually timed your own wash against a clock at least once, and corrected it. - Your routine includes backs of hands, between fingers, under nails and both thumbs, deliberately, because none of those happen by accident. - You dry completely, on something clean, every time. - You know the three things sanitiser does not handle: norovirus, *Cryptosporidium* and *C. difficile*, and you know it also fails on dirty or greasy hands and on chemicals. - You have checked that the sanitiser in your house is at least 60 percent alcohol. - If your water is limited, you have a station that pours rather than a basin that sits, and its runoff goes somewhere that is not uphill of your drinking water. - Your hands are not cracked. When all of those are true you have taken the most-used bridge between the world's germs and your body out of service, using soap, water and twenty seconds. There is no other intervention in this entire curriculum with that ratio of effect to effort, which is the only real argument this guide has been making. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. United States federal government publications are listed first because they are public domain and can be redistributed with this guide; the rest cannot, and their content is restated in our own words above rather than quoted. ### United States government (public domain) - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About Handwashing (key times to wash, the five steps, the 20 seconds, soap versus sanitiser, how germs reach the body). https://www.cdc.gov/clean-hands/about/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Handwashing Facts (diarrhoeal and respiratory reduction figures, school absenteeism, child mortality, the 19 percent global figure, the gram of faeces). https://www.cdc.gov/clean-hands/data-research/facts-stats/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Hand Hygiene Frequently Asked Questions (the 20 seconds, water temperature, antibacterial soap, drying, which areas to scrub). https://www.cdc.gov/clean-hands/faq/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Hand Sanitizer Guidelines and Recommendations (the 60 percent threshold, norovirus, *Cryptosporidium* and *C. difficile*, chemicals and lead, dirty and greasy hands, technique, supervising children). https://www.cdc.gov/clean-hands/about/hand-sanitizer.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. What You Should Know about Hand Hygiene (thumbs, fingertips and between the fingers as commonly missed; *C. difficile*). https://www.cdc.gov/patient-safety/stories/what-you-should-know-about-hand-hygiene.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Clinical Safety: Hand Hygiene for Healthcare Workers (the 60 to 95 percent alcohol range, when soap and water is required instead, lotions, artificial nails). https://www.cdc.gov/clean-hands/hcp/clinical-safety/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Keeping Your Hands Clean and Healthy (hand dermatitis thresholds and symptoms, moisturising, why sanitiser stings cracked skin). https://www.cdc.gov/patient-safety/stories/keeping-hands-clean-and-healthy.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Nail Hygiene (germs under nails, nail length, scrubbing under nails, cuticles). https://www.cdc.gov/hygiene/about/nail-hygiene.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Guidelines for Personal Hygiene During an Emergency (washing water during advisories, the jug station, what not to bathe in, wounds and contaminated water). https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/safety/guidelines-for-personal-hygiene-during-an-emergency.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Global WASH Posters (the tippy tap build posters, soapy water handwashing solution, container-based handwashing stations). https://www.cdc.gov/global-water-sanitation-hygiene/communication-resources/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. How to Prevent Norovirus (hand sanitiser does not work well against norovirus). https://www.cdc.gov/norovirus/prevention/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Preventing Crypto (alcohol-based hand sanitisers are not effective against *Cryptosporidium*). https://www.cdc.gov/cryptosporidium/prevention/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Potential Sanitation Solutions During an Emergency Response, archived (handwashing stations at every sanitation facility). https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/healthywater/global/sanitation/sanitation-emergency-response.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Clean Hands Publications, Data and Statistics (CDC's own evidence listing, including the Patrick 1997 hand drying study cited above). https://www.cdc.gov/clean-hands/data-research/index.html - Larson, E. Hygiene of the Skin: When Is Clean Too Clean? *Emerging Infectious Diseases*, Vol. 7, No. 2, 2001. A CDC journal, so public domain (skin barrier, damaged skin harbouring more pathogens, soaps as damaging, over-washing). https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/7/2/70-0225_article - National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards: Sodium hydroxide (lye synonyms, eye and skin burns, exposure limits, first aid). https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0565.html - Food and Drug Administration. Frequently Asked Questions on Soap (what soap is chemically, fats or oils plus alkali, no lye in the finished product, detergents versus soap). https://www.fda.gov/cosmetics/cosmetic-products/frequently-asked-questions-soap - Environmental Protection Agency. Onsite Non-Potable Water Reuse Research (greywater as a reusable non-potable stream, the reference pathogens, regulation by state and local jurisdictions). https://www.epa.gov/water-research/onsite-non-potable-water-reuse-research ### International organisation (copyrighted, restated not quoted) - World Health Organization. Hand Hygiene (the Five Moments framework, up to half of avoidable health-care-associated infections preventable, the roughly sixteenfold economic return, the compliance figures). https://www.who.int/teams/integrated-health-services/infection-prevention-control/hand-hygiene ### Peer-reviewed literature (copyrighted, restated not quoted) - Patrick, D.R., Findon, G. and Miller, T.E. Residual moisture determines the level of touch-contact-associated bacterial transfer following hand washing. *Epidemiology and Infection*, Vol. 119, No. 3, 1997, pages 319 to 325 (the organism counts transferred from wet versus dried hands). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2809004/ - Mbakaya, B.C., Kalembo, F.W. and Zgambo, M. Use, adoption, and effectiveness of tippy-tap handwashing station in promoting hand hygiene practices in resource-limited settings: a systematic review. *BMC Public Health*, Vol. 20, article 1005, 2020 (the tippy tap design, 50 mL versus up to 500 mL per wash, the school programme outcomes). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7316639/ ### Labelled as rules of thumb in the text, and not sourced - That cold, dry weather worsens hand cracking. - That harsh or strongly scented soap worsens it. Both are consistent with the mechanism CDC describes, which is loss of the skin's protective oils, but no figure in this guide rests on them.

Call for help now if any of these are true
The burns that need professional care whatever their size

docs.text: # Burns Someone has been burned. Before you read another word, the first minute matters more than anything else in this guide: 1. **Stop the burning.** Get the person away from the heat. If clothing is alight, stop them, get them on the ground, and roll them or smother the flames with something heavy. If it is electricity, the power goes off before anyone touches them. 2. **Get things off before the swelling starts.** Rings, watch, bracelets, belt, boots, and any clothing that is not stuck to the skin. Anything still stuck to the skin stays where it is. 3. **Cool the burn under running water.** Twenty minutes, cool not cold. No ice, ever. 4. **While the water is running, decide whether this needs a hospital.** The list is a few paragraphs down. If you are not sure, it does. Everything after this is the explanation. Do the four things first. One honest boundary before we go further. **This guide is not a substitute for medical care, and it does not qualify you to manage a serious burn at home.** What it can do is help you act correctly in the first minutes, tell you which burns you must hand to someone trained, and stop you doing the things that make a burn worse. Many of the remedies people reach for instinctively cause real harm, and that is the single most useful thing in here. The moment a burn is on the list of burns that need professional care, your job stops being treatment and becomes getting the person to someone who can treat it. Its companion, [Building a Fire Staff](/library#fire-staff-materials), covers the other side of this: how to build a thing that burns, and how to not get burned by it in the first place. ## Cooling: the numbers, and why ice is not a shortcut Cool running water is the whole of burn first aid. It is not a comfort measure. A systematic review in the *Journal of Burn Care & Research* covering seven studies and 11,383 patients found that people who got twenty minutes of cool running water within three hours of injury had "significantly decreased odds of requiring skin grafting or other surgical intervention." That is the difference between a burn that heals and a burn that gets operated on. The numbers: - **How long.** MedlinePlus says to keep the area under water for at least 5 to 30 minutes. The burn-care guidance summarised by CADTH is firmer, calling for at least twenty minutes for any major burn or burn over 10 percent of the body. Twenty minutes is the number to aim at. - **How cool.** The 2024 international consensus on second-degree burn wounds recommends running water between 12 and 25 degrees Celsius, roughly 54 to 77 Fahrenheit. CADTH's summary cites 15 degrees Celsius, about 59 Fahrenheit. As a rule of thumb, an ordinary cold tap is usually in that band already, which is exactly why this works without a thermometer. - **How soon.** Sooner is better, but the window is wider than people assume. The studies that found the grafting benefit measured cooling begun within three hours of injury. If you did not cool it at the time, it is still worth doing. **Ice and iced water are harmful, and this is not a small point.** The 2024 consensus is explicit about the mechanism: ice cubes are cold enough to cause "vasoconstriction of the wound blood vessels, leading to ischaemic necrosis," and also carry a risk of frostbite and hypothermia. Read that plainly. The burn has already damaged the tissue, and the blood supply is what will repair it. Ice clamps that blood supply shut. You can take living tissue at the edge of a burn and kill it with an ice pack. The CADTH summary gives the same two reasons, hypothermia and impaired blood flow, and says ice or ice water should not be used. MedlinePlus lists ice among the things never to put on a burn. There is one more wrinkle worth understanding, because it looks like a contradiction. MedlinePlus says not to put a severe burn into cold water, because doing so can cause shock. Both things are true. Running cool water over a burn is right. Immersing a large burn, or a whole person, in cold water is not, because burned skin loses heat fast and a cold person is a new emergency on top of the burn. Military burn guidance notes that casualties with burns over 20 percent of the body are at high risk of hypothermia and says plainly to keep the patient warm. So for a large burn: cool the burned area with running water, then cover the person and keep them warm. Cool the burn, warm the patient. ## Call for help now if any of these are true MedlinePlus says to call emergency services if: - The burn is large, about the size of your palm or bigger - The burn is full thickness - You are not sure how serious it is - The burn was caused by chemicals or electricity - The person shows signs of shock - The person breathed in smoke - Physical abuse is the known or suspected cause - There are other symptoms alongside the burn Notice the third one. "You are not sure how serious it is" is on the official list, in those words. You are allowed to not know. ## How deep is it Three depths, described by what you can actually see and feel. These descriptions come from US military burn care guidance and from the National Library of Medicine, and they agree with each other. **Superficial, also called first degree.** The outer layer of skin only. Red, painful, swollen. It does not blister, and it blanches readily, meaning the redness goes pale when you press it and floods back when you let go. Sunburn is the everyday example. **Partial thickness, also called second degree.** Outer and underlying layers. Red, moist, swollen, blistered, and it still blanches. Military guidance describes these as "moist and sensate," meaning they hurt, and they hurt a lot. A shallower partial thickness burn is red and wet and extremely painful. A deeper one turns paler, drier, mottled white, and blanches less and hurts less. **Full thickness, also called third degree.** All the layers of skin, sometimes deeper. It looks leathery and dry, white or brown or blackened. It does not blanch. And here is the thing nobody expects: > **The deepest burns can hurt the least.** Military guidance describes > full thickness burns as "insensate," and the National Library of > Medicine describes them as causing little or no pain, with skin that > may be numb. The nerve endings that report pain are in the skin. A burn deep enough to destroy them destroys their ability to complain. So "it does not hurt much" is not reassurance. On a burn that is white, leathery, dry and numb, it is the finding that tells you this is the worst kind. Two practical consequences. A big burn is usually a patchwork of all three depths, so judge the worst part, not the average. And a burn often declares itself over the first day or two, so the depth you see in the first hour is a first guess, not a verdict. ## How big is it Two methods, one for small burns and one for large. **The rule of palm.** The flat of a hand is about 1 percent of that person's body. Federal emergency medicine guidance gives the palmar hand surface as approximately 1 percent of total body surface area, stated there for a child. Published clinical teaching gives the finer version for patients generally, separating the palm alone, about 0.5 percent, from the whole hand including the fingers, about 1 percent. Use the injured person's own hand, not yours, because the whole point is that it scales with the body you are measuring, and MedlinePlus uses exactly this as the household threshold: a burn about the size of your palm or larger means call for help. **The rule of nines.** For larger burns, the body is divided into regions worth 9 percent or a multiple of it. For an adult: | Region | Percent | |---|---| | Head and neck | 9 | | Each arm | 9 | | Front of the trunk | 18 | | Back of the trunk | 18 | | Each leg | 18 | | Genitals | 1 | Those add to 100. It is a rough field estimate, deliberately coarse, and in hospital it gets refined against a proper chart. **Children are not small adults, and the rule of nines does not fit them.** Federal guidance notes that children have proportionally larger heads, up to 20 percent, and smaller legs, 13 percent in infants. This is one of several reasons a child's burn is not something to size up by eye at home. **The counterintuitive rule: superficial burns do not count.** Military guidance states that first degree burns are not included in the estimate of burn size at all. Only partial thickness and full thickness are counted. So a whole sunburned back is a 0 percent burn by this measurement, which sounds absurd until you realise that what is being measured is how much skin has stopped working, and a first degree burn has not stopped working. **The size thresholds that matter.** The American Burn Association is the authority here, and its criteria are copyrighted, so this is a summary in our own words rather than their text. A published consensus study that updated those criteria, in the *Journal of Burn Care & Research*, puts the transfer thresholds at full thickness burns over 5 percent of the body, and partial thickness burns over 10 percent. Below those, it still recommends outpatient burn referral rather than nothing, and recommends specialist consultation for any burn that might be deep, at any size. Translated for a household: a partial thickness burn bigger than about ten palms, or any full thickness burn bigger than about five, is a hospital problem. In practice you will not be measuring. MedlinePlus gives the household version, which is that one palm or larger means call. ## The burns that need professional care whatever their size Size is only one of the reasons a burn goes to a specialist. These go regardless of how small they look. The list is drawn from the American Burn Association's referral criteria, restated here, and from the published consensus study that updated them. - **Face.** Also because of what it implies about the airway. - **Hands.** Scarring across a hand costs function permanently. - **Feet.** - **Genitals and perineum.** - **Anything over a joint**, for the same reason as hands. Healing burn tissue contracts as it matures, and a contracture across a joint locks it. - **Circumferential burns**, meaning a burn that goes all the way around a limb, a finger, the neck, or the chest. Military guidance explains why: a deep circumferential burn to an arm or leg can act "like a tourniquet, reducing arterial circulation," and around the chest it can physically stop the ribcage expanding. The burned skin is stiff, the limb underneath swells, and the pressure has nowhere to go. This needs a surgeon, sometimes urgently. - **Every chemical burn.** The consensus criteria say all chemical injuries should be cared for in a burn center. - **Every electrical burn.** High voltage and lightning injuries go straight in; even low voltage injuries warrant follow-up, because some of the damage shows up late. - **Any inhalation injury**, or a good reason to suspect one. - **Burns in young children and in older adults.** The published criteria treat both groups as benefiting from specialist involvement beyond what the size thresholds alone would trigger, and the American Burn Association's guidance is that paediatric burns generally warrant referral. As a rule of thumb for a household: have a child's burn or an older person's burn looked at even when you would shrug off the same burn on yourself. The reasons are real. The same patch of skin is a bigger fraction of a smaller body, older skin is more fragile, and older adults are already the group most at risk around fire. The US Fire Administration recorded adults aged 65 and over as having 2.5 times the risk of dying in a fire compared with the population as a whole in 2020. - **Any burn on someone with other significant health problems**, or who was injured in some other way at the same time. ## Smoke, enclosed spaces, and why the airway comes first A burn that happened in an enclosed space is an airway emergency until proven otherwise, even if the skin looks fine. The blunt number, from MedlinePlus: "Over half of deaths from fires are due to inhalation injuries." Not the flames. The air. Three separate things are going on in a house fire or a vehicle fire or any fire in a closed room: - **Heat and smoke particles damage the lining of the airway.** Federal emergency medicine guidance notes that the lung symptoms of inhalation injury "rarely grossly manifest within first 24hrs" and generally evolve over 48 to 72 hours. Someone can walk and talk and look fine and be in serious trouble the next day. - **The airway swells shut.** The same guidance describes swelling at the vocal cords, from local injury or from the whole-body swelling that follows a large burn, which "can eventually occlude airway." Swelling in a tube that is already narrow is a race against a clock. - **The smoke poisons.** Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin and displaces oxygen. Hydrogen cyanide, released when synthetic materials burn, is described as "a potent and rapid cellular poison." Neither has anything to do with the burn on the skin. Signs worth taking seriously: the fire was in an enclosed space, soot around the nose or mouth, singed nose or facial hair, a hoarse or changed voice, a cough with black phlegm, a scratchy throat, chest tightness, shortness of breath, confusion, or drowsiness. Any of those, or just the fact that they were breathing smoke in a closed room, means emergency care now rather than a wait-and-see. MedlinePlus adds one small mechanical detail for someone with an airway burn: do not put a pillow under their head. It closes the airway further. ## What not to put on a burn MedlinePlus is unambiguous, and names the list: no oil, butter, ice, medicines, cream or oil spray, and no household remedy of any kind, on a severe burn. Taking them one at a time, because knowing why makes it stick: - **Butter, oil, grease, lard.** A layer of fat over a burn holds heat against tissue you are trying to cool. It is not sterile. It has to be cleaned off before anyone can see the burn, and cleaning it off means scrubbing a wound that already hurts. The MedlinePlus sunburn guidance separately says to avoid oil-based products including petroleum jelly and butter. - **Ice and iced water.** Covered above. Vasoconstriction, ischaemic necrosis, frostbite, hypothermia. The one that people are most confident about is the one most likely to deepen the injury. - **Toothpaste.** A genuinely common practice: published surveys of burn first aid in several countries found people reaching for toothpaste, honey, oil, yogurt and aloe ahead of running water. Toothpaste is not sterile, it is mildly abrasive and alkaline, it traps heat, and it has to be removed. The research literature classes these as unsafe practices, and finds they cluster where formal first aid teaching has not reached. - **Honey, egg white, yogurt, flour, mud.** Same reasoning. Unsterile material pressed into broken skin, which then has to be picked out. - **Creams, ointments and sprays, including anaesthetic sprays.** Not on a severe burn. They obscure the wound, and MedlinePlus specifically advises against benzocaine and lidocaine products for sunburn. For a small superficial burn with unbroken skin, a plain moisturising lotion or aloe is fine; that is a different situation from a raw wound. - **Adhesive dressings directly on the burn.** MedlinePlus advises against putting adhesive bandages on an electrical burn, and generally a dressing that sticks to a burn becomes part of the problem when it comes off. - **Your own breath.** MedlinePlus says not to breathe, blow or cough on a burn. Blowing on it to cool it feels natural and puts mouth bacteria straight onto an open wound. - **Anything by mouth, if the burn is severe.** No water, no food, no painkillers, because they may need surgery. And one that is not a substance: **do not remove clothing that is stuck to the skin.** Cut around it and leave the stuck part alone. Pulling it takes skin with it. ## Blisters: leave them alone The evidence here is weaker than most people assume, and the honest summary is worth giving straight. **What to do in the moment is not in doubt.** Leave blisters intact. Military burn guidance says not to debride blisters until the patient has reached a facility with emergency medical or surgical capability. The 2024 international consensus rates preservation of the intact blister during early first aid as highly recommended. MedlinePlus says do not disturb blistered or dead skin. Every source agrees: not at home, not by you. **The reason is mechanical.** An intact blister is a sterile dressing that fits perfectly and that your own body made. The consensus describes it as a physical barrier that protects the wound and prevents bacterial colonisation, provides pain relief, and maintains the moist environment in which skin heals. **What the evidence does not settle** is what a clinician should do with a blister afterwards. The same 2024 consensus rates its own recommendation to preserve blisters as based on low-quality evidence, and separately allows removal, weakly and also on low-quality evidence, when a blister is already damaged, or is large, thin-walled, likely to burst, or badly contaminated. A randomised trial in *Medicine* comparing draining a blister with a needle against cutting the roof off concluded that neither is superior, with healing times around twelve days either way. A 2021 case report in the *Journal of Cutaneous and Aesthetic Surgery* states it outright: "There is no consensus for burn blister management." So the guidance to leave blisters alone is firm advice resting on modest evidence, and the argument among specialists is about a decision you are not the one making. Leave them intact, and let someone trained decide. ## Dressing it with what you have After cooling, cover the burn. The purpose is to keep it clean and keep the air off it, and that is all. MedlinePlus: cover with a dry, sterile bandage or a clean dressing, keep pressure and friction off it, and where the skin is broken an ointment is preferred so the dressing does not stick. For a major burn, cover with a dry sterile bandage if you have one or a clean cloth if you do not. Military guidance says the same thing in field terms: cover burns with loose, dry gauze or a clean sheet. The word doing the work is **loose**. A burn swells. Anything snug now will be a tourniquet in an hour. Burned fingers and toes get separated from each other with non-stick dressings so they do not heal stuck together. Elevate a burned limb above the level of the heart if you can, which reduces the swelling. A rule of thumb for having nothing: clean kitchen cling film, laid over the burn in loose sheets rather than wrapped around a limb, is widely taught as an improvised burn cover, because it is clean, it does not stick, and a clinician can see through it. That is not something a US federal source specifies, so treat it as a practical fallback. The sourced instruction remains loose dry gauze or a clean sheet. ## Infection and tetanus A burn is an open wound with its defences removed, and the infection risk runs for days after the injury. MedlinePlus lists the signs to watch for: drainage or pus from the burned skin, fever, increased pain, red streaks spreading out from the burn, and swollen lymph nodes. Red streaks in particular mean go now, not tomorrow. **Tetanus.** The CDC lists burns among the wounds that carry dead tissue and therefore tetanus risk, alongside crush injuries, fractures and frostbite. Adults are recommended a tetanus booster every ten years. For wound management the interval tightens: for a clean minor wound, a booster is indicated if the last dose was ten or more years ago, and for a dirty or major wound, including a burn, the trigger is five or more years. So a burn is a reason to check the date of your last tetanus shot, and if you cannot remember it, that itself is the answer. The CDC also notes that antibiotics are not a substitute for this. ## Chemical burns are a different problem A chemical burn keeps burning until the chemical is gone. Time under water is not comfort, it is removal. MedlinePlus gives the sequence: 1. Protect yourself first. Eye and skin protection. You are no help contaminated. 2. Get the person away from the source. 3. **Brush dry chemical powder off before any water touches it.** Brush it away from yourself and away from their eyes. 4. Remove contaminated clothing and jewellery. 5. Flush the skin with cool running water for 15 minutes or more. 6. Cover loosely with a sterile dressing or clean cloth. **The exception that matters.** Do not flush with water if the exposure involves dry lime, which is calcium oxide, or the elemental metals sodium, potassium, magnesium, phosphorus or lithium. Those react with water, and adding water makes the injury worse. **Do not try to neutralise a chemical** with an acid or an alkali unless a professional tells you to. The neutralisation reaction releases heat, so you end up adding a thermal burn to a chemical one. Call emergency services for difficulty breathing, seizures or loss of consciousness. For a chemical that was swallowed or inhaled, in the United States, Poison Control is **1-800-222-1222**, free, and staffed around the clock. Every chemical burn should be seen by a burn service. ## Electrical burns are a different problem again With electricity, the visible burn is often the least of it. **Before you touch anyone.** MedlinePlus says not to get within 20 feet, about 6 metres, of someone being electrocuted by high-voltage current until the power is confirmed off. For household current, unplug it, pull the fuse, or throw the breaker. If you cannot cut the power, push them clear with something non-conducting and dry, a wooden broom handle or a rubber mat, never metal and never anything wet. **Then check breathing and pulse.** Electricity kills mainly by stopping the heart. If they are unconscious with no pulse, start CPR. **Why a small electrical burn is not a small injury.** Current enters at one point and leaves at another, and it cooks tissue along the path in between. Military burn guidance is explicit that with high voltage injuries, above 1,000 volts, "skin contact points (cutaneous burns) of limited extent can hide extensive soft-tissue damage." MedlinePlus puts it plainly: some electrical burns look minor but there may be serious internal damage, especially to the heart, muscles or brain. One sign worth knowing, from the same military guidance: muscle destroyed by current releases its contents into the blood, which damages the kidneys, and the visible clue is **urine that is red or brown**. That is an emergency finding. Call emergency services for any electrical injury, including the ones that look trivial. MedlinePlus adds: no ice, no ointments, no adhesive bandages, do not break blisters or remove dead skin, and do not move the person unless they are in ongoing danger. ## Pain Ordinary over-the-counter painkillers are appropriate for minor burns. MedlinePlus recommends them for minor burns and names ibuprofen for sunburn. Follow the label, respect the dosing, and ask a pharmacist if anything about the person makes you unsure. Cool running water is itself a good analgesic, which is one more reason the twenty minutes is worth doing properly. Two limits. Do not give anything by mouth if the burn is severe, because they may need an anaesthetic. And avoid anaesthetic sprays and creams containing benzocaine or lidocaine, which MedlinePlus advises against. If pain is poorly controlled despite sensible painkillers, that is itself one of the American Burn Association's reasons to get a burn service involved. ## What healing actually looks like So you know what is normal and what is not. **A superficial burn** is red, warm and sore, and it settles over a few days. With sunburn, MedlinePlus notes the first signs may not appear for a few hours and the full effect may take 24 hours or longer, pain is worst somewhere between 6 and 48 hours, and peeling arrives several days in. Peeling is the burn resolving, not an infection. **A partial thickness burn** blisters, weeps, and is very painful for the first days. The 2024 international consensus gives the healing times by depth: a superficial second degree burn heals in under two weeks, a shallower deep one in two to three weeks, and a deeper one mostly takes longer than three weeks. Those weeks are the reason depth matters. A burn still open after about three weeks is the kind that scars badly and is usually better off surgically treated, which is why a burn that is not clearly healing by then needs review. **A full thickness burn** does not heal from the middle, because there is nothing left in the middle to heal from. It closes from the edges, slowly and with scar tissue, which is why these are grafted. What to expect along the way: swelling that peaks in the first day or two, weeping that gradually dries, itching as it heals, and skin that stays pink, tight and sensitive for months and burns easily in the sun. Keep new skin covered from sunlight. What is not normal: increasing rather than decreasing pain after the first day or two, spreading redness, red streaks, pus, a smell, fever, or a burn that has not closed within about three weeks. Any of those, get it seen. ## How you know you got it right - You stopped the burning before you did anything else. - Rings, watch and non-stuck clothing came off before the swelling did. - Cool running water ran over it for twenty minutes, and nothing colder than a tap went near it. - You covered the person up and kept them warm while you cooled the burn. - You looked at where the burn is, not just how big it is, and you know that face, hands, feet, genitals, joints, anything circumferential, anything chemical or electrical, and any burn in a child or an older adult goes to a professional whatever its size. - Nothing went on the burn except water and a loose clean covering. - Blisters are intact. - You asked when their last tetanus shot was. - If someone was in a closed space with smoke, they were seen by a clinician even though their skin looked fine. The one that carries the most weight is the fifth. Almost all of burn first aid is a short, known procedure that anyone can do. The skill that actually matters is recognising the burn that is past you, and handing it over before you have made it worse trying to help. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. Government publications are listed first because they are public domain and can be redistributed with this guide; the rest cannot. ### United States government (public domain) - National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Burns (burn degrees and appearance, cooling duration, the complete do-not list, when to call 911, dressings, infection signs, prevention). https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000030.htm - National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Chemical burn or reaction (brushing off dry chemicals, flushing duration, the dry lime and elemental metal exception, not neutralising, Poison Control). https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000059.htm - National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Electrical injury (the 20 foot rule, cutting power, CPR, hidden internal damage, what not to apply). https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000053.htm - National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Inhalation injuries (over half of fire deaths are due to inhalation injury; symptoms). https://medlineplus.gov/inhalationinjuries.html - National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Sunburn (onset and progression, peeling, pain timing, avoiding oil-based and anaesthetic products). https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003227.htm - US Department of Defense, Joint Trauma System. Burn Care Clinical Practice Guideline, CPG ID 12, version 1.3, 10 June 2025 (burn depth definitions and blanching, superficial burns excluded from size estimates, do not debride blisters before reaching a facility, loose dry gauze or clean sheet, hypothermia risk above 20 percent body surface area, circumferential burns acting as a tourniquet, high voltage injury hiding soft tissue damage, red or brown urine). https://jts.health.mil/assets/docs/cpgs/Burn_Care_CPG_10_June_2025_ID12_v1.3.pdf - US Department of Health and Human Services, Radiation Emergency Medical Management (REMM). Burns (burn depth appearance, the Rule of Nines percentages, palmar surface as approximately 1 percent, larger heads and smaller legs in children, inhalation injury evolving over 48 to 72 hours, airway occlusion, carbon monoxide and hydrogen cyanide). https://www.remm.hhs.gov/burns.htm - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About Tetanus (burns among wounds carrying tetanus risk). https://www.cdc.gov/tetanus/about/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Tetanus vaccination (adult booster every 10 years). https://www.cdc.gov/tetanus/vaccines/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Clinical guidance for tetanus (the 10 year and 5 year wound management intervals; antibiotics are not a substitute). https://www.cdc.gov/tetanus/hcp/clinical-guidance/index.html - US Fire Administration, Federal Emergency Management Agency. Older adults and fire safety (2.5 times the fire death risk for adults 65 and over, 2020). https://www.usfa.fema.gov/prevention/home-fires/at-risk-audiences/older-adults/ ### Peer-reviewed literature - Ji, S., Xiao, S., Xia, Z., Chinese Burn Association Tissue Repair of Burns and Trauma Committee, and Cross-Straits Medicine Exchange Association of China. Consensus on the treatment of second-degree burn wounds (2024 edition). *Burns & Trauma*, volume 12, 2024, tkad061 (running water at 12 to 25 degrees Celsius for no less than 20 minutes within 3 hours; ice causing vasoconstriction, ischaemic necrosis, frostbite and hypothermia; preserving intact blisters and the limits of that evidence; healing times by depth; removing rings and bracelets). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10858447/ - Singer, Y.M., et al. Effect of 20 minutes of cool running water within 3 hours on burn patient outcomes: a systematic review. *Journal of Burn Care & Research*, 2023 (seven studies, 11,383 patients, significantly decreased odds of requiring skin grafting or other surgical intervention). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10464582/ - Bettencourt, A.P., Romanowski, K.S., Joe, V., et al. Updating the Burn Center Referral Criteria: Results From the 2018 eDelphi Consensus Study. *Journal of Burn Care & Research*, volume 41, issue 5, 2020, pages 1052 to 1062 (transfer thresholds of full thickness above 5 percent and partial thickness above 10 percent of total body surface area; anatomical sites; all chemical injuries; high voltage and lightning; children and older adults; consultation for any potentially deep burn). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7510842/ - Ro, H.S., Shin, J.Y., Sabbagh, M.D., Roh, S.G., Chang, S.C., and Lee, N.H. Effectiveness of aspiration or deroofing for blister management in patients with burns: a prospective randomized controlled trial. *Medicine (Baltimore)*, 2018 (neither aspiration nor deroofing superior; healing around twelve days either way). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5944508/ - Gupta, S., Chittoria, R.K., Chavan, V., et al. Role of burn blister fluid in wound healing. *Journal of Cutaneous and Aesthetic Surgery*, 2021 ("There is no consensus for burn blister management"). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8611715/ - Solak, M. First aid practices about wounds and burns in rural areas. *BMC Research Notes*, 2025 (34.1 percent used traditional first aid practices such as honey, oil and yogurt). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12548283/ - La Ramba, H., et al. Local understandings of burn first aid. *Acta Medica Philippina*, 2026 (first aid based on toothpaste, honey or aloe vera, while running water was rarely mentioned). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13233781/ - Alsiaghi, Y.A., et al. Community knowledge of burn first aid. *International Wound Journal*, 2026 (applying honey or toothpaste and improper handling of chemical or electrical injuries classed as unsafe practices). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13042722/ ### Health technology assessment - Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health. Cooling for Thermal Burns: Clinical Effectiveness and Guidelines, 2019 (at least 20 minutes for any major burn or burn over 10 percent of total body surface area; running cool water at 15 degrees Celsius; ice or ice water should not be used due to the risk of hypothermia and impaired perfusion). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK541209/ ### Copyrighted authorities, cited but not reproduced The text of these is under ordinary copyright. Every statement drawn from them above is written in our own words. - American Burn Association. Guidelines for burn patient referral (the referral criteria: anatomical sites, all chemical injuries, high and low voltage electrical injuries, suspected inhalation injury, paediatric burns, comorbidities, poorly controlled pain). https://ameriburn.org/burn-care-team/resources/guidelines-for-burn-patient-referral - StatPearls, via the NCBI Bookshelf. Burn Evaluation and Management (the palm alone at approximately 0.5 percent of body surface area against the whole hand including fingers at approximately 1 percent; full thickness burns causing little or no pain). Distributed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, so cited rather than copied. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430741/
