Very few amputations were solely due to tourniquet use, and those that were traced mainly to improvised tourniquets and prolonged application time; complications seemed tightly related to application time, with times under two hours reasonably safe in previously healthy patients and times over two hours increasing fasciotomy rates; and 96 percent of patients survived when the tourniquet was placed before the onset of shock against 4 percent when it was placed later. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7844612/ - Charlton, N., Schuler, K., Ho, C.H., et al. Provider Fatigue During Direct Manual Compression for Life-Threatening Bleeding. *Cureus*, volume 13, issue 8, 2021, e17487. 33 adult laypeople compressing a bleeding-control simulator: the primary cause of failure in a simulated model of life-threatening bleeding was the inability to maintain adequate direct pressure for three minutes. Simulation, not patients. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8476202/ - Jensen, T.W., Moller, T.P., Viereck, S., et al. Danish first aid books compliance with the new evidence-based non-resuscitative first aid guidelines. *Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine*, volume 26, 2018, article 7. Used only for its verbatim quotation of the European Resuscitation Council's 2015 first aid recommendation not to try to control major external bleeding by proximal pressure points or elevation of an extremity. The paper quotes that guideline rather than issuing it. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5764019/ - Quinn, J.V., Polevoi, S.K., and Kohn, M.A. Traumatic lacerations: what are the risks for infection and has the "golden period" of laceration care disappeared? *Emergency Medicine Journal*, volume 31, issue 2, 2014, pages 96 to 100. 2,663 patients completed follow-up and 69 (2.6 percent) developed infection; no difference in infection rates for lacerations closed before or after 12 hours; independent predictors were diabetes (odds ratio 3.1), lacerations longer than 5 cm (2.4), a location other than head and neck (2.5), and moderate or heavy contamination (1.9); human and animal bites were excluded; and the conclusion that time from injury to closure is not as important as previously thought. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3797169/ - Weiss, E.A., Oldham, G., Lin, M., Foster, T., and Quinn, J.V. Water is a safe and effective alternative to sterile normal saline for wound irrigation prior to suturing: a prospective, double-blind, randomised, controlled clinical trial. *BMJ Open*, volume 3, issue 1, 2013, e001504. Infection in 3.5 percent of the tap water group against 6.4 percent with sterile saline; the conclusion of no difference with a trend favouring tap water; and the exclusion criteria, which are quoted in the text because they bound the claim: immunocompromising illness, current antibiotics, puncture or bite wounds, underlying tendon or bone involvement, and wounds more than 9 hours old. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3549228/ - Moscati, R.M., et al. A multicenter comparison of tap water versus sterile saline for wound irrigation. *Academic Emergency Medicine*, volume 14, issue 5, 2007, pages 404 to 409. 715 enrolled, 634 (88 percent) followed up; infection in 12 of 300 (4 percent) with tap water against 11 of 334 (3.3 percent) with saline; equivalent rates. Adults with acute simple lacerations requiring closure, three emergency departments. Abstract read through the NLM service above; PMID 17456554. - Valente, J.H., et al. Wound irrigation in children: saline solution or tap water? *Annals of Emergency Medicine*, 2003. 530 children aged 1 to 17 with simple lacerations; infection in 2.8 percent with saline against 2.9 percent with tap water; no clinically important difference. Abstract read through the NLM service above; PMID 12712026. - Fernandez, R., Green, H.L., Griffiths, R., Atkinson, R.A., and Ellwood, L.J. Water for wound cleansing. *Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews*, 2022, CD003861. 13 trials, 2,504 participants aged 2 to 95, with open fractures, surgical wounds, traumatic wounds, anal fissures and chronic wounds. The effect of tap water compared with normal saline is uncertain (risk ratio 0.84, 95 percent confidence interval 0.59 to 1.19), and all the evidence identified was low or very low certainty. Read through the open-access PMC copy; the Cochrane Library page returned 403. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9473482/ - FLOW Investigators. A Trial of Wound Irrigation in the Initial Management of Open Fracture Wounds. *New England Journal of Medicine*, volume 373, issue 27, 2015, pages 2629 to 2641. 2,447 patients analysed; reoperation in 13.2 percent with high pressure (above 20 psi), 12.7 percent with low pressure (5 to 10 psi) and 13.7 percent with very low pressure (1 to 2 psi), with the conclusion that very low pressure is an acceptable low-cost alternative; and reoperation in 14.8 percent of the castile soap group against 11.6 percent of the saline group (hazard ratio 1.32). Open fractures of the extremities irrigated in theatre. Abstract read through the NLM service above; PMID 26448371. - Lineaweaver, W., Howard, R., Soucy, D., et al. Topical antimicrobial toxicity. *Archives of Surgery*, volume 120, issue 3, 1985, pages 267 to 270. Four antiseptics applied directly to cultured human fibroblasts, including 3 percent hydrogen peroxide and 1 percent povidone-iodine: all four were cytotoxic; all of the cytotoxic agents except hydrogen peroxide were subsequently found to adversely affect wound healing in an animal model; the cellular toxicity of hydrogen peroxide and acetic acid exceeded their bactericidal potency; and the conclusion that these agents are unsuitable for use in wound care. Abstract read through the NLM service above; PMID 3970664. - Zhu, G., Wang, Q., Lu, S., and Niu, Y. Hydrogen Peroxide: A Potential Wound Therapeutic Target? *Medical Principles and Practice*, volume 26, issue 4, 2017, pages 301 to 308. The dose-dependent reversal: very dilute hydrogen peroxide promoting wound closure in animal models while 3 percent delayed healing, and no beneficial effect of 3 percent on wound healing found in the literature. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5768111/ - Ortega-Llamas, L., Quinones-Vico, M.I., Garcia-Valdivia, M., et al. Cytotoxicity and Wound Closure Evaluation in Skin Cell Lines after Treatment with Common Antiseptics for Clinical Use. *Cells*, volume 11, issue 9, 2022, article 1395. In vitro, on immortalised human keratinocytes and human fibroblasts: povidone iodine, chlorhexidine digluconate and ethanol were the most cytotoxic of those tested, povidone iodine reduced fibroblast viability to zero and inhibited migration in the scratch assay, and sodium hypochlorite was least detrimental. Hydrogen peroxide was not among the agents tested. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9099882/ - Cheng, H.T., Hsu, Y.C., and Wu, C.I., and others. Primary closure versus delayed or no closure for traumatic wounds due to mammalian bite. *Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews*, 6 December 2019. Four randomised trials, 998 participants, all concerning dog bites: it is uncertain whether primary suturing improves the proportion of wounds free of infection compared with no closure or with delayed closure, both very low certainty, and the benefits and harms of primary closure for mammalian bites remain uncertain. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6894945/ - Eliya-Masamba, M.C., and Banda, G.W., and others, as summarised in the systematic review of wound age and infection: Impact of wound age on infection rate of simple lacerations. *Injury*, 2012. Four trials, 3,724 patients; the existing evidence supports neither a golden period nor a role for wound age in the infection rate of simple lacerations. Abstract read through the NLM service above; PMID 22424703. - Forsch, R.T., Little, S.H., and Williams, C. Laceration Repair: A Practical Approach. *American Family Physician*, volume 95, issue 10, 2017, pages 628 to 636. That studies have been unable to define a golden period; primary closure up to 18 hours for non-infected wounds caused by clean objects and up to 24 hours for head wounds; 50 to 100 mL of irrigation solution per centimetre of wound length; and that potable tap water instead of sterile saline does not increase infection risk. https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2017/0515/p628.html ### What could not be sourced - **That a correctly applied tourniquet is painful.** Stated in the text as an observation, because none of the federal materials opened here says it in those words. What they do say, and what the guide relies on instead, is that the tourniquet should be tightened as much as possible and tightened further if bleeding persists. - **An instruction to bystanders to loosen a tourniquet.** This one resolved in the guide's favour: the Uniformed Services University's public page tells the bystander to leave the tourniquet in place until medical professionals arrive, so "leave it alone" is sourced and not merely inferred. What is still absent from every source opened here is any mention of the old folk practice of periodically loosening one, in either direction. - **Why military guidance prefers a tourniquet on bare skin while other federal guidance prefers padding or clothing.** The disagreement is reported as it stands. No source opened here explains it, and none is invented. - **Why a scalp wound bleeds so heavily.** The first aid guidance gives the scalp as its example of a minor injury that bleeds a lot but does not say why, and the military note about high blood flow in the face and scalp is made in the context of infection, not bleeding. No mechanism is asserted here. - **The rule against wrapping a bandage right around a neck.** No source opened here states it. It is presented in the text as reasoning, with the reasoning shown, rather than as guidance. - **A plain prohibition on packing the chest or abdomen.** No source opened here says it in those words. The torso is excluded structurally instead: packing is scoped to compressible bleeding and the torso is classified as non-compressible. The text shows that reasoning rather than presenting a quotation. - **Wound packing technique taught to lay rescuers.** The widely taught civilian packing course material is published by a copyrighted professional body and was not used. What is here comes from the military junctional-haemorrhage guidance, the federal clinical reference on haemorrhage control, and the first aid guidance on torso wounds. - **Numerical failure rates for improvised tourniquets applied by genuinely untrained people to real limbs.** The closest figures available are from a manikin model and from a randomised trial of people tested immediately after training, and both are reported with those limits attached. - **When first aid teaching changed its position on tourniquets.** No page opened here gives a date or decade, so none is given. The change is evidenced only by what the sources currently say. - **A resolution of the syringe pressure conflict.** Two sources opened here give figures roughly four times apart for the same hardware. The conflict is reported rather than resolved. - **A resolution of the elevation disagreement.** A 2015 European guideline says not to use elevation for major bleeding; a federal consumer page reviewed in 2025 still tells the public to raise the bleeding part. Both are reported. The reconciliation offered in the text is labelled as this guide's own. - **The current edition of the Tactical Combat Casualty Care Guidelines.** The 25 January 2024 edition was read in full and is what is cited. A later edition dated 1 May 2026 exists, but its PDF is encrypted and would not yield text here, so it was not read and nothing is attributed to it.

docs.title: Cold and Hypothermia
headings: Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead
Rewarming: what helps and what harms
Wet feet, which is the injury that actually happens in a wet climate
Wind chill, and what the chart actually says
Prevention, which is where the real gains are
Copyrighted authorities, cited but not reproduced
docs.text: # Cold Someone is cold and not acting right. Before you read another word: 1. **Get them out of the wind and out of the wet.** A building, a vehicle, a tent, the lee side of anything. Wind and wet are what turn survivable cold into hypothermia, and neither of them stops while you think. 2. **Get the wet clothes off and dry cover on.** CDC's order is: warm shelter, remove wet clothing, warm the centre of the body, which means chest, neck, head and groin. Not the hands. Not the feet. 3. **Get them off the ground.** The National Park Service says to "Insulate the body from the ground using any material available such as clothing, space blanket, etc." As a **rule of thumb**, ground takes heat out of a person faster than air does; the sourced part is the instruction, and what it means in practice is that a casualty lying on cold ground with blankets piled on top is still losing. 4. **Handle them gently, and do not let them walk.** This is the one that is not obvious and the one that kills. It is explained two sections down. Move them slowly, keep them flat, do not let them walk it off, do not rub them. 5. **Call for help.** MedlinePlus says to call 911 if the person is confused or has trouble thinking. CDC says a body temperature below 95 F (35 C) needs medical attention immediately. Everything after this is the explanation. Do those five things first. One honest boundary. **This guide is not a substitute for medical care, and nothing in it qualifies you to manage severe hypothermia on your own.** Severe hypothermia is an intensive-care problem. What a person without training can genuinely do is stop the heat loss, avoid the handful of instinctive actions that make things worse, and get the casualty to people who can rewarm them properly. That is not a small job. Done right it is most of the outcome. Two companions carry parts of this subject, so they are not repeated here. Cold water is its own emergency on a much faster clock, and [Reading the Tide](/library#reading-the-tide) covers cold shock, the gasping reflex and the 1-10-1 rule in full. The cold dark house after a windstorm, and the carbon monoxide deaths that come from trying to heat it, are in [The Hazards Your Place Actually Has](/library#the-hazards-where-you-live). ## What you can actually see Hypothermia is defined by core temperature, and you will not have a core temperature. You will have a person in front of you. So here it is by what you can observe. **The shivering stage.** NIOSH lists the early symptoms as shivering, fatigue, loss of coordination, and confusion and disorientation. CDC's list for adults is shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech and drowsiness. For infants, CDC says "bright red, cold skin" and very low energy, which is worth knowing because a baby does not shiver the way an adult does. Shivering is the body working. It is a good sign in the sense that the furnace is still lit. It is a bad sign in the sense that the furnace should not have needed to light. **The umbles.** The National Park Service teaches the four signs with a mnemonic: "The four main signs of hypothermia can be easily remembered using the mnemonic device 'umbles'. These signs include: stumbles, mumbles, fumbles, and grumbles." The same guide notes that "These signs indicate changes in motor coordination and levels of consciousness." That is the most useful field test there is, because you do not need equipment for it. Can they walk a straight line, speak clearly, work a zip or a buckle, and hold a civil conversation? Losing any of those is a neurological sign, and a neurological sign means the cold has reached the brain. **Denial belongs on the symptom list.** Point Reyes National Seashore puts it plainly: "Victims of hypothermia often deny that they are cold and often attempt to reassure others that they are 'Okay.'" Rocky Mountain National Park adds that someone with hypothermia "is not aware of their condition because symptoms begin gradually and their confused state hinders self-awareness." So the patient's own report is the least reliable evidence you have. Trust the umbles over the reassurance. **The stage where shivering stops.** This is the one people misread. NIOSH's late symptoms are: no shivering, blue skin, dilated pupils, slowed pulse and breathing, loss of consciousness. MedlinePlus makes the same point about shivering: it describes shivering that cannot be controlled as a symptom, and notes that at extremely low body temperatures the shivering may stop altogether. Read that again with the person in front of you. They were shivering violently. Now they are calm and still. Nothing improved. The body ran out of the fuel and the nerve signalling that shivering needs, and it gave up on the one defence it had. **Shivering stopping is a deterioration, not a recovery**, and it is the moment the problem becomes an emergency rather than a discomfort. The published staging behind this, for context rather than for you to apply: the Swiss system used in the clinical literature runs from HT I, "Conscious, shivering," through HT II, "Impaired consciousness; may or may not be shivering," to HT III, "Unconscious; vital signs present," and HT IV, "Apparent death; vital signs absent." Note that the staging the professionals use is also built on what can be observed, because they cannot measure a core temperature in a snowdrift either. StatPearls places the loss of shivering at a core temperature of about 30 to 32 C. **Paradoxical undressing.** At some point in deep hypothermia, some people take their clothes off. It is real and it is common enough to have been counted. A study of 207 fatal hypothermia cases in a sub-arctic region found "Some degree of paradoxical undressing was documented in 63 of 207 (30%) cases," most often shoes, then upper body clothing, then lower. The authors attribute it to "a combination of vasodilatation with consequent skin-warming, and diminished mental capacity," reasoning that "a sudden opening of previously constricted peripheral vessels could induce a sense of warmth, and, hence, a desire to undress." Two practical consequences. If you find someone cold and partly undressed, do not assume assault or intoxication as the explanation and do not let that assumption slow the rewarming. And if someone you are with starts shedding layers in the cold and telling you they feel hot, that is not them warming up. That is a late sign. ## Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead This is the single most counterintuitive fact about cold, it is real clinical guidance rather than folklore, and the federal sources say it in plain words. MedlinePlus is explicit on the point: **a person found lying motionless in the cold must not be assumed to be dead.** CDC's winter weather guidance says the same thing operationally: give CPR and keep giving it, because people who appear dead from hypothermia have been revived. The clinical reasoning is in the 2021 international update on accidental hypothermia. In a hypothermic patient, "rigidity (apparent rigor mortis) is not a reliable sign of death." And the list of findings that do **not** rule out resuscitation is remarkable: "asystole, unwitnessed CA, low core temperature, long no-flow or low-flow time, fixed, dilated pupils, hypocapnia, old age, or trauma (even major trauma)." Every one of those is something a bystander, and for that matter a paramedic, would ordinarily read as death. Cold slows the metabolism of the brain and heart enormously. That is the same effect that surgeons deliberately induce for some operations. A person cooled to the point of apparent death may have an intact brain that is simply running very slowly, and that brain can come back. What this means for you: **start CPR and keep going.** The decision that someone cold is beyond help belongs to a clinician who has rewarmed them, not to you at the scene and not to the first responder either. The guidance does list genuine stopping conditions, such as a valid do-not-resuscitate order or clear signs of irreversible death like fixed dependent lividity, but those are deliberately narrow and none of them is "they look dead." ## Why gentle handling matters A severely hypothermic heart is electrically unstable. Move it roughly and it can go into a fatal rhythm. The clinical term for this is rescue collapse, and the 2021 update defines it as "Cardiocirculatory collapse during extrication or transfer of hypothermic patients," attributed "most frequently, by mechanical stimuli such as sudden movement." The scale of it: **"rescue collapse appears to double the risk of death in severely hypothermic patients."** The instruction that follows is "Patients should be transported gently and horizontally to avoid triggering hypothermic CA." A 2003 review in CMAJ gives the same instruction from the arrhythmia angle: "Because of the risk of arrhythmia, patients should have cardiac monitoring and should be transferred gently." The National Park Service gives the plain-language version: "Be gentle. Sudden movements can cause severe pain." So: no shaking them awake. No hauling them upright. No slinging them over a shoulder. No jogging them to the truck. Keep them flat. If they cannot walk, "A patient who is unable to walk, should be placed in a horizontal position on a stretcher." And do not let them exercise their way warm. Walking generates heat, but "Walking increases heat production but increases afterdrop." The 2021 guidance is that a hypothermic patient found lying down should not be allowed to walk until they have taken calories and been allowed to shiver for about 30 minutes. ## Rewarming: what helps and what harms **Afterdrop** is the thing that makes rewarming counterintuitive. When a body gets cold, it shuts blood out of the arms and legs to protect the core, and those limbs get very cold. The 2021 update describes what happens next: "After extrication from a cold environment, cooling continues by redistribution of the heat from the warm core to the cold periphery." The CMAJ review says it more briefly: an afterdrop "may occur when blood supply to the cold periphery is recirculated to the core." In other words, the limbs are a reservoir of cold blood. Open them up and that cold blood comes back to the heart, and the core gets colder after the rescue than it was during it. That single mechanism explains almost every rewarming error. **A hot bath is wrong.** It dilates every peripheral vessel at once, which is the fastest possible way to flush cold blood into an unstable heart. MedlinePlus is direct about it, saying not to apply direct heat and naming hot water, a heating pad and a heat lamp as the things to avoid. The Park Service guidance says direct heat "can do extreme damage to the skin" and to use slow methods instead. **Rubbing the limbs is wrong**, for the same reason plus a second one. It drives cold blood back to the core, and on frostbitten tissue it physically destroys cells. The military guidance for cold injury is explicit: "Rubbing the affected areas is to be avoided as this will further traumatize the skin." **Alcohol is wrong**, and the reason is worth knowing because the folklore is so strong. The CMAJ review sets out three separate mechanisms: "Alcohol and sedative drugs dull mental awareness of cold and impair the judgement necessary to seek shelter or put on warm clothing. In addition, alcohol inhibits shivering, perhaps by causing hypoglycemia, and causes cutaneous vasodilatation, which counteracts the thermoregulatory response." So it stops you noticing, stops you shivering, and opens the vessels that were protecting your core. The feeling of warmth is the heat leaving. CDC, NIOSH, MedlinePlus and the Park Service all say the same thing in one line: do not give alcohol. **What does help**, from CDC and NIOSH, in this order: - Get them somewhere warm and dry. - Remove wet clothing. - Warm the centre of the body first: chest, neck, head and groin. An electric blanket if you have one, or skin-to-skin contact under loose dry layers of blankets, clothing, towels or sheets. - If they are conscious and alert, warm drinks help. Not alcoholic, and nothing by mouth for someone who is not fully awake. - Once they are warming, keep them dry and wrap the whole body including the head and neck. - If there is no pulse, start CPR. Notice that the warming is aimed at the trunk. The CMAJ review explains why heat goes "to the trunk rather than the extremities" in exactly the afterdrop terms above. Heat packs, where used, go on the trunk and should not be put directly against skin. The recurring beginner's instinct is to warm the parts that feel coldest and complain loudest, which are the hands and feet. Those are the last parts to warm, not the first. ## Wet feet, which is the injury that actually happens in a wet climate In a mild marine climate, frostbite is rare and non-freezing cold injury is not. It gets the most space here for that reason. **Trench foot, also called immersion foot, does not require freezing and barely requires cold.** NIOSH states that it "can occur at temperatures as high as 60 F if the feet are constantly wet." Sixty Fahrenheit is about 15.6 C. That is an ordinary autumn afternoon, and that is the point. The military guideline is blunt about the cause: it is "a syndrome related to prolonged exposure to moisture. Classically it has been associated with cold water, but can happen in all climates." The timing matters: "The syndrome generally happens slower in warm water, taking approximately 48 hrs, than cold water (earliest estimate 12 hours)." Twelve hours of cold wet feet is one long day of work in the rain. **What it looks like**, from the same guideline: it begins as "water logging of the feet, most pronounced in the soles." Then, with continuing exposure, "the foot becomes hyperemic, mottled, painful and edematous, gradually progressing into blistering, hypoperfusion, ulceration and gangrene." NIOSH's symptom list is the practical version: reddening of the skin, numbness, leg cramps, swelling, tingling pain, blisters or ulcers, bleeding under the skin, and gangrene, where "foot may turn dark purple, blue, or gray." **Treatment is not what you would guess.** For frostbite you immerse in warm water. For immersion foot you do the opposite. The military guideline: rewarming "is done by air drying at room temperature," and its quality metric for the condition is that patients "have dry heat administered." Do not soak these feet. NIOSH's field version: remove shoes and boots and wet socks, dry the feet, and "Avoid walking on feet, as this may cause tissue damage." That last one is easy to get wrong because the person can usually still walk. Walking on a foot in this state damages it further, and the damage can be permanent. **Chilblains** are the mild relative and they are worth naming so you do not mistake them for something worse. NIOSH describes them as caused by "repeated exposure of skin to temperatures just above freezing to as high as 60 F," producing redness, itching, possible blistering, inflammation, and in severe cases ulceration. Their first aid is: avoid scratching, warm the skin slowly, keep any blisters clean and covered. **Prevention is dry socks and a chance to dry out.** That is the entire intervention and it is nearly free. Spare socks in a pocket. Boots that actually keep water out. Feet out of wet boots at breaks. NIOSH's prevention list for cold work includes waterproof insulated boots and carrying extra socks, and that unglamorous line is the one that matters most in a rainy climate. ## Frostbite Frostbite is tissue freezing. It needs an air temperature well below freezing, which is why it is the rarer problem in a mild wet climate and the more likely problem on a clear cold night inland or at altitude. **Check the core before the fingers.** The military guideline is explicit that hypothermia comes first: "patients are likely hypothermic and should be warmed expediently before focusing on cold injuries of the extremities." MedlinePlus gives the same order. A warm-handed corpse is not the goal. **What it looks like, by depth.** The military guideline uses four degrees: - **First degree.** Superficial skin injury. Numbness, then pain on rewarming, redness, sometimes blue mottling, swelling, and peeling that starts around day 5. - **Second degree.** Partial thickness. Everything above plus blistering surrounded by redness and swelling, appearing around day 2. - **Third degree.** The full thickness of the skin and into the tissue beneath. Skin that is bluish to black and will not deform. Blood-filled blisters. Ulceration later. - **Fourth degree.** As above but through to bone. The area may be cold to the touch and "may feel stiff or woody." CDC's version for spotting it early: "Redness or pain in any skin area may be the first sign of frostbite," followed by "a white or grayish-yellow skin area," "skin that feels unusually firm or waxy," and numbness. The parts that go first are the nose, ears, cheeks, chin, fingers and toes. **The grade is not knowable at the time.** The military guideline warns that "The ultimate grade will not be truly known until treatment has been attempted and a period of time has passed." Do not write anyone off at the scene on the basis of how bad it looks. **Rewarming, if and only if it can be finished.** The sourced number is consistent across three of them. The military guideline: "Rapid active re-warming is done in 104-108 F (40-42 C) water for 15- 30 minutes as long as care can occur in an environment where there is no risk of refreezing." MedlinePlus gives the same window, recommending water between 104 and 108 degrees F, which is 40 to 42.2 C, with the part soaked for 15 to 30 minutes. The CMAJ review: "Rapid rewarming of a frostbitten extremity in a bath of water between 40 C and 42 C for 15 to 30 minutes may minimize tissue loss." That range is narrow on purpose. The military guideline explains both edges: "The temperature is important, as there is reduced effect with cooler temperatures and higher temperatures will cause burns." Use a thermometer. Water that feels comfortably hot to your hand is already too hot for tissue that cannot feel it. Expect it to hurt. The guideline notes the process "can be expected to be very painful," and that the temptation to warm slowly because it is better tolerated is a mistake, since "tissue survival is improved with rapid re-warming." **Do not thaw what may refreeze.** MedlinePlus lists among the things not to do: thaw a frostbitten area if it cannot be kept thawed. The military guideline is stronger: "It is imperative to prevent refreezing of the impacted extremity as it results in more tissue damage," and "refreezing after partial thawing will result in more severe injury." A frozen foot walked out to a road is a bad outcome. A thawed foot that refreezes on the way is a worse one. **The rest of the do-not list**, from CDC and MedlinePlus: - Do not rub or massage the area. - Do not use a fireplace, heat lamp, radiator or stove. - Do not use a heating pad or electric blanket on frostbite. - Do not walk on frostbitten feet or toes unless you have no choice. - Do not break the blisters. The heating pad item looks like it contradicts the hypothermia advice, where CDC does recommend an electric blanket. Both are right, and the difference is what you are heating. An electric blanket on the trunk of a hypothermic person warms a core that can still feel and complain. Anything hot against frostbitten tissue is being applied to skin that has lost sensation, and NIOSH gives the reason directly: affected areas "are numb and can be easily burned." A numb patient cannot tell you that you are burning them. If you want the other half of that problem, see [Burns](/library#treating-burns). ## Wind chill, and what the chart actually says Wind chill is one of the most misused numbers in weather reporting, so it is worth being precise. **What it is.** The National Weather Service defines it as "how cold people and animals feel when outside," based on "the rate of heat loss from exposed skin caused by wind and cold." It is a heat-loss index for living skin, not an air temperature. **What it is not.** From the NWS: "The only effect wind chill has on inanimate objects, such as car radiators and water pipes, is to shorten the amount of time for the object to cool. The inanimate object will not cool below the actual air temperature." Wind makes things reach the air temperature faster. It does not make them colder than the air. Your pipes do not care about the wind chill number, and neither does a thermometer. **The formula**, published by the NWS and effective 1 November 2001, is: ``` Wind Chill (F) = 35.74 + 0.6215T - 35.75(V^0.16) + 0.4275T(V^0.16) ``` where T is air temperature in Fahrenheit and V is wind speed in mph. The NWS notes it applies for temperatures at or below 50 F and wind speeds above 3 mph. **The frostbite bands.** The NWS chart shades three regions, labelled 30 minutes, 10 minutes and 5 minutes, meaning the approximate time in which exposed skin can freeze. The NWS gives one worked example in words: "If the temperature is 0 F and the wind is blowing at 15 mph, the wind chill is -19 F. At this wind chill temperature, exposed skin can freeze in 30 minutes." Reading the shading off the published chart, the coldest air temperature at which each band begins, for a few representative wind speeds: | Wind | 30 min band begins at | 10 min | 5 min | |---|---|---|---| | 5 mph | -5 F | -35 F | not reached down to -40 F | | 15 mph | 5 F | -15 F | -35 F | | 30 mph | 10 F | -5 F | -20 F | | 60 mph | 15 F | 5 F | -5 F | The shape of that table is the useful part. **Wind buys the cold a great deal of ground once you are already below freezing, and almost none above it.** Going from 5 mph to 60 mph moves the 30 minute threshold only from -5 F to 15 F, twenty degrees. But at a fixed -20 F, going from 5 mph to 30 mph moves you from skin freezing in 30 minutes to skin freezing in 5. Same air, six times the hurry. **And here is the number that matters in a mild wet climate.** Across the entire published chart, at every wind speed up to 60 mph, no frostbite band appears at any air temperature warmer than 15 F, about -9 C. Silverdale's January mean low is 2.0 C, about 35.6 F. Its coldest recorded temperature is -13.9 C, about 7 F, and its winter design temperature is -6 C, about 21 F. Those and the rest of the local setting are in [Where You Are: Silverdale, Washington](/library#silverdale-wa). So in an ordinary local winter, **frostbite is essentially off the table, and that is exactly why the wind chill number is dangerous here.** A 35 F day with a 60 mph wind, which is well inside this area's windstorm record, produces a wind chill of about 17 F by the NWS formula. Damaging winter windstorms here are near-annual and the recorded peak is 77 mph, on 14 December 2000, so this is an ordinary bad day rather than an extreme. That is a genuinely alarming-sounding number and skin still cannot freeze in it. What the wind is doing at that temperature is stripping heat out of a whole person at a rate their metabolism cannot match. The injury on offer is hypothermia, not frostbite, and the chart does not have a band for that. ## Who this actually happens to **Most hypothermia deaths are not in the wilderness.** CDC recorded 1,024 deaths attributed to excessive cold or hypothermia in the United States in 2023, with the majority in January and February and November and December, January highest at 19.9 percent. In the earlier national review covering 1999 to 2002, 4,607 death certificates carried hypothermia-related diagnoses, 49 percent of the deceased were over 65, 67 percent were male, and only 22 percent were married against 52 percent of the general population. Of those deaths, "Most deaths were not work related (63%); 23% of affected persons were at home when they became hypothermic," and an Alabama study cited in the same report found that "almost half of the hypothermia-related deaths occurred indoors." Even in a genuinely cold and outdoors-heavy setting, the picture is less like mountaineering than you would expect. In the sub-arctic series of 207 fatal cases, 93 percent were found outdoors, but "a large proportion (81/207) of events occurred within close proximity to other people and buildings," many within 500 metres of a structure. Ethanol was found in 43 percent of the victims. The mean age was 62. The population this kills is old, often alone, frequently indoors in a house that has lost its heat, and frequently within sight of help. **Who is at higher risk**, from CDC and MedlinePlus: - Older adults without adequate food, clothing or heating - Infants sleeping in cold bedrooms - People who stay outdoors for long periods, including people who are unhoused, and outdoor workers - People drinking alcohol in excess or using drugs - People with chronic illness, especially heart and circulation problems - People who are malnourished or exhausted - People taking certain medications NIOSH adds a point that transfers directly to a mild climate: "In regions unaccustomed to winter weather, near freezing temperatures are considered factors for cold stress." A place that is never very cold is a place where nobody owns the right coat. ## Prevention, which is where the real gains are **Cold plus wet plus wind is a different problem from cold.** CDC states it outright: "Hypothermia often occurs at very cold temperatures, but can occur at cool temperatures (above 40 F), if a person is wet (from rain, sweat or cold water) and becomes chilled." Forty Fahrenheit is about 4.4 C. Silverdale's mean low is under 4.4 C for five months of the year, and December and January together bring about 488 mm of rain out of an annual 1,446 mm. Read those two facts together. The local winter is a machine for producing the exact combination CDC names: not very cold, very wet, and regularly windy. That is why this guide spends more words on wet feet than on frostbite. **Cotton is the problem.** Rocky Mountain National Park: "Avoid clothing that will absorb and hold water, like cotton and jeans." Cotton holds water against you, loses its loft when wet, and then evaporates that water using your body heat. A cotton shirt under a rain jacket, soaked with your own sweat, is a cooling system you are wearing. Wool and synthetics keep some insulating value wet; cotton keeps almost none. **Layers, loose ones.** NIOSH: "Wear several layers of loose clothing for insulation," and specifically that "Tight clothing reduces blood circulation to the extremities." A tight boot is a cold foot. So the extra pair of socks that does not fit in the boot is not extra insulation, it is a circulation problem. The rest of the NIOSH list is ordinary and complete: waterproof insulated boots, a hat, protection for ears, face, hands and feet, warm locations for breaks, limits on time outside, and a bag with spare socks, gloves, hat, jacket and a thermos of something hot. **Stay fed.** Shivering is muscular work and it runs on food. MedlinePlus lists going without enough food, drink or rest in cold weather among the causes of hypothermia, in the same breath as falling into cold water. The 2021 clinical guidance treats calories as part of the recovery, saying a patient should have taken calories and shivered for about 30 minutes before being allowed to walk. **Stay hydrated.** MedlinePlus names inadequate fluids as a cause alongside inadequate food. Cold suppresses thirst and cold air is dry, so the mistake is easy. **Keep the ground in mind.** Everything in the emergency section about insulating from the ground applies before the emergency too. A bed roll without a sleeping pad, a folding chair versus a rock, a stop on wet grass versus a stop on a log: those are the same decision made in advance and for free. If you want the physics of where household heat goes and how to stop it leaving, that is a separate subject and it has its own guide: [Insulation and Heat Loss](/library#insulation-and-heat-loss). ## You own this when - Your first five actions are out of the wind, out of the wet, off the ground, gently, and call, and you can do them without reading. - You warm the chest, neck, head and groin, not the hands and feet, and you can say why. - You know that shivering stopping is a deterioration. - You would start CPR on someone cold who looks dead, and you know that the decision to stop is not yours. - You know that a hot bath, rubbing the limbs and a drink are three versions of the same mistake, and that the mistake is called afterdrop. - You would not let a hypothermic person walk to the vehicle. - You treat immersion foot by drying it in air, and frostbite by immersing it in water at 104 to 108 F, and you do not confuse the two. - You would not thaw a frozen foot you could not keep thawed. - You read a wind chill number as a rate of heat loss from a person, not as a temperature anything reaches. - You carry spare socks in the rain. The one carrying the most weight is the sixth. Almost everything on this list is knowledge. That one is a decision you will have to make while a cold, confused adult is insisting they are fine and would rather just walk, and it has to have been made in advance. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. Federal government publications are listed first because they are public domain and can be redistributed with this guide; the rest cannot. ### United States government (public domain) - National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Hypothermia (definition and the 95 F threshold, symptoms including shivering stopping at extremely low temperatures, causes including inadequate food, drink and rest, first aid order, do not assume someone motionless in the cold is dead, no direct heat, no alcohol, risk groups). https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000038.htm - National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Frostbite (appearance and progression, checking for hypothermia first, the 104 to 108 F rewarming range and the 15 to 30 minute duration, do not thaw what cannot be kept thawed, no dry heat, no rubbing, do not disturb blisters). https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000057.htm - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Preventing Hypothermia, Winter Weather (warning signs in adults and infants, the below 95 F rule, the treatment order, warming the centre of the body, electric blanket and skin-to-skin, warm non-alcoholic drinks, CPR, who is at risk). https://www.cdc.gov/winter-weather/prevention/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Preventing Frostbite, Winter Weather (early signs, body parts affected, what to do, and the four do-nots: no walking on frostbitten feet, no rubbing, no fireplace or heat lamp or radiator or stove, no heating pad or electric blanket). https://www.cdc.gov/winter-weather/prevention/preventing-frostbite.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Avoid, Spot, Treat: Frostbite and Hypothermia, publication CS253565-A (hypothermia can occur above 40 F if a person is wet and becomes chilled; the at-risk list; the numbered treatment and caution steps). https://www.cdc.gov/winter-weather/media/pdf/avoid-spot-treat-frostbite.pdf - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. Cold-related Illnesses in Workers (early and late hypothermia symptoms, frostbite first aid and why numb skin burns easily, trench foot at temperatures as high as 60 F with its symptom list and first aid, chilblains). https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/cold-stress/about/related-illness.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, NIOSH. Cold and Work: Types, Causes, Preparation (the four cold-related illnesses; regions unaccustomed to winter weather; loose layers; hats; warm liquids). https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/cold-stress/about/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, NIOSH. Fast Facts: Protecting Yourself from Cold Stress, DHHS (NIOSH) Publication No. 2010-115 (the same illness descriptions in compact form, plus the prevention list: loose layers, tight clothing reducing circulation, waterproof insulated boots, spare socks, chemical hot packs). https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/docs/2010-115/pdfs/2010-115.pdf - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Hypothermia-Related Deaths, United States, 1999-2002 and 2005, MMWR (4,607 death certificates, 49 percent over 65, 67 percent male, 22 percent married, 63 percent not work related, 23 percent at home, the Alabama indoor finding). https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5510a5.htm - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. QuickStats: Percentage Distribution of Deaths Attributed to Excessive Cold or Hypothermia, by Month, United States, 2023, MMWR volume 74 (1,024 deaths in 2023; January highest at 19.9 percent). https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/74/wr/mm7406a6.htm - National Weather Service. Understanding Wind Chill (the definition as how cold people and animals feel, the rate of heat loss from exposed skin, the formula, and the worked example of 0 F with 15 mph wind giving a wind chill of -19 F at which exposed skin can freeze in 30 minutes). https://www.weather.gov/safety/cold-wind-chill-chart - National Weather Service. Wind Chill Questions (inanimate objects such as car radiators and water pipes will not cool below the actual air temperature; the formula applies at or below 50 F and above 3 mph). https://www.weather.gov/safety/cold-faqs - National Weather Service. Wind Chill Chart, effective 1 November 2001 (the full temperature and wind speed matrix, and the shaded frostbite time bands of 30, 10 and 5 minutes that the table in this guide is read from). https://www.weather.gov/media/safety/windchillchart3.pdf - National Weather Service. Cold Water Hazards and Safety (cold shock, the 77 F gasping threshold, incapacitation within seconds). Used here only to point at the companion guide. https://www.weather.gov/safety/coldwater - National Park Service, Rocky Mountain National Park. Winter Ecology Teacher Guide (the "umbles" mnemonic and what it indicates; be gentle because sudden movements cause severe pain; do not apply direct heat; insulate the body from the ground; that a person with hypothermia is often unaware of their own condition). https://www.nps.gov/romo/learn/education/upload/Winter-Ecology-Teacher-Guide-for-web.pdf - National Park Service, Rocky Mountain National Park. Hypothermia (warning signs; avoid cotton and jeans; ensure a barrier between the ground and the person; warm non-alcoholic drinks; get professional help immediately). https://www.nps.gov/romo/planyourvisit/hypothermia.htm - National Park Service, Point Reyes National Seashore. Your Safety: Hypothermia (signs including fumbling hands and memory lapse; that victims often deny being cold and reassure others they are okay; get out of wind and rain; heat packs to neck, armpit and groin; never alcohol). https://www.nps.gov/pore/planyourvisit/yoursafety_hypothermia.htm - US Department of Defense, Joint Trauma System. Frostbite and Immersion Foot Care, CPG ID 59, 26 January 2017 (the four degrees of frostbite and their appearance; that the grade is not knowable until later; warm the hypothermic core before the extremities; rapid rewarming at 104 to 108 F for 15 to 30 minutes and why that range is narrow; rewarming is very painful and should not be done slowly; no rubbing; refreezing causes worse injury; immersion foot from prolonged moisture in any climate, roughly 12 hours in cold water and 48 in warm, its clinical progression, and that it is rewarmed by air drying at room temperature rather than by soaking). https://jts.health.mil/assets/docs/cpgs/Frostbite_and_Immersion_Foot_Care_26_Jan_2017_ID_59.pdf ### Peer-reviewed literature - Paal, P., et al. Accidental Hypothermia: 2021 Update. *International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health*, volume 19, issue 1, 2022, article 501 (the Swiss staging system HT I to HT IV described by observable signs; afterdrop by redistribution from core to periphery; rescue collapse and that it appears to double the risk of death in severely hypothermic patients; transport gently and horizontally; walking increases afterdrop; calories and about 30 minutes of shivering before walking; apparent rigor mortis is not a reliable sign of death; the list of findings that are not contraindications to rewarming a hypothermic patient in cardiac arrest, and the narrow list that is). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8744717/ - Biem, J., Koehncke, N., Classen, D., and Dosman, J. Out of the cold: management of hypothermia and frostbite. *CMAJ: Canadian Medical Association Journal*, volume 168, issue 3, 2003, pages 305 to 311 (the three mechanisms by which alcohol worsens cold exposure: dulled awareness and judgement, inhibited shivering, and cutaneous vasodilatation; afterdrop and why heat is applied to the trunk rather than the extremities; gentle transfer because of arrhythmia risk; frostbite rewarming at 40 to 42 C for 15 to 30 minutes). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC140473/ - Brandstrom, H., Eriksson, A., Giesbrecht, G., Angquist, K.-A., and Haney, M. Fatal hypothermia: an analysis from a sub-arctic region. *International Journal of Circumpolar Health*, volume 71, 2012, article 18502 (paradoxical undressing documented in 63 of 207 cases, 30 percent, and which garments went first; the vasodilatation and diminished mental capacity explanation; 93 percent found outdoors but 81 of 207 events close to people and buildings; ethanol in 43 percent; mean age 62). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3417546/ ### Copyrighted authorities, cited but not reproduced The text of this is under ordinary copyright. Every statement drawn from it above is written in our own words. - StatPearls, via the NCBI Bookshelf. Hypothermia (the mild, moderate and severe core temperature bands, and that shivering typically ceases at a core temperature of about 30 to 32 C, at which point paradoxical undressing may be observed). Distributed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, so cited rather than copied. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK545239/ ### Project data - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/climate.json`. The local temperature and precipitation figures: January mean low 2.0 C, December mean low 1.7 C, December and January precipitation of 252 mm and 236 mm against an annual 1,446 mm, record low -13.9 C, winter design temperature -6 C. That file's own provenance is NOAA NCEI 1991-2020 Normals for station USC00450872 near Bremerton, with the design temperature from Bremerton National Airport. - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/hazards.json`. The near-annual winter windstorm record for the Kitsap Peninsula, including the 77 mph peak of 14 December 2000, which is where the 60 mph figure in the wind chill worked example comes from. ### Computed rather than quoted - The wind chill value of about 17 F for 35 F air with a 60 mph wind was computed here from the National Weather Service formula above, not read from a published table. The formula is valid in that range, being at or below 50 F and above 3 mph. - The frostbite band table was read off the shading of the published NWS wind chill chart rather than from a written list, because the NWS publishes the bands graphically. It reproduces the one example the NWS does state in words, 0 F with a 15 mph wind falling in the 30 minute band, which is the check that it was read correctly. ### Not sourced to any authority - **The claim that ground conducts heat out of a person faster than air does.** It is the reason every source above tells you to insulate from the ground, but none of the federal sources consulted states the physical comparison, so treat the mechanism as a **rule of thumb** and the instruction, which is sourced to the National Park Service, as the part to act on. - **The advice to carry spare socks specifically.** NIOSH's prevention list includes carrying extra socks, so the practice is sourced; the emphasis placed on it here for a wet marine climate is this guide's own judgement, drawn from the sourced fact that immersion foot needs only wet feet and about 12 hours.
