docs.text: # Sharpening: Why the Dull Blade Is the Dangerous One Most people believe a sharp blade is the hazard and a dull one is merely annoying. It is the other way round, and getting this backwards is how people end up in an emergency room. The decision you are actually making is this: **every time you pick up a cutting tool, you are choosing between spending five minutes on the edge and pushing harder than the job needs.** Pushing harder is the dangerous option. Everything below serves that one choice. Here is the mechanism, and it is not complicated. A dull edge does not start the cut. You lean on it. When it finally goes, it goes with all that stored force behind it, and it goes somewhere you did not plan, which is usually into the hand holding the work. A sharp edge starts where you put it, needs almost no push, and if it does slip it is not carrying much energy. Sharpening is therefore a safety skill first and a quality skill second. Where a number appears here it comes from a government publication or a peer-reviewed study that measured it. The best sources on this subject are unusually good: the USDA Forest Service has published detailed public-domain manuals on filing axes and crosscut saws, and the Army and Navy jointly publish a hand tool manual that is better on sharpening stones than most books you can buy. Every number traces to something in the Sources list at the bottom. Where a figure is trade practice rather than a measured value, it says so in the text. ## What the evidence actually says, and what it does not Be careful here, because the argument at the top of this page is made confidently all over the internet and the supporting evidence is partial. **The force half is measured.** Researchers instrumented knives and followed fifteen professional meat cutters through lamb shoulder boning, beef rib trimming and beef loin trimming in two packing plants. Sharper blades required statistically significantly lower peak and mean cutting moments, and lower grip forces, than dull knives. The numbers give a sense of scale: peak cutting moments reached 17.2 newton metres on shoulder boning, and grip forces averaged 28.3% of each worker's maximum voluntary contraction with peaks at 72.6%. A dull knife pushes those numbers up. That is a real measurement, not a saying. **The authority half is stated but not quantified.** OSHA's hand and power tools guidance puts it plainly: knives and scissors must be sharp, and dull tools can cause more hazards than sharp ones. The same document tells you to direct saw blades and knives away from walkways and away from anyone working near you. **The injury half is inference.** No study found for this guide directly measures injury rate against edge sharpness. What is measured is the scale of the problem: an analysis of the federal injury surveillance system found an estimated 434,259 knife-related injuries treated in United States emergency departments every year, about 1,190 a day, or 1.56 per thousand people per year. Fingers and thumbs were hurt in 66% of cases, and 94% of injuries were lacerations. The same paper opens by noting that knives cause more disabling injuries than any other type of hand tool. Pocket and utility knives accounted for 47% of the injuries where a knife type was recorded, and kitchen knives for 36%. So: the force increase is proven, the hazard claim is the position of the federal safety regulator, the mechanism is obvious, and the direct injury comparison has not been published. That is an honest summary. It is still more than enough to sharpen your tools. ## What an edge actually is An edge is not a thing added to a blade. It is a **geometric coincidence**: two surfaces meeting so precisely that the line where they meet has almost no width. That line is the **apex**. This matters because it changes what you think you are doing. You are not putting an edge on. You are **removing metal from two surfaces until they intersect cleanly**. Every stroke of every stone is subtraction. If the two surfaces do not yet meet, no amount of polishing will make them cut, and this is the single most common reason a beginner sharpens for twenty minutes and ends up with a blade that still will not cut paper. They polished two surfaces that never touched. How small is small? A straight razor is honed to a wedge with a total included angle of about 17 degrees and a tip radius of roughly 40 nanometres. Forty nanometres is smaller than many of the individual structural features inside the steel itself. That last fact is the key to how edges die. Research published in *Science* in 2020 followed razor blades cutting human hair inside an electron microscope. The blades did not simply wear smooth. They **chipped**: microscopic cracks started where the steel's internal structure varied from point to point along the edge, and a chunk of the apex broke away. The chipping happened before any appreciable wear had occurred. The authors are careful that the conditions have to line up, so it is not every stroke, but it is what took the blade out. That study is about razors and hair, so do not stretch it into a law about every blade. What it does establish is that **an edge can go from sharp to useless by fracturing rather than by rounding over**, and two practical consequences follow: - **A dull edge is often a damaged edge, not a worn one.** You may not be restoring a gently rounded curve at all. You may be cutting back past a chipped line until you reach sound metal, which takes more removal than people expect. - **Thinner is sharper and also more fragile.** The Forest Service crosscut saw manual says this about saw teeth in exactly these terms: the more pointed a tooth is filed, the deeper it sinks and the hungrier the saw is, but a sharply pointed tooth wears faster than one less sharply pointed. That trade is the whole of edge geometry, in one sentence, for every tool you own. ## The burr: your one reliable checkpoint This is the most useful thing a beginner can learn, and it turns sharpening from guesswork into a procedure with a test you can pass. When you grind one side of a blade far enough that the two surfaces finally meet, the metal at the apex has nowhere left to go. It folds over to the far side as a thin ragged lip. This is the **burr**, also called a wire edge or a feather edge. You cannot usually see it. You can feel it by sliding a fingertip **off the edge, across it, never along it**. A burr is not a defect. It is proof. **It is the only unambiguous signal that you have removed enough metal to reach the apex at that point on the blade.** No burr means the surfaces have not met yet and you are not finished, however long you have been at it. The procedure the Forest Service ax manual gives, which is the same procedure for a kitchen knife, is: 1. Work one side until **a burr can be felt along the whole length of the edge**. Not part of it. The whole length, from heel to tip. If the middle burrs and the tip does not, keep going on the tip. 2. Turn the blade over and work the other side until **the burr flips back across to the first side**, again along the whole length. 3. Move to a finer abrasive and repeat, more lightly. The burr gets smaller each time. 4. Remove the last of it, which is what stropping is for. More on that below. The ax manual is blunt about step 1: stop filing once you have filed one side so that a burr of metal can be felt on the back side, then turn the ax over and continue on the other side until the burr goes back over to the side where you started. The crosscut saw manual adds a warning worth carrying over to every tool. Remove the burr periodically as you go, because **a burr can hide the true shape of the edge** and make you think you are further along than you are. Its instruction for saw teeth is to knock the burr off with a whetstone, a light stroke of the file, or even a piece of hardwood. ## Angle: consistency beats the number The exact number matters far less than people think. Holding the same number for every stroke matters enormously, because a wobbling angle grinds a rounded shoulder instead of a flat surface, and a rounded shoulder never meets its partner at a clean apex. The Forest Service says this in the plainest possible way in its handtool manual: blade and edge bevels may vary with individual preference and with the task at hand, an ax bevel for softwoods might be thinner than one for hardwoods, and experience and experimentation will determine the right bevel for each tool and job. The crosscut saw manual says the same about saw teeth, that the consensus is less bevel on a cutter tooth for hardwood than for softwood. Read that as permission to stop agonising. Pick an angle, hold it, and adjust later if the edge chips or will not bite. The working ranges below give the total included angle where that is what the source specifies, and the per-side angle where that is the convention. Read the last column carefully. | Tool | Working angle | Where this comes from | |---|---|---| | Straight razor | About 17 degrees total | Measured, from published research on razor steel | | Kitchen knife | About 15 to 20 degrees per side | **Trade practice.** No federal source found. Softer steels and heavier work want the higher end | | Woodworking chisel or plane iron | About 25 degrees primary, often a 30 degree micro-bevel at the very tip | **Trade practice.** No federal source found | | Axe | About 25 degrees, and **slightly convex**, filed back 2 to 3 inches from the edge | USDA Forest Service ax manual, which supplies a printed gauge template | | Machete | Keep the factory bevel | USDA Forest Service handtool manual: use a mill bastard file or whetstone to maintain the factory edge bevel | | Hoe, McLeod, grub hoe | 45 degrees, outside bevel | USDA Forest Service handtool manual | | Shovel | About 45 degrees, bevel on the inside (top) face | USDA Forest Service handtool manual | | Twist drill | 118 degrees included, that is 59 degrees each side of the axis, with 8 to 12 degrees of lip clearance | US Army machine tool manual: the general purpose drill point | **Convex, flat or hollow.** The ax manual asks for a rounded, slightly convex profile and a fan shape spreading back over the cheek of the head. The handtool manual explains why: when you grind, arc the blade toward its midpoint so it ends up with a full-width convex bevel, and be careful not to hollow grind, which leaves the bevel dished to the radius of the grinding wheel. A hollow bevel is thinner just behind the apex, which is exactly where an impact tool needs steel. The crosscut manual makes the same point from the other direction: a saw tooth whose filed surface is flat develops a concave cutting edge and a thin, weak point. Short version: for anything you swing or lever, convex. For anything you push through a controlled cut, flat is fine and easier to hold. ## Abrasives, honestly Every abrasive does the same job, which is scratching metal off. They differ in how fast, how flat they stay, how much mess they make and what they cost. The Forest Service handtool manual publishes a comparison of sharpening stones with a speed rating for each. The prices are from 2005 and are useless now, so they are left out; the ranking is not. | Stone | Natural or synthetic | What it is for | Speed | |---|---|---|---| | Washita | Natural | Shaping and roughing | Fast | | Soft Arkansas | Natural | Sharpening | Medium | | Hard white Arkansas | Natural | Edge finishing | Slow | | Black hard Arkansas | Natural | Edge polishing | Very slow | | Silicon carbide | Synthetic | Roughing to sharpening | Fast to medium | | India | Synthetic | Roughing to sharpening | Fast to medium | | Crystolon | Synthetic | Roughing to sharpening | Fast to medium | | Diamond on nickel | Synthetic | Sharpening hard steels | Medium | | Silicon carbide in rubber | Synthetic | Deburring | Fast | That manual's own recommendation is **synthetic**, because synthetic abrasives are harder than natural stones, their uniform particle size gives an even surface, and they cost less. If you want a natural stone for the final polish, do the rough work on a synthetic first so you do not wear out the expensive stone on work it is not needed for. What the common types mean in practice: - **Oilstones.** Light oil floats the swarf, the metal and grit, off the surface so it does not lodge in the pores. Use oil on an oilstone. If it glazes because the pores have filled, clean it with a citrus-based solvent and a stiff brush. - **Waterstones.** Water does the same floating job. They cut fast and polish well, and the ax manual warns they are much softer than oilstones and tend to cup and wear faster. They need flattening often. - **Diamond plates.** Steel plate with diamond grit bonded to it. They stay flat, they cut hard steels that ordinary stones struggle with, and there is nothing to glaze. They are the low-fuss choice. - **Ceramic.** Very hard, very slow, almost no wear. A finishing abrasive, not a shaping one. - **Sandpaper on glass.** Wet-and-dry paper laid on a sheet of glass or a machined flat. The Forest Service uses exactly this arrangement to reshape worn stones: rub the stone over coarse sandpaper, or over glass sprinkled with carborundum powder, keeping it wet. If it will flatten a stone it will sharpen a chisel. It is cheap, it is flat, and the paper is consumable. - **Files.** For axes, mower blades, mattocks, machetes and anything else too soft and too battered to bother a stone with. A 10 inch mill bastard file is the Forest Service's all-round recommendation. **Understanding file cut.** Files are graded two ways at once and the labels confuse everyone. The pattern of teeth: **single-cut** files have one series of parallel teeth set at 60 to 80 degrees to the edge and are for finishing; **double-cut** files have two crossing series at 45 degrees to each other and are for restoring shape. The coarseness, for files of the same length: **bastard** is coarsest, then **second cut**, then **smooth**. Longer files of the same grade are coarser than shorter ones. **Grit numbers.** An abrasive grain number is a sieve mesh count: grain number 40 means the grains passed through a sieve with about 40 openings to the linear inch. Bigger number, smaller grit, finer finish. That is the definition. The specific progressions people recommend, such as 1000 then 4000 then 8000 on waterstones, are trade practice, not standards, and any three reasonably spaced grits work. **When coarse is the right answer.** This is where beginners waste the most time. If the edge is chipped, rolled, or has simply never met itself, a fine stone cannot fix it, because a fine stone removes almost no metal. More strokes on a fine stone is not equivalent to fewer strokes on a coarse one. The rule: - **No burr after a few minutes on a fine stone?** You are on the wrong stone. Drop to coarse. - **Visible chips or a rolled edge?** Coarse, or a file. - **Edge is there but not keen?** Fine, then finer. - **Edge was sharp yesterday and is merely tired?** No stone at all. See the keeping-it section. The general shape of this, as the Army and Navy tool manual describes a two-sided stone, is that the coarse face removes nicks and reshapes, and the fine face completes the job and puts a keen edge on. ## Stropping is not sharpening A strop is a piece of leather, canvas, or a block of soft clear wood. Drawing the blade **backwards**, spine first, along it does two things: it tears off the last of the burr, and it aligns and burnishes the very apex. The Forest Service ax manual gives the direction precisely: strop by drawing the ax toward the edge, the opposite of the direction used during sharpening, on finished leather or a piece of soft clear wood such as pine. The Army and Navy manual says the same about any blade, that the wire edge left by a stone may be removed by stroking both sides on a soft wood block, canvas, or leather. What a strop does **not** do is remove meaningful metal or change the geometry. If a blade will not cut, stropping will not save it. Strop after sharpening, and strop between sharpenings to keep an edge pleasant, but do not mistake it for the work. Compounds, the waxy abrasive bars sold to charge a strop with, do add a little cutting action. That is trade practice rather than a specified process, and a bare leather strop already does the job the Forest Service describes. ## Tool by tool ### Kitchen knife The easiest place to learn, because the steel is soft enough to respond quickly and the angle is forgiving. Medium stone until you raise a burr along the entire edge, flip, raise it back, go to a fine stone, strop. Hold the same angle; a guide clip or a folded matchbook under the spine is a legitimate beginner's crutch. ### Chisel and plane iron The only tools here where flatness is as important as the bevel. The back of a chisel is one of the two surfaces that form the apex, so if the back is not flat and polished near the edge, the edge cannot be sharp no matter what you do to the bevel. The usual practice, which is trade practice rather than a specification, is to flatten the back once, properly, on a coarse abrasive, and then to sharpen only the bevel from then on. ### Axe The best-documented tool in this guide, because the Forest Service wrote a manual about it. Clamp the head so both hands are free. Wear leather gloves. Fit the file with a knuckle guard, which can be made from leather, wood, a piece of fire hose, or old linen hose. File **into** the edge, toward the middle of the handle, because that creates the least burr to remove on the other side. A single-cut file only cuts on the push stroke, so lift it clear on the return; sawing back and forth loads the file with metal and ruins it. Work back 2 to 3 inches from the edge with a fan shape across the cheek, keeping the profile rounded, chasing the burr from side to side, then hone with a stone and strop. ### Machete and brush tools Keep the factory bevel with a mill bastard file or a whetstone. Repair nicks and dull spots **immediately**, before the next use, and do not work with a dull or defective brush tool at all, because a brush tool that skates off a springy stem goes somewhere unpredictable at swing speed. ### Scissors and shears Sharpen, do not grind. The Army and Navy manual is specific and useful here: dull shears can usually be sharpened on an oilstone or with a file; do not grind them if sharpening is all that is needed, because **most shears become useless after two or three grindings**. Grind only if the edges are actually nicked, damaged or distorted. And never touch the flat inside faces, because two scissor blades cut by shearing past each other and that contact plane is the mechanism. ### Drill bit Sharpenable by hand on a grinder, with practice, to 118 degrees included with 8 to 12 degrees of clearance behind each lip. Both lips must come out the same angle and the same length. The Army manual spells out what happens otherwise: if the lip angles differ, only one lip cuts as the drill revolves, the hole comes out oversized, and the drill wears very rapidly. A drill point gauge, set at 59 degrees, removes the guessing, and the manual says to use it frequently to check both lip angle and lip length. This is the tool most likely to be ruined by heat, so read the temper section below before trying. ### Saw Depends entirely on which saw. A traditional handsaw is sharpenable with a triangular file and is a reasonable second-year skill. A crosscut felling saw is a trade in itself: the Forest Service manual walks through cleaning, hammering out kinks, jointing the teeth to a circle, fitting and swaging the rakers, pointing up the cutter teeth, and setting the teeth to about 0.010 inch for a felling saw or 0.015 inch for a heavy bucking saw, each step with its own gauges. Two saws you cannot sharpen at all, and this is **trade knowledge** rather than anything sourced here: a modern hardpoint handsaw has hardened teeth and is sold as a consumable, and a carbide-tipped circular blade needs diamond wheels and a machine. For any saw, the Army and Navy manual's maintenance advice still applies: never cut nails or other metal with a woodcutting saw, do not force a saw that binds but spread the cut with a wedge, and touch up the teeth with a file occasionally rather than waiting until it will not cut. ### What a beginner should not attempt yet Only the shears entry below comes from a manual. The rest is judgement, offered as trade practice. - **Crosscut and bandsaw blades.** Not because they are dangerous to sharpen, but because a badly filed saw is worse than a dull one and you will not know which mistake you made. Learn from a person. - **Scissors and shears you care about.** See above. The material budget is two or three grindings for the life of the tool. - **Carbide anything.** Wrong abrasive, wrong machine. - **Serrated knives.** Each scallop needs a tapered rod of the right diameter, and the flat side must never be ground. - **Reshaping a good chisel or plane iron on a dry bench grinder.** The next section explains why. ## Testing sharpness, safely **Do not run a thumb or finger along the edge.** It is the commonest test and it is how people cut themselves while checking whether they might cut themselves. Three tests that do not require touching the apex with soft tissue: - **The light test.** Look straight down into the edge with a light over your shoulder. A properly honed edge has no flat at the apex, so there is nothing to reflect, and **it reflects no light**. Any bright line or bright dot is a flat spot or a nick. The Forest Service ax manual uses exactly this test, and notes that a single point of light is usually a ding that will disappear over several sharpenings and need not be chased. - **The fingernail test.** Rest the edge lightly **across** your thumbnail, not along it, and try to slide it. A sharp edge bites in and stays. A dull one skates. The ax manual gives this as the safer alternative to the traditional test of shaving hair off the back of the hand, and calls it equally effective. - **Cutting something.** Paper held by one corner, or a tomato skin, or for a woodworking edge a slice of end grain in softwood. If it needs a push, it is not sharp. ## Keeping it, which is most of the work Sharpening is the small part. Nearly all edge life is decided by what happens in between. **A steel or ceramic rod is not a sharpener.** A rod realigns an edge that has rolled over rather than removing metal to make a new one. That distinction is trade practice rather than a measured specification, but the working consequence is solid: a rod restores an edge that is tired, and does nothing for one that is chipped or genuinely blunt. Ten seconds on a rod before each use, and a real sharpening when the rod stops helping. **What ruins edges.** The mechanism in each row is just relative hardness or repeated impact. The ordering is judgement about ordinary domestic use, not data. | Cause | What it does | |---|---| | Cutting on glass, stone, ceramic or steel | Chips the apex outright. Glass, stone and ceramic are harder than blade steel; a steel surface usually is not, and there the apex fails against something that simply will not yield | | Cutting down onto a plate | Same, in miniature, every meal | | Cutting through bone, staples, nails or wire | One impact, one chip | | Letting blades touch each other in a drawer | Random nicks along the whole edge | | Dishwashers | Heat, alkaline detergent and knocking about | | Rust | Pits the apex, which is the thinnest and most exposed metal | Cutting boards of wood or soft plastic, and never on a plate, is the single largest change most people can make. Which board material is kindest to an edge is trade practice and not something this guide can source, but the general rule that a surface harder than your steel will chip your steel is simply hardness. **Storage** should stop the edge touching anything hard. A sheath, a block, a magnetic bar, an edge guard. The Forest Service, the Army and the Navy all say some version of the same thing: protect sharpened edges at all times, store to protect the cutting edge, coat metal with light oil for long storage, and never store a saw in a wet sheath. **Two conditions worth knowing.** The Army and Navy manual warns that in very cold weather a chopping tool should not be used before the blade is warm, because a cold blade is brittle and will break easily. And a rusty tool is a dull tool, because rust attacks the thin metal at the apex first. ## Safety ### The injuries sharpening itself causes Sharpening puts your fingers next to a freshly sharpened edge on purpose, repeatedly, for an extended period. The four defences, all from federal manuals: - **Gloves.** Wear leather gloves throughout, on both hands. The ax manual is explicit that this is because the blade becomes razor-sharp during the process, and the handtool manual repeats it for all filing. - **A file guard.** A knuckle guard on the file keeps your fingers off the edge when the file skips, which it does. Leather, wood, a piece of fire hose or old linen hose all work. - **Secure the tool, free both hands.** Clamp the head to a bench at a comfortable height, or wedge it. Holding a tool in one hand and a file in the other is how the file slips. - **Choose the stone that does not put fingertips in the path.** The ax manual notes that traditional round pocket stones can be dangerous because your fingertips are always in jeopardy, and that the version with a finger groove in the middle exists precisely to fix that. ### Which way to stroke **Always cut away from the body.** The Army and Navy manual gives that rule for knives with a single named exception, the draw knife, which is designed to be pulled. OSHA's guidance adds the other half: direct saw blades, knives and other tools away from walkways and away from anyone working near you. Sharpening has its own directions, and they are not the same: - **Filing an axe:** file **into** the edge, because it raises the least burr. - **Using a stone on a blade:** stroke with **the sharp edge trailing**, in a circular motion, light even pressure. - **Stropping:** draw the blade **backwards**, spine first, away from the edge. - **A wet pedal grindstone:** rotate it **toward you and into the blade**. ### Power grinders A bench grinder is the fastest way to reshape a damaged tool and the fastest way to destroy one. Both federal regulation and the shop manuals converge on the same short list. - **Eye protection, always.** The Army machine tool manual calls eye protection the most important safety rule in the shop and specifies safety glasses with side shields, with goggles worn over prescription glasses. The Army and Navy hand tool manual's warning on bench grinders is to wear eye protection and watch the fingers, and to hold the work firmly so it cannot catch in the wheel. The Forest Service adds heavy leather gloves, long sleeves and a leather apron against sparks and hot shavings, plus shields and hood guards on the grinder itself. - **Ring test every wheel before you mount it.** Tap it gently with a light non-metallic implement. A ringing note means sound. A dull note means cracked, and OSHA says a wheel that sounds dead shall not be used. - **Check the speed.** OSHA requires the machine's spindle speed to be verified before mounting, so it cannot exceed the maximum operating speed marked on the wheel. - **Set the work rest close.** OSHA sets a maximum opening of one eighth of an inch between rest and wheel, to stop work being dragged into the gap. The Army manual says one sixteenth to one eighth. The adjustable tongue guard at the top must never sit more than one quarter of an inch from the wheel. - **Keep the guards.** OSHA's exposure figures put the open arc of a bench or floor stand wheel at not more than 90 degrees, one quarter of the periphery, and a portable grinder at not more than 180 degrees with the top half of the wheel enclosed at all times. - **Never grind on the flat side of a wheel**, which weakens it and can break it, and never clamp a hand-held grinder in a vice. ### Heat: the failure you cannot undo This is the one that ruins tools permanently, and it is silent while it happens. Tool steel is hard because it was **hardened**, heated and quenched, and then **tempered**, reheated to a lower temperature to take the brittleness out. Tempering is a one-way trade: the higher the tempering temperature, the softer the steel becomes. That is the whole mechanism. A grinding wheel puts heat into a thin edge faster than the mass of the tool can carry it away, and the edge tempers itself further, in seconds, with nobody deciding to do it. **You cannot put it back by cooling it down.** The steel is permanently softer, and it will not hold an edge again until the softened metal is ground away. **The colour tells you.** Heat grows an oxide film on bright steel, and the film changes colour as it thickens. The colour these two manuals name, and the only one you need, is **blue**. The Army machine tool manual, on grinding a drill: overheating turns the drill edges blue, which indicates the drill's temper has been lost, and **the blue area must be ground completely away** to get back to sound steel. The Forest Service ax manual: you can always tell when the temper is drawn because the colour of the steel at the edge turns blue, and at minimum you have drawn the temper for at least three sixteenths of an inch back from the edge. So blue is not a stain to polish off. It is a map of the metal you now have to remove. The Forest Service's advice on grinders is worth quoting in substance because it is stronger than most people expect. Never use an electric high-speed dry bench grinder to sharpen an axe, because that type of grinder will almost certainly draw the temper and ruin it, and very few people have the skill to avoid it. The grinder it recommends instead is an old-style pedal grindstone kept wet by a constant application of water. Failing that, a file and a whetstone, which is how most quality axe sharpening is done today. The handtool manual is a little more permissive and gives the conditions: electric grinders reshape damaged tools quickly but improper grinding ruins both the bevel and the temper; high speeds remove metal fast, which can leave the blade weak and prone to chipping, and they let heat build in the head until the temper is destroyed and the blade can no longer hold an edge. Its instructions are to grind slowly, keep the blade cool, inspect frequently so you do not take off too much, and dip the tool in water or let it cool in open air. One trap: the Army manual warns that a drill which has already got too hot can **crack** when dipped into cold water or coolant. Do not let it get hot in the first place; cool it early and often rather than rescuing it late. ### Dust Dry grinding produces very fine airborne particles of both the metal and the wheel. The Army machine tool manual's instruction is direct: some machines have a vacuum dust collector, and when operating a grinder without one, wear an approved respirator; use coolant whenever possible, because it also controls dust. Where the material contains crystalline silica, the dust is a recognised long-term hazard rather than a nuisance. That is the case for concrete, stone and masonry, which is what the federal guidance below was written about, and it is worth assuming for a sandstone grinding wheel or a quarried natural stone until you know otherwise. NIOSH sets a recommended exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica of 0.05 milligrams per cubic metre as a time-weighted average and designates it a **potential occupational carcinogen**, with lung cancer the associated site. The listed effects are cough, shortness of breath, wheezing, decreased lung function and progressive respiratory symptoms of silicosis, with the eyes and respiratory system as target organs. The federal engineering answer for silica dust from a handheld grinder is one of two things: **water applied continuously to the wheel**, or **a shroud with vacuum dust collection**. OSHA also says not to clean up with compressed air, because it puts the dust back in the air, and to clear slurry before it dries out and becomes dust again. There is a happy coincidence here. Working a stone wet, which is what the oil or water on a sharpening stone is for anyway, is also the dust control. Keep the stone wet and you have very little to breathe. ### If you do cut yourself From the National Library of Medicine's public first aid guidance: - Wash your hands, then wash the cut thoroughly with mild soap and water. Use direct pressure to stop the bleeding. Apply an antibacterial ointment and a clean non-stick bandage. - For a puncture, rinse for 5 minutes under running water, then wash with soap. Look for objects in the wound but do not poke around, and if something is stuck in there do not pull it out. - **Call emergency services** if the bleeding is severe or will not stop, for example after 10 minutes of pressure, if the area has lost feeling or does not work properly, or if the person is otherwise seriously hurt. - **Contact a healthcare provider right away** if the wound is more than a quarter inch, 0.64 centimetre, deep, is on the face, or reaches bone, because stitches may be needed; if it was caused by a rusty object or a fishhook; if debris is stuck in it; if it shows signs of infection such as warmth, redness, throbbing, fever, swelling, a red streak spreading from the wound, or pus-like drainage; or if you have not had a tetanus shot in the last 10 years. A tetanus vaccine is generally recommended every 10 years. ### One legal note if you employ anyone Federal regulation makes each employer responsible for the safe condition of tools and equipment used by employees, **including tools and equipment furnished by the employees themselves**. A worker's own dull, mushroomed or cracked tool is still the employer's responsibility. OSHA's guidance adds the related rules: impact tools such as chisels, wedges and drift pins must be kept free of mushroomed heads, wooden handles must not be splintered, cracked saw blades must be taken out of service, and wrenches with sprung jaws must not be used. ## You own this when - You can say out loud that a dull tool takes more force, and that more force is what makes a slip dangerous. - You think of sharpening as removing metal until two surfaces meet, not as adding something to a blade. - You do not stop working a side until you can feel a burr along its entire length, and you know that no burr means not finished. - You pick the coarse stone when the edge is damaged, instead of doing four hundred more strokes on a fine one. - You know that stropping finishes an edge and never makes one. - You test with light and a fingernail, never with a fingertip along the edge. - You have never seen blue on an edge you ground, because you cooled it before it got there. - Your edges are stored where nothing hard can touch them, and you cut on wood, not on a plate. When those are true you can put a working edge on almost anything, which is one of the few skills that makes every other physical skill cheaper and safer at the same time. The underlying habit transfers well past blades: find the signal that tells you the job is actually done, trust that signal instead of elapsed effort, and stop when it appears. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. Government publications are listed first because they are works of the United States federal government, are therefore in the public domain, and can be redistributed with this guide. The rest cannot, so their facts are restated here in our own words and cited to the body that established them. ### United States government (public domain) - USDA Forest Service, Missoula Technology and Development Center. Weisgerber, B. and Vachowski, B., *An Ax to Grind: A Practical Ax Manual*, 9923-2823-MTDC, 1999. The Sharpening section (the warning against high-speed dry bench grinders and the loss of temper; blue as the visible sign and the three sixteenths of an inch of damage; the wet pedal grindstone and its direction of rotation; leather gloves and file guards; filing into the edge and why; the single-cut file cutting on the push stroke only; the fan shape and the 2 to 3 inch filing distance; the burr procedure and chasing the burr from side to side; the 25 degree slightly convex angle and the gauge template; Arkansas, Carborundum and water stones and the use of oil or water to float particles; the round pocket stone finger hazard; stropping direction on leather or soft clear wood; the light test and the fingernail test; protective oil and beeswax). Read as the page 15 text on the Federal Highway Administration mirror and as the full manual text at the Internet Archive. https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/environment/recreational_trails/publications/fs_publications/99232823/page15.cfm and https://archive.org/details/an-ax-to-grind - USDA Forest Service, Missoula Technology and Development Center. *Handtools for Trail Work, 2005 Edition*, 0523-2810-MTDC (the sharpening stone comparison table and its speed ratings; the recommendation of synthetic abrasives and the reason; oil to float swarf and citrus solvent for a glazed stone; using the whole stone surface and reshaping it on glass with carborundum powder or on coarse sandpaper; single-cut, double-cut, curved and rasp file patterns and their tooth angles; bastard, second cut and smooth coarseness; the 10 inch mill bastard file; knuckle guards; the wet sandstone wheel as the best all-round grinder; the electric grinder warnings on bevel, temper, weakening and chipping, and the instruction to grind slowly, cool often and avoid the flat sides of wheels; leather gloves, sleeves, aprons, eye shields and hood guards; that bevels vary with preference and task; the 45 degree bevels for hoes and shovels; the machete instruction to keep the factory bevel; the Pulaski fan-shaped bevel tapered back 2 to 3 inches). https://www.fs.usda.gov/t-d/pubs/pdfpubs/pdf05232810/pdf05232810dpi72.pdf - USDA Forest Service, Missoula Technology and Development Center. Miller, W., *Crosscut Saw Manual*, 7771-2508-MTDC, June 1977, revised December 2003 (the order of operations from cleaning through setting; the burr forming on the back of the tooth and obscuring its true shape; removing it with a whetstone, a light file stroke or a piece of hardwood, and the final pass with a flat fine stone; not filing the back of the tooth; that a flat-filed surface develops a concave edge and a thin weak point; that a more pointed tooth is hungrier but wears faster; that there should be less bevel for hardwood than softwood; set of about 0.010 inch for a felling saw and 0.015 inch for a heavy bucking saw). https://www.fs.usda.gov/t-d/pubs/pdfpubs/pdf77712508/pdf77712508dpi72.pdf - Departments of the Army, Navy, Air Force and Marine Corps. *Use and Care of Hand Tools and Measuring Tools*, TM 9-243, issued jointly as Navy M6290-AJ-MAN-010, Air Force TO 32-1-101 and Marine Corps TM 10209-10/1. Chapter 29, Grinders and Sharpening Stones (coarse and fine faces and what each is for; natural stones being finer grained than artificial; oiling a stone before and during use and preventing glazing; stroking with the sharp edge trailing in a circular motion with light even pressure; removing the wire edge by stroking both sides on soft wood, canvas or leather; the bench grinder warning to wear eye protection, watch the fingers and hold work firmly; never using a cracked wheel and the tap test). Chapter 34, Knives (always cut away from the body except with a draw knife; sheathing after use). Chapter 45, Chopping Tools (storing tools so heads and cutting edges are protected; wiping with oil for prolonged storage; a cold blade being brittle and breaking easily). Chapter 46, Saws (never cutting nails or other metal with a woodcutting saw; wedging rather than forcing a binding saw; touching up the teeth with a file occasionally). Chapter 37, Shears and Nippers (dull shears sharpened on an oilstone or with a file, the caution against grinding when sharpening is all that is needed, and most shears becoming useless after two or three grindings). Chapter 47, Brush-Cutting Tools (do not use a dull or defective tool; repair nicks and dulled edges immediately). Read at the Internet Archive. https://archive.org/details/use-and-care-of-hand-tools-and-measuring-tools-1983 - Department of the Army. *Fundamentals of Machine Tools*, TC 9-524, 1996 (grinding machine safety: goggles for all operations, ring test before mounting, never exceeding the wheel's rated speed, and a bench grinder tool rest set one sixteenth to one eighth of an inch from the wheel; silicon carbide against aluminium oxide and their characters; abrasive grain number as a sieve mesh count; wheel glazing and dressing; the 118 degree twist drill point, the 8 to 12 degree lip clearance, the 59 degree drill point gauge, and the oversized hole and rapid wear that follow from unequal lips; overheating turning drill edges blue as the sign that temper has been lost, the blue area having to be ground completely away, and an overheated drill cracking when quenched; honing a ground cutter with a fine oilstone to remove burrs; grinding dust being fine metal and wheel particles, the respirator requirement without a vacuum collector and coolant as dust control; eye protection as the most important shop rule and safety glasses with side shields; hardening, tempering, annealing and normalising and the fact that a higher tempering temperature leaves softer metal). Read at the Internet Archive. https://archive.org/details/tc-9-524-fundamentals-of-machine-tools-1996 - Occupational Safety and Health Administration, US Department of Labor. 29 CFR 1910.215, Abrasive wheel machinery (work rest maximum opening of one eighth of an inch; adjustable tongue guard never more than one quarter of an inch from the wheel; the tap test and the rule that a wheel sounding cracked shall not be used; checking spindle speed against the wheel's marked maximum before mounting; the 90 degree maximum exposure on bench and floor stands). https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title29-vol5/xml/CFR-2024-title29-vol5-sec1910-215.xml - Occupational Safety and Health Administration, US Department of Labor. 29 CFR 1910.242, Hand and portable powered tools and equipment, general (employer responsibility for the safe condition of tools including those furnished by employees; the requirement that compressed air used for cleaning be reduced to less than 30 psi and used only with chip guarding and protective equipment). https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title29-vol5/xml/CFR-2024-title29-vol5-sec1910-242.xml - Occupational Safety and Health Administration, US Department of Labor. 29 CFR 1910.243, Guarding of portable powered tools (safety guards for abrasive wheels, the 180 degree maximum angular exposure with the top half enclosed, and the ring test and speed check before mounting). https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title29-vol5/xml/CFR-2024-title29-vol5-sec1910-243.xml - Occupational Safety and Health Administration, US Department of Labor. *Hand and Power Tools*, OSHA 3080 (knives and scissors must be sharp and dull tools can cause more hazards than sharp ones; directing saw blades and knives away from aisle areas and other workers; employer responsibility and the prohibition on issuing unsafe hand tools; mushroomed impact tool heads, splintered wooden handles, cracked saw blades and sprung wrench jaws; eye or face protection when using a powered grinder and never clamping a hand-held grinder in a vice). https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA3080.pdf - Occupational Safety and Health Administration, US Department of Labor. *Control of Silica Dust in Construction: Handheld Grinders for Tasks Other Than Mortar Removal*, Fact Sheet FS-3628 (continuous water to the wheel or a shroud with vacuum dust collection as the two engineering controls; cleaning up slurry before it dries; not using compressed air to clean surfaces). https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA_FS-3628.pdf - National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. *NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards*: Silica, crystalline (as respirable dust) (the 0.05 milligrams per cubic metre recommended exposure limit, the potential occupational carcinogen designation with lung cancer as the site, target organs, symptoms and exposure routes). https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0684.html - National Library of Medicine, National Institutes of Health. MedlinePlus, *Cuts and puncture wounds* (washing and pressure; the 5 minute rinse for a puncture; the 10 minutes of pressure threshold for calling emergency services; the quarter inch, 0.64 centimetre, depth threshold and the face and bone criteria; rusty objects and fishhooks; the signs of infection; the 10 year tetanus interval). https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000043.htm ### Peer-reviewed literature - McGorry, R.W., Dowd, P.C. and Dempsey, P.G., Cutting moments and grip forces in meat cutting operations and the effect of knife sharpness, *Applied Ergonomics* 34(4):375-382, 2003 (fifteen professional meat cutters in two plants; mean and peak cutting moments by operation; mean grip force of 28.3% and peak of 72.6% of maximum voluntary contraction; sharper blades requiring significantly lower peak and mean cutting moments and grip forces than dull knives). Abstract read at PubMed, PMID 12880746. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12880746/ - McGorry, R.W., Dowd, P.C. and Dempsey, P.G., A technique for field measurement of knife sharpness, *Applied Ergonomics* 36(5):635-640, 2005 (that blade sharpness is measurable in the field rather than merely judged, and that measured cutting force tracks sharpness). Abstract read at PubMed, PMID 15904890. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15904890/ - Smith, G.A., Knife-related injuries treated in United States emergency departments, 1990-2008, *Journal of Emergency Medicine* 45(3):315-323, 2013 (an analysis of the Consumer Product Safety Commission's National Electronic Injury Surveillance System: an estimated 434,259 knife-related injuries annually, 1,190 per day, 1.56 per 1,000 population per year; 66% to fingers and thumbs; 94% lacerations; 47% pocket and utility knives and 36% kitchen knives; and the statement that knives cause more disabling injuries than any other type of hand tool). Abstract read at PubMed, PMID 23849364. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23849364/ - Roscioli, G., Taheri-Mousavi, S.M. and Tasan, C.C., How hair deforms steel, *Science* 369(6504):689-694, 2020 (a straight razor honed to a wedge of about 17 degrees with a tip radius of about 40 nanometres; blades failing by chipping through mixed-mode cracking at microstructural heterogeneities, before appreciable wear; and that individual structural constituents in the steel can be larger than the tip radius itself). Read as the authors' copy hosted by MIT. https://fisherp.mit.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/689.full_.pdf ### What could not be sourced, and is labelled in the text Several things in this guide are trade practice rather than measured or specified values, and each says so where it appears: - **Bevel angles for kitchen knives, chisels and plane irons.** The figures everyone quotes, roughly 15 to 20 degrees per side for a kitchen knife and 25 to 30 degrees for a chisel, do not appear in any federal publication found for this guide. The sourced angles in the table are the axe, the hoe, the shovel and the drill. - **That a steel or ceramic rod realigns an edge rather than removing metal.** Universally stated by makers and cooks, not found as a measured claim in any authority cited here. - **Grit progressions.** The definition of a grit number as a sieve mesh count is sourced. The specific ladders people recommend are convention. - **Which cutting board material is kindest to an edge.** The general rule that a surface harder than the blade will chip the blade is just hardness, but the ranking of boards is not sourced here. - **The full temper-colour sequence.** Straw, brown and purple before blue are commonly quoted and are not in any source opened for this guide. Blue is, from two of them, and blue is the one that matters. - **Angle guides, hardpoint saws and serrated knives.** The suggestion of an angle guide or a folded card under the spine, the statement that a hardpoint handsaw is a consumable, and the method for serrations are all ordinary shop knowledge, labelled as such in the text. One further limitation is worth stating plainly rather than hiding in a footnote: **no study was found that directly compares injury rates between sharp and dull blades.** The force difference is measured, the hazard statement is the federal regulator's, and the step between them is mechanical reasoning. Nothing in this guide depends on that step being more than reasoning. ### A note on what is not cited Knife retailers, sharpening-equipment makers and woodworking publications carry a very large amount of sharpening advice, some of it excellent. None of them is an authority on an angle, a temperature, or an injury statistic, and where a number here exists only in that literature it has been left out or labelled as trade practice. Nothing in this guide rests on a vendor's claim about a product.
